articles.title: Getty Images deja de cotizar en la Bolsa de Nueva York: una pérdida de USD 206,1 millones en 2025
articles.text:
Getty Images se declaró en quiebra en Estados Unidos y dejará de cotizar en la Bolsa de Nueva York como parte de un acuerdo para reorganizar su deuda con los principales acreedores. La empresa anunció un plan preacordado que incluye una inversión de hasta USD 533 millones por parte de integrantes de la familia Getty y filiales de Koch Equity Development.
La decisión afecta a una de las compañías más conocidas del mercado global de fotografía, video y contenidos visuales. Getty Images asegura que mantendrá su actividad durante el proceso y que no prevé consecuencias para proveedores, clientes, socios comerciales ni empleados. La reorganización llega después de una pérdida de USD 206,1 millones en 2025 y una caída del 68% de sus acciones tras el anuncio.
Getty Images buscará reorganizar su deuda bajo el Capítulo 11
La compañía planea acogerse al Capítulo 11 de la ley de quiebras de Estados Unidos, un mecanismo que permite a las empresas reorganizar sus obligaciones financieras bajo supervisión judicial. Este procedimiento no implica necesariamente el cierre de la compañía, sino que ofrece un marco legal para renegociar compromisos, reducir deuda y asegurar recursos para continuar operando.
Getty Images informó que la reestructuración ya cuenta con el respaldo de la mayoría necesaria de sus acreedores. El objetivo es presentar ante el tribunal un acuerdo previamente negociado, lo que evita iniciar el proceso sin una propuesta financiera definida.
La empresa espera completar la reorganización antes de que termine el año. Durante ese periodo, continuará ofreciendo licencias de fotografías, videos, ilustraciones y otros contenidos para medios de comunicación, empresas, instituciones y usuarios de todo el mundo.
“No prevemos consecuencias para los proveedores de contenido, socios comerciales, clientes o empleados en todo el mundo”, señaló Getty Images al informar sobre el acuerdo.
La familia Getty y Koch aportarán hasta USD 533 millones
La operación contempla una inversión de hasta USD 533 millones para reducir el endeudamiento de la empresa. Los fondos procederán de miembros de la familia Getty y de filiales de Koch Equity Development, la división de inversiones del conglomerado estadounidense Koch.
Además de esa inyección de capital, Getty Images tendrá acceso a hasta USD 143 millones en financiación aportada por Koch. Estos recursos, junto a los ingresos procedentes de la actividad habitual de la empresa, servirán para sostener las operaciones durante el proceso judicial.
La compañía no detalló el reparto exacto de la inversión ni las condiciones finales de la nueva estructura accionarial. Sin embargo, la entrada de recursos forma parte de un plan para aliviar la presión financiera y mantener la continuidad del negocio mientras avanza la negociación con acreedores.
La salida de la Bolsa de Nueva York marca el cambio
La reestructuración también implica que Getty Images dejará de cotizar en la Bolsa de Nueva York. La empresa ya había advertido que podía perder su presencia en el mercado bursátil después de que el valor de sus acciones descendiera por debajo de un dólar.
Tras conocerse el acuerdo con los acreedores, los títulos registraron una caída del 68%. El descenso reflejó la reacción del mercado ante el anuncio de la quiebra preacordada y la futura salida de bolsa.
Dejar de cotizar permite a la empresa avanzar con la reorganización fuera de la presión diaria de los mercados financieros. A cambio, los accionistas actuales afrontan un escenario de incertidumbre sobre el valor de sus participaciones y sobre la estructura que tendrá la empresa una vez concluya el proceso.
Una empresa clave en el mercado de contenidos visuales
Getty Images opera en un sector que reúne fotografía editorial, material de archivo, imágenes comerciales, video e ilustraciones. Su catálogo abastece a medios de comunicación, agencias de publicidad, compañías tecnológicas, marcas y organizaciones de diferentes países.
La continuidad de su actividad resulta relevante para fotógrafos, agencias y creadores que distribuyen su trabajo a través de la plataforma. También lo es para empresas y redacciones que utilizan su material mediante licencias para publicaciones, campañas y producciones audiovisuales.
El anuncio sitúa a Getty Images ante una etapa de reorganización financiera. La compañía confía en reducir su deuda, mantener sus operaciones y cerrar el proceso antes de finalizar el año, mientras deja atrás su cotización pública en Nueva York.

articles.title: Chainguard puts Claude Mythos on flaw hunting, secures coding agents and widens Libraries - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Chainguard puts Claude Mythos on flaw hunting, secures coding agents and widens Libraries
Secure software supply chain solution provider Chainguard Inc. today unveiled a vulnerability-hunting service that uses frontier artificial intelligence models such as Anthropic PBC’s Claude Mythos 5.1, as well as two products for securing AI coding agents and an expansion of Chainguard Libraries.
All four arrived at the company’s Assemble London conference today.
Vulnerability hunting falls to Chainguard Harness, which reports only the flaws it can reproduce against a live build of a customer’s application. Developers and their agents get a hardened, credential-free cloud environment from Chainguard Workspaces.
Because that work still has to be tested, Chainguard paired Workspaces with Chainguard Checks, which runs continuous integration tests on the code before anyone opens a pull request. Go and .NET developers are the new audience for Chainguard Libraries, the company’s service for vetted open-source dependencies.
Harness is aimed at organizations that want frontier-model vulnerability hunting without direct access to the models themselves. According to Chainguard, those models have mostly gone to a small set of groups doing defensive security work, and static scanners miss the logic flaws that only surface once an application is running.
Customers connect a repository through Chainguard’s Guardener GitHub app. From there, Harness compiles the application as it would ship, and the build boots in an isolated virtual machine cut off from the outside network. A frontier model then probes that running copy the way an attacker would. Nothing gets reported until it reproduces in a fresh environment on every replay, according to the company. A Chainguard engineer signs off on every report and fix before a customer sees it.
“Every time we’ve pointed Harness at code, it has found serious, exploitable vulnerabilities, including in software that’s been scanned many times over and code that runs critical infrastructure,” said co-founder and Chief Executive Dan Lorenc.
For now, Chainguard’s own staff run Harness for customers. Scans of the open-source artifacts the company distributes end in patched builds shipped through Chainguard Repository.
When Harness runs against a customer’s own code, the customer receives a write-up covering severity, reproduction steps and a recommended fix. Flaws turned up in open-source projects go to upstream maintainers through Athena, a disclosure coalition Chainguard set up in June.
Anthropic is also selling Harness. The service is listed on the Claude Marketplace, which opened in March, and enterprises can put part of an existing Anthropic spending commitment toward it. Daniela Hurtado, head of commercial cyber at Anthropic, said how a model like Mythos 5.1 gets deployed “matters as much as the capability itself.”
Harness looks for flaws in software a company already ships. The two agent products step in earlier, at the point where coding agents are still writing the code. Chainguard Workspaces and Chainguard Checks are built for teams whose agents run long migrations with the same permissions as the developer who launched them, within reach of cloud keys and production systems. Approval prompts depend on the agent following the rules, and a developer juggling a dozen agents can end up clicking “allow” all day.
Each workspace is a remote virtual machine built entirely from Chainguard OS packages. Syncing with the developer’s local working tree keeps the editor and git workflow on the laptop while execution happens remotely.
Real credentials stay outside the machine. Tools that need one on disk get an encrypted, short-lived stand-in, and teams can switch on egress policies that block any connection they have not approved. Lorenc described the result as an isolated machine “with nothing in it worth stealing.”
Checks takes aim at the queue that forms when agents push code far more often than continuous integration systems were designed for. Each run starts from a warm snapshot with dependencies already installed. An agent working in a workspace has its session suspended during testing, then picks up again with any failure logs fed straight into its context.
Passing runs produce a signed attestation tied to the environment, test result and commit. Merge gates can verify that attestation and merge the code without running the suite again.
James Governor, co-founder of analyst firm RedMonk LLC, said existing continuous integration platforms are “struggling under the massive increase in load” that agentic development has brought. Australian payments infrastructure provider Cuscal Ltd. is an early design partner on both products.
The Libraries update takes the service to five languages. Java was the only language Libraries supported when Chainguard introduced the service in March 2025, and Python and JavaScript have joined it since. Teams building on .NET can now swap NuGet for a Chainguard-managed endpoint.
Go and .NET both come with configurable blocking policies and malware scanning that also catches greyware. Chainguard applies the term to packages that work as advertised while also doing something malicious, such as harvesting credentials.
Chainguard is pitching the Go libraries at teams that build cloud and infrastructure software in the language. Older Go packages also get backported upstream fixes when a critical- or high-severity known vulnerability is found, sparing teams pinned to them a forced major upgrade. JavaScript libraries now carry the same remediation.
Java and Python get zero-day protection drawn from findings that Athena members pool. Chainguard says patched artifacts for flaws found by frontier AI models will be ready the day each one is made public.
Workspaces and Checks are available in beta test starting today. Harness is open through a waitlist for its own beta, and early access has started for the Go and .NET libraries.
Chainguard is a venture capital-backed startup that has raised about $892 million since its founding in 2021. The latest $280 million came from General Catalyst’s Customer Value Fund last October.

articles.title: Top 10 notebooks com placa de vídeo dedicada para comprar em 2026 • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Top 10 notebooks com placa de vídeo dedicada para comprar em 2026
Selecionamos os melhores notebooks com GPU dedicada para jogos, edição de vídeo e tarefas de alto processamento gráfico em diversas faixas de preço
Notebooks com placa de vídeo dedicada são voltados principalmente a quem precisa de mais recursos do que os oferecidos pelas GPUs integradas aos processadores. Esses modelos são recomendados para designers, editores de vídeo, arquitetos, gamers e outros usuários que lidam com processamento gráfico intenso.
Mas ao escolher o melhor computador com GPU dedicada, é importante entender o nível de exigência das suas atividades. Modelos de entrada e intermediários, com RTX 3050 ou RTX 4050, são ideais para atividade gráfica leve e moderada, enquanto máquinas com RTX 5060, RTX 5070 e até RTX PRO 1000 são recomendadas para quem quer máxima performance.
Além disso, a escolha não depende apenas da GPU: processador, quantidade e tipo de memória e armazenamento também influenciam o perfil de cada equipamento.
A seguir, o Tecnoblog apresenta 10 notebooks com placa de vídeo dedicada para comprar em 2026. Veja prós e contras de cada modelo.
O Acer Predator Helios Neo 16 é um notebook avançado para jogos, edição de vídeo, criação gráfica e outras atividades que aproveitam processamento e aceleração gráfica. Ele combina o Intel Core Ultra 9 275HX, com 24 núcleos, à GeForce RTX 5070 com 8 GB de memória GDDR7 e recursos de IA.
Seu painel IPS tem 16″, resolução WQXGA de 2560 x 1600, 240 Hz de taxa de atualização, brilho de até 500 nits e cobertura de 100% do espaço DCI-P3 — que pode ser útil para trabalhos de imagem e vídeo.
O conjunto ainda traz 32 GB de RAM DDR5 e SSD NVMe de 1 TB, com possibilidade de expansão de memória e armazenamento nessa configuração. Por ser um equipamento voltado a desempenho gráfico, o Helios Neo 16 tem dimensões e peso maiores que os notebooks comuns e a conectividade inclui Wi-Fi 6E, Ethernet, além de USB e HDMI.
O Galaxy Book6 Ultra é o notebook da Samsung recomendado para quem trabalha com edição de vídeo, criação gráfica, projetos em 3D e outras tarefas que podem aproveitar uma GPU dedicada, mas também precisa de um notebook fino: são 15,4 mm de espessura e 1,89 kg.
No hardware, o conjunto reúne o Intel Core Ultra 7 356H, 32 GB de memória LPDDR5X, SSD NVMe de 1 TB e GeForce RTX 5060 com 8 GB de GDDR7. A NPU do processador pode ser utilizada por aplicações compatíveis com recursos de IA executados localmente.
O principal diferencial físico está na tela. O painel Dynamic AMOLED 2X de 16 polegadas tem resolução de 2880 x 1800, é sensível ao toque e trabalha com taxa adaptativa de 30 a 120 Hz. O brilho chega a 500 nits em SDR e 1.000 nits em HDR, enquanto o acabamento antirreflexo ajuda na visualização em ambientes iluminados.
A bateria é acompanhada de carregador USB-C de 140 W, e a Samsung informa autonomia de até 30 horas em condições específicas de reprodução de vídeo. Há ainda Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 5.4, duas portas Thunderbolt 4, USB-A, HDMI 2.1 e leitor SD.
O ASUS ROG Strix G16 é recomendado para quem prioriza jogos e aplicações gráficas e quer combinar uma GPU dedicada com uma tela de alta resolução e frequência. Ele traz chip Intel Core i9-14900HX, com 24 núcleos e 32 threads, acompanhado da GeForce RTX 5060 com 8 GB de GDDR7.
A tela ROG Nebula é um dos componentes centrais do modelo. O painel de 16 polegadas usa proporção 16:10, resolução 2.5K, taxa de atualização de 240 Hz e tempo de resposta de 3 ms. Também há G-Sync, MUX Switch e Nvidia Advanced Optimus, recursos voltados ao gerenciamento gráfico e à sincronização da imagem.
O modelo traz 16 GB de RAM DDR5 e SSD PCIe 4.0 de 512 GB, capacidade que pode exigir gerenciamento de arquivos para quem mantém muitos jogos ou projetos grandes instalados simultaneamente. O sistema operacional é Windows 11 Home, com Wi-Fi 6E e teclado ABNT2 retroiluminado.
O Lenovo Legion 5i é voltado a quem pretende usar o notebook para jogos, criação de conteúdo e multitarefa, mas prefere investir em um painel OLED. Esse modelo traz chip Intel Core Ultra 7 255HX e uma GeForce RTX 5060 com 8 GB de GDDR7.
Seu painel OLED de 15,1″ tem resolução de 2560 x 1600, proporção 16:10, taxa de atualização de 165 Hz, brilho de até 500 nits e cobertura de 100% do DCI-P3, além de suporte a HDR.
Na prática, a resolução favorece maior área de trabalho que um painel Full HD tradicional, enquanto o OLED é relevante principalmente para quem valoriza contraste e reprodução de conteúdo.
São 16 GB de RAM DDR5 e SSD de 1 TB, além de Wi-Fi 7 e Bluetooth 5.4. O teclado em português possui retroiluminação RGB e a webcam de 5 MP inclui obturador eletrônico. É uma configuração que equilibra uso em jogos com características que também interessam a quem trabalha com criação visual.
O Dell Pro Max 16 é voltado ao público profissional, que precisa de uma GPU dedicada para aplicações gráficas, projeto e criação, em vez de um notebook desenvolvido exclusivamente para jogos. A RTX PRO 1000 Blackwell disponível no modelo possui 8 GB de GDDR7 e pertence à linha profissional da Nvidia.
A Dell oferece o modelo com Core Ultra 7 265H ou Ultra 9 285H, diferentes quantidades de memória e opções de SSD, portanto, a configuração exata deve ser conferida no anúncio antes da compra. Na versão com Ultra 7, por exemplo, há opções com 16 ou 32 GB de RAM DDR5 em módulos expansíveis.
Na configuração exibida pela Dell, a tela tem 16 polegadas, resolução FHD+ e 300 nits, com opções de touchscreen, enquanto a conectividade inclui duas Thunderbolt 4 com Power Delivery e DisplayPort, USB-A, HDMI 2.1, Ethernet e leitor de cartão SD.
O Alienware 16 é recomendado para quem procura um notebook gamer com tela de alta resolução e uma configuração intermediária de GPU dedicada. A versão reúne o Intel Core 7 240H, de 10 núcleos, com a GeForce RTX 4050 de 6 GB GDDR6, 16 GB de memória DDR5 e SSD de 512 GB.
A GPU dedicada acrescenta capacidade para jogos e aplicações gráficas que dependem de processamento paralelo, enquanto os 16 GB de RAM atendem a um cenário de multitarefa mais exigente que o de notebooks básicos.
A tela é de 16 polegadas com resolução de 2560 x 1600, 120 Hz de taxa de atualização, 300 nits e cobertura de 100% do sRGB para melhor visualização de cores. Essa resolução oferece mais pixels do que o Full HD, enquanto os 120 Hz favorecem movimentações mais fluidas do que em notebooks comuns.
O modelo tem Wi-Fi 7 e Bluetooth, Ethernet RJ-45, HDMI 2.1 e duas portas USB-A, além de duas USB-C com DisplayPort, e seu peso fica na faixa de 2,5 kg.
O Lenovo LOQ 15IRX9 é um modelo para quem quer um notebook gamer com uma GPU de entrada/intermediária, mas não pretende abrir mão de um processador Core i7. Ele tem o chip de 13ª geração da Intel, com 14 núcleos e 20 threads, 16 GB de DDR5 e GeForce RTX 4050 de 6 GB.
A tela de 15,6 polegadas utiliza resolução Full HD, painel WVA, 144 Hz, 300 nits e cobertura de 100% do sRGB. Para jogos, essa frequência favorece a fluidez quando o hardware consegue gerar taxas de quadros compatíveis; para trabalho com edição de imagens, a cobertura de sRGB pode ser interessante para maior gama de cores.
O conjunto ainda traz teclado retroiluminado, webcam Full HD com obturador eletrônico, Wi-Fi 6 e Ethernet. Entre as conexões estão três USB-A, USB-C com DisplayPort e Power Delivery, HDMI 2.1 e RJ-45.
O ASUS TUF Gaming F16 é um notebook com GPU dedicada mais acessível. Ele combina o Intel Core i7-13620H, de 10 núcleos e 16 threads, com a GeForce RTX 4050 de 6 GB GDDR6 e SSD de 512 GB, além do sistema KeepOS baseado em Linux.
Como a memória instalada é de apenas 8 GB, esse é um ponto que merece atenção para quem pretende utilizar simultaneamente jogos, navegadores e programas mais pesados; a plataforma, por outro lado, possui dois slots de RAM e suporta expansão.
A tela de 16 polegadas é de alta resolução, com revestimento antirreflexo e taxa de atualização de 144 Hz. A ASUS também informa suporte a G-Sync, MUX Switch e Advanced Optimus na plataforma. O TUF Gaming F16 também tem Wi-Fi 6, Ethernet, HDMI e Thunderbolt 4.
O Acer Nitro V15 é recomendado para quem procura um notebook gamer de entrada com GPU dedicada para jogos e aplicações gráficas, sem partir para as configurações mais caras da linha Nitro.
A versão com Intel Core i5-13420H combina um processador de 13ª geração com 8 núcleos e 12 threads, à GeForce RTX 4050 de 6 GB GDDR6. Há versões com 8 GB de RAM e SSD de 512 GB, enquanto outras configurações utilizam 16 GB; por isso, a memória instalada deve ser conferida no momento da compra.
Na configuração i5/RTX 4050, a tela tem 15,6 polegadas, resolução Full HD e taxa de atualização que pode chegar a 165 Hz. A família Nitro também traz Wi-Fi 6, Bluetooth e Thunderbolt 4, além de HDMI e conexões USB. O peso fica próximo de 2,1 kg.
O LOQ-e é o notebook da Lenovo para quem quer entrar na categoria com GPU dedicada gastando menos em componentes do que nas configurações mais avançadas da linha LOQ. O modelo combina o Intel Core i5-12450HX, de 12ª geração, com a GeForce RTX 3050 de 6 GB, 8 GB de RAM e SSD de 512 GB.
Essa GPU é mais antiga, mas ainda permite utilizar aceleração gráfica dedicada em jogos e aplicações que aproveitam processamento paralelo, mas os 8 GB de RAM merecem atenção em cenários de multitarefa mais pesada.
A tela de 15,6 polegadas trabalha em Full HD, com painel antirreflexo e taxa de atualização de 144 Hz. O conjunto também inclui teclado retroiluminado e numérico, características que podem ser úteis tanto para jogos quanto para quem utiliza o equipamento em tarefas de produtividade.
Diferentemente de boa parte dos notebooks gamers deste guia, essa configuração é comercializada com Linux, o que pode ser um ponto negativo para quem não é acostumado com esse sistema operacional. O modelo possui Wi-Fi 6, Bluetooth, USB-C, USB, HDMI, Ethernet e leitor de cartões.
A escolha deve considerar o conjunto de componentes e o tipo de atividade que será realizada. Entre os principais pontos estão:
A GeForce RTX 5090 ocupa o topo da linha em especificações, com 10.496 núcleos CUDA e 24 GB de GDDR7. A RTX 5080, RTX 5070 Ti e RTX 5070 aparecem em níveis inferiores, enquanto a RTX 5060 é uma opção intermediária da geração.
O Acer Nitro V15 aparece como uma opção de custo-benefício na categoria notebook gamer. Ele traz configuração com Core i7-13620H, RTX 4050, 16 GB de RAM e SSD de 512 GB na faixa de R$ 7 mil no varejo brasileiro.

articles.title: Tinybox pairs an older 32-core EPYC processor with DDR4 memory
articles.text:
Tinygrad refreshes Tinybox with an 'old' EPYC CPU running DDR4 RAM to feed four AMD 9070XT — slaps a $11,000 price tag on a new 'computer for deep learning'
'We strongly encourage others to compete with us,' spokesperson says after being called out for a rather expensive SRP.
- Tinygrad's new Tinybox supports four AMD Radeon RX 9070 XT GPUs
- The four-GPU configuration raises the G4 workstation's price to $11,000
- Tinygrad retains DDR4 memory and PCIe 4.0 in its G4 platform
Tinygrad has introduced a redesigned Tinybox workstation built around a server processor and capable of accommodating four AMD Radeon RX 9070 XT graphics cards.
The device combines water cooling, a server-grade motherboard and a spacious internal layout intended for demanding deep-learning workloads.
Its standard platform uses DDR4 memory and PCIe 4.0, while an alternative configuration offers newer memory and connectivity technologies.
An older server platform anchors the design
The standard G4 configuration uses a 32-core AMD EPYC processor with 32 GB of DDR4 memory and a 1 TB boot SSD.
Its motherboard includes a baseboard management controller, while a 1,700 W power supply supports the system's demanding graphics configurations.
The controller also has a VGA output, allowing administrators to connect a display without using the installed graphics cards.
The system also includes two 1GbE network ports and an OCP 3.0 interface for connecting compatible networking hardware.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
The enclosure measures 12 inches wide, 19.25 inches high, and 18 inches deep, and weighs 42 pounds.
This size feels like a PC from the 2000s, but TinyCorps defends this dimension on X, saying, “Everything old is new again. We're reentering an era where there are programs people want to run but can't because their computers are too small.”
The spacious enclosure leaves ample room between the graphics cards, allowing better airflow to keep them cool under heavy workloads.
Customers can also choose the G5 platform, which uses AMD's Genoa generation and supports DDR5 memory alongside PCIe 5.0 connectivity.
The company has not identified the exact processor model in the supplied specifications.
GPU and storage choices determine the final configuration
Tinygrad offers four AMD Radeon RX 9070 XT graphics cards, alongside Nvidia alternatives including the RTX 5090 and professional RTX 6000 models.
The company says acoustic output influenced its graphics selection, prompting it to exclude certain alternatives because their cooling systems generated more noise.
To maintain noise levels below 50 dB, Tinygrad combines low-speed Noctua fans with liquid cooling for the processor inside the workstation.
Two printed circuit boards (PCBs) at the system's bottom connect NVMe storage drives to MCIO interfaces, supporting the optional RAID configuration available to customers.
The G4 platform starts at $7,000, while the newer G5 configuration costs $12,000 before buyers select additional graphics cards, memory, or storage upgrades.
Adding four Radeon RX 9070 XT cards costs $4,000, bringing the complete G4 configuration to $11,000 before any optional upgrades are selected.
Nvidia configurations include one RTX 5090 for an additional $8,000, two RTX 5090 cards for $16,000, or RTX 6000 options costing $19,000 individually and $38,000 for two.
Memory can be upgraded from 32 GB to 128 GB for an additional $3,000, while storage options include a 4 TB RAID array for $2,000 or a 16 TB RAID array for $6,000.
After being called out for the rather expensive SRP, a spokesperson for the company said, “We strongly encourage others to compete with us”
Tinygrad builds each workstation to order, with estimated delivery between one and eight weeks after the purchase process is complete.

articles.title: Scimplify raises $25M to challenge China's grip on critical materials with AI | TechCrunch
articles.text:
As manufacturers across industries strive to reduce their reliance on Chinese suppliers, Indian startup Scimplify has raised $25 million to expand its AI-powered approach to producing specialty chemicals and critical materials, with semiconductors, defense and energy emerging as key growth markets.
The all-equity strategic round was led by Hitachi Ventures, with customers Henkel and Teknor Apex joining as new investors. Existing backers Accel India, Bertelsmann India Investments, Omnivore, and 3one4 Capital also participated. The round values the Bengaluru-based startup at $250 million after the investment, according to a person familiar with the transaction, up from $150 million after a $40 million Series B round in March 2025. The latest investment brings Scimplify’s total equity funding to $80 million, the startup said, though it declined to disclose its valuation.
The growing adoption of AI and advanced computational tools has accelerated materials discovery and research. However, turning promising chemistry into commercially available products at scale remains a slow and complex process. Manufacturers need to develop production processes, qualify facilities, and meet stringent quality standards, all while navigating supply chains limited to a handful of countries. Scimplify is seeking to shorten that process.
In some cases, the startup, founded in 2023, has gone from receiving a customer’s requirements to delivering the finished material in just two months, compared with the 12 to 18 months such work would typically take, co-founder Sachin Santhosh (pictured above) said in an interview.
Once it receives an order, Scimplify develops chemical manufacturing processes at its research facilities in Bengaluru and Hyderabad and then transfers them to partner factories for commercial production. Its proprietary AI platform, Scinode, helps coordinate the work by identifying suitable production routes and manufacturing facilities, while tracking quality and regulatory requirements. The platform uses specialized AI agents for different functions, including research, manufacturing and quality control, Santhosh told TechCrunch.
“Each of these agents is basically solving for what [a customer] would want, working backward from the customer’s requirement,” Santhosh said. “This helps us move a lot faster and remember customer context even for future references.”
Scimplify’s in-house team of scientists and engineers oversees production across a network of more than 500 manufacturing facilities. It helps customers establish alternative sources for materials whose supply is concentrated in China and a few other countries.
About 90% of Scimplify’s manufacturing currently takes place in India. The startup, however, plans to expand its production network to the U.S. and Japan over the next year as it seeks to attract more customers in both markets, Santhosh said.
The U.S. has emerged as a key growth market, with Simplify’s annualized revenue run rate in the country rising sixfold to about $60 million from $10 million a year ago, according to Santhosh. The market now accounts for roughly 30% of its business, while customers outside India collectively contribute more than half of its revenue, compared with less than 5% about 18 months ago.
Overall, Scimplify, which serves more than 1,000 customers and has delivered products to more than 40 countries, has reached an annualized revenue run rate of about $200 million, tripling from a year earlier, Santhosh told TechCrunch. The startup is targeting a $400 million annualized revenue run rate over the next year. Scimplify has also been EBITDA-positive for the past two months and expects to turn profitable after tax this month, he said.
Energy, electronics and defense now account for about 45% to 50% of Scimplify’s revenue, up from less than 15% a year ago, Santhosh stated. The growth comes as AI fuels demand for materials used in electronics and energy infrastructure, while ongoing wars drive demand from the defense industry.
Scimplify is working on producing tungsten derivatives from scrap, offering customers an alternative source of materials whose supply is heavily concentrated in China. The startup is also working on rare earth materials, another category where global supply chains remain heavily dependent on China.
The startup works with customers including Japanese electronics manufacturer TDK, German chemicals group BASF, and Hitachi. Santhosh cited a project involving TDK as an example of how the startup can shorten the time needed to develop and deliver specialty materials. Timelines, he said, vary depending on the project.
With its latest funding, Scimplify plans to deploy around $7.5 million for its U.S. expansion, including building out its manufacturing network, Santhosh said. It also earmarked another $2 million for further development of Scinode.
The startup employs about 340 people, including roughly 70 scientists. Most of its workforce is based in India, though it also has local teams in the U.S., Japan, Indonesia, and the UAE.

articles.title: Biostar Introduces the BIWCL-PAT Industrial Motherboard for Edge Computing and AIoT Applications
articles.text:
Tuesday, October 13th 2026
Biostar Introduces the BIWCL-PAT Industrial Motherboard for Edge Computing and AIoT Applications
BIOSTAR, a leading manufacturer of consumer and industrial motherboards, edge computing solutions, graphics cards, and storage devices, today introduced the BIWCL-PAT industrial motherboard. Powered by Intel Core Series 3 (Wildcat Lake) processors, the BIWCL-PAT brings triple independent displays, high-speed NVMe storage expansion, and versatile wired and wireless connectivity into a small-form-factor platform. Designed for system integrators, it supports applications across industrial automation, AIoT, and edge computing, as well as human-machine interfaces (HMI), POS systems, and self-service kiosks.
With a 148 × 102 mm footprint, the BIWCL-PAT is built for integration into space-constrained equipment. It supports processor options from Intel Core 3 to Intel Core 7, and its single DDR5-6400 SO-DIMM slot supports up to 64 GB of memory, providing capacity for multitasking and local data processing. This combination gives developers a solid foundation for systems that bring computing closer to factory equipment, retail terminals, and networked devices.Triple independent display support through LVDS, HDMI, and DisplayPort lets one platform drive multiple screens with different content. HDMI 2.1 and DisplayPort 1.4 each support 4K resolution at 60 Hz, while the LVDS interface drives embedded panels at up to 1920 × 1200. Industrial operators can use separate displays for control interfaces, equipment status, and operational data, while POS and kiosk developers can combine operator screens with customer-facing information.
Three dedicated M.2 slots support storage, cellular, and wireless expansion. The M.2 Key-M slot accommodates 2242/2280 NVMe SSDs through PCIe 4.0 x2, enabling high-speed access to applications and locally stored data. An M.2 Key-B slot supports 3042/3052 4G/5G modules over PCIe 4.0 x1 and USB 3.2, with an onboard SIM slot for cellular network access. An M.2 Key-E 2230 slot supports Wi-Fi and Bluetooth modules. Together, these options let integrators configure storage and wireless access for each deployment.
For always-on networking, the BIWCL-PAT features dual Intel 2.5GbE LAN ports powered by Intel I226-LM and I226-V controllers. The two interfaces let developers connect local equipment and upstream networks through separate ports, supporting reliable data exchange between embedded devices and wider infrastructure. Cellular and Wi-Fi expansion add further options for installations with different network access requirements.
The BIWCL-PAT also offers a practical mix of modern and industrial interfaces, with two USB 3.2 Gen 2 ports, four USB 2.0 connections, two RS232/422/485 interfaces, two RS232 interfaces, and an 8-bit digital I/O header. These connections accommodate peripherals such as barcode scanners and industrial controllers.
Onboard TPM 2.0 provides hardware-based security capabilities, while supported operating systems include Windows 11 IoT Enterprise 24H2 or later and Ubuntu 24.04. A 9-24 V DC input range and an operating temperature range of 0°C to 60°C further support deployment across industrial and commercial environments.
With the BIWCL-PAT, BIOSTAR gives system integrators the tools to build compact, connected systems for factory terminals, interactive kiosks, and retail installations. Its combination of multiple displays, dedicated M.2 expansion, and dual 2.5GbE networking helps power the edge across practical embedded applications.

articles.title: 32GB of DDR5 6000 RAM now costs $450 — AI-induced shortage reaches worst milestone yet
articles.text:
32GB of DDR5 6000 RAM now costs $450 — AI-induced shortage reaches worst milestone yet
$449.97 to be precise.
The AI-induced PC component shortage, which has caused drastic increases in the cost of DIY building, continues to get worse. Since last year, RAM prices have increased by more than 500% and show no sign of slowing down. In August, we reported that DDR5 6000 RAM — the sweet spot benchmark for both performance and pricing — had reached $400; now, the price is $450.
As mentioned, because DDR5 6000 RAM is a de facto standard configuration and capacity in terms of performance, tracking the price of this particular spec has proven to be a strong barometer of the industry overall. While we track RAM prices across multiple models and kits, we also track the price of 32GB DDR5 6000 RAM daily.
We've been creeping closer to $450 for some time. As of today, the cheapest 32GB DDR5 6000 kit on the market costs $449.97, or three cents shy of $450. Cheaper RAM is still available; this 32GB DDR5 4800 kit is $399 at Corsair, but good, speedy RAM is now harder to buy than ever before. The 4800 Corsair kit once cost just $80.
As RAM prices and other component hikes have a knock-on effect on PC pricing as a whole, it was recently reported that PC shipments in 3Q26 have tumbled by a massive 20%, with the top three vendors shipping 11.6 million fewer units than the same period last year.
Combo deals remain a rare bright spot. Various Newegg bundles could save you as much as $358 when you buy RAM alongside a motherboard, CPU, and even an SSD, and we've seen a recent resurgence in stock on these.
Pre-builts also continue to offer some solace to wannabe DIY builders, with price hikes trickling down to systems more slowly. With industry figures warning that memory shortages could persist well into next year, or even last up to a decade, in the space of just 12 months RAM has gone from being a PC gaming commodity to a luxury few

articles.title: Canada built nearly 100 EV charging stations in Q3 2026
articles.text:
Canada is continuing to improve its national EV infrastructure, adding nearly 100 new stations and 400 new charging ports in the third quarter of 2026.
Paren, a data intelligence company focused on North American electric vehicle (EV) charging infrastructure, released its “State of the EV Charging Industry” report for Q3 2026, which is focused on the current quarterly situation of Canada’s EV Charging infrastructure.
To start, the report notes that Canada added 103 new stations and 391 new charging ports in Q3 2026, bringing the national network to 2,740 stations and 9,615 fast-charging ports year over year. That’s up from 2,275 stations and 7,585 ports in Q3 2025. Of the 103 new stations, 93 were new sites, and 10 were existing stations adding ports, compared with 77 new sites and 24 expansions in Q2 2026.
Interestingly, Paren notes that non-Tesla stations in Q3 averaged 3.2 new ports per site, in line with last quarter. In contrast, Tesla stations averaged 9.8 new ports per site. This is still a wide margin over non-Tesla stations, but significantly down from 16.3 new ports per station last quarter and the lowest since Q1 of 2026, when Tesla added only 10.6 ports per station.
Continuing with Tesla, Paren notes that the automaker installed 88 of the quarter’s 391 new ports (22.5 per cent, down from 24.4 per cent in Q2), and is slowly losing share of the amount of ports deployed — now holding less than a third of Canada’s DC Fast Charging (DCFC) ports (32.1 per cent, down from 36.0 per cent in 2025) depite its all time amount of ports rising from 2,729 to 3,091.
Rounding out the top three is Circuit Électrique, which added 61 total ports in Q3 to hold 15.6 per cent of the ports deployed, and ChargePoint, which added 41 ports to hold 10.5 per cent of the total ports deployed. Other charging networks, essentially just a combined 27 networks outside of the top 10, hold 1,697 ports total (17.6 per cent of the base) and added 90 ports in Q3 (23.0 per cent).
Provincially, Paren notes that eight provinces and territories have at least added one station in Q3, up from seven last quarter. However, 86.4 per cent of the stations were added in three provinces; Quebec added the most stations with 49 (up from 44 in Q2), and Ontario added 22 (up from 21 in Q2). British Columbia added only 18 this quarter, down from 21 in Q2.
Interestingly, British Columbia (13.1 per cent) and Ontario (11.5 per cent) have the highest charger utilization, with PEI right behind at 10.1 per cent. Paren also notes that the Northwest Territories have the lowest utilization with 0.3 per cent, with Yukon and Saskatchewan being the next closest at 3.9 per cent.
Source: Paren

articles.title: The Internet’s undersea backbone is slipping into the danger zone
articles.text:
A fiber optic cable is pulled ashore from the cable-laying ship "Pleijel" at the entrance to the port of Sassnitz on the island of Rügen, Germany in November 2023.
Credit:
Stefan Sauer/picture alliance via Getty Images
A fiber optic cable is pulled ashore from the cable-laying ship "Pleijel" at the entrance to the port of Sassnitz on the island of Rügen, Germany in November 2023.
Credit:
Stefan Sauer/picture alliance via Getty Images
Despite the expansion of Starlink and other communications satellite services, most of the world’s Internet traffic still travels through subsea cables crisscrossing the ocean floors. Those fiber-optic cables coexist with a network of oil and gas pipelines and submarine power cables—and all these crucial links connecting countries and continents now face growing sabotage risks as gray-zone warfare and open conflicts have become widespread.
The rising risks to the world’s invisible infrastructure beneath the waves are the main subject of a new book by Elisabeth Braw, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council who leads the Threats to the Global Maritime Order Initiative. Her book, titled Undersea War, explores the modern rise in suspicious incidents in which ships dragging their anchors for unusually long periods have cut or damaged undersea cables and pipelines from the Baltic Sea to the Pacific Ocean.
Braw acknowledges that about 60 percent of undersea cable damage is primarily due to human error during fishing and shipping activities, when weighted nets or anchors drag across the seabed. Natural hazards such as storms and undersea landslides also account for a smaller proportion of such incidents. In total, between 150 and 200 cables are damaged each year and usually repaired quickly.
But international tension between superpowers and open war in Europe and the Middle East have led to increased scrutiny of cable-cutting incidents, with governments investigating and sometimes prosecuting crews for allegedly causing deliberate damage to subsea cables. One of the more notorious incidents documented in the book is the “Christmas Day massacre” of 2024, when a Russian-linked oil tanker named Eagle S dragged its anchor across the seabed for about 56 miles (90 kilometers), cutting or damaging four data cables and the Estlink 2 submarine power cable connecting the Baltic and Nordic power grids.
One of those data cables had also previously been severed by the Chinese cargo ship Yi Peng 3 just one month earlier in November 2024, when that ship damaged two data cables in the Baltic region. That ship’s crew was not prosecuted by European authorities, whereas the Finnish government has attempted to prosecute three senior officers of the Eagle S.
On the other side of the world, the captain of the Chinese-owned ship Hong Tai was convicted by a court in Taiwan of severing an undersea telecommunications cable in February 2025 and sentenced to three years in prison in June 2025. The island democracy’s legislature later amended its laws to increase penalties for intentional damage to undersea cables or pipelines and allow for up to seven years in prison.
This year has seen several notable incidents involving both overt and covert threats to undersea infrastructure, including Iranian efforts to impose fees on operators of undersea cables running through the contested Strait of Hormuz. Separately, a joint operation involving the UK, Norway and the United States confronted Russian submarines that were practicing using a new technology to disable undersea cables in Arctic waters near Norway’s Svalbard archipelago.
What happens when the Internet’s undersea backbone, not to mention crucial energy infrastructure, is no longer protected by near-universal international agreement? Ars spoke with Braw to find out more. (The interview has been condensed and edited for clarity.)
Elisabeth Braw is the author of the book Undersea War.
Credit:
Hachette Book Group (cover art) / Annabel Moeller (author photo)
Elisabeth Braw is the author of the book Undersea War.
Credit:
Hachette Book Group (cover art) / Annabel Moeller (author photo)
Ars Technica: Right now there’s so much suspicion and tension around undersea infrastructure. But it does seem like for quite a few decades, even during the Cold War, there was a broad international framework that mostly worked where countries generally agreed not to mess around too much.
Braw: Exactly. It worked for so long, and that’s why it’s so frightening to see that system that really depends on everybody doing the right thing and being a good seabed citizen, as it were, may not work for that much longer.
Ars Technica: I know it’s not really any single factor, but I’m curious what you would highlight as the key contributing factors to why we’re seeing a breakdown in that general agreement.
Braw: If you think about the absolutely crucial nature of subsea cables and pipelines, especially subsea cables… if they were to be disrupted for even just a minute, it would cause massive disruption to not just the New York City area, but also New York as a financial hub. It would cause operational losses, but also the loss of all that money that goes through the cables every second of every day.
So if you think about the utter importance of subsea cables to modern societies and modern economies, then that makes them incredibly attractive as a target. Whereas during the Cold War, we had telephone cables, but there weren’t that many of them, and we didn’t use them as much. Yes, they were used for international phone calls, and there were also telegraph messages that could be sent. But nobody sent telegrams around the clock, and nobody made international phone calls around the clock. So they were there, but they were just less crucial.
Also, despite it being a Cold War and a very dangerous few decades, there was some sort of agreement that when you sign a treaty, you uphold it. In fact, the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea was adopted in 1982 during the height of the Cold War. So there was a commitment to creating some sort of rules of the road.
Today that commitment is, I don’t want to say it’s vanishing, but it’s declining among key countries in the world. And at the same time, we are seeing Russia has discovered that it’s really quite beneficial to use non-military means to weaken other countries, and this is something that Russia has come to specialize in, and other countries may yet come to specialize in. That makes the cables around the seabed highly attractive as a target.
Ars Technica: There was even recent reporting on how NATO countries apparently foiled a Russian attempt to practice undersea cable sabotage, although that incident took place back in the spring.
Braw: The fascinating thing about subsea cables and pipelines, but especially subsea cables, is not just that we are utterly dependent on them. They don’t sit only within countries’ territorial waters. They connect countries, so they are in international waters [where] countries don’t have jurisdiction. The oceans are a global commons, and that’s where cables live, and that’s why it’s so utterly important for countries and everybody using the oceans to take care around them so that they don’t get damaged.
Then what we have seen in the past few years is that, all of a sudden, merchant vessels in the Baltic Sea and off the coast of Norway and in Taiwanese waters, all of a sudden, they got extremely sloppy and dragged anchors for long stretches, which is something that is not supposed to happen as a seafarer. You should know whether your anchor is dragging on the seabed or not, and you know where the cables are.
So this is not supposed to happen, and yet it happened not just once, not just twice, but several times, and caused considerable anxiety, obviously, in the countries affected. It also caused considerable expenses to the operators because they have to get the cables repaired, and in the case of the electricity cables, it’s extremely expensive to repair them and takes a very long time.
We don’t know what has caused these merchant vessels to drag their anchors across the border sea and damage cables, and we may never know because it’s not like those crew members are going to tell us what happened. We just know that these incidents were extremely suspicious.
But then we have what you just brought up, that Russia and other countries may develop tools to damage other countries’ subsea cables using submarines or gadgets or drones attached to submarines, and that’s where we are today. That might yet happen, and that’s why it’s always so concerning when Russian research vessels loiter around subsea cables. What are they doing there? What is it that they are looking at? What is it they are measuring?
China does the same thing. It sends research vessels that loiter in other countries’ waters for long periods of time. And you’re supposed to inform the country in whose waters you are conducting research that you are conducting research and what the nature of your research is, but China doesn’t do that. So what is it that these research vessels are doing? What is it they are researching?
This is all in the context of increasing geopolitical tension, and by the way, also rapid expansion of submarine fleets: Western ones and the Russian one and the Chinese one. But also the expansion of other undersea equipment, gadgets, drones, and so forth.
Ars Technica: Another point your book touched on was everything that’s been happening around the Strait of Hormuz, and how we have seen Iran either threaten to put a fee on companies that want to run undersea cables through there, or threaten to attack them. At the same time, it sounds like a number of companies have rethought undersea cable projects that were intended to run through that region.
Braw: This is another fascinating aspect of the situation for subsea cables. So in the Persian Gulf, in the Strait of Hormuz, there are subsea cables, and they are indispensable not just for the countries connected by them, but also for other nearby countries. For example, one third of India’s westbound Internet traffic or digital connectivity goes through the Persian Gulf. So it just illustrates how important these cables are, and not just to countries that are immediately connected.
In February of this year, the situation was that three cable projects were about to be launched or were being conducted. Then the war began, and you can imagine that when missiles are flying, drones are flying around, it’s impossible to install cables on the seabed. Because if you think about ships, that is dangerous enough, but ships are moving. Installation ships are stationary. You really are like a sitting duck, and so those projects had to be suspended or abandoned and the companies declared force majeure.
But we need subsea cables. So what will happen as the world becomes more contentious, as there are more conflicts, or as more conflicts erupt? How are cable installation crews and cable repair crews supposed to do their work when there are various projectiles and other weapons flying around them or next to them on the ocean? This is where geopolitics is truly clashing with modern economies, and at the front line are cable installation crews and repair crews.
And then you asked about the toll that Iran said it was going to impose. This was a new and, I have to say, unsurprising twist on the Iran war. So everybody has heard about the fact that, a few weeks into the war, Iran said it was going to charge tolls on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, and that is a violation of UNCLOS, the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea. Iran said it was going to do that anyway, and Iran could claim that it didn’t need to uphold UNCLOS, which it has signed but not ratified. But until February, it had upheld UNCLOS, and shipping had worked well in the Strait of Hormuz.
Then in March, Iran could say that it wasn’t bound by UNCLOS anymore because the US and Israel had violated the UN Charter by attacking it. So why should it uphold UNCLOS? And this is the dangerous situation we’re in, where countries can say, “Well, why should I uphold my treaty obligations when such and such country isn’t upholding that?”
So what Iran said a few months into the war—after having imposed tolls on shipping for a while—was that it was going to charge tolls on the subsea cables in the Strait of Hormuz. And yes, it is a violation of UNCLOS. But it could say, “Well, the US has violated the UN Charter, so we get to do as we like too.”
If you think about the implications of that, it’s not just implications for cable operators in the Strait of Hormuz. How would they make payments to Iran? How would that work? And if they don’t make payments, what would happen? But it’s also a question for other cable owners. What if other countries say, “Well, there are cables in our water, so we are going to charge a toll because countries aren’t adhering to UNCLOS anyway, so we might as well.”
It’s not just that you know the world was harmonious, and all of a sudden there were some suspicious cable incidents. It is that the order on the ocean—and even on land too—is deteriorating, and in the midst of all that we are experiencing suspicious cable incidents.
Ars Technica: These undersea cables are obviously of great national interest to governments and may require even military protection in some cases. But at the same time they’re being developed by private operators, including a lot of tech giants. We just saw Meta announcing it was going to lay the first petabit capacity cable across the Atlantic, and that’s part of a much broader buildout of undersea cables. What does this private ownership but public interest collision mean for who takes responsibility, especially as there are increasing threats?
Braw: It’s such an important question. Ever since the first cables were laid on the seabed, they have been privately owned. The cables that then joined them were also privately owned. Then, in the 1900s, postal services in different countries took over the operation of cables. So many cables were state-owned.
Then later in the 1900s, we started seeing more privately owned cables again. And today, virtually all cables are privately owned, typically by consortia. But shorter cables are often owned by one company. And a crucial development is what you also mentioned, that the hyperscalers are building their own cables for their own traffic. So, these are private operators, but [the cables are] critical national infrastructure. And what governments want may be different; in fact, it is different from what operators want.
So people often ask me, “Shouldn’t operators install more cables to make sure that they always have cables that are operational?” And yes, you can say they should, but each cable is an expense in the installation and the operation of the cable. Companies will look at figures and the hard facts, and are likely to conclude in many cases that the risk of their cables being damaged in some malicious way is smaller than the expense of adding more cables, and that’s a commercial calculation, right? Whereas for national governments, it would clearly be in their interest and they would want to see more redundancy. But they don’t own the cables, and commercial operators exist to make money.
The only other alternative is for governments to subsidize new cables. And I write about this in the book as well, what happened with the Matsu Islands [governed by Taiwan]. But we don’t have that sort of money to create backups for every cable on the seabed. So this is the clash, as it were, the interests of cable owners and the interests of national governments.
Ars Technica: It was interesting to see how that first cable, when it was laid, was used to send a message of hope and peace. And then there were also newspapers declaring that having this near-instant communication across the oceans would basically usher in an era of world peace. So again, viewing this technology as finally bringing about world peace when clearly it hasn’t done that.
Jeremy Hsu is a reporter exploring a wide range of topics across deep tech and AI. He has previously written for New Scientist, Scientific American, IEEE Spectrum, Wired, Undark Magazine and MIT Tech Review, among many other publications, about topics such as deepfakes, data centers, drones, battery tech, robotics, and GPS jamming. He also has a Master of Arts in Journalism from NYU, and a bachelor's degree from University of Pennsylvania in History and Sociology of Science, with a minor in English.

articles.title: Trump's super intelligence is rapidly catching up in the USA with 3X rise in search as Google Trends shows decreasing interest in 'Enemy' AI — while the rest of the world blissfully ignores it
articles.text:
Trump's super intelligence is rapidly catching up in the USA with 3X rise in search as Google Trends shows decreasing interest in 'Enemy' AI — while the rest of the world blissfully ignores it
In the US, "super intelligence" is the Trumpian new name for artificial intelligence
- Google Trends highlights the term “super intelligence” is replacing “artificial intelligence” in the US – but not elsewhere
- In a Truth Social post, the POTUS described anyone that doesn’t use the “super intelligence” name as “THE ENEMY”
- The US government’s AI website domain remains ai.gov
Donald Trump has declared that anyone using the term “artificial intelligence” is “the enemy,” as Google Trends demonstrates an increase in search volume for the US President’s preferred term, while the rest of the world obliviously goes about its business.
Following the signing of Executive Order 14434, the purpose of which is “Inaugurating the Age of Super Intelligence,” the POTUS has taken to social media to emphasize the preferred term for artificial intelligence in the Land of the Free.
While the rest of civilization continues with the term “artificial intelligence,” it seems the US public quite likes the term “super intelligence,” which is believed to have been introduced to cast AI in a more positive light.
Subhead
Since the executive order was passed, interest in the term “super intelligence” grew considerably, increasing by around three times at one point. Of course, this only happened in the USA - worldwide, attention was not drawn to the revised nomenclature.
While that initial excitement appears to have settled down, the term certainly seems to have made its mark. As the chart above illustrates, interest in "artificial intelligence" as a search term has been seriously impacted by the sudden existence of "super intelligence."
Posting on Truth Social – the social network he founded via his Trump Media & Technology Group – Donald Trump stated: “The White House considers anyone that uses the term, “Artificial Intelligence,” as opposed to the highly accepted new and more accurate term, “Super Intelligence,” THE ENEMY! President DONALD J. TRUMP
Despite the determination to remove the term “artificial intelligence” from the public lexicon, however, the move doesn’t appear to have been wholly repeated across the US Government.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
For example, Politico has identified that while the websites have converted with references to “super intelligence” and “SI” replacing “artificial intelligence” and “AI,” the main website for super intelligence has retained its ai.gov URL.
Rein it in a bit
Despite various emergencies and concerns caused by artificial intelligence – which range from the Hugging Face Incident to the growing environmental costs and impacts on rural communities of data centers – Donald Trump has been steadfast in his support for the technology.
Seemingly viewing it as the equivalent of the nuclear arms race, the POTUS has refused calls for guardrails on AI, preferring instead not to hamper the technology when the competition – namely, China – is not taking the same precautions.
Renaming the technology as super intelligence seems to have had a positive short-term impact, but whether this spreads beyond the US remains to be seen. It is unlikely – but then, the United States of America has long existed in a paradox of colloquial contradictions...

articles.title: Indra Bets on Qilimanjaro Quantum for Sovereign Deep Tech - EE Times
articles.text:
BARCELONA, Spain — In Spain, a new alliance between a state-backed investment entity, an industrial defense giant, and a deep-tech startup aims to offer a blueprint for building domestic alternatives in strategic computing infrastructure.
Qilimanjaro Quantum Tech, a Barcelona-based full-stack quantum computing startup, has completed a €19.6 million (~$21.3 million) first close of its Series A financing round. Spanish defense and technology multinational Indra Group led the round, investing €10 million (~$11.2 million) through its AI subsidiary, IndraMind.
The partnership is twofold: IndraMind acts as an investor and as a technology partner to develop quantum solutions for AI and cybersecurity, which are essential to protect areas of national and European interest.
The Spanish Society for Technological Transformation (SETT), a public fund under Spain’s Ministry for Digital Transformation and Public Administration, also renewed its backing with a €9.6 million (~$10.5 million) injection. This deal is part of a broader European effort to combine public funding with established industry partners to protect key intellectual property.
Qilimanjaro intends to use the funds to advance the development of quantum computing solutions and integrate them with high-performance classical computing in multimodal systems.
Hybrid capital model for deep tech
For deep-tech founders, securing multi-million-euro investments means managing technical development while continuously raising capital. “You always have the double job of working on the technological side and, on the other hand, looking for the money for it,” Qilimanjaro CEO Marta Estarellas told EE Times in an interview. Speaking about the initial Series A tranche, Estarellas emphasized that the capital raise remains an active process: “We were in this process of capital raising, and we still are. This is not a final closing of the round, simply the first entry of funds.”
Indra’s and SETT’s entry brought together two distinct financial levers. SETT channeled its contribution through instruments such as the PERTE Chip facility, designed to strengthen Spain’s microelectronics and semiconductor ecosystem under NextGenerationEU recovery funds.
Estarellas noted that the deal moved unusually fast because of institutional deadlines and corporate execution. “Everything came accelerated because SETT had to move a series of funds within specific dates, and Indra demonstrated diligence and agility to move this operation that was completely amazing,” she said.
She observed that Indra is undergoing a major internal restructuring to guarantee technological sovereignty in strategic industries. In an official statement, Estarellas summarized the rationale behind the partnership: “SETT’s renewed commitment and Indra’s entry bring together sovereign capital and industrial capital to protect, but also accelerate, national technological autonomy.”
From flood management to AI
This partnership marks a change in how defense companies work with quantum hardware specialists. “I had a vision of Indra as a very typical defense company, but what we have seen is that it is not like that,” Estarellas told EE Times. She highlighted Indra’s work in emergency management, space, and AI.
Among the immediate joint opportunities is emergency response—a pressing priority following severe floods in Spain. “The convergence of quantum computing along with quantum tech with space, and something that interests them enormously—and us as well—is the convergence between quantum computing and artificial intelligence,” Estarellas said.
Indra Group, with €5.46 billion (~$6.1 billion) in revenue in 2025 and operations in over 140 countries, gives Qilimanjaro access to markets such as transportation, logistics, and network optimization. Through IndraMind, Indra Group said it aims to integrate quantum AI across different projects, combining synthetic data, flexible architectures, and realistic environments.
For Qilimanjaro, the partnership with an established company provides access to distribution channels and markets that could help bring its technology to market. “It is very transversal, and for us it works well because it is like going with a big cousin who helps you, opens doors, introduces you to new markets, and ultimately helps you scale and grow,” Estarellas said.
Scaling hardware for the global race
Founded in Barcelona in 2019, Qilimanjaro employs 80 workers from over 22 nationalities and has deployed eight quantum systems. The company builds full-stack quantum platforms—integrating proprietary chips, control electronics, cryogenics, and software based on superconducting fluxonium qubits.
Three of its systems operate directly within the Barcelona Supercomputing Center (BSC). One of them is Europe’s first analog quantum computer integrated into a high-performance supercomputing hub.
Qilimanjaro initially focused on making analog quantum chips that can be used right away for simulation and optimization and require less error correction. Now, the company is expanding its technology approach by starting to develop digital quantum chips. “We are making a much more ambitious technological roadmap, and once we have it completely aligned, it puts us in a global race,” Estarellas told EE Times. “We are going a bit beyond what was purely analog quantum computing and starting to enter the digital modality, because our hardware is giving us very good results.”
By anchoring manufacturing and design capabilities in Barcelona, the alliance aims to ensure that European quantum research translates into long-term commercial value, rather than intellectual property that is developed or owned elsewhere. As Estarellas put it: “Together, we are joining forces to bring quantum computing closer to strategic industrial sectors and to ensure that the quantum technology built in Spain continues to grow in Spain.”

How Spain Built a Quantum Ecosystem Without Calling It One

articles.title: Pluto Security nabs $42M to help enterprises secure their AI agents - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Pluto Security nabs $42M to help enterprises secure their AI agents
Pluto Security Inc., a provider of artificial intelligence security software, today announced that it has raised $42 million in funding.
The company raised about a fifth of the sum through a seed round led by TLV Partners. The rest arrived in the form of a Series A investment led by Jump Capital. The latter deal also included contributions from several other backers including Skinos, a fund affiliated with Point Software Technologies Ltd. co-founder Shlomo Kramer.
Manually identifying every single AI agent in a corporate network is often prohibitively time-consuming. As a result, administrators can overlook agents that pose cybersecurity risks. Tel Aviv-based Pluto offers a platform designed to address that challenge. It can automatically map out agents across employee endpoints, cloud infrastructure and software-as-a-service applications.
The platform collects detailed telemetry about each agent that it detects. Pluto identifies the AI model that powers an agent, the tool it uses to carry out its work and whether users have added any customizations. Those customizations often take the form of plugins, file repositories that contain prompts and integrations with external applications.
According to TechCrunch, Pluto collects agent telemetry using customers’ other cybersecurity tools. It also deploys lightweight data collection programs called sensors. Pluto’s sensors rely on hardware-efficient AI models to identify malicious activity. When an agent attempts to perform a risky action, Pluto sends it a prompt that instructs it to stop the workflow.
Companies can customize how Pluto mitigates risks by defining cybersecurity policies. A software startup, for example, can create a policy that only allows developers to run AI-generated scripts if they don’t interact with a sensitive system. It’s also possible to regulate AI agents’ tools and user-created customizations.
The company offers its cybersecurity platform alongside a free service called Plutonium. It enables companies to check publicly available agent extensions, application connectors and MCP servers for risks before installing them. Plutonium provides data about more than 4,500 such tools.
Pluto’s third focus area is cybersecurity research. Earlier this month, the company’s researchers uncovered a hacking campaign that targeted users of Solidity, a programming language optimized for smart contract projects. A smart contract is a transaction processing script that runs on a blockchain.
Pluto reportedly generates more than $2 million in annualized revenue from over 30 enterprise customers. Its free Plutonium service has several thousand users. The company will use its new funding to grow its workforce, enhance its commercial offering and finance more cybersecurity research.

articles.title: TechSparks 2026: meet the innovators exhibiting at India’s premier startup tech summit
articles.text:
TechSparks 2026: meet the innovators exhibiting at India’s premier startup tech summit
In our photo essay from YourStory's flagship TechSparks 2026 conference, we showcase a range of innovators. Sign up to attend!
Launched in 2014, PhotoSparks is a weekly feature from YourStory, with photographs that celebrate the spirit of creativity and innovation. In the earlier 1,020 posts, we featured an art festival, cartoon gallery. world music festival, telecom expo, millets fair, climate change expo, wildlife conference, startup festival, Diwali rangoli, and jazz festival.
TechSparks is India’s most beloved startup conference and exhibition, organised for the past 17 years by YourStory. In this photo showcase, we feature teams from many startups and ecosystem enablers exhibiting at TechSparks in Bengaluru.
See our earlier exhibitor showcases from TechSparks in 2025, 2024, 2023, 2019, 2018, 2017, and 2016. Also check out our quotes compilations from the conference editions in 2022, 2021, 2020, 2019, 2018, 2017, 2016, 2015, and 2014.
The theme of TechSparks this year is The New Tech Order. AI, deep tech and new digital infrastructure are changing how technology is built, who can build it, and how quickly ideas can reach billions.
TechSparks 2026 is about the people, technologies and businesses shaping what comes next, and putting ideas into action. A galaxy of industry leaders, founders and investors are addressing a wide range of questions.
What happens when every business can build its own software? What will India’s next technology advantage be? What does Indian deeptech need to become globally iconic? Does every founder need to build an audience?
In this photo essay, we feature some of the dozens of exhibitors at TechSparks – Startup Park, Sushi Tech Tokyo, PayU, Incred Wealth, Bhasha Bharat, Niti Bodh, Mitra for Life, Feltiv, XSpecies, SearchJob.AI, Pro1 Analytics, Dolphin AI, RentenPe, Aria, Makers Hive, and Rapyder.
Startup Park is an entrepreneurial ecosystem platform designed to help founders turn early-stage ideas into scalable businesses. Its offerings include coworking spaces, innovation labs, incubation programmes, mentorship, networking opportunities, business education, and startup support services.
SusHi Tech Tokyo is an international innovation conference and startup ecosystem initiative led by the Tokyo Metropolitan Government. An abbreviation for the Sustainable High City Tech Tokyo, its focus is on using advanced technology to address urban and societal challenges.
PayU is a financial technology company that provides digital payment infrastructure to businesses, enabling them to accept and process online payments through multiple payment methods. Its services support merchants with payment processing, transaction management, and related financial technology capabilities for digital commerce.
InCred Wealth is a wealth management and financial advisory business serving affluent individuals, professionals, entrepreneurs, and families. Its offerings include personalised investment strategies, wealth creation, family office services, estate planning, wealth protection, and support for business owners managing complex financial needs.
Mitra for Life is a nonprofit organisation focused on improving access to care, therapy, and inclusion for children and young people with developmental disabilities. Its approach emphasises community-based support, working with families and schools, parent education, specialised therapies, and care delivered closer to where children live.
Feltiv is a technology company focused on AI-powered localization to help businesses adapt content for different languages and markets. Its focus on localisation is relevant to businesses expanding internationally, as well as digital platforms that need multilingual content at scale.
xSpecies is a Bengaluru-based deep-tech robotics company developing physical AI systems that combine artificial intelligence, robotic hardware, perception, and dexterous manipulation. Its technology includes DexteraX, a robotic hand designed for precise object interaction.
SearchJob.AI is an AI-powered recruitment and candidate-assessment platform designed to help organisations identify, evaluate, and hire suitable talent. By using generative AI and data-driven insights, the platform aims to reduce the time and manual effort involved in recruitment while helping employers identify candidates.
RentenPe is a proptech and fintech platform focused on making residential rental payments more valuable for tenants and more transparent for landlords. By connecting rental history with financial identity, RentenPe aims to address a gap in which regular rent payments do not traditionally contribute directly to a tenant's credit profile.
Makers Hive is an assistive-technology initiative focused on developing affordable solutions for people with disabilities. Its products include KalArm, a mobile-app-enabled bionic hand intended to help people with upper-limb amputations regain practical hand functionality.
Rapyder Cloud Solutions is a Bengaluru-headquartered cloud consulting and technology services company. It helps organisations build, migrate, modernise, and manage their digital infrastructure.
Each year, YourStory also presents and felicitates the Tech30 startups. These featured entrepreneurs regarded as having the most promise and potential in India's innovation journey.

Now what have you done today to pause in your busy schedule and harness your creative side for a better world?
