articles.title: 800 000 prévues, 350 000 autorisées : l’Europe bride fortement les hybrides chinoises — Frandroid
articles.text:
L’Union européenne va limiter à 350 000 voitures par an les hybrides et hybrides rechargeables importés de Chine. Un haut responsable européen l’a confirmé ce lundi 12 octobre au Wall Street Journal, au lendemain des révélations de Bloomberg.
Le dispositif est prévu pour quatre ans, avec un quota relevé de 6 % chaque année à partir de la deuxième, et doit s’appliquer dès début décembre 2026. Pour MG, BYD ou Chery, qui ont misé sur l’hybride pour échapper aux surtaxes européennes sur leurs voitures électriques, ça représente moins de la moitié des volumes que Bruxelles voyait arriver cette année.
D’après Eurostat, l’UE a importé environ 107 000 hybrides chinoises en 2024, puis environ 302 000 en 2025, soit presque le triple. Sans intervention, le responsable européen estime que le chiffre pourrait grimper jusqu’à 800 000 en 2026. Le quota revient donc à diviser par plus de deux les volumes attendus.
Les marques chinoises se sont ruées sur l’hybride parce qu’il échappe aux surtaxes décidées en octobre 2024. Certains constructeurs paient jusqu’à 45,3 % de droits sur une voiture électrique fabriquée en Chine (droit de base de 10 % compris), contre 10 % seulement sur un modèle hybride. En clair, les surtaxes ont surtout déplacé le problème, et Bruxelles avait déjà commencé à viser les hybrides rechargeables venues de Chine.
Selon les chiffres de l’ACEA, l’association des constructeurs européens, relayés par L’argus, les marques chinoises pesaient 14 % du marché européen des hybrides et 25 % de celui des hybrides rechargeables au premier semestre 2026, contre 2 % dans chaque catégorie en 2024.
Jusqu’à 330€ d’avantages avec nos offres Hello Prime ou Hello Prime Duo, dont 80€ cash à l’ouverture de compte !
Trois groupes concentrent l’essentiel de ces volumes. SAIC (maison mère de MG), BYD et Chery réalisent plus de 90 % des ventes des marques chinoises dans l’UE, et l’hybride pèse plus de la moitié de leurs ventes européennes.
Bruxelles a négocié ce plafond avec Pékin. Maros Sefcovic, commissaire européen au Commerce, a passé deux jours dans la capitale chinoise avec le ministre chinois du Commerce, Wang Wentao, et les deux camps ont annoncé un accord de principe le 9 octobre. Dans le même accord, la Chine a accepté de baisser ses droits de douane sur environ 4 milliards d’euros de produits européens, dont des pièces automobiles, des chaussures, des glaces et de l’huile d’olive.
Pékin s’en accommode plutôt bien, même si son ministère du Commerce se réserve le droit de saisir l’OMC pour réclamer des compensations. La Chine a salué le 10 octobre des compromis qui permettent d’« éviter une escalade » et constituent « un nouveau départ », avec au passage une promesse de faciliter les licences d’exportation de terres rares vers l’Europe.
De son côté, l’UE a enregistré en 2025 un déficit commercial de près de 360 milliards d’euros avec la Chine, selon Eurostat, un pays qui pèse lourd dans la transition énergétique mondiale, et les Européens répètent depuis des mois vouloir être moins naïfs face aux voitures chinoises.
Quelles voitures comptent dans le quota ?
Le quota couvre toutes les motorisations hybrides. Stéphane Séjourné, vice-président de la Commission européenne, a parlé de « tous types d’hybrides (MHEV, HEV et PHEV) ». Pour l’acheteur, ça regroupe les micro-hybrides (un petit moteur électrique qui assiste le moteur thermique sans jamais rouler seul), les hybrides classiques, dont la batterie se recharge en roulant, et les hybrides rechargeables, qu’on branche sur une prise.
Le plafond porte sur les voitures importées de Chine, donc sur le pays de fabrication. Une hybride de marque chinoise assemblée dans l’UE n’entre pas dans le calcul, ce qui donne une bonne raison à BYD, dont l’usine hongroise de Szeged doit démarrer au quatrième trimestre 2026, et à Chery, qui prévoit d’assembler des Omoda et des Jaecoo dans l’usine d’Ebro à Barcelone à partir de fin 2026, de produire sur place.
Pour respecter le principe de non-discrimination de l’OMC, la mesure de sauvegarde s’applique en théorie aux hybrides importées de tous les pays, à l’exception de l’Espace économique européen, de l’Ukraine, du Kenya et des petits pays exportateurs en développement. La Chine doit recevoir un quota au moins égal à celui de tout autre pays. Le critère reste le lieu de fabrication : une hybride de marque européenne produite en Chine entre dans le quota au même titre qu’une MG ou une BYD.
Les Échos ont passé en revue les points pratiques du dispositif : la règle d’origine, la répartition du volume entre constructeurs et la gestion du quota par les douanes. Par contre, le texte réglementaire n’a pas encore été publié. La Commission n’a donc pas dit comment les 350 000 places seront partagées entre MG, BYD, Chery et les autres.
Le sort des voitures arrivées une fois le quota épuisé n’est pas tranché non plus : des responsables européens ont assuré au Guardian qu’elles resteraient bloquées en douane, sans surtaxe, alors que le Financial Times évoquait la veille des droits supplémentaires élevés. Le quota passe par une mesure de sauvegarde, un outil prévu par les règles de l’OMC pour freiner une hausse brutale des importations, plus rapide à déclencher qu’une enquête antidumping.
Moins de choix pour l’acheteur français ?
Les modèles concernés sont faciles à repérer en concession : la MG3 Hybrid+, le MG ZS Hybrid+, le BYD Seal U DM-i ou le Jaecoo 7 de Chery sont tous fabriqués en Chine. Pour autant, le quota ne les fera pas disparaître du jour au lendemain. Avec 350 000 voitures la première année, il dépasse encore d’environ 16 % les importations de 2025. Il passe ensuite à 371 000 voitures la deuxième année, environ 393 000 la troisième et 417 000 la quatrième.
Le problème viendrait plutôt de la demande. Si les commandes dépassent le quota, les marques devront choisir quels modèles envoyer en priorité. Elles pourraient privilégier ceux qui rapportent le plus, ou allonger les délais de livraison. Les prix très bas qui ont fait le succès de ces hybrides auraient alors moins de raison d’être, ce qui arrangerait Renault, Dacia ou Toyota, qui fabriquent leurs hybrides hors de Chine. Bref, la mesure protège d’abord les constructeurs installés en Europe, et l’acheteur d’une hybride abordable risque de le sentir sur le prix.
La mesure doit entrer en vigueur le 1er décembre, d’après le document interne consulté par Bloomberg, une fois le texte réglementaire publié. Si vous comptez commander une hybride MG, BYD ou Chery d’ici là, faites inscrire une date de livraison ferme sur le bon de commande.

articles.title: LineageOS 24 sauve des millions de smartphones de l'obsolescence en leur offrant Android 17
articles.text:
Le 28 octobre 2021, Google lançait les Pixel 6 et 6 Pro en France à 649 et 899 euros, avec la promesse de cinq ans de mises à jour de sécurité. Le correctif diffusé depuis le 6 octobre est le dernier que la firme garantit aux deux smartphones. Google les avait écartés du programme bêta dès le 20 juillet, avec une mention claire : « l’appareil atteindra sa fin de vie ». Cinq jours plus tard, LineageOS 24 les inscrivait à son programme officiel, Android 17 à la clé.
Une fin de vie actée depuis juillet
Les deux téléphones continueront de fonctionner, mais chaque faille découverte restera désormais sans rustine, un détail qui pèse pour un appareil qui paie sans contact et stocke la moitié de nos comptes. Le Pixel 6a conserve, lui, un sursis jusqu’en juillet 2027, les Pixel 7 tiennent jusqu’en octobre 2027, et Google promet sept ans de suivi à partir des Pixel 8.
Le Pixel 4a a déjà vécu ce scénario : abandonné en août 2023 sur Android 13, il figure toujours au catalogue officiel de LineageOS. La nouvelle version l’emmène jusqu’à Android 17, soit quatre versions majeures après son arrêt. Les Pixel 6 rejoignent la même liste, aux côtés de 27 modèles Google au total, du Pixel 4 de 2019 jusqu’aux Pixel 10.
174 appareils, mais une installation qui se mérite
LineageOS 24 démarre avec 174 appareils, contre 104 pour la version 23.0 lancée un an plus tôt jour pour jour, et 148 pour la 23.2 de février. Les correctifs de sécurité publiés entre août 2025 et octobre 2026 ont par ailleurs été fusionnés sur les branches 18.1 à 24.0.
L’installation réclame toujours un bootloader déverrouillé et une remise à zéro du téléphone. Un outil de flash par navigateur, ouvert en juillet sur flash.lineageos.org, allège une partie de la procédure en gérant les protocoles ADB, Fastboot ou Odin. La compatibilité varie toutefois selon l’appareil, le navigateur et même le câble. Les guides du wiki restent la référence pour chaque modèle, et l’outil n’en dispense pas. Le système arrive enfin sans les services Google, que le projet n’a jamais embarqués et n’embarquera pas.
Depuis le 20 juin 2025, un règlement européen garantit au moins cinq ans de mises à jour du système aux smartphones commercialisés dans l’Union, décomptés à partir de leur mise sur le marché. Sortis quatre ans trop tôt pour en profiter, les Pixel 6 s’arrêtent précisément au plancher que Bruxelles impose désormais aux autres.

articles.title: The developer who cloned Photoshop using AI has now created Word, Excel, and PowerPoint replicas with Claude
articles.text:
First look: Though vibe-coded apps are often slammed as "AI slop" by users and developers alike, generative AI can now produce complex productivity apps that rival market leaders. After building free, open-source alternatives to Adobe's Creative Cloud apps using Claude AI, developer Brandon Thomas is now turning to replicas of Microsoft Office apps like Word, Excel, and PowerPoint.
Called WordCraft, GridCraft, and DeckCraft, respectively, the open-source applications are written in Rust with Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5, as the Adobe replicas were, and are available for download under MIT or Apache 2.0 licenses. They are, however, still at a relatively early stage of development and need a lot more work before they can be considered viable alternatives to Microsoft Office.
According to its GitHub page, WordCraft is an "open-source, clean-room reimplementation of Microsoft Word" that runs natively on Windows, macOS, Linux, and BSD. It can also be used in the browser via WebAssembly. The app uses a single Rust codebase for all platforms, without falling back on Electron or Tauri.
WordCraft reads and writes .docx, the native file format of Microsoft Word. It also supports a range of other formats, including .odt, .rtf, .html, .md, and .txt, and can import the legacy .doc format. It can export PDFs with real, selectable text, links, and bookmarks, too. Thomas noted that spelling, grammar, and many other critical features work offline.
WordCraft is visually almost identical to the software it's modeled after, offering the same ribbon, styles, tables, track changes, and references as Word. It also implements features like mail merge, which lets users create personalized letters by pulling in data from a CSV file or Outlook contacts list.
GridCraft, which replicates Microsoft Excel, already implements 89% of Excel's ribbon and menu commands, according to the developer, and about 98% of its worksheet functions. It offers Excel's familiar interface, including the ribbon, formula bar, keyboard shortcuts, and more. It uses .xlsx as its native file format and is fully scriptable by AI agents.
DeckCraft, which opens and saves .pptx files, aims for full feature parity with PowerPoint and to be "better and faster" than the original. Its GitHub page claims 79% "feature parity" across 191 PowerPoint features, including advanced formatting, and export to PDF.
WordCraft development is the furthest along, with 88% of Word's ribbon-based commands implemented.
Overall, the project estimates it has reached around 60% feature parity with the Microsoft app. All three apps are in alpha, with GridCraft around 50% "ready for real work" and DeckCraft around 55%.

articles.title: Intel bets the next phase of AI belongs to the rightsized system, not the biggest one - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Intel bets the next phase of AI belongs to the rightsized system, not the biggest one
For three years, artificial intelligence infrastructure has been dominated by one idea: Bigger is better. Bigger models, bigger clusters, and bigger checks written to a small group of suppliers. At this week’s Open Compute Project Global Summit, Intel Corp. argued that the next phase of AI will look very different and that Intel is well-positioned to benefit.
During his keynote, Nicolas Dubé (pictured), corporate vice president at Intel, framed his OCP keynote around a simple phrase: “Put every prompt in its place.” He shared new details about the Intel GPU D-series, formerly code-named Crescent Island, as well as Xeon rack designs built largely on OCP’s Open Rack v3 spec and open software work.
Underneath is a strategic argument worth attention: Intel believes inference, not training, will define enterprise AI economics and that agentic AI will bring the CPU back to the center of the data center. If that’s right, Intel’s turnaround gets a second engine at exactly the right time.
Not every prompt needs a frontier model
Today, most organizations default to sending every request to a frontier model, whether or not the task warrants it. That’s like hiring a senior law partner to proofread a memo. Intel’s alternative is an orchestration layer that evaluates each request based on the required depth of intelligence, context length, latency, data sensitivity and sovereignty, and cost and energy.
Deep research may justify using a frontier model. Proprietary documents may need to remain within the enterprise. Routine coding, summarization or operational tasks can run on a smaller open model at a small fraction of the cost.
“Open models are expanding the options enterprises have for deploying AI,” said Dubé. “To realize their full potential, organizations need infrastructure that can match different workloads with the right intelligence, compute resources and economics.”
The momentum behind open models has never been stronger. In recent months, I’ve spoken with dozens of companies aggressively shifting to them. Intel cited Vercel AI Gateway data showing that open-weight models’ share of observed token traffic rose from roughly 31% in early July to about 78% by late September. One gateway isn’t the market, but it aligns with what I hear from IT leaders who are uneasy about runaway token bills and about sending sensitive data to someone else’s model.
Crescent Island targets the enterprise middle
The D-series, first disclosed at last year’s OCP Summit, is the hardware embodiment of that thesis. It’s built on the Xe3P architecture and delivers 1.3 petaflops of FP8 compute and 1.5 terabytes per second of memory bandwidth in a 350-watt, air-cooled PCIe form factor. The design supports up to 480 gigabytes of LPDDR5X memory. Intel’s own branded card carries 160 gigabytes, and partners can build higher-capacity cards.
The most interesting decision is the memory choice. Rather than chase Nvidia Corp. and Advanced Micro Devices Inc. with expensive, supply-constrained high-bandwidth memory, Intel chose LPDDR, trading peak bandwidth for capacity and cost. That’s the right trade for inference, where the bottleneck is often fitting the model and its context into memory. Intel says it supports models up to 300 billion parameters on a single card and more than 1 trillion in an eight-GPU system.
Just as important is what it doesn’t require. Most enterprise data centers weren’t built for liquid-cooled racks drawing 100-plus kilowatts. A 350-watt card that fits in a standard air-cooled server lets a company start with a single card, move to an eight-way server, and scale to rack-level systems only when the workload demands it. Inference is becoming the defining AI workload, and enterprises need infrastructure that makes the transition easier and more cost-effective.
Agentic AI is a CPU story
The most underappreciated part of the announcement is the Xeon rack work. Agentic AI turns inference into a multi-step workflow spanning retrieval, reasoning, tool calls, database queries and application execution. Every agent generates tokens and a significant amount of general-purpose work that runs on CPUs.
Intel showcased partner-built Xeon rack designs, many based on ORv3, with select Xeon 6+ configurations scaling beyond 46,000 cores per rack at 133.45 kilowatts. Xeon 6+ with dense, efficient cores targets high-concurrency agent workloads, while Xeon 6 with performance cores handles tasks that depend on single-thread speed. Intel argues that the right metric is no longer core count but how many concurrent agents a rack can sustain at target latency, a useful lens for buyers.
The result is a heterogeneous system: Xeon for orchestration, data processing and tool execution; the D-series for open-model inference; and SambaNova as an optional fast-token engine where speed is the priority. During his presentation, Dubé explained that Intel is tying the system together with a software architecture it’s building with the community, which’s open, downloadable today, and designed to run across the broad silicon.
Fuel for the Lip-Bu Tan rebound
All of this underscores Intel’s turnaround under Chief Executive Lip-Bu Tan, which is moving from hopeful to measurable. In the second quarter, Intel posted $16.1 billion in revenue, up 25% year-over-year, with Data Center and AI revenue up 59%, to $6.3 billion. It marked the seventh consecutive quarter of beating its own guidance. The stock has more than tripled over the past year.
It’s important to understand what’s driving growth. It isn’t Intel winning the graphics processing unit war. It’s the recognition that AI needs many central processing units. At Splunk’s .conf26 in September, Tan said Intel could meet only about half of customer CPU demand, even after Intel had already raised 2026 capital spending to more than $20 billion.
The OCP announcements extend that momentum in two ways. The agentic rack work reinforces the Xeon demand already driving the numbers, positioning Intel as an essential agent infrastructure provider rather than a legacy supplier. And Crescent Island gives Intel an accelerator play where it doesn’t have to beat Nvidia on peak performance. This could be the most practical, power-efficient way to run open models in an existing data center.
That’s the discipline Tan has brought: Stop trying to win every fight and focus on the fights where Intel has a structural advantage. Intel doesn’t need to own frontier training. It needs to own the enterprise middle, a much larger opportunity than most give it credit for.
What IT leaders should do now
The shift from scale to fit doesn’t happen to an organization. It must be planned. Here’s where I’d focus:
- Audit your prompt mix. Most organizations have limited visibility into what their AI spend is buying. Pull a few weeks of usage logs and sort requests by task type: deep reasoning, retrieval-heavy questions, coding help, summarization and classification. In my conversations with IT leaders, I often find that a large share of traffic is routine work a smaller open model could handle at a fraction of the cost. Do this before your next model contract renewal, not after.
- Treat orchestration as a strategic layer, not a feature. Routing based on cost, latency, context length and data sensitivity is where the savings and control come from. Whether you build it or buy it, the orchestration layer should be model-agnostic so that switching providers or bringing a workload in-house is a policy change rather than a re-architecture. It’s also the natural place to enforce governance, such as ensuring that regulated data never leaves your environment.
- Change how you evaluate infrastructure. Peak FLOPS and core counts are vendor metrics, not business metrics. Ask suppliers to demonstrate concurrent agents sustained at a target latency, cost per million tokens and tokens per watt on a model you plan to run. Then run the tests yourself with your own prompts and context lengths. A system that wins a benchmark at short context can look very different at the long contexts that agentic workflows generate.
- Plan for the data center you have. Liquid cooling has its place, but retrofitting facilities is expensive, slow and often constrained by available power. Before committing capital, run a proof of concept using air-cooled PCIe inference in existing racks. Start small, with one card or one server, and scale only when utilization justifies it. For many enterprise workloads, that path will be sufficient, and it is far faster to deploy.
- Don’t overlook the CPU budget. Agentic AI shifts a meaningful share of work to general-purpose compute: tool calls, data retrieval, database queries and code execution. Organizations that size only for accelerators will find their agents bottlenecked elsewhere. Model CPU demand alongside GPU demand, and account for tight supply. Intel itself says it can’t meet all current demand, so lock in capacity early.
- Insist on open standards and open software and hardware. ORv3, PCIe, and the Open Adapter Card, combined with open frameworks and orchestration layers, protect your ability to mix vendors and adapt as the market shifts. Note that OAC, while close, is not a final spec. Until then, PCIe, a proven standard, is a fine option. It’s not PCIe versus OAC but about delivering openness everywhere. Ask every supplier how quickly new open models run on its hardware and whether its optimizations live in mainstream frameworks or in a proprietary stack. Lock-in at the software layer is harder to unwind than at the hardware layer.
Final thoughts
Intel has spent much of the past few years being written off in AI, and for a while that criticism was deserved. The company chased Nvidia on Nvidia’s terms and lost. What’s different now is that Intel is playing a different game, one built around where enterprise AI is heading rather than where it has been.
The bet is that inference will be heterogeneous, that open models will continue to close the gap with proprietary ones, and that agents will make the CPU as important to AI as the GPU. None of those ideas is particularly controversial anymore, and the data increasingly supports all three. What’s still open to debate is whether Intel can execute. Crescent Island needs to ship on time and perform as promised; the software stack needs to keep pace with an open-model ecosystem that evolves weekly; and the company has to fix its supply constraints to capitalize on the Xeon demand it already has.
That’s where the Lip-Bu Tan era differs from what came before. Under Tan, Intel has been more disciplined about where it competes, more candid about what it can deliver, and more focused on customers than on roadmaps. Seven straight quarters of beating guidance don’t happen by accident. If Intel brings that same discipline to the D-series and its agentic Xeon platforms, OCP 2026 may be remembered as the moment Intel stopped trying to catch up in AI and started defining its own lane.
The first phase of AI rewarded scale. The next will reward fit. Intel’s message at OCP is that it understands the difference, and its recent results suggest the market is beginning to believe it.
Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

articles.title: Este es HomeView de Apple, la nueva pantalla que controla el hogar con Siri AI
articles.text:
Apple presentó HomeView, una pantalla inteligente diseñada para reunir en un solo dispositivo el control del hogar conectado, el entretenimiento y algunas funciones de comunicación. La compañía apuesta por Siri AI, su asistente de inteligencia artificial, para que los usuarios puedan buscar contenido, controlar accesorios y consultar información mediante la voz.
El equipo tiene una pantalla Liquid Retina de siete pulgadas y puede colocarse sobre una mesa o instalarse en la pared. También permite hacer videollamadas con FaceTime, reproducir música y acceder a funciones de vigilancia del hogar. Apple indicó que HomeView reconoce a las personas por su rostro y adapta el contenido para cada usuario, como mensajes, calendario y recordatorios.
Las reservas comenzaron el martes 13 de octubre y la disponibilidad en tiendas de Estados Unidos está prevista para el 13 de noviembre. HomeView no estará a la venta en la Unión Europea, porque Siri AI todavía no está disponible en iOS en esa región.
Siri AI lleva la conversación al hogar
Apple describe Siri AI como una versión más conversacional del asistente, con conocimiento general y capacidad para comprender mejor las solicitudes. En HomeView, permitirá descubrir música y controlar dispositivos inteligentes mediante comandos de voz. También podrá responder preguntas y mostrar información en pantalla.
Cuando se empareja con un dispositivo compatible con Apple Intelligence, como un iPhone, HomeView puede utilizar ciertos datos personales para dar respuestas más relevantes. Por ejemplo, Siri AI puede consultar información de aplicaciones como Calendario o Mensajes para responder a solicitudes relacionadas con la rutina de cada usuario.
El reconocimiento facial también permite que la pantalla compartida cambie de perfil según quién la esté utilizando. Así, cada persona puede acceder a su contenido sin que el dispositivo se limite a mostrar una experiencia común para toda la casa. Apple afirma que la privacidad y la seguridad son parte central del diseño.
Un centro para los dispositivos inteligentes
HomeView está pensado para controlar luces, cámaras, persianas, cerraduras y otros accesorios compatibles con Apple Home. El dispositivo puede ejecutar automatizaciones y permitir que los usuarios manejen escenas del hogar por voz.
Si se conecta un timbre compatible, las notificaciones pueden aparecer en la pantalla. Desde allí, el usuario podrá ver quién está en la puerta y comunicarse con esa persona. La pantalla también puede servir para vigilar cámaras del hogar y consultar información sobre la actividad detectada.
El producto busca ofrecer una alternativa a controlar la casa desde un iPhone o una tableta. Apple ya permite gestionar accesorios desde esos dispositivos y mediante sus altavoces HomePod, pero HomeView incorpora una pantalla dedicada a permanecer en espacios comunes de la vivienda.
Precio y disponibilidad en Europa
Apple todavía no ha publicado el precio de HomeView ni todos los detalles sobre su disponibilidad en cada mercado. La falta de una fecha para Europa está relacionada con la disponibilidad de Siri AI en la Unión Europea: según la compañía, el dispositivo no se venderá en la región mientras el asistente no esté disponible allí.
La restricción deja pendiente el lanzamiento europeo de la nueva pantalla. Apple señaló que está trabajando con las autoridades de la Unión Europea para encontrar un camino que permita llevar Siri AI a iOS en ese mercado. Hasta que haya un acuerdo o un cambio en la disponibilidad del asistente, los usuarios de la UE no tienen una fecha anunciada para comprar HomeView.

articles.title: Cerebras CEO says we're nearing a future where everyone has a personal AI assistant at home | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Cerebras Systems CEO and co-founder Andrew Feldman believes we’re nearing a future where everyone will have an AI appliance in their own home.
Speaking on stage at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 on Tuesday, the chipmaker executive answered a question about what would need to happen for AI to become a home appliance, saying, “Actually, I don’t think that’s very far away.”
He pointed to the advances in consumer AI agents, like Meta’s Muse and Instinct, the startup now valued at $10 billion, as examples of how AI is finding its footing with everyday users.
As for home AI? He predicts that we’ll have personal AI assistants that run locally.
“Just like your cell phone, they’ll do some work on device and some work going back to the cloud,” Feldman explained. “But I think they will get to know you very well, and you will have a security perimeter around them. And they will certainly have access to credit cards and be able to buy things for you,” he continued. “I think they will make a meaningful impact in making our lives better.”
Of course, for an AI chipmaker, the vision of a home AI appliance, or at least widespread consumer adoption of agentic technology, is certainly appealing.
But Feldman isn’t just working on the hardware infrastructure; he’s a personal AI user himself, saying that he now uses “a collection of agents” to sweep his calendar, pull up information about the people he’s going to have a call with, and more. While AI is already doing many of the things we used to do manually, Feldman is most excited about the new possibilities — things that weren’t possible before.
He’s leaving it up to other founders to figure out what those might be, though.
“One of the reasons I love being in infrastructure is because I don’t need the consumer-facing idea … I like building the platforms that other people’s ideas take flight on,” he said.

articles.title: ESA targets Anbernic emulation handhelds as "superfake" piracy enablers
articles.text:
For years, Chinese hardware manufacturers have carved out a market niche with an array of handheld Android gaming devices focused on retro emulation and/or more modern game-streaming capabilities. Now, though, a major game industry trade group is targeting one of those manufacturers, Anbernic, asking the US Trade Representative (USTR) to add the company to its list of “Notorious Markets” that “engage in or facilitate substantial copyright piracy or trademark counterfeiting.”
TorrentFreak was among the first to notice the request from the Entertainment Software Association (ESA), which was submitted to the USTR last week. In it, the US trade group—which represents major publishers including Nintendo, Microsoft, PlayStation, Amazon, Epic, EA, Ubisoft, and more—notes that Anbernic devices “are routinely offered or shipped with removable memory cards preloaded with hundreds or thousands of unauthorized copies of copyright-protected video games published by ESA members.”
While many online sellers do include an SD card full of ROMs alongside emulation hardware of all types, Anbernic itself does not appear to do the same when selling directly from its website. Regardless, the ESA argues that these ROM-laden Anbernic devices selling through “normal retail channels” help to “normalize hardware-based piracy by delivering illicit catalogues through a polished consumer product.” This, the ESA says, meets the threshold for a “superfake,” an ill-defined designation that applies to “high-quality counterfeit trademark goods … on a commercial scale.”
Being included on the USTR’s Notorious Market List wouldn’t bring any additional direct legal consequences for a company like Anbernic. However, the USTR says the list “encourages the responsible authorities to step up efforts to combat piracy and counterfeiting” and notes that the list itself “increase[s] public awareness and help market operators and governments prioritize intellectual property enforcement efforts that protect American businesses and their workers.” Inclusion on the list could also presage a Section 301 investigation that could lead to legal consequences or restrictive import controls on the devices.
@Kyle Orland I think you should have read a bit further in the reddit comments you linked to:
View: https://www.reddit.com/r/Handhelds/comments/1x4u2zp/comment/pghpclh/
I have ordered direct from anbernic, and that second SD card most definitely came chock full of ROMs.

articles.title: Thermaltake Launches the OB360 AIO Liquid Cooler
articles.text:
Tuesday, October 13th 2026
Thermaltake Launches the OB360 AIO Liquid Cooler
Thermaltake, a leading PC DIY brand for premium hardware solutions, introduces the OB360 AIO Liquid Cooler, combining powerful cooling performance with refined industrial aesthetics. Featuring a 360 mm single-frame fan design, support for up to 360 W TDP, and distinctive textured detailing, the OB360 simplifies installation while delivering efficient thermal management. Its black, non-RGB design offers a minimalist and understated look for modern PC builds.
Industrial Textured Aesthetics
The OB360 features a black water block with diagonal textured grooves that create a distinctive finish. Embossed detailing on the fan frame complements the water block, establishing a cohesive industrial aesthetic throughout the cooling assembly.Single-Frame Fan Design
The OB360 integrates three 120 mm high static pressure PWM fans into a single 360 mm frame, simplifying installation and reducing cable clutter. The unified structure makes fan installation easier and helps keep the interior organized.
Powerful Cooling Performance
Engineered to support thermal loads of up to 360 W TDP, the OB360 combines high static pressure fans with PWM speed control for efficient heat dissipation. Each fan delivers up to 53.9 CFM of airflow and 2.36 mm-H₂O of static pressure, with a maximum noise level of 32.3 dB-A. Operating between 500 and 2000 RPM, the fans dynamically adjust their speed to meet varying cooling demands.
Slim Radiator for Effective Heat Dissipation
The OB360 incorporates a 27 mm slim radiator with a thickened 20 mm copper chamber, designed to facilitate efficient heat dissipation while maintaining a compact profile. The slim construction supports easier installation and provides greater flexibility for integration into compatible chassis.
High-Performance Pump and Copper Base Plate
The OB360 features a high-performance PWM pump operating between 1500 and 2500 RPM to maintain consistent coolant circulation. Paired with a copper base plate for effective thermal transfer from the CPU, the cooling system helps maintain stable temperatures under demanding workloads.
Minimalist Black Design for Non-RGB Builds
Designed for users who prefer a non-RGB setup, the OB360 features a black finish without integrated lighting. Its understated industrial styling complements minimalist and performance-focused PC builds, maintaining a cohesive look without RGB lighting effects.
Features of the OB360 AIO Liquid Cooler
- Diagonal textured grooves and embossed fan frame detailing create a refined industrial aesthetic.
- Supports up to 360 W TDP for demanding cooling applications.
- Single-frame design integrates three 120 mm high static pressure PWM fans into one module.
- Each fan delivers up to 53.9 CFM of airflow and 2.36 mm-H₂O of static pressure.
- PWM fan speeds from 500 to 2000 RPM provide responsive cooling performance.
- 27 mm slim radiator with a thickened 20 mm copper chamber supports efficient heat dissipation.
- PWM pump operates from 1500 to 2500 RPM for consistent coolant circulation.
- Copper baseplate enables effective thermal transfer from the CPU.
- The black, non-RGB design complements minimalist, performance-focused builds.

articles.title: Framework Laptop 12 (Wildcat Lake) review: Growing up amid an unprecedented shortage
articles.text:
Tom's Hardware Verdict
The Framework Laptop 12 is a highly portable and repairable budget laptop, but it’s lacking features compared to the competition and lands at a higher price — unless you’re willing to supply your own RAM and SSD.
Reasons to buy
- + Decent performance for single-channel DDR5
- + Highly repairable and customizable
- + Easy to save money if you already have RAM and SSD
Reasons to avoid
- - Configurations often reach about $1,000
- - Display is middling and locked to 1080p60
- - Webcam quality is poor
Why you can trust Tom's Hardware
Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.
When Framework introduced the Laptop 12 early last year, it offered an affordable, repairable, and relatively capable laptop, especially aimed at students. Between a 2-in-1 convertible design, a touchscreen with an optional stylus, the slim frame, and a $699 starting price, it was an attractive option. The updated Framework Laptop 12 targets that same group, though it’s entering a very different market, with some of the biggest brands gunning to become frontrunners for the best college laptops. Framework still makes one of the best laptops on the market with the Laptop 13 Pro, but the entry-level market is a different beast, especially today.
Apple’s MacBook Neo has prompted a wave of more affordable Windows laptops, with Intel’s Wildcat Lake taking center stage in devices like Dell’s refreshed XPS 13. The Framework Laptop 12 provides competitive performance with these devices, though at a higher price point and with less premium amenities.
The 1080p, 60Hz display is a reminder that the otherwise-premium-feeling Laptop 12 is a budget device, and although the Laptop 12 starts at just $549 without memory or storage, it ends up around $200 to $300 more expensive than the competition when fully configured. The laptop begs a question: how much are you willing to pay for repairability?
Design
Like Framework’s previous Laptop 12 with 13th-Gen Intel CPUs, the updated version with Wildcat Lake comes in a variety of colors: Black, Gray, Lavender, Bubblegum, and Sage. Our review unit, as you can see, is the Lavender variation. At the time of writing, you need to purchase the DIY version to choose your color; the prebuilt version is currently only available in Sage.
Unlike Framework’s more expensive Laptop 13 Pro, you don’t have the option to customize the color of the bezels, and only Gray and Lavender keyboard options are available now (though, presumably, Framework will expand these options). USB-A and USB-C modules come in a wide array of colors, as well, though other expansion modules are limited to a standard silver color. Framework also offers an optional $59 stylus, matching the color options available for the Laptop 12.
The Framework Laptop 12 is a highly portable device, though perhaps not as thin and light as you’d expect out of a 12-inch laptop. It's 0.72 inches thick and clocks in at 2.8 pounds, which is thin enough and light enough, though not on the level of its enclosed competitors. The MacBook Neo weighs about the same at 2.7 pounds, but it’s covered in aluminum and it’s 0.5 inches thick. The XPS 13 with Wildcat Lake is much lighter at 2.2 pounds, thinner at 0.5 inches, and also finished with aluminum.
Considering the bulk of modularity, the fact that Framework managed to get the weight and thickness of the Laptop 12 close to closed-door competitors is remarkable. However, the fact remains that you’re often paying a premium with the Framework Laptop 12 compared to the Neo and XPS 13 and, in both cases, getting a laptop that feels less like a premium ultrabook out of the box.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
Although the Framework Laptop 12 isn’t finished in aluminum, it still has a metal structure. On top is plastic, which is then coated with thermoplastic polyurethane to absorb impacts. That leads to a plastic feeling externally, though with a smooth, slightly grippy surface that feels good in the hands.
Framework offers an optional backlight on the keyboard (our review unit didn’t have one), as well as four module slots for expansion ports. The back two support Thunderbolt 4 and DisplayPort Alt mode, and all four support USB 3.2 Gen 2 speeds and USB-PD. A 3.5mm headphone jack is standard on the Framework Laptop 12, regardless of the additional modules you choose.
Specifications
| CPU | Intel Core 7 350 | 
| Graphics | Intel Xe3 (2 cores) | 
| Memory | 16GB LP | 
| Storage | 1x 16GB DDR5-5600 SODIMM | 
| Display | 12.2-inch, 1920x1200, touch, 60Hz | 
| Networking | Intel BE213 Wi-Fi 7 / Bluetooth 6.0 | 
| Ports | Up to 4 user-selectable expansion cards | 
| Camera | 2MP sensor, 1080p30, hardware privacy switch | 
| Battery | 50Whr | 
| Power Adapter | 60W USB-C GaN (optional) | 
| Operating System | Fedora 44 | 
| Dimensions (WxDxH) | 11.29 x 8.42 x 0.72 | 
| Weight | 2.8 pounds | 
| Price (as configured) | $1,491 ($1,384 without expansion cards and power adapter) | 
Productivity Performance
This isn’t our first outing with Intel’s Wildcat Lake, so we went into this review with a good idea about what to expect from the Framework Laptop 12’s performance. Our test machine came with the highest-end chip Framework offers in this laptop, which is the Core 7 350. It’s a 6-core / 6-thread CPU with a maximum turbo clock of 4.8 GHz, and it can operate between 15W and 35W.
If you’re unfamiliar, Wildcat Lake is the younger, weaker sibling of Panther Lake. It uses Intel’s cutting-edge 18A node but with several cut corners. For starters, the 350 comes with just two faster P-cores (the remaining four are an LPE cluster). It also comes with just 6MB of last-level cache, half of what you get with Panther Lake.
The cores matter less here than the memory, however. Wildcat Lake exclusively uses single-channel DDR5 or LPDDR5X, regardless of capacity (support goes up to 64GB). In practice, that often means you need to overbudget your capacity, at least compared to something like the MacBook Neo with unified memory. Performance drops at 8GB with Wildcat Lake (see our Dell XPS 13 review).
The Core 7 350 comes in behind in single- and multi-core performance in Geekbench 6 compared to the A18 in the MacBook Neo (though multi-core to a much lesser extent). Compared to the 6-core Core 5 320 in the XPS 13, the Framework Laptop 12 is in lockstep with multi-core speed, and just shy of 5% ahead in single-core speed.
Compared to full-fat Panther Lake in the Framework 13 Pro, Wildcat Lake actually looks better than expected. The 13 Pro here is for context, not as a true comparison point; it costs a few thousand dollars. What’s interesting in Geekbench is how the X7 358H in the Framework 13 Pro scales, relative to the Core 7 350.
The X7 358H is a 16-core chip with a 4.8 GHz boost and access to up to 80W of total power (though much of that is allocated to the 12-Xe3-core GPU). Despite more than doubling total core count, and offering a doubling of P-cores, we’re not seeing twice the performance. And, even with access to less power, the Core 7 350 is within 5% of Panther Lake’s single-core performance.
With Geekbench, Apple silicon tends to perform especially well, particularly in single-core tasks, so keep that in mind.
Even with a bit of extra clock speed, however, the Framework Laptop 12 with the Core 7 350 came in behind the Core 5 320 in the XPS 13 in Handbrake. Here, the Geekbench swing toward Apple levels out; the A18 was 8% ahead in Geekbench 6 multi-core, but it’s less than 3% ahead here in Handbrake.
The Panther Lake-based 13 Pro gives some much-needed context, showing compounding factors between higher core counts, higher power limits, and true dual-channel memory. Again, it’s a far more expensive laptop, and the Framework Laptop 12 performs in line with our expectations for laptops in this class.
Perhaps the biggest takeaway is how similar the Core 5 320 is, at least in this laptop. You get an extra 200 MHz on the CPU and 100 MHz on the GPU with the Core 7 350, which isn’t moving the needle a ton here given how limited Wildcat Lake is as a platform. That’s good news, as the Core 5 320 will save you $220 in the Framework Laptop 12 compared to the Core 7 350.
Unfortunately, many of our gaming tests for laptops won’t run on Linux, and given that devices are often shipped back, we can’t go back and retest a dozen devices. That’s not too important here, though. The Core 7 350 has just two Xe3 cores, as do other Wildcat Lake chips, which doesn’t provide enough horsepower to power most titles.
We were able to achieve 30 FPS in Civilization VI at 1080p, which underscores the limitations of the integrated graphics. Intel’s dual-core Xe3 is plenty capable of running Balatro, Vampire Survivors, or whatever 2D sidescroller is currently popping off on Steam. Otherwise, it’s there to give you a display output.
Display
The display is what separates the Framework Laptop 12 from the various other Wildcat Lake-based devices we’ve seen in the wake of the MacBook Neo, and not for the better. Color performance, especially, is weak in our testing, and although peak brightness is in line with similar laptops, the 60Hz refresh rate is a severe downgrade compared to other devices, as is the 1080p resolution.
For metrics, you can see the display peaked at 451 nits, right in line with the MacBook Neo and Framework 13 (non-Pro). However, gamut coverage is poor, with just 64.9% of the sRGB gamut measured, compared to wide-gamut coverage on the competing machines. This is a “budget” laptop, but it’ll easily run over $1,000 with most configurations, and the display is not worthy of that price.
The XPS 13 provides some important context. It doesn’t get as bright — though, it’s hard to split hairs over 50 nits — but it comes with a 120Hz refresh, a higher 2.5K resolution, and it’s a touchscreen like the Framework Laptop 12. That gap in display performance would be understandable with a big gap in price, but that’s not the case. In fact, the Framework Laptop 12 clocks in at $1,271 with a Core 5 320, 16GB of memory, and 500GB of storage. The XPS 13, meanwhile, is $1,000 for that configuration.
Framework naturally needs to cut corners at this price, and it needs to engineer its devices to be repairable and upgradable. So, it’s hard holding the Framework Laptop 12 to the standard of a device like the XPS 13 that doesn’t come with those serviceability upsides. Still, the display is a consistent reminder that this is a budget laptop, whereas with the XPS 13 and MacBook Neo, it’s easy to forget that when doing day-to-day web and office task, due to the premium screens and build quality.
Keyboard and Touchpad
The Framework Laptop 12 comes with a standard keyboard/touchpad combo unit, which is available in several different layouts. There’s currently just a gray and lavender option for the keyboard unit, though presumably Framework will expand its offerings to cover the other colors available on the Framework Laptop 12 (at least with an American English layout).
I achieve 85 WPM with 99% accuracy in a MonkeyType test, compared to 92 WPM at 97% accuracy on my desktop (using the keyboard I type on every day). The keys have standard 19mm spacing and generous 1.5mm of key travel, which makes it comfortable to type on, even considering the small footprint of the Framework Laptop 12.
The touchpad is naturally small given the size of this device, and it’s mechanical, leading to sharp dips during presses on the bottom corners and no responsiveness near the top. It’s a serviceable touchpad, what you’d expect to see on this class of device. Just don’t go in expecting to be spoiled with a large glass surface or haptics.
Upgradeability
Framework built its brand on upgradability, so it’s no surprise that the Framework Laptop 12 earns near-perfect marks here. Like other devices, you can ship the Framework Laptop 12 pre-assembled, or as a barebones system that can accept your own M.2 2230 SSD, DDR5 SODIMM, and operating system. Even then, you can swap out the keyboard, display, mainboard, and ports if you choose (though only within the Framework Laptop 12 form factor).
However, the Framework Laptop 12 brings up the important distinction between serviceability and upgradability. The Framework Laptop 12 is the gold standard (among all Framework devices) for serviceability.But the Wildcat Lake chip brings up concerns about upgradability with its single-channel memory interface.
You can upgrade the memory up to a 64GB DDR5-6400 SODIMM, but there’s only one physical memory slot on the board. Wildcat Lake exclusively uses single-channel memory; it’s not simply a single-channel configuration for a budget price point. You can upgrade to more capacity down the line, but you can’t simply add in a second SODIMM to double your RAM.
You won’t find a more serviceable laptop on the market (outside of the other options from Framework) than the Framework 12, but you primarily have two narrow upgrade paths: more storage and more memory capacity, but not a true dual-channel configuration. Hopefully Framework will continue this line in the future, allowing you to swap the mainboard.
On the serviceable end, however, Framework makes things simple. You get a matching Torx screwdriver with the laptop that can detach the bottom cover. The cover has eight captive screws, so you don’t need to worry about losing them, and it’s primarily there to keep everything together; you actually service the laptop from the top, under the keyboard.
Considering you’re meant to go inside the laptop, Framework has everything clearly labeled, along with QR codes that link to repair guides for various components. With our barebones kit of modules, the laptop was powered on and assembled within five minutes, and this is my first time ever assembling a Framework device from scratch.
Battery Life
Our typical laptop battery tests are based on Windows, and we can’t replicate the testing process on Linux. Framework assured us that Fedora 44 offers the best experience out of the box, so that is what we tested. Instead of a direct comparison, we designed a basic web browsing test loop to see how long the 50WHr battery would hold up away from a charger.
About 9 hours is the answer, with a 9:16 average across three runs. We ran the laptop through a series of live websites with the screen set to 150 nits, Wi-Fi on, and Bluetooth disabled for the test. Again, we can’t make direct comparisons with Windows laptops, but getting around a full day of work is solid for the small 50Whr battery. And with USB-C charging, you can pretty easily top off with a portable GaN brick.
Audio
The stereo 2W speakers inside the Framework Laptop 12 are surprisingly powerful, considering the size of the machine, though the quality of the speakers and dual internal microphones is a clear cut corner to reach the more affordable price of the device. Thankfully, there’s a 3.5mm headphone jack built in (it doesn’t take a module slot), along with Bluetooth 6.0 support for wireless headphones.
The microphone poses a larger issue than the speakers. It’s heavily compressed, which helps make your voice come through clearly, though at the cost of heavy background noise (including keyboard and trackpad noise). You’ll want to use something like EasyEffects in Linux to clean up the microphone audio.
As for the speakers, they’re not as bad as they could be. As mentioned, they’re loud considering the size of the device, and they didn’t distort at full volume. They’re tuned for this type of device, as well. Rather than overemphasizing the highs or pumping too much low-end and exposing distortion, the speakers in the Framework Laptop 12 have a heavy emphasis on the upper midrange.
This range, somewhere between 500Hz and 4kHz, is typically described as “boxy,” and that emphasis works well for the small drivers in the Framework Laptop 12. It implies a low end that the drivers aren’t actually capable of producing. Further, the higher-end of this range, around 1kHz to 2kHz, is where many human voices fall, with sharp consonants pushing higher-end harmonics that come off as harsh. Again, the emphasis helps, allowing voices to come through clearly, without sounding tinny.
Heat
The Framework Laptop 12 stays fairly cool, even under load. The hottest point we measured on the laptop was the underside, directly in the middle, which peaked at 101 degrees Fahrenheit (about 38 degrees Celsius). Under normal usage in a browser with a handful of tabs open, there’s very little noticeable heat, even at this hottest point.
Up where your hands are, we measured 94 degrees Fahrenheit (about 34 degrees Celsius) between the G and H keys on the keyboard, and 86 degrees Fahrenheit (30 degrees Celsius) on the touchpad. That’s warm for your hands, but again, the heat only crops up during heavy load.
Webcam
It’s unsurprising for a laptop at the price of the Framework Laptop 12, but the webcam quality is poor. The camera oddly uses a 4:3 aspect ratio, and the 2MP sensor creates an image more reminiscent of a watercolor than a sharp, Full-HD picture. It struggles with low-light especially, with even moderate shadows in an otherwise brightly-lit room showing visible noise.
The image above was taken in my office in the middle of the day. A window behind me was fully open, about three and a half feet away, and I have a lamp serving somewhat as a key light about three feet off-screen to my left. I’m on the second floor of a two-story house, on a hill without any trees obstructing sunlight (and it was a sunny day). There was a generous amount of natural light in the room.
Yet, you’d think I was sitting in near darkness from the webcam image. The stark brightness from the window darkens my face, filling it with visible noise, as the camera struggles to handle the dynamic range. Sitting in front of an unobstructed window during the middle of the day is the time and place where you’re likely to have the webcam turned on, and it fails that test.
Software and Warranty
Framework offers a standard one-year limited warranty on the Framework Laptop 12, with an optional three-year warranty available for $89 extra. You can read over Framework’s limited warranty, but the limitations are fairly straightforward. Normal wear and tear, damage due to negligence or misuse, and use of third-party parts (or first-party parts from third-party sources) will void the warranty.
Broad warranty protection isn’t as important here as it is elsewhere, however. If, for example, your USB-C port stops working, you can just buy another one rather than going through the RMA process and potentially paying for a repair on the other side (even if you’re under warranty).
You’re free to bring your own OS, but Framework also offers the Framework Laptop 12 with either Windows 11 or Fedora 44 pre-installed. Framework normally uses Ubuntu; however, Fedora 44 has moved to the newer Linux 7.1 kernel, which has optimizations specifically for Wildcat Lake. Using a slower-moving distro like Ubuntu is fine, though you’ll want to make sure to manually upgrade your kernel (and packages) for the best performance if you’re not already using a distro with kernel 7.1 or newer.
Configurations
Framework offers three mainboard configurations: Core 3 204, Core 5 320, or Core 7 350. As we covered in the performance section, the Core 5 320 in the XPS 13 offered largely similar performance to the Core 7 350 in the Framework Laptop 12, so that seems like the sweet spot here. The Core 3 304 is effectively a single-core CPU, with just one P-core alongside a four-core LPE cluster, and it lacks a fingerprint reader, which is available with both other mainboards.
With the DIY edition, Framework ships the laptop without memory, storage, or expansion cards. There’s a single SODIMM slot for memory and a single M.2 2230 slot for the SSD. Framework offers up to 2TB of PCIe 4.0 storage at checkout, as well as up to 48GB DDR5-5600 (again, via a single SODIMM). Framework has USB-C, USB-A, HDMI, Ethernet, 10G Ethernet, DisplayPort, microSD, and SD card modules available, ranging from $10 to $99.
There aren’t any display options aside from the standard 60 Hz 1080p panel in our unit. For the keyboard and trackpad, Framework offers backlit and non-backlit options in various different native layouts.
Framework offers prebuilt versions of the Framework Laptop 12 at a discounted price. The Core 3 304 comes with 8GB of memory ($699), the Core 5 320 comes with 16GB (1,099), and the Core 7 350 comes with 32GB (1,399), and all three configurations use 512GB of storage. All of the configurations come with Framework’s standard expansion card bundle: two USB-C, a USB-A, and an HDMI module.
Dell starts higher with the XPS 13 at $799, but that’s with the Core 5 320 and 8GB of memory. Jumping up to 16GB, the XPS 13 is $999 with the Core 5 320, $100 less than the preconfigured Framework Laptop 12.
Bottom Line
The Framework Laptop 12 is caught between an unprecedented memory and storage shortage and a wave of budget-oriented Windows laptops that skip the repairability angle in favor of better trimmings out of the box. At the same price, it’d be a solid alternative with understandable downsides. The killer for the Laptop 12 is that you’ll likely spend more on it compared to other Wildcat Lake options.
With the Core 5 320, the Framework Laptop 12 is nearly $300 more expensive than the XPS 13, when both are configured with 8GB of memory and 500GB of storage. The Acer Swift Air 14 is $700, and a similarly configured Framework Laptop 12 is $1,074 before adding on the extra cost of a power adapter and modules. For many Wildcat Lake devices, we see prices top out around $1,000; with the Framework Laptop 12, you’ll often spend at least $1,000, assuming you push beyond the Core 3 304.
Modularity comes at a cost, which is more relevant in the case of the Framework Laptop 12 where $100 or $200 makes all the difference in value (it’s less relevant up at the Framework Pro 13, where you expect premium pricing). That extra cost is especially damaging here, when Framework’s competitors are offering better display performance (and more pixels) and all-aluminum bodies for less money.
There are situations where the Framework Laptop 12 is a great option, even compared to the other Wildcat Lake devices on the market. If you already have a SODIMM module you can harvest from other devices, along with an SSD, this is a cheap way to get some of Intel’s latest silicon. But for everyone else, unless you don’t mind paying significantly more for repairability, there are better options available that typically cost less, look better, and feel more premium.
Jake Roach is the Senior CPU Analyst at Tom’s Hardware, writing reviews, news, and features about the latest consumer and workstation processors.

articles.title: Most U.S. drone shipments went to Ukraine while Iran’s went to Russia
articles.text:
The US exported the most drones over the past few years — but the second-biggest exporter might surprise you
US and Iran account for 86% of global military drone exports
- The US exported 7,592 military drones, narrowly ahead of Iran's 6,800
- Iran overtook America in 2025 after US deliveries dropped to 402
- Russia received 99% of Iran's exported drones, mostly Shahed-136 attack systems
The United States exported the most military drones between 2022 and 2025, narrowly beating Iran, which ranked second worldwide during the period.
Data from the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI) records 7,592 American exports against 6,800 Iranian deliveries, while Germany ranked a distant third with 1,000 exports.
Together, the US and Iran accounted for 86% of global exports, with Ukraine receiving 95% of American shipments while Russia got 99% of Iran’s deliveries, most of which were Shahed-136 one-way attack drones.
Iran overtakes the US as exports shift
Although Washington maintained the lead across most of the period, annual figures changed significantly in 2025, when Iranian deliveries exceeded American shipments.
Iran exported 2,002 drones that year, compared with 402 delivered by the United States.
The decline of American shipments is due to the suspension of military assistance to Ukraine, which had received most US exports during the preceding years.
Subsequent American deliveries were directed mainly toward Taiwan, marking a change in the destinations receiving these systems.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
The figures cover military drones weighing at least 150 kilograms, equivalent to approximately 331 pounds, including loitering munitions and one-way attack aircraft.
Small first-person-view drones and commercial models were excluded, meaning the figures do not capture every type of unmanned aircraft supplied internationally.
One-way attack platforms accounted for 97% of recorded exports, indicating that expendable systems dominated the shipments measured by SIPRI during the period.
Their prevalence also explains why the figures should not be interpreted as a comprehensive count of military drones worldwide.
Poland and others trail the leading exporters
In addition to the top exporters, within the same period, Poland exported 690 drones to take fourth place while Turkey occupied fifth place with 381 exports, despite supplying customers across a considerably wider international network.
Ankara delivered drones to 28 countries, including Pakistan, Kuwait and Romania, which belong to the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO).
Its Bayraktar TB2 accounted for 58% of worldwide exports of reusable drones, distinguishing Turkey’s position within that category.
The Czech Republic, Sweden and the next seven countries in the rankings collectively exported just 89 drones, considerably fewer than Germany or Poland.
Their combined deliveries also fell far below Turkey’s total, despite the latter ranking behind both European countries in overall export numbers.
The figures therefore distinguish the country’s leading total military drone shipments from those supplying particular categories of aircraft.
However, SIPRI’s weight threshold and exclusion of smaller commercial and first-person-view models limit comparisons with estimates covering the entire unmanned aircraft market.

articles.title: No Man's Sky is coming to iPhone and iPad
articles.text:
No Man’s Sky will fly onto iPhones and iPads on Oct. 28, developer Hello Games has announced.
In a blog post, the studio outlined the new ports, which come just over 10 years after the space exploration game debuted on PS4 and PC. Impressively, No Man’s Sky will work on iPhone 11 and 3rd-generation iPad Air and above, albeit with some limitations.
In particular, multiplayer isn’t available on Apple devices, while Planetary Settlements, which are alien towns that the player can build and manage, are only supported on iPhone 15 Pro and above.
Still, it’s commendable that so much of this vast and ever-expanding game is playable on Apple’s mobile devices. In addition to having streamlined touch controls, Hello Games says it will offer support for controllers, TV casting and even mouse and keyboard on iPad.
The game will also be free to try at launch and come in at under 4GB.
The No Man’s Sky Apple ports come as Hello Games toils away at its next game, Light No Fire. The open-world adventure MMO is currently in development for PC, although no release window has been confirmed.

articles.title: Dunkle Energie: So könnten schwache Radiowellen sein Geheimnis lüften
articles.text:
Dunkle Energie: Ein schwaches Radiosignal aus der Frühzeit des Universums könnte ihr Geheimnis lüften
Was steckt hinter Dunkler Energie? Dies ist eines der großen Rätsel der Kosmologie. Die unsichtbare, hypothetische Form der Energie gilt als verantwortlich für die Ausdehnung des Universums, nachdem der erste Schub durch den Big Bang abgeklungen war.
Neuer Weg zum Verständnis von Dunkler Energie?
Direkt nachgewiesen werden konnte die Dunkle Energie, die fast 70 Prozent der Energiedichte des Universums ausmachen soll, noch nicht. Ein Forschungsteam könnte aber nun einen Weg gefunden haben, Dunkle Energie künftig besser zu verstehen.
Die Resultate ihrer Forschung haben die Wissenschaftler:innen in gleich zwei Papern vorgestellt, die beide in der Fachzeitschrift The Astrophysical Journal erschienen sind.
Analyse von neutralem Wasserstoff
Die Forschenden haben mit dem Radioteleskop Canadian Hydrogen Intensity Mapping Experiment (CHIME) nach Spuren von kosmischem Wasserstoff gesucht. Genauer gesagt nach neutralem atomaren Wasserstoff, der nicht ionisiert und also elektrisch ungeladen ist.
Neutraler Wasserstoff sendet eine Radiostrahlung mit einer Wellenlänge von etwa 21 Zentimetern aus. Durch die Expansion des Universums wird die Strahlung auf dem Weg zur Erde zu niedrigeren Frequenzen verschoben.
Je stärker die Verzerrung im Vergleich zur ursprünglichen Wellenlänge ist, desto länger waren die Strahlen unterwegs. Daraus kann man ablesen, aus welcher Zeit die Signale stammen. Die Strahlung des neutralen Wasserstoffs, die CHIME auffing, wurde vor acht bis neun Milliarden Jahren ausgesendet. Sie stammt also aus dem relativ jungen Universum.
CHIME beobachtete erstmals direkt neutralen Wasserstoff
Bei der Analyse von neutralem Wasserstoff gibt es eine Schwierigkeit. Sein Signal ist so schwach, dass es von anderen Radioquellen überlagert wird.
Bisher konnten Forschende mit CHIME Wasserstoff nur indirekt wahrnehmen. Sie mussten die empfangenen Signale mit bereits kartierten Galaxien abgleichen.
Mit Hilfe neuer Algorithmen ist es den Wissenschaftler:innen nun gelungen, mit CHIME die Wellenlängen des Wasserstoffs unmittelbar zu erkennen. Das Radioteleskop konnte eigenständig Störsignale erkennen und ausblenden. So soll die Detektion von neutralem Wasserstoff künftig einfacher werden.
Verteilung von Wasserstoff gibt Aufschluss über Ausdehnung des Universums
Was hat dies alles nun mit Dunkler Energie zu tun? Um diese mysteriöse Kraft zu verstehen, ist es wichtig, die Verteilung von Materie im Universum zu unterschiedlichen Zeiten zu kennen.
Nur daraus kann man ablesen, wie schnell sich das Weltall ausgedehnt hat und welche Rolle die Dunkle Energie dabei gespielt hat. Und da Wasserstoff das häufigste Element im Universum ist, ist es der beste Marker, um die Verteilung von Materie und ihre Veränderung zu analysieren.

articles.title: OPPO's Find X10 Series will offer a new standard of photo and video quality on a smartphone - Tech Guide
articles.text:
OPPO will launch its new flagship Find X10 smartphone series which includes a Hasselblad True-to-Life Camera and a next-generation LUMO True Image Engine to take your photography to a new level.
The Find X series continues the minimalist design language and uses premium materials and crafted detail that’s all brought together in a new borderless design which includes one piece of sculpted glass that seamlessly flows from the screen to the camera module.
The OPPO Find X10 Pro Max in Luna White has a LUMO camera island in a matte silver metallic finish that houses the True-Colour Cameras and dual flash system.
It’s also complemented by Hasselblad’s signature matte orange accent ring to create a distinctive two-tone finish.
“Find X Series reflects our relentless pursuit of exceptional mobile imaging,” said Pete Lau, SVP and Chief Product Officer at OPPO.
“Together with Hasselblad, we are taking another significant step forward with Find X10 Series, bringing true-to-life detail, colour and tone to everyday photography.
“Simply open the camera and capture the moment as you see it, with no extra settings required.”
The Find X10 camera includes a dual 200MP camera system co-developed with Hasselblad.
The Find X10 Pro Max has the industry’s first triple 200MP camera system, bringing 200MP sensors to the ultra-wide, main, and telephoto cameras for the first time on a smartphone.
Now it’s one thing to have great cameras but the OPPO Find X10 also has next-generation computational photography – the LUMO True Image Engine.
It works with OPPO’s image expertise deliver precise colour and quality.
On the video side the Find X10 Pro Max supports 4K 120fps and 8K 30fps through all three rear cameras, while the Find X10 has the same capabilities on its two 200MP cameras.
The Find X10 is powered by the MediaTek Dimensity 9600M chip while the Find X10 Pro Max is among the first smartphones to include the 2nm MediaTek Dimensity 9000 Pro which offers a major boost to performance and power efficiency.
Both Find X10 models feature a massive 7,150 mAh OPPO silicon carbon battery to 2 days of use on a single charge.
The battery is also engineered to retain more than 80 per cent of its original capacity even after five years of typical use.
The OPPO Find X10 will be available in Glacier Blue, Glow Coral, and Mist Grey while the OPPO Find X10 Pro Max will come in Titanium Grey and Luna White.
Pricing and availability will be announced at the global launch event on October 21.

articles.title: Seulement 11 mètres de haut : pourquoi le premier vol de la fusée réutilisable RV-X de la JAXA est aussi le dernier
articles.text:
C’était cet été, et l’agence spatiale japonaise (JAXA) a mis en ligne ce mercredi 14 octobre une vidéo qui raconte de bout en bout le premier vol de RV-X. Sous ce nom se cache un « petit » démonstrateur de fusée réutilisable, qui montre tout l’intérêt qu’a la JAXA pour une approche à la SpaceX : tirer des fusées, les récupérer et les remettre sur le circuit ensuite.
Ce vol, qui remonte au 11 juillet, a eu lieu au centre d’essais de Noshiro, dans la préfecture d’Akita, au nord du Japon. Dans la vidéo, on voit la préparation, le vol et ce qui se passe une fois l’engin posé. Pendant la phase de vol, RV-X est monté à environ 11 mètres et s’est décalé de 16 mètres en restant vertical. Le vol a duré une quarantaine de secondes.
Onze mètres de haut, ça peut faire sourire, quand on compare au Starship de SpaceX : l’immense lanceur de l’entreprise américaine en est maintenant à faire des vols orbitaux. Mieux que ça : il devrait bientôt y avoir le premier test de capture de l’étage supérieur par la tour de lancement (le propulseur, lui, a déjà été rattrapé).
Mais c’est oublier que SpaceX aussi a commencé modestement. Le Starhopper, premier engin d’essai du programme Starship, ressemblait beaucoup à ce RV-X : un prototype extrêmement incomplet. Lors de son premier vol libre, en juillet 2019, il ne s’était élevé que d’une vingtaine de mètres.
Le Japon n’est pas le seul à courir derrière SpaceX. La veille du vol de RV-X, les médias d’État chinois annonçaient que la Chine avait récupéré pour la première fois le premier étage d’une fusée, une Longue Marche 10B, rattrapé par un filet sur une plateforme en mer après un lancement orbital. Pour Tokyo, l’enjeu est de préparer un successeur moins cher au lanceur jetable H3, l’actuel pilier du spatial japonais.
Un moteur allumé 166 fois au sol, avant de se lancer dans les airs
Avant son premier saut, RV-X a passé beaucoup de temps au sol.
Il y a d’abord eu une campagne de mises à feu à l’été 2018, rappelle la page du projet, puis une deuxième de mars 2020 à septembre 2021, en pleine pandémie de covid. Des essais de chute ont aussi vérifié que les jambes d’atterrissage encaissent bien le choc. Enfin, les équipes ont répété la manutention et l’installation sur le pas de tir.
En tout, le moteur a été allumé 166 fois, vol compris. La JAXA avait d’abord annoncé 165 allumages lors de sa conférence de presse du 11 juillet, avant de corriger. Sur une fusée jetable, un moteur finit sa carrière après un seul vol. L’agence met en avant une conception pensée pour la sécurité, qui a permis de mettre l’engin hors danger rapidement après l’atterrissage.
Un saut plus modeste que prévu
En octobre 2024, la JAXA prévoyait encore un premier vol de RV-X à 100 mètres d’altitude, donc plus ambitieux, selon le quotidien Nikkei cité par European Spaceflight.
Une première tentative, en mars 2026, a été annulée à cause de la panne d’un raccord à déconnexion rapide, la pièce qui détache l’engin de ses conduites au sol.
Le 11 juillet, RV-X est finalement monté à 11 mètres, environ neuf fois moins haut que les 100 mètres envisagés en 2024. Entre-temps, la JAXA avait ramené son objectif à une dizaine de mètres. RV-X ne revolera pas, alors que la JAXA prévoyait encore en juillet, selon Space.com, de nouveaux vols jusqu’à environ 100 mètres. Après avoir inspecté l’engin et analysé les données, la JAXA a mis fin à la série d’essais en vol. Elle estime avoir obtenu les résultats attendus.
La suite se jouera donc avec Callisto, un démonstrateur d’environ 13 mètres développé par le CNES français, l’agence allemande DLR et la JAXA.
Cet engin doit voler depuis Kourou, en Guyane française. Le programme accumule pourtant les reports : le DLR a confirmé en septembre que ses premiers sauts, prévus en 2026, glissaient à 2027, a rapporté European Spaceflight. Avant de partir pour la Guyane, la partie moteur de Callisto doit encore passer des essais à feu à Noshiro, là où RV-X a volé.
