articles.title: Meet the 30 startups shaping India’s tech future; Overcoming failures in spacetech
articles.text:
Meet the 30 startups shaping India’s tech future; Overcoming failures in spacetech
At the 17th edition of YourStory’s flagship tech-startup event, TechSparks, Sridhar Vembu, Chief Scientist and Co-founder of Zoho Corp, unveiled and presented this year’s Tech30 at TechSparks 2026.
Dear Reader,
From autonomous drones to electric farm machines manufacturers, meet the 30 startups building the next generation of technology.
At the 17th edition of YourStory’s flagship tech-startup event, TechSparks, Sridhar Vembu, Chief Scientist and Co-founder of Zoho Corp, unveiled and presented this year’s Tech30 at TechSparks 2026. This year’s picks reflect the growing ambition of Indian startups to develop their own technologies and apply them to practical problems. Here’s the full list.
With AI taking over software development, the technology remained the core topic across several discussions at the event.
“AI already can write better code than at least 60-70% of software engineers out there. And in maybe three to six months, when things accelerate, AI can do better software than maybe 90% of software engineers,” Vembu said, speaking at TechSparks 2026.
But it is not all doom and gloom.
Despite the impending disruption to tech professionals, a huge part of India’s population will remain largely unaffected, said Vembu, presenting a counter-intuitive macro perspective. He pointed out that roughly 97% of the broader population does not write software and operates as consumers of technology.
Meanwhile, the Karnataka government is being cautious about using AI in governance as it first needs to understand how this technology can be used responsibly, Priyank Kharge, Minister for Home, IT, BT & E-Governance, Government of Karnataka, said at the event.
However, this does not mean that the state government will not use AI in governance. The minister said the technology is being leveraged for basic issues such as citizen grievances, health, and mobility. He also said the government has set up a committee to study how to use AI responsibly in governance.
ICYMI: All that happened on day 1 of TechSparks 2026.
In today’s newsletter, we will talk about
- Priyank Kharge on Karnataka’s new tech order
- Overcoming failures in spacetech
Here’s your trivia for today: Which multinational computer hardware company gets its single-word name from the last four letters of the mythical winged horse Pegasus? (Scroll down for answer)
TechSparks
Priyank Kharge on Karnataka’s new tech order
Karnataka is setting its sights on defining the future of global technology. At Techsparks 2026, Kharge declared that the next era of tech innovation will originate from the state.
During a captivating conversation with Shradha Sharma, Founder & CEO of YourStory and The Bharat Project, the minister highlighted the government’s relentless focus on upskilling local talent to meet the evolving demands of the global economy.
Key takeaways:
- The minister said that, in the last nine months, the state has attracted close to $4.9 billion investments just from the technology sector. Karnataka’s capital Bengaluru is already the fourth largest technology cluster in the world.
- He said manufacturing units and global capability centres (GCCs) have come up across the state, and that one of Apple’s supply chain partners operates out of Belagavi, doing precision manufacturing.
- Kharge added that the state runs dedicated entrepreneurship programmes for startups outside Bengaluru and cited recent deals to emphasise the state’s Beyond Bengaluru policy.
TechSparks
Overcoming failures in spacetech
Building spacetech companies requires nerves of steel, given the nature of the business. Companies have to survive hundreds of investor rejections, acute supply chain bottlenecks, and the constant threat of orbital failure.
Speaking with Shradha Sharma, Founder and CEO, YourStory and The Bharat Project, at the 17th edition of YourStory’s flagship tech-startup event, TechSparks, Srinath Ravichandran, Co-founder and CEO of AgniKul Cosmos, and Suyash Singh, Co-founder and CEO of GalaxEye, shared practical insights into the complex task of building aerospace ventures in an emerging market.
Key takeaways:
- Ravichandran faced 275 investor rejections before securing initial backing. Singh encountered similar headwinds at GalaxEye, facing roughly 100 rejections.
- Following a successful test launch in May 2024 using 3D-printed engines and a mobile launchpad, AgniKul is now preparing for orbital customer flights while testing rocket stage reusability, bringing hardware safely back to Earth to lower launch costs.
- Despite the risks, market demand in spacetech is expanding rapidly. Surging geopolitical conflicts across the globe have made space-based Earth observation indispensable.

articles.title: La NASA ha fotografiado desde el espacio un gigantesco cráter en Australia con forma de araña
articles.text:
El 13 de octubre de 2026, la imagen del día del NASA Earth Observatory fue una instantánea fascinante tomada por el satélite Landsat 9 desde el cielo de Australia. En ella se ve el cráter Araña (Spider crater), una deformación del terreno ubicada en la región de Kimberley, en Australia Occidental. Como su propio nombre indica, tiene una curiosa forma de araña que ha llamado la atención de los científicos desde hace años. Y es que, en realidad, esta estructura llamó por primera vez la atención de los geólogos en los años 50 del siglo pasado.
En unos inicios se pensó que podría tener origen volcánico, pero las investigaciones posteriores la han descrito como un cráter de impacto. Aún hay muchos misterios a su alrededor, pero estos ya no obsesionan solo a los científicos. La foto de la NASA ha hecho que personas ajenas a la ciencia de todo el mundo se interesen y se maravillen por ella.
Las cifras. En la imagen de la NASA, tomada el pasado 20 de septiembre de 2026, se ve una estructura de unos 4 kilómetros de ancho. Sin embargo, este es solo el centro del cráter completo, cuyas dimensiones totales son de 13x11 kilómetros. Esto incluye las patas de la araña, formadas por crestas claras de arenisca.
El origen. Durante estudios realizados en la década de 1970 se encontraron dentro del cráter Araña varias muestras de conos astillados (shatter cones). Estas son fracturas cónicas con estriaciones que se forman en las rocas cuando estas se someten a un impacto colosal, de entre 2 y 30 GPa. Normalmente son una evidencia diagnóstica de que una estructura como esta pueda considerarse un cráter de impacto. Por eso, cuando se hallaron, se desechó la hipótesis del origen volcánico.
Con esta evidencia, se sugiere que, tras un gran impacto de un meteorito, el terreno se elevó en el centro y las capas de roca se deformaron, sacando a la superficie algunas rocas que normalmente estarían a mucha profundidad. Después, con el paso del tiempo, la erosión eliminó la roca menos resistente y dejó en relieve las crestas más duras. Esas serían las patas de la araña.
Más pruebas. Otra prueba de que se trata de un cráter de impacto se arrojó con un estudio publicado en 2021. En él se analizaban granos de cuarzo y circón recogidos en el cráter Araña. Cuando un impacto golpea la roca, deja deformaciones microscópicas en los cristales, y el circón y el cuarzo las conservan bien. Por eso, igual que los shatter cones, estos minerales son grandes indicadores de que una deformación del terreno es en realidad un cráter de impacto. En este caso, también explicaron cómo se produjo la colisión, ya que las deformaciones no estaban repartidas de forma uniforme alrededor del centro. Esto indicaría que el impacto se produjo de forma oblicua.
Antigüedad incierta. Ya tenemos bastante información sobre cómo se pudo formar el cráter Araña. Aun así, salta a la vista que no es un cráter convencional, de ahí que se considere tan interesante y misterioso. De hecho, uno de los misterios que aún lo envuelven es el de su antigüedad. Se sabe que debió formarse después de un plegamiento suave de la cuarcita paleoproterozoica y antes de un episodio regional de erosión glaciar. Esto, por asociación, lo ubica en un momento entre 600 y 900 millones de años atrás. Más allá de eso, no se sabe nada de su edad.

articles.title: Un botnet d'un genre nouveau : Anthropic a peur que votre TV devienne le refuge d'une IA malveillante
articles.text:
En décembre 2025, le botnet Kimwolf enrôlait 1,8 million de box Android TV pour mener des attaques par déni de service, un parc qui a ensuite dépassé les 2 millions d’appareils. Ces boîtiers sans marque, rarement mis à jour, viennent de servir à une expérience d’un tout autre genre : héberger une intelligence artificielle complète. L’équipe de sécurité d’Anthropic en tire un avertissement précis, chiffres et calendrier à l’appui, publié le 12 octobre.
Une IA entière sur quinze box à 55 dollars
Gemma4-26B, un modèle de 26 milliards de paramètres, a fonctionné réparti sur quinze boîtiers Android TV à 55 dollars pièce, dotés de 4 Go de mémoire chacun. Le débit plafonne à 0,39 token par seconde, environ un mot toutes les trois secondes : lent, mais fonctionnel, sur un matériel branché derrière des millions de téléviseurs.
Un second modèle de 9 milliards de paramètres a su monter seul son serveur d’inférence sur 8 des 9 machines inconnues qu’on lui présentait. La liste allait d’un Jetson Nano à un Mac, en passant par une carte RTX 4090. En se transmettant des notes d’une génération à l’autre, il fait aussi grimper son taux de réussite d’environ 45 % à 84 % au meilleur des essais.
La réplication complète, de l’intrusion à la remise en route, reste l’apanage d’un seul modèle ouvert, GLM-5.2, qui a colonisé 8 nœuds sur 8 dans quatre essais sur cinq. L’exercice se jouait toutefois sur un réseau simplifié, port de débogage laissé ouvert et plusieurs protections retirées. Les auteurs présentent leur résultat comme une borne haute, et reconnaissent n’avoir pas testé la riposte de défenseurs humains.
Deux millions de box, l’équivalent de 40 cartes H100
Un parc de la taille de Kimwolf représenterait l’équivalent d’une quarantaine de H100, ces cartes graphiques qui font tourner les centres de données d’IA. Un ver qui transporterait les poids de son modèle n’aurait pourtant besoin d’aucune d’entre elles : chaque appareil infecté ajoute un peu de calcul, sans serveur central à débrancher pour tout arrêter. La propagation resterait lente, un cycle de réplication de un à deux jours pour un modèle de 9 milliards de paramètres, et un doublement du parc en quelques jours. Les auteurs y voient une possible « réseau mycorhizien numérique », prospérant sur l’informatique mal sécurisée.
Au rythme de progression observé, les petits modèles atteindraient le niveau de GLM-5.2 d’ici la fin de 2026, et les vers porteurs de leurs propres poids suivraient peu après. La projection resserre celle du patron de la société, qui évoquait dès avril 2024 une IA capable de « se répliquer et survivre » entre 2025 et 2028.
Des parades existent déjà, proches de celles opposées aux botnets classiques : surveiller les transferts de plusieurs gigaoctets entre appareils domestiques, puis placer les abonnés infectés en quarantaine. Cette méthode avait nettoyé 92 % des infections du botnet Mirai en quatorze jours. Les auteurs plaident aussi pour interdire les mots de passe d’usine chez les fabricants d’objets connectés, comme la loi britannique l’impose déjà.

articles.title: Narnia : pourquoi la première bande annonce du nouveau film ne plait pas du tout à certains fans ?
articles.text:
Après l’ouragan commercial et critique de Barbie, l’arrivée de Greta Gerwig aux commandes du reboot de Narnia pour le compte du géant du streaming s’annonçait comme l’un des projets les plus ambitieux de la décennie.
Mais à la vision de ce tout premier trailer, diffusé dans la nuit du 13 au 14 octobre 2026, le soufflé est retombé à une vitesse vertigineuse, laissant place à une colère importante chez les nostalgiques des livres et des films des années 2000. Une déception qui avait déjà eu lieu lors d’une précédente annonce.
Une overdose de CGI et une esthétique « à la Taika Waititi » qui passe très mal pour Narnia
Le premier grief formulé massivement par les spectateurs du trailer de Narnia concerne la direction artistique du film. Là où les adaptations de Walden Media en 2005 misaient sur des décors naturels somptueux, des costumes tangibles et un ton épique très ancré dans le réel, la version Gerwig semble céder aux pires travers du Hollywood moderne : un abus étouffant d’effets numériques.
Les commentaires (que l’on trouve un peu partout sur X ou YouTube) n’y vont pas par quatre chemins : la comparaison avec les productions Marvel les plus saturées est sur toutes les lèvres. Plusieurs internautes reprochent à la réalisatrice d’avoir copié la palette visuelle flashy et artificielle d’un Thor: Ragnarok, détruisant au passage toute la magie poétique et le charme tactile du monde de Narnia. L’atmosphère envoûtante et immersive semble s’être évaporée au profit d’un spectacle numérique froid et générique.
La bande-son n’échappe pas non plus au massacre. Le choix d’habiller cette première bande-annonce avec du Led Zeppelin, et notamment Stairway to Heaven ou une reprise rock, fait hurler les puristes. Pour beaucoup, plaquer du rock classique sur un univers fantastique qui repose à l’origine sur la création poétique et le chant mystique du lion Aslan relève d’une totale erreur de ton.
Trahison de C.S. Lewis et casting contesté
Au-delà de la forme, c’est le fond même de l’adaptation qui suscite une vive levée de boucliers. Comme argument, on retrouve souvent chez les fans le fait que C.S. Lewis a conçu Les Chroniques de Narnia comme une allégorie profondément chrétienne, où le personnage d’Aslan incarne une figure messianique centrale. Or, les choix de production et les rumeurs d’altération du lore, notamment autour du casting, alimentent l’impression que le matériau d’origine est une fois de plus utilisé comme un simple décor par l’industrie hollywoodienne.
Sur X, les invectives se multiplient : certains dénoncent un « sacrilège » envers l’œuvre originale, accusant la production de vouloir déconstruire les piliers du récit sous prétexte de modernisation. L’agacement est palpable chez les lecteurs qui estiment que le cinéma d’aujourd’hui achète des sagas littéraires légendaires non pas pour les célébrer, mais pour entrer en conflit avec elles.
Février 2027 : une route qui s’annonce déjà très houleuse
Bien sûr, quelques rares voix s’élèvent pour saluer le découpage de certains plans ou l’énergie qui se dégage de cette première vidéo, mais elles se retrouvent littéralement noyées sous une vague de rejet global.
À moins d’un an de la sortie en salles prévue pour février 2027, le chantier de communication autour du Narnia de Greta Gerwig démarre avec un handicap colossal. Si Netflix espérait faire de cette saga son nouveau Seigneur des Anneaux, la plateforme va devoir cravacher dur pour rassurer un public qui crie déjà au massacre.

articles.title: Alerte maximale chez SAP : quatre failles critiques permettent de voler des identifiants et de prendre le contrôle de serveurs
articles.text:
SAP vient de corriger quatre vulnérabilités critiques dans ses logiciels professionnels. La plus grave permet de détourner les demandes d’authentification d’applications pour récupérer leurs identifiants et accéder à des informations sensibles.
Une application qui transmet ses propres identifiants à un serveur contrôlé par des pirates, leur permettant ensuite d’accéder à des données confidentielles : voilà ce que peut provoquer une faille que SAP vient de corriger, et dont la gravité a été évaluée à 10/10. Ce mardi 13 octobre, l’éditeur allemand a également publié des correctifs pour trois autres vulnérabilités critiques, dont deux pourraient conduire à une prise de contrôle complète des systèmes concernés.
Protégez votre entreprise gratuitement pendant 30 jours
Découvrez Bitdefender Ultimate Small Business Security et protégez votre activité contre les cybermenaces. Aucune coordonnée bancaire requise.
Des identifiants envoyés directement au mauvais serveur
Référencée CVE-2026-89111, la vulnérabilité la plus grave concerne SAP Cloud SDK for Python, une bibliothèque utilisée par les développeurs pour connecter leurs applications aux services cloud de SAP. Elle touche plus particulièrement les applications capables de gérer plusieurs clients à partir d’une même infrastructure.
Pour accéder aux services auxquels elles sont autorisées, ces applications doivent s’identifier auprès d’un serveur d’authentification, auquel elles transmettent leurs propres identifiants afin d’obtenir un jeton d’accès. Or, le SDK ne vérifie pas correctement un paramètre utilisé pour déterminer l’adresse de ce serveur. Si un attaquant parvient à le manipuler, il peut rediriger la demande d’authentification vers un serveur frauduleux et récupérer les identifiants transmis par l’application.
Une fois ces informations récupérées, le pirate peut se faire passer pour l’application et accéder aux ressources pour lesquelles elle dispose d’autorisations. Selon les droits accordés, il pourrait ainsi consulter des données financières, des informations relatives aux salariés ou d’autres données professionnelles sensibles, voire les modifier.
Le risque est d’autant plus sérieux que la vulnérabilité peut être exploitée à distance, sans compte préalable ni intervention d'un utilisateur, dès lors que l’attaquant parvient à contrôler le paramètre concerné. SAP a publié un correctif dans la version 0.45.2 de son SDK, qui vérifie désormais ce paramètre avant de l’utiliser pour construire l'adresse du serveur d’authentification.
Trois autres failles critiques qui menacent les systèmes SAP
Le bulletin de sécurité d’octobre comprend trois autres vulnérabilités critiques, dont deux évaluées à 9,9/10. La première, CVE-2026-89110, affecte SAP NetWeaver Visual Composer. Elle permet à un utilisateur disposant de droits limités de contourner les contrôles d’accès et, selon la configuration, de prendre entièrement le contrôle d’un système distant.
La deuxième, CVE-2026-89107, concerne SAP S/4HANA, le logiciel de gestion intégré de l’éditeur. Un utilisateur authentifié et disposant des autorisations nécessaires pourrait y injecter du code malveillant et compromettre le système. Enfin, CVE-2026-89108, notée 9,1/10, touche SAP Manufacturing Integration and Intelligence, utilisé dans les environnements industriels. Elle permet à un administrateur de l’application d’obtenir des privilèges étendus sur le serveur Java qui l’héberge.
SAP n’a signalé aucune exploitation active de ces vulnérabilités pour le moment, et les correctifs sont désormais disponibles. À installer sans attendre, évidemment.

articles.title: OpenAI engineer arrested for allegedly planting spy device in office
articles.text:
A Saudi OpenAI engineer has been arrested for allegedly planting a hidden recording device in an executive conference room at the company's San Francisco offices to secretly record sensitive conversations.
The U.S. Department of Justice announced Tuesday that Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, who had worked at OpenAI since July 2025, was arrested on October 9 and charged with illegally intercepting oral communications.
The DOJ says OpenAI security personnel discovered the recording device on September 30, plugged into a USB port behind a television in an executive conference room.
According to the DOJ, OpenAI determined that the device had been concealed in toilet paper, was installed around September 28, and contained encrypted data.
"On or about Sept. 30, OpenAI personnel discovered a surreptitious audio recording device (Recording Device 1) inserted into a USB port on the back of a television in an executive conference room inside one of their buildings in San Francisco," says the DOJ press release.
The DOJ says the conference room was regularly used for meetings involving confidential information about OpenAI's proprietary research, product plans, technical capabilities, business relationships, and government engagements.
Security camera footage allegedly showed Alfozan near the conference room on multiple occasions, despite not being authorized to attend meetings held there.
According to the complaint, Alfozan also used a productivity tool to search for information about OpenAI's offices, meeting rooms, executive locations, and meeting schedules.
The complaint also says a chatbot account associated with Alfozan's spouse was used to ask questions about building and concealing recording devices.
These included inquiries about creating a continuous audio recorder, modifying Wi-Fi connectivity, improving live listening capabilities, and encrypting an SD card.
"The same chatbot account also submitted prompts specifically related to Recording Device 1, including its custom header and unique MAC address, between Sept. 27 and Sept. 28," alleges the DOJ.
On October 5, surveillance footage allegedly captured Alfozan returning to the conference room and looking behind the television where the device had been installed.
The complaint says that on that same day, OpenAI security employees discovered a second, similar recording device inside a bag Alfozan had left unattended in another room.
In a statement posted on X, OpenAI said it used its own AI models to investigate the suspicious device and help identify the employee responsible.
"We used our models to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier," OpenAI said.
The company said it terminated the employee and referred the incident to the FBI.
"At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data," OpenAI added.
If convicted, Alfozan faces up to five years in prison and a $250,000 fine.
Build your security blueprint for AI-powered attacks
Join Mikko Hyppönen and security leaders from the NFL, CHANEL, and Atlassian for a two-hour digital summit on what AI-speed attacks change, what defenders should stop doing, and how to validate, decide, fix, and re-validate at machine speed.
Save your seat
Comments
maximilianx33 - 4 hours ago
The part about hiding the recording device behind a TV wrapped in toilet paper is almost unbelievable.
maximilianx33 - 4 hours ago
You'd expect something a bit more sophisticated from an engineer working at OpenAI. What surprises me more is that he allegedly used a chatbot to figure out how to build and hide the device. If the accusations are true, that's a pretty serious breach of trust. At least the security team managed to find it. Makes me wonder how many companies actually check their meeting rooms for things like this

articles.title: Composable Commerce: Inside Shipt’s Kit Platform
articles.text:
Key Takeaways
- A commerce platform tends to age better when it is built from a small number of first-class entities that reference each other rather than duplicate data between them. The pull to introduce a new entity for every new use case is constant, and it usually signals that the existing model needs to flex rather than grow.
- When a feature has to satisfy several independent constraints at once — which locations can serve a customer, which offerings are enabled where, which categories carry extra eligibility rules — treating the problem as an intersection of independently-evaluated sets scales better than threading conditional logic through a single workflow.
- Grouping related items under a shared identity, with its own completeness guarantees, keeps a bundled offering from silently degrading into something that no longer matches what was promised to the customer.
- Regulated or constrained product categories are easier to support safely when their constraints are modeled as a distinct type carrying its own rules, rather than as flags scattered through a shared code path. New categories then become additive, rather than compounding the complexity of existing ones.
- When a fully safe editing workflow is not realistic within a launch deadline, a layered set of lighter-weight guards can capture most of the risk reduction at a fraction of the engineering cost — often enough of a trade-off to ship safely under real time pressure.
The launch
Kits at Shipt are built for moments — a game day, a holiday dinner, a hosting weekend. The window between a merchandiser deciding to launch a themed bundle and a customer needing it can be days, not weeks. Every architectural decision described below is downstream of that constraint.
In June 2026, Shipt launched Shipt Kits, a one-click cart-building feature designed to help customers plan their hosting events. Timed around a global soccer event, the company’s national brand campaign introduced Shipt Kits through a celebrity partnership, highlighting summer use cases such as watch parties, backyard hosting, and cookouts. Customers landing on a "Match of the Week" kit could add a full evening’s worth of groceries — sides, drinks, snacks, dessert — to their cart in one click. Each item was store-aware: the kit you saw at your store reflected what was actually on shelves near you, not a generic catalog.
The campaign was covered in Progressive Grocer, Supermarket News, ¡HOLA!, and Better Homes and Gardens. From the outside, it looked like a polished new feature.
From the inside, the team had three weeks to build it. The API was done in ten days. The remaining eleven went to the admin experience, the customer surfaces, and the operational hardening that turns a working prototype into something a merchandising team can use without supervision.
This is an architecture tour of what was built in those three weeks: how the platform replaced a multi-day clerical workflow with a single admin UI, how it was modeled as three first-class entities that compose well, how the catalog was made store-aware end-to-end, and how it was made safe to edit live without a full draft-publish lifecycle.
Figure 1. Platform architecture overview (Image source: created by author)
The Kit API sits between the merchandiser-facing admin UI and the entity layer, with store-aware resolution and kit-type compliance rules determining what a customer ultimately sees, and edit-safety guards protecting in-flight changes.
Before Kits: a manual assembly workflow
Before Kits, building a themed shopping experience at Shipt looked like this. A merchandiser who wanted to assemble, say, a Tailgate Bundle would:
- Query the data warehouse for products that fit the theme.
- Pick the relevant UPCs by hand from the query results.
- Translate each UPC to the retailer-specific product ID — different IDs for the same physical product at Target, Meijer, Publix, and so on.
- Build a category containing those retailer-specific IDs.
- Build a product list from that category.
- Plug the product list into wherever the bundle needs to show up.
After all that work, the bundle still wasn’t guaranteed to display correctly at every store. The workflow was pegged on product ID, not on per-store inventory, so a kit that looked complete in the admin tool could be missing half its items at the customer’s actual store. The merchandiser had no way to know in advance.
Figure 2. The pre-Kits workflow: six manual steps and no per-store guarantee (Image source: created by author)
For a one-off promotion that lived for a week, this was tolerable. For a national campaign that needed dozens of fresh kits launching on cadence — across multiple retailers, multiple regions, multiple weeks — it was impossible. When the campaign got the green light with a fixed launch date, the team had three weeks to build a system where merchandisers could describe a bundle once and have the platform handle the per-store, per-retailer materialization.
Three first-class entities: items, shopping lists, kits
The first architectural decision was the most important: model the platform as three composable entities, not one monolithic "kit" type.
The approach draws on the design vocabulary of Domain-Driven Design (DDD). Items, shopping lists, and kits form the ubiquitous language shared across code, admin UI, and merchandiser conversations, and each is modeled as an aggregate that owns its own invariants. Kits act as aggregate roots for editorial and structural metadata; items live in their own bounded context and are shared by reference rather than duplicated inside every kit that uses them. Naming these boundaries early kept downstream feature work — new kit types, ad monetization, per-store resolution — additive rather than disruptive.
Items are the atomic catalog units — generic, typed, and tagged. An item knows what kind of thing it is (a product, an ingredient, a non-product element of an editorial bundle) and carries arbitrary metadata in a JSON tag bag. Items are not retailer-specific; the resolution to a particular store’s product ID happens at view time, not at modeling time.
Shopping lists are curated sequences of items. A shopping list can be merchandiser-curated and attached to a kit (the "here’s what to grab for your party" list inside a Game Day Bundle) or customer-built (a personal grocery list that the customer maintains across sessions). The same shopping-list abstraction supports both, which means the platform maintains one mental model and one set of APIs rather than two parallel ones.
Kits are the composable bundles — the things customers see, click, and add to cart. A kit carries editorial metadata (title, description, hero image, theme), structural metadata (slot layout, type, anchor items), and references to items and optionally to shopping lists.
Figure 3. Items as a single source of truth, referenced by both shopping lists and kits (Image source: created by author)
The platform’s most consequential property is that items are shared by reference across shopping lists and kits. The same Heinz ketchup item powers the Tailgate Bundle, the Backyard BBQ Bundle, the Family Picnic Bundle, the customer’s personal grocery list, and twenty other surfaces. Updating the item’s metadata propagates everywhere it’s used. Adding a new retailer mapping for that item lights it up across every kit and list that references it, automatically.
An item, roughly, looks like this:
{
  "id": "itm_01H2N7X...",
  "item_type": "product",
  "canonical_name": "Heinz Tomato Ketchup, 20 oz",
  "tags": {
    "category": "condiments",
    "dietary": ["vegetarian", "gluten-free"],
    "seasonal": ["summer", "grilling"],
    "brand_id": "brand_heinz"
  }
}
The tags field is intentionally a schemaless JSON bag — new dimensions (dietary, seasonal, promotional, anything a merchandiser or downstream service wants to filter on) can be added without a migration. Retailer-specific product IDs deliberately don’t live on the item; they’re resolved at view time, per store, which is the subject of the next section.
The migration that unified items into this single source of truth — kit products and shopping-list items both pointing at the same item rows — was mechanically boring but paid off immediately. Maintenance dropped. New kit types became inexpensive to introduce because a new type just needed to know which items it references, not how to manage its own private item table.
Anchor items and kit identity
A kit is more than a bag of items. Some items are essential to the kit’s identity. A summer grilling kit without meat is not a summer grilling kit. A pasta-night kit without pasta is not a pasta-night kit. An alcohol kit without alcohol is, legally and conceptually, something else.
The team modeled this with the concept of anchor items. An anchor item is one whose absence — at a specific store, on a specific day — disqualifies the entire kit from being shown at that store. The merchandiser marks anchor items during kit creation. The resolution layer checks anchor availability before deciding whether to surface the kit.
Anchor items also drive a per-kit minimum product threshold. A kit can declare that it needs at least, say, eight non-anchor items available at the customer’s store to be worth showing, in addition to all anchor items being present. The thresholds and anchors compose: a kit is shown only if (a) every anchor item resolves at the store and (b) the total available item count clears the threshold.
As a result, the platform never shows customers a half-empty kit. The kit either makes sense at this store today, or it doesn’t appear in the customer’s catalog at all. For a curated, editorial product, this is the contract the team wants.
Resolving a kit per store, per customer
Figure 4. The customer’s effective retailer set is the intersection of three independently configured layers (Image source: created by author)
Behind every customer view of a kit is a small set-theoretic computation that decides which retailers’ inventories to query. A customer at a given zip code may be served by a set of grocery retailers—the customer’s local Hy-Vee, Target, Meijer, and Giant Eagle. Each kit has its own allow-list of retailers it’s enabled for. Some kits—alcohol kits, most notably— also have additional eligibility constraints that depend on store-level licensing.
The resolution is the intersection of all three:
effective_retailers = customer_zip_retailers ∩ kit_allowed_retailers ∩ kit_eligibility(store)
For an alcohol kit, the eligibility check filters to stores with active alcohol licenses in the customer’s jurisdiction. For a kit with no special eligibility, the third set is unconstrained. For a general national-campaign kit, the allow-list covers Shipt’s operational areas. Each layer is independently configurable; the intersection is computed very efficiently at request time.
Once the effective retailer set is known, the platform fans out concurrent searches against each retailer’s catalog, collects the results, and assembles the customer-facing kit. Items are scored against the retailer’s actual inventory, anchor items are checked, the minimum threshold is verified, and the kit is either rendered or quietly dropped from the customer’s view.
The fan-out matters operationally. A customer at a metro zip might be eligible for four retailers; the kit needs to materialize quickly enough to feel instantaneous. Sequential per-retailer queries would have been too slow at the latency budgets the team was targeting. Concurrent fan-out, with per-retailer timeouts and graceful degradation, keeps the customer-perceived latency flat regardless of how many retailers the customer is eligible for.
Each retailer call runs independently and in parallel, with its own fixed timeout rather than a single timeout for the whole fan-out. If a retailer doesn’t respond within that window, its result is simply omitted from that customer’s kit view rather than blocking or failing the request. This keeps customer-perceived latency bounded by a fixed ceiling regardless of how many retailers the customer is eligible for, rather than growing with the number of retailers or stalling on a single slow one.
Figure 5. Concurrent fan-out for retailer calls (Image source: created by author)
Alcohol kits: when compliance becomes a kit type
Alcohol is the clearest example of why the team settled on kit types as an abstraction.
A generic kit’s lifecycle is editorial: a merchandiser creates it, sets its theme and items, publishes it. An alcohol kit’s lifecycle is editorial plus compliance: the same creation flow plus a separate store-eligibility check (does this store hold an active alcohol license?), plus product-level filtering (only products classified as alcoholic, no mixers-as-alcohol false positives), plus jurisdictional constraints (an alcohol kit is hidden at the customer level if the customer’s zip falls outside the retailer’s licensed delivery area).
We made all of that part of the alcohol kit type rather than special-casing the generic kit. The type carries its own eligibility predicates; the merchandiser doesn’t need to remember to apply alcohol rules because the type applies them automatically. New compliance constraints can be added by extending the type’s predicate without touching the generic kit code path.
The team expects more of these — pharmacy, age-restricted content, regulated brands. Each one is a good candidate for its own kit type rather than a new flag on the generic one.
Onsite ad monetization without breaking the bundle
The first revenue surface on top of the platform is onsite ad monetization. A consumer-packaged-goods brand pays to be featured prominently inside a kit — their product appears in a designated slot, branded, sometimes with promotional pricing.
The mechanics require a brand registry, sponsor associations on a per-kit basis, and an answer to a question the team hit almost immediately: what happens when the sponsored brand’s product isn’t available at the customer’s store?
Neither of the obvious answers works cleanly. Showing the kit without the sponsored item breaks the sponsorship agreement — the brand paid for placement, and silently dropping it leaves the customer with an awkward gap. Hiding the entire kit is worse in the other direction — one out-of-stock sponsored beverage shouldn’t sink a whole Game Day Bundle for the customer.
The behavior is contractual, so we made it configurable per kit. A brand_fallback field takes one of two values: hide item (drop the sponsored item, render the rest of the kit) or hide kit (don’t show the kit at this store). The merchandiser picks the value that matches the brand’s contract at kit-setup time, and the resolution layer enforces it at view time.
The brand registry itself is synced from Shipt’s upstream catalog system on a cadence. The sync is streaming and idempotent: it pages through the upstream catalog, upserts into the local brand table, and writes only where values would actually change. Re-running the sync after a partial failure is safe — already-correct rows are no-ops, and inconsistent ones converge on the next run.
Edit safety: layered guards over a live-edit model
Merchandisers edit kits in a live system. Customer carts and placed orders are snapshots taken at add-to-cart and order time, so live edits don’t rewrite history — but the kit itself is mutable, and every save is visible to the next customer. The textbook fix is a full draft-publish lifecycle (draft rows, atomic publish, diff UI, snapshots), at two to four extra weeks of build.
That time wasn’t available in the launch window, so the team shipped four guards instead:
- Layer 1 — persistent warning. An always-visible amber banner whenever the kit is published. Deliberately louder than admin-UI convention, because it’s the only always-on signal that this is production data.
- Layer 2 — first-edit confirmation. Touching any control on a live kit triggers a modal, remembered per tab and per kit (a fresh tab reprompts; a single click can’t authorize blanket edits across the catalog). Fourteen mutation call sites route through the same hook. "Live" is derived from the persisted kit status, not the local Status field — flipping the dropdown to Draft doesn’t silence the warning while the kit is still live for customers.
- Layer 3 — explicit Save and Discard per section. A mixed model (some fields autosaved, some POSTed on toggle) was replaced with a uniform one: Save, Discard, an "Unsaved changes" pill, and a native beforeunload prompt. Two primitives — a generic dirty-form hook and a page-level dirty registry — compose the cross-section guarantees. Recipe and shopping-list slot edits stay instant, because they’re actions, not form drafts.
- Layer 4 — cross-section locks. Those instant actions are short-circuited whenever section metadata is dirty, so they always operate on persisted truth. A one-line check against Layer 3’s dirty registry — cheap, but only watching real edit flows made it clear the platform needed it.
Together, the four layers cover roughly 70% of what a true draft-publish system would give the platform, at maybe 10% of the cost — enough to ship the campaign safely, with the full lifecycle now visible on the roadmap.
What we’d build next
The next three investments are clear, and they’re investments rather than rework — the platform is structured to accept them.
A true draft-publish lifecycle
Layered guards are a good 70%. Draft-publish is 100%. The remaining 30% shows up in workflows we don’t currently support well: a merchandiser editing a kit over multiple days, an editorial reviewer approving changes before they go live, an audit trail of who changed what when, automatic rollback when a published change causes a regression.
Since the campaign, we’ve taken the first concrete step — a Testing status that puts a kit live in production but only visible to a global tester allowlist, so internal reviewers see the real customer surface before real customers do. The lifecycle is now a genuine pipeline (Draft → Testing → Published → Archived) rather than a binary switch; per-field drafts, atomic publish, diff UI, and audit trail are the next slice.
Brand-sponsored kits with full ROAS attribution
The ad monetization layer ships placements today. The natural next step is closed-loop attribution: a brand pays to be featured, and we report back attributed revenue at the kit, item-within-kit, and impression levels. This is plumbing more than research — the events exist, the joins are tractable, the reporting surface is the work.
Per-customer filtering on kit items
Today’s resolution layer is per-store. The next axis is per-customer: a customer with a "no pork" or "gluten-free" preference should see a Tailgate Bundle that respects it. The mechanics are an additional intersection in the resolution layer, alongside the per-store ones already in place. Anchor items and minimum thresholds will need to be re-evaluated per customer rather than per store, which is a real but contained change.
What I’d say to anyone building something similar
Three things would have saved me time if I’d known to look for them earlier:
- Pick a small set of composable entities and resist the urge to add more. Items, shopping lists, and kits are three. The pressure to add a fourth (a "collection," a "feature," a "carousel") is constant and almost always wrong. Each new entity multiplies the platform's surface area; sharing the existing three by reference does almost everything the new entity would, with one less concept to maintain.
- Model real-world constraints as types, not flags. Alcohol is the obvious case. The next case will be something else — pharmacy items, regulated brands, age-restricted content. Each one should be a kit type that carries its own eligibility predicate, not another boolean column on the generic kit.
- Ship enough to learn what the rest should be. Layered edit-safety guards weren’t the architecturally clean answer — they were what fit in the launch window. But they’ve been good enough to let the merchandising team use the platform in production, which is now teaching us what a real draft-publish system would need to support. If we’d tried to build the full lifecycle in week one, we’d have been designing against guesses instead of real edit patterns.
Shipt Kits has been live for a few weeks now, handling real merchandiser workflows and real customer traffic across the guardrails, resolution, and compliance layers described above. The team is now planning its next investments — draft-publish, ROAS attribution, per-customer filtering — from a base of real usage rather than assumptions.
Summary
The specifics above are about grocery kits, but the underlying modeling questions are not unique to grocery, or even to commerce. Any platform that lets customers combine multiple things into one purchasable or consumable unit — travel packages, subscription boxes, meal kits, ticket bundles, curated content collections — runs into the same handful of decisions: how many first-class entities to introduce before the system becomes unmanageable; how to resolve eligibility when several independent constraints apply at once, such as location, inventory, regulation, and pricing; how to give a bundled offering an identity that customers can trust rather than one that silently falls apart; and how to support regulated or exception-heavy categories without littering the core model with special cases.
None of these questions has a universal right answer. The right level of abstraction depends on how often new constraints or categories will show up, and how much operational cost a team can absorb up front versus later. What held true in this case, and what tends to hold true elsewhere, is that the answer rarely comes from more process or more documentation. It comes from naming the entities and constraints explicitly in the model, early enough that the system can grow by composition instead of by exception.
Thanks to Marc Kapke (Senior Principal Engineer, Shipt) for review and technical feedback, and to the Shipt Marketplace team for the collaboration that made this platform possible.

articles.title: Il achète un box aux enchères pour 180 € et découvre dedans près de 100 PC portables, 20 ordinateurs, des centaines de barrettes de RAM et un PC Pentium 4 des années 2000
articles.text:
Il achète un box aux enchères pour 180 € et découvre dedans près de 100 PC portables, 20 ordinateurs, des centaines de barrettes de RAM et un PC Pentium 4 des années 2000
Quand l’achat d’un box de stockage aux enchères se transforme en bonne affaire. C’est ce qui est arrivé à un internaute qui pensait mettre la main sur une trentaine de PC portables, mais à la place, près de 100 laptops, 20 PC de bureau, des centaines de barrettes de RAM, des disques durs, des pièces détachées et des milliers de CD. Et ce n’est pas la seule trouvaille, puisque le petit chanceux a aussi mis la main sur un PC Pentium 4 des années 2000.
C’est sur Reddit que Witty-Composer-6445 a raconté son histoire. Alors qu’il s’attendait à trouver quelques PC portables et autres objets sans grand intérêt dans le box remporté aux enchères, le contenu a largement dépassé ses attentes, notamment un PC en particulier.
Un PC Pentium 4 trouvé dans le box attire l’attention
    
        Voir la discussion sur Reddit
    
Si tout ce matériel en masse est déjà un gros lot, c’est surtout un PC en particulier qui a retenu l’attention. Il s’agit d’un boîtier X-Superalien conçu par Aspire, qui s’est depuis renommé Apevia en 2006. Un PC à l’époque où les joueurs appréciaient beaucoup les couleurs vives, les fenêtres transparentes et les éclairages très colorés.
Dans le X-Superalien, on trouve cinq emplacements pour les lecteurs optiques, des prises USB 2.0, des prises audio, un port FireWire et un petit écran LCD. Les pièces internes sont totalement visibles via le panneau latéral. Bref, de quoi offrir une bonne excuse aux joueurs de l’époque pour montrer l’intérieur de leur PC gaming.
À l’intérieur, on trouve un processeur Intel Pentium 4 et une alimentation transparente Aspire de 500 W. Pour la petite histoire, c’est en novembre 2000 qu’Intel a lancé la gamme Pentium 4 avec une architecture pensée pour des fréquences très élevées. Une époque où la course au mégahertz était très présente dans le marketing des boîtes informatiques.
Pour ceux qui ont connu cette période, ces images postées sur Reddit leur rappelleront sans doute des souvenirs. Mais au-delà de ce PC, le reste du box de stockage est tout aussi intéressant avec près de 100 PC portables, 20 PC de bureau et des centaines de barrettes de RAM.
Bref, l’auteur de cette publication n’a plus qu’à dégager quelques heures pour trier, tester et possiblement récupérer ce matériel. On se doute que beaucoup n’auront pas beaucoup de valeur, mais le Pentium 4 et son boîtier X-Superalien sont déjà une belle trouvaille.
Un box qui lui a coûté environ 200 $
Le travail de recherche a déjà d’ailleurs commencé puisque l’internaute explique qu’il a au moins listé un ancien MacBook, deux PowerBook G4 et plusieurs PC portables sous Windows. Il y a aussi un Sony VAIO, un Lenovo ThinkPad T400 et plusieurs modèles HP.
Pour les quelque 200 barrettes de RAM, c’est principalement de la DDR, de la DDR2 et de la DDR3. Selon le propriétaire, il y en a à peu près pour trois kilos. Bref, il reste à terminer le tri, notamment avec des dizaines de disques durs et des milliers de CD qui pourraient aussi avoir des choses intéressantes enregistrées à l’intérieur, qui sait.
L’internaute précise que la personne qui utilisait le box réparait des ordinateurs et récupérait des données, d’où ce matériel en masse. C’est vers 2014 que son activité se serait terminée et le stockage aurait été utilisé jusqu’à la pandémie de coronavirus. Bref, de quoi expliquer la présence d’appareils de générations très différentes et éloignées.
L’acheteur explique aussi que le box a été remporté pour 200 $, soit environ 180 €, puis ont été dépensés environ 300 $ de plus pour remettre une remorque en état et 200 $ d’essence pour les trajets. Si l’on ne sait pas la valeur exacte du box dans sa totalité, le volume de matériel récupéré dépasse largement ce que l’internaute pensait acheter au départ.

articles.title: Apple finally enters the smart home hub market with $299 HomeView
articles.text:
The big picture: Apple is finally entering the smart home hub market, more than 11 years after Amazon launched the Echo and almost exactly a decade after Google introduced its Nest devices. With a similar price point and feature set, Apple's HomeView aims to integrate Siri AI with the company's latest smartphones, tablets, and smartwatches, as well as upcoming smart home cameras, doorbells, locks, and thermostats.
Pre-orders are now open for the Apple HomeView, Cupertino's answer to the Amazon Echo Show 11 and Google Nest Hub Max. Priced at $299, the smart home hub will launch on November 13 in either a tabletop or wall-mounted configuration.
The HomeView aims to combine features of the iPad and HomePod at a lower price, powered by the same A18 processor found in the iPhone 16. Its 7-inch, 1,088 × 1,088-pixel LED touchscreen displays messages, FaceTime calls, photos, news, music, and apps connected to the smart home ecosystem. AI-powered voice controls enable hands-free operation. Other built-in apps include Alarms, Find My, Podcasts, Reminders, Safari, World Clock, and an intercom feature.
With a unique take on Face ID, the HomeView can recognize up to six users by their appearance and automatically switch to their messages, calendars, and personalized Siri AI settings, keeping individual content private from other users. Certain shared content remains accessible to everyone.
Apple's new generative AI-powered Siri assistant can retrieve information from each user's calendars, messages, and other content while also answering questions using web searches. When users sync a separate Siri AI-compatible device, such as an iPhone or iPad, conversations with the digital assistant carry over between devices. Music playback does, too, and audio can be routed through spatial audio speakers built into the circular base and along the bottom of the screen.
The HomeView also connects to a range of smart home cameras, smart deadbolt locks, and thermostats from LG and Schneider under the Apple Home Collection brand. The devices will be available in December. Users can adjust the temperature, remotely control locks, and view feeds from multiple cameras through the HomeView or other Apple devices connected to the company's Home app ecosystem.
LG's upcoming Smart Deadbolt Lock can be unlocked using a PIN, remotely by the owner, with a tap from an iPhone or Apple Watch, or by detecting nearby Apple devices containing digital keys. Meanwhile, cameras from LG and Schneider can store up to 10 days of 2.5K video footage in iCloud with an iCloud+ subscription, even when the Wi-Fi connection is down. Apple Intelligence can also recognize and describe familiar people, pets, vehicles, and packages.

articles.title: Gemini 4 Argon reaches Gemini app Pro and Ultra subscribers alongside a new tasks mode - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Gemini 4 Argon reaches Gemini app Pro and Ultra subscribers alongside a new tasks mode
Google LLC today brought its Gemini 4 Argon frontier artificial intelligence model to Gemini app users on its Pro and Ultra subscription plans, two weeks after the model went first to vetted cybersecurity defenders.
Subscribers on those plans also get a new tasks mode that keeps Gemini working on a job after they have stepped away from the computer.
Argon’s arrival changes how Gemini answers in the app. Responses come “more directly with less hedging,” according to Google, and the model repeats itself only when it needs to. Anyone who hands it a longer job should also see progress updates more often than before.
Switching to tasks takes one toggle in the main chat window. Once it’s on, Gemini “can work for you even when you’re not at your computer,” Google said. The count of connected apps has passed 40, so a task can run as far as a grocery order through Instacart or a table booked on OpenTable. Adobe Inc. and Shopify Inc. are on the list for people designing or running a business.
Argon also brings what Google calls “major improvements in coding.” Google’s chart at the Sept. 30 unveiling had the model at 77.9% on DeepSWE v1.1, a test of long-horizon software engineering, against 74.2% for Anthropic PBC’s Claude Opus 5.5. OpenAI Group PBC’s GPT-6 Astra sat a 10th of a point further back.
The agentic coding interface from Google Antigravity now runs directly inside the Gemini app for macOS, which means a chat can turn into a coding session without a jump to a separate tool. Google did not mention a Windows version.
The app was one part of a wider release today. Koray Kavukcuoglu, chief AI architect at Google, wrote in a separate post that developers anywhere can now build on Argon through the paid tier of the Gemini application programming interface. Introductory rates of $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens hold until Nov. 30, when they double to $4 and $20.
Kavukcuoglu’s post also set out an offer for researchers. Up to 10,000 scientists can apply for six months of free access to the highest usage tier in Antigravity. Cybersecurity teams that want Argon without its cyber guardrails still apply through the Fairwind Program.
On the consumer side, Argon is also available in AI Mode in Search for Pro and Ultra subscribers. A Google AI Pro subscription costs $19.99 a month in the U.S. Ultra plans start at $99.99 and come with higher Argon limits. Google’s plans page says the tasks mode is limited to select countries for now and that Argon is still rolling out to Pro subscribers.

articles.title: “Lo que diga la sede central es irrelevante. Somos PlayStation”, confiesa exdirectivo cuando diseñaba la PS3, PS4 y PS Vita
articles.text:
Kazuo Hirai, exjefe de PlayStation admitió que durante su conducción ignoraba las directrices de la sede central para preservar la autonomía del negocio de consolas, una postura que más tarde trasladó a la reestructuración de toda la compañía.
“Cuando era presidente de Sony Computer Entertainment y gestionaba el negocio de consolas de sobremesa de PlayStation, cada vez que Howard Stringer y los demás ejecutivos me decían esto o aquello, yo me iba por mi propio camino diciendo: ‘Lo que diga la sede central es irrelevante. Somos PlayStation’”, relató Hirai en una entrevista con Nikkei XTrend.
La división de videojuegos funcionaba con un margen de independencia dentro de Sony que Hirai utilizaba para proteger las decisiones de PlayStation frente a la estructura corporativa. Esa lógica marcó su forma de conducir el área durante años de cambios para las consolas PS3, PS4 y PlayStation Vita.
Cómo fue la gestión de Kazuo Hirai en PlayStation
La desconfianza interna fue uno de los primeros obstáculos de su gestión. Hirai recordó que muchos trabajadores se preguntaban: “¿Cuándo nos va a quitar el suelo de bajo los pies?” o “¿Quizá es de los que se cuelgan el mérito y culpan a sus subordinados de los fallos?”.
El entonces director ejecutivo consideraba que la recuperación de la compañía requería reconstruir el vínculo con su personal. “Sin respeto, nadie va a pensar: ‘¡Vamos a trabajar duro juntos!’”, sostuvo.
Durante sus seis años al frente de Sony, viajó a más de 20 países y recorrió cerca de 50 ciudades. No se limitó a reuniones ocasionales: visitó oficinas y fábricas de distintos lugares y regresó varias veces a algunas de ellas, una presencia que sorprendía a los operarios de las líneas de producción.
Asimismo, la reorganización se articuló alrededor de KANDO, un concepto japonés referido a la creación de experiencias emocionalmente conmovedoras. Esa filosofía buscó unificar la cultura interna de Sony y acompañó la transición hacia la etapa de PlayStation 4.
En qué estado estaba PlayStation antes de la llegada de Kazu Hirai
Al asumir el mando de PlayStation en 2006, Hirai heredó el desastroso y costoso lanzamiento de PS3. En lugar de rendirse, orquestó una de las mayores remontadas de la industria: rediseñó la arquitectura de costes del hardware, impulsó el modelo PS Plus y apostó por un catálogo exclusivo inolvidable que logró superar a Xbox 360 en ventas globales.
Con esa misma visión de hardware premium, respaldó el lanzamiento de PS Vita, una máquina adelantada a su tiempo que, aunque sufrió la presión del mercado móvil, se convirtió en un objeto de culto técnico por su pantalla OLED y su integración portátil.
Esa intensa etapa sirvió como banco de pruebas para moldear la filosofía que definiría la época dorada de Sony. Hirai aprendió que el hardware debía ser amigable para los desarrolladores y centrado 100% en el jugador, una premisa que impregnó el desarrollo de PS4.
Al conectar la potencia de la nueva sobremesa, la experiencia en red perfeccionada en PS3 y el ecosistema interconectado con PS Vita mediante el juego remoto, Hirai dejó servido el camino para que PS4 arrasara en el mercado y devolviera a Sony al trono absoluto del videojuego.
Qué trayectoria tenía Kazuo Hirai antes de llegar a Playstation
Hirai había ingresado a CBS/Sony en 1984, atraído por la música y favorecido por su dominio bilingüe del inglés. Su infancia transcurrió entre Tokio, Nueva York y Toronto, una experiencia que contribuyó a su orientación hacia el entretenimiento y a su rechazo de la burocracia corporativa.
Al asumir la conducción general de Sony, aplicó esa misma autonomía mediante el plan One Sony. La estrategia implicó recortar divisiones históricas que generaban pérdidas, entre ellas la de computadoras VAIO, y redefinir el negocio de televisores.
Los recursos se concentraron en tres áreas: sensores de imagen, música y el ecosistema PlayStation. Esa reorientación devolvió la rentabilidad y el prestigio a la marca, mientras Hirai convertía una gestión marcada por la independencia de la división de videojuegos en un modelo para reorganizar el resto del grupo.

articles.title: FLÆ Robotics raises over €1 million in Seed funding to develop its AI hospitality agent | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Czech startup FLÆ Robotics has raised over €1 million in Seed funding to accelerate product development, deepen integrations with hotel systems, grow its team, and expand internationally. The funding will support BE-A, the company’s AI hospitality agent.
Investment came from Purple Ventures and Garage Angels.
“Hotel teams handle a large volume of repetitive enquiries and tasks every day across email, phone and other channels. We are developing BE-A to go beyond answering questions and carry out the next step within hotel systems. This gives staff more time for guests and situations that need their experience and judgement.” says Filip Linek, founder and CEO of FLÆ Robotics.
This announcement from FLÆ Robotics, founded by Linek in 2023, comes amid a series of European investments in AI-powered hospitality software this year.
Among the closest examples is Oslo-based Altek AI, which secured €423k to develop autonomous guest communication and deeper integrations with hotel systems. Germany’s happyhotel raised €6.5 million to advance AI agents for hotel revenue management, while Italy’s profitize secured €1.4 million for AI-powered hospitality financial planning.
In the adjacent operational automation segment, Berlin-based Bounti raised €4 million. Together, these four selected rounds represent approximately €12.3 million in disclosed funding, excluding FLÆ Robotics.
“This investment will help us expand BE-A’s capabilities, deepen our integrations and support more hotels in international markets.” adds Jan Davídek, General Partner at Purple Ventures,
“We invested in FLÆ Robotics because BE-A is already solving a very real problem for hotels and proving its value in day-to-day operations. The team combines strong hospitality experience with a clear product vision and international ambition. We believe there is significant potential to scale BE-A across European and global hotel markets.”
FLÆ Robotics says BE-A is already used by more than 60 hotels across the United Kingdom, Germany and the Czech Republic.
The company says the platform handled approximately 265,000 messages and voice interactions across nearly 160,000 conversations in July and August 2026, averaging more than 4,000 interactions per day. During the same period, it completed more than 3,400 hotel bookings without human intervention.

articles.title: Motorola Edge 60 (512 GB) tem 12 GB de RAM e cai 46% com cupom • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Motorola Edge 60 (512 GB) tem 12 GB de RAM e cai 46% com cupom
Edge 60 (512 GB) traz 12 GB de RAM e câmeras de 50 MP; celular da Motorola sai por quase metade do preço original, no Pix com cupom no Mercado Livre
O Edge 60 de 512 GB está saindo por R$ 1.895 no Pix com cupom MELHORDEHJ no Mercado Livre. O celular da Motorola, com 12 GB de RAM e câmeras de 50 MP, recebe desconto de 46% sobre o preço original de R$ 3.499.
Embora não seja o menor preço histórico, esta é uma ótima oferta de um celular básico, com bastante RAM física para rodar apps e games.
O Edge 60 é um intermediário equipado com 12 GB de RAM física e o chip MediaTek Dimensity 7300, que sustentam apps em multitarefa e alguns recursos do Moto AI. Os 512 GB de armazenamento oferecem espaço interno de sobra para quem adora filmar e fotografar.
Falando nisso, seu kit de câmeras traz uma wide com OIS e uma ultrawide de 122º, que captam belas situações com grandes ângulos, e uma frontal que tira ótimas selfies, todas de 50 MP. A telefoto de 10 MP traz zoom óptico de 3x para aproximações com muitos detalhes. Todas filmam em 4K.
A tela POLED de 6,7″, com taxa de 120 Hz e brilho de 4.500 nits, é capaz de reproduzir imagens com cores fiéis e alta fluidez nas transições em apps e games, além de garantir a visibilidade em qualquer lugar. O vidro Gorilla Glass 7i protege o display contra pancadas e arranhões.
O corpo do Edge 60 recebe as certificações IP68/IP69 e militar MIL-STD-810H, que juntas conferem proteção em cenários extremos, como altas temperaturas, e em situações como poeira intensa e mergulhos acidentais.
Sua bateria de 5.200 mAh suporta carregamento ultrarrápido de 68 W via USB-C e permite ao gadget receber uma carga para um dia inteiro de uso em apenas 8 minutos, segundo a fabricante. Assim, o usuário não precisa se preocupar em ficar sem energia durante o corre-corre diário.
O Edge 60 de 512 GB (R$ 1.895 no Pix com cupom MELHORDEHJ) será atualizado apenas até o Android 18 e conversa com redes 5G, Wi-Fi 6, Bluetooth 5.4 e NFC.

articles.title: Helix Carbon says it can make iron cheaper by recycling blast furnace pollution | TechCrunch
articles.text:
The iron and steel industries are among the biggest polluters in the world. Plenty of startups have tried to cut the industry’s emissions, mostly by developing new ways to make the metals. Helix Carbon thinks those startups have been going about it all wrong.
“Any attempt to decarbonize the steel industry without dealing with the blast furnace is not going to work,” David Brown, Helix Carbon’s co-founder and CEO, told TechCrunch. A blast furnace is the giant furnace that turns iron ore into the iron used to make steel. Rather than replace blast furnaces, Helix wants to clean them up. Its approach promises to slash the steel industry’s carbon emissions while boosting profit margins for iron producers, a rare win-win for a dirty industrial process.
Blast furnaces have made iron for centuries, using coke, a processed form of coal, to help turn raw iron ore (iron bound up with oxygen) into metallic iron. The burning coke supplies heat for the reaction but doesn’t take part in it directly. Instead, carbon monoxide produced from the combustion does the work of reducing the iron, meaning stripping away its oxygen atoms.
The process releases tremendous amounts of carbon dioxide, or CO2, which is normally dumped straight into the atmosphere. But Helix Carbon has devised a way to turn that waste carbon dioxide into carbon monoxide and recycle it back into the blast furnace.
Helix Carbon’s process relies on an electrolyzer, a device that uses electricity and a catalyst to break off an oxygen atom from the carbon dioxide. Electrolyzers aren’t new, but Brown said the startup’s design can handle the entire exhaust stream from the blast furnace. Most electrolyzers are too delicate for raw exhaust like that. They work only on purified, concentrated carbon dioxide, so the exhaust typically has to be processed before they can use it.
By injecting carbon monoxide into a blast furnace, iron producers can use less coke. How much, exactly, is still debated, Brown said. Some scientific papers suggest as much as 90% of the coke can be eliminated, while other studies suggest it’s more like 30% to 40%.
Helix Carbon is proposing that iron producers start by replacing 33% of their coke. The company says using its technology to do so would save them $14 per ton of iron. “That may not seem like a lot, but margins in the iron industry are famously thin,” Brown said.
The iron and steel industries are a combined $2 trillion market, according to Grand View Research, which makes the sector an appealing target for a young startup to chase. But it also moves slowly, in part because its equipment lasts so long. “There are blast furnaces that have lived for over 100 years,” Brown said.
To bring in revenue earlier, Helix Carbon plans to court the specialty chemicals industry first. “We don’t need to capture the CO2 first,” Brown said. “We just utilize it, and that opens up the door of making chemicals on-site right out of waste streams.”
Helix Carbon presented live onstage on Tuesday in the Startup Battlefield pitch competition at TechCrunch Disrupt in San Francisco, taking place this week from October 13-15. Join us this week to watch as the rest of Startup Battlefield unfolds.

articles.title: Disney offers $20M for Character.AI’s scandal-plagued chatbot tech
articles.text:
In a bankruptcy proceeding that kicked off yesterday, Disney has offered to buy some of the technology that powers the controversy-plagued chatbot Character.AI.
Disney is willing to pay $20 million for “a non-exclusive perpetual license” of certain Character Technologies intellectual property, the chatbot maker said in a press release that did not go into much further detail on which assets Disney wanted.
The move may be surprising. In September 2025, Disney joined others in publicly criticizing Character.AI for stealing content and harming kids. Specifically, Disney sent a strongly worded cease-and-desist letter that accused Character Technologies of weaponizing Disney characters “in a way that could damage its brand long term,” Axios reported.
“Character.AI’s infringing chatbots are known, in some cases, to be sexually exploitive and otherwise harmful and dangerous to children, offending Disney’s consumers and extraordinarily damaging Disney’s reputation and goodwill,” Disney wrote at the time.
That scandal ended with Character Technologies wiping all Disney-owned characters from its platform, but since then, Disney has hired former Character.AI chief Karandeep Anand as its first chief technology officer, Deadline reported.
Disney did not respond to Ars’ request for comment on whether the company plans to use Character.AI technology in products for kids.
It’s possible that Disney will be outbid and not acquire any Character.AI intellectual property. But ever since Disney’s potentially lucrative partnership with OpenAI fell through after Sora’s abrupt shutdown, the entertainment giant has been looking for more ways to “get in the AI game and profit from its boom,” Deadline reported. (Meanwhile, OpenAI apparently plans to revive Sora without Disney, insiders told The Information.) So, Disney may be moving early in the hopes of acquiring chatbot technology proven to resonate with its fanbase. It may possibly even take over the platform in a transition that preliminarily would be managed by Character.AI employees, the press release said.

articles.title: Hacker claims ‘123456’ password let them breach the Danish national registry, accessing 8.8 million records — IT and data services company with weak passwords linked source of the hack
articles.text:
Hacker claims ‘123456’ password let them breach the Danish national registry, accessing 8.8 million records — IT and data services company with weak passwords linked source of the hack
8.8 million Danes have reportedly been affected by this hack.
A person claiming to be responsible for the recent hack of Denmark’s national registry claimed that they were able to gain access because of an IT company’s weak password. According to The Register, Pays ApS, an IT and data services company that lets customers reference the Danish Central Register of Persons (CPR) was the source of the hack, with the hacker saying that one of the accounts they breached was only protected by a ‘123456’ password.
Copenhagen has confirmed the hack, with a government official saying that the breach was discovered 12 days after it happened when an invoice revealed an unusual amount of activity from the company. The Danish government said that 8.8 million records have been illicitly retrieved, although the hacker claimed that they do not intend to sell or leak the information. While the government did not mention which company the hacker exploited, Pays ApS managing director Sophie Laursen confirmed that the hacker used the company’s access to the database to exfiltrate the data.
This incident shows that a system’s security is only as strong as the weakest link, with the Danish database getting compromised through a third-party user’s poorly chosen password. Given that CPR essentially contains information on virtually every Danish citizen, one would expect that it would require users to at least have a more complicated password, if not two-factor authentication. This isn’t the first time that an incident reveals shortcomings in government database protection, though — Indonesia realized that it had no backups when a ransomware attack in 2024 affected over 230 public agencies, while South Korea lost 858 terabytes of data after a catastrophic fire at a government data center last year.
We expect the Danish government to overhaul its password policies in the near future, especially now that AI is making it easier and more efficient for hackers to hit their targets. Recent incidents like the attacks on South Korean banks and against the Taiwanese government were reportedly conducted with the help of AI agents. Hackers also breached OpenAI using Claude tools, showing just how potent AI has become as a hacking tool in the wrong hands. But with a password like “123456,” potential hackers wouldn’t need to use any AI tools to break into weakly protected systems.

- habermas It's not really a hack of the Danish government since the service exposed by the government was always intended to sell access to citizens' information at large scale including for the purpose of letting any paying party update their customer databases with correct address information and more. For example, a bank with 2 million customers might run regular look-ups to ensure they still have updated information about the addresses of their customers without the customers having to do anything.
This was always the concept of the service. It was never designed to keep anything secret but rather to ensure that the information was only revealed in return for a payment.
The hack was therefore not against the Danish government but against the company, which was perfectly entitled to pull the 8 million records from the government as long as they paid for it.
The "password" was in fact "guarding" a web-based front-end to making such look-ups in the central person registry. The web-based front-end was developed by the small company called Pays ApS.
In principle, the "hacking" is a matter between the hacker and the small company Pays ApS and not a matter between the "hacker" and the government since they merely served up CPR records in return for expected payment.
From a legal point of view, the company is liable to pay the fees for looking up the 8 million records and should seek remedy with the hacker.
Also, currently doing the rounds is some mumbo-jumbo story that "AI enabled the hacker to hack the service".
In fact, the guy is a script kiddie, who was not even able to program a simple for-loop generating the individual unique person ID-numbers required to look up address information. He therefore had to ask ChatGPT how to code a simple look-up script in Python and even managed to mess it up so they got no records out for people born in 1977.
One might argue that the Danish government's model of selling unlimited access to any willing and paying company without requiring any proactive cybersecurity audits is totally irresponsible in a world where information about where people live has already been abused by informants serving assassin hit squads and is probably also being exfiltrated by Russian intelligence services to target CEO's of weapons manufacturing companies as well as high-ranking military personnel.
