articles.title: Hollywood sería el próximo destino de Sora, la herramienta de video que OpenAI dejó de lado
articles.text:
OpenAI estudia dar un nuevo uso a Sora, su modelo de generación de videos con inteligencia artificial (IA), después de cerrar la aplicación dirigida al público en marzo. La compañía conversa con una startup que desarrolla herramientas de video para cineastas y que busca acceder a Sora para ofrecer programas y servicios destinados a la industria del cine, según informó The Information, citando a una persona familiarizada con las negociaciones.
La propuesta supondría un cambio de enfoque: Sora dejaría de presentarse como una aplicación general para crear y compartir videos y podría convertirse en tecnología para profesionales de la industria audiovisual. El acuerdo no se ha concretado. Según el reporte, OpenAI recibiría una participación en la startup si las conversaciones llegan a buen puerto.
La empresa emergente fue fundada por Jeffrey Katzenberg, exdirector de Disney y cofundador de DreamWorks; Bill Peebles, quien lideró la investigación de Sora en OpenAI; y Sujay Jaswa, exdirector financiero de Dropbox. La compañía mantiene un perfil discreto y su objetivo es desarrollar modelos de video y herramientas orientados a cineastas.
Del cierre de la aplicación a un posible uso profesional
OpenAI retiró Sora en marzo, cuando decidió concentrar sus recursos de computación y desarrollo en otras prioridades. Generar video requiere una gran capacidad de procesamiento, un recurso que la compañía también necesita para sus modelos y servicios de inteligencia artificial.
El cierre de la aplicación para consumidores fue un revés para quienes esperaban usarla en proyectos audiovisuales. También coincidió con el fin de la colaboración entre OpenAI y Disney, que había anunciado una inversión de 1.000 millones de dólares y un acuerdo para permitir el uso de personajes de sus franquicias en Sora. La alianza no llegó a materializarse como estaba prevista.
El nuevo planteamiento podría permitir que parte de la tecnología se aproveche en un entorno más especializado. En lugar de ofrecer una herramienta abierta para crear clips, la startup buscaría adaptar modelos y servicios a las necesidades de las producciones: desde tareas de creación visual hasta otras etapas del proceso cinematográfico. Sin embargo, el reporte no detalla qué funciones tendría el producto ni cuándo podría estar disponible.
La industria explora el uso de IA en el cine
La posible alianza aparece mientras estudios y empresas tecnológicas buscan formas de integrar herramientas generativas en la producción audiovisual. Para los grandes estudios, estas tecnologías pueden acelerar ciertas tareas y reducir costos; también podrían facilitar el uso comercial de catálogos de personajes y obras mediante licencias.
Al mismo tiempo, el avance de la IA genera preocupación entre guionistas, actores, artistas y otros trabajadores del sector. El uso de modelos para crear imágenes, voces o escenas plantea dudas sobre la sustitución de empleos, la remuneración de los creadores y el consentimiento para utilizar obras protegidas en el entrenamiento de sistemas.
Esas tensiones estuvieron presentes en las huelgas de Hollywood de 2023 y siguen formando parte del debate sobre las condiciones laborales y los derechos de autor. Una herramienta diseñada para profesionales no elimina esas preguntas: su impacto dependerá de los acuerdos sobre licencias, el control creativo y la manera en que los estudios la incorporen a sus producciones.
Un acuerdo aún sin confirmar
La negociación entre OpenAI y la startup no implica que Sora ya haya regresado ni que vaya a producir películas por sí sola. Por ahora, se trata de conversaciones reportadas por The Information, sin anuncio oficial de las compañías sobre los términos o el calendario.
Si se concreta, la operación podría abrir una vía para que OpenAI mantenga su tecnología de video en el mercado sin volver a la aplicación que cerró. También acercaría a la compañía a los estudios y cineastas en un momento en que Hollywood evalúa cómo aprovechar la IA sin dejar de lado los derechos de quienes crean sus contenidos.

articles.title: Helsinki’s Ambio raises €5.1 million to scale its AI-powered recycled plastics procurement platform | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Ambio, a Helsinki-based startup building an AI-native end-to-end procurement solution for recycled plastics, has raised a €5.1 million Seed round to make recycled plastics procurement faster and more reliable.
The round was led by b2venture, with participation from Montis and existing investor Lifeline Ventures.
“We are backing Ambio not only because of the talented team led by Tommi and Elmo but also because of the compounding competitive moat the business is built on: a proprietary dataset on recyclate quality, a principal model that builds trust with buyers and sellers, and an agentic engine that turns every transaction and quality data point into improved matchmaking. We are convinced that Ambio will become the central marketplace for recycled plastics in Europe and beyond,” said Mathias Ockenfels, Partner, b2venture.
Founded in 2023 by Tommi Bergström and Elmo Pakkanen, Ambio is building an AI-native, end-to-end procurement solution for recycled plastics that covers the full purchasing cycle, from material discovery to long-term deliveries.
Highlighting the advantages of using recycled plastics for European manufacturers, such as sustainability, price advantages, and meeting tightening regulatory requirements, Ambio states that customers increasingly ask for them. It further notes that every tonne recycled and used in Europe stays in the European supply chain, increasing supply chain resilience and reducing dependence on imported fossil fuels needed in virgin plastics production.
However, recycled plastics procurement remains fragmented, manual and difficult to scale, says the Finnish startup. According to the company, that is because recycled polymers vary significantly in quality, depending on source, batch and processing history.
The most pressing challenge is that data is scattered or missing, and quality is often confirmed only at the production line. “Industrial buyers want recycled materials to behave like any other input: consistent quality, reliable delivery, no surprises – but today that is still the exception,” the company mentioned.
It argues that to reach broad adoption and drive market growth, a verification infrastructure is needed to turn recycled plastics from a gamble into a reliably obtainable material at scale.
“People in the industry like to talk about regulation and the EU. We are a startup, we cannot yet impact what happens in Brussels. What we can impact is the purchasing experience for the buyer. When you’re buying virgin plastics, you know exactly what you’re getting. When you’re buying recycled, you’ll know if it works when it’s running in your production line. Our goal is to predict if the material works or not before sampling even happens,” said Bergström, co-founder and CEO of Ambio. He believes widespread adoption of recycled plastics is held back more by trust than by regulation alone.
Ambio’s solution makes recycled plastics predictable: verified materials, structured quality data and one accountable partner from first sample to long-term deliveries. Materials are qualified through samples, documentation, and defined quality.
It states that materials are qualified through samples, documentation, and defined quality protocols. Ambio’s matching engine learns from this growing dataset, with each transaction adding structured data on materials, suppliers, pricing and outcomes. The startup uses this growing dataset to improve matching, quoting and execution over time.
The company plans to use this capital to scale internationally and across polymer types. The funding will support its goal to make recycled plastics procurement as predictable as buying virgin polymers, driving adoption across Europe and beyond. Ambio aims to become the central, pan-European trust layer of the growing recyclates market and a reliable supplier of recycled plastics for industrial buyers.

articles.title: Judge orders OpenAI to turn over hiring records in Apple trade secrets case | TechCrunch
articles.text:
A judge has ruled that Apple will gain expedited access to OpenAI’s hiring materials in the trade secrets-focused lawsuit the iPhone maker filed against OpenAI in July.
Specifically, the court will allow Apple to view documents associated with OpenAI’s interviews with former Apple employees who applied for roles within its consumer hardware and robotics groups ahead of the rumored launch of OpenAI’s first hardware device.
These documents could include interview checklists, guides, instructions, manuals, and scripts, as well as technical presentations and records showing that interview discussions had included references to Apple technology or components.
The court gave OpenAI five days to turn over materials it has already collected and 14 days for any other materials related to this request, agreeing with Apple that these documents should be expedited.
The case comes as OpenAI develops a consumer hardware device that could one day potentially rival the iPhone — or smartphones more generally — if the AI device becomes a central part of consumers’ lives and how they engage with software and services.
In its lawsuit, Apple accused OpenAI of a pattern of theft, which includes direct complaints about former employees using Apple laptops to download confidential material and files that contained information about unannounced technologies, features, and products, including technical specifications, engineering presentations, and proprietary project data.
Apple also said that former Apple employees at OpenAI coached others considering leaving Apple for OpenAI on what information to bring to their interviews, among other allegations.
U.S. District Judge Edward Davila didn’t greenlight all of Apple’s requests for expedited access to OpenAI documents and messages relevant to the case. But he did rule that Apple could access the interview materials, alongside private LINE messages (from a messaging app) between individuals named in the case, including OpenAI employees Chang Liu and Alyssa Peng.
The judge also approved depositions for Liu and Peng, along with a third individual, OpenAI’s chief hardware officer, Tang Yew Tan. All three are former Apple employees.
However, the judge denied Apple’s request to expedite its access to OpenAI’s research and development in specific areas, like metal finishes and power management. He also denied several of Apple’s broader discovery requests, like access to OpenAI’s hardware research or information about what its former employees created while working at OpenAI.
That denial isn’t final, though; the judge left the door open for Apple to narrow its requests and try again.

articles.title: The Paris Auto Show is full of interesting cars Americans can’t have
articles.text:
Perhaps the days when auto shows debuted new models aren’t entirely over. The big trade shows for cars were a gateway drug for many, expos where you could see the newest models of today and the concepts of tomorrow. But automakers increasingly got tired of sharing the spotlight with each other. New reveals moved offsite to events the night or even the week before the show itself. One by one, brands pulled out of auto show after auto show until there was little left to see. And then the pandemic hit.
But the news out of Paris, where its auto show held media day yesterday, seems like we stepped back into a time when automakers would debut new cars aplenty. That retro vibe extends to the cars themselves, with plenty of familiar nameplates reimagined.
France’s Renault has a long and glorious history of delightful concept cars, and more on what it brought to Paris later. But the star of the show was arguably Stellantis, with strong work from Citroen, Peugeot, and Fiat, to name but three. But this article is meant to irritate you, because I’m pretty sure none of the stuff you’re seeing here will come to the United States. And it’s doubly irritating considering what Stellantis’ brands do offer us over here, doubling down on the same malign trends I saw back in 2020: did you know they’re about to relaunch a V8 Hellcat-powered Charger?
EVs can be small and cheap, apparently
The European concepts show us that, as those Kneecap chaps have it, there’s a better way to live. A sense of utopia was responsible for the original Citroen 2 CV; it had to be cheap enough for a farmer to buy it and rugged enough to get produce to market without breaking it. I’m not sure whether the 2 CV Concept also has to be able to transport eggs across a rutted field without breaking any (although the glove box is a clue), but Citroen says that affordability, lightness, practicality, and versatility were top of mind during the design process. The press release probably didn’t need to also say the company imbued it with distinctive character or charm; that’s quite obvious from the design.

The interior feels particularly refreshing compared to the touchscreen overload we’re usually presented. It might be stripped back, but it still has plenty of whimsy—the display in front of the driver has a bande dessinée theme, and the radio is portable and removable from the car. Technology fans don’t despair, there’s still the 8-inch touchscreen, but this too features more of Belgian comic artist Jean-Luc Delvaux’s work.
I’m even confident some of that whimsy will make it into production, because Citroen is going to build the 2 CV within the next two years, it says, and at a starting price of just 15,000 euros ($16,766). That slots it between low-speed microcars like the Renault Twizy, Citroen Ami, and the Fiat Topolino (which you can buy if you live in Michigan), and superminis like Volkswagen’s Polo.

Audi’s first attempt at a supermini was the esoteric A2, an aluminum and aerodynamic experiment from the wild days of Ferdinand Piëch. Like the original, the Audi A2 e-tron is an efficient little thing—its most efficient car ever it says, with a WLTP rating of 4.9 miles/kWh (100 km/12.8 kWh). As one might expect, I was a big fan of the original A2, which was always a rarer sight on the roads than it deserved to be. I can definitely see that car in the A2 e-tron’s design, and the promised efficiency sounds impressive even if there might not be quite the same excessive and cost-ineffective overengineering under the skin. I can’t see any way that Audi brings this car to America, just like we never saw the first A2, or the A1.

The Peugeot 205 GTi was a Gallic alternative to the late ’80s-era Golf GTIs that Americans will be familiar with, and it’s into this well that Peugeot dipped for Paris. Or rather, the wild 205 T16 Group B rally homologation special that the 205 GTi gave birth to, a car that won the world Rally Championships in 1985–86. Like the Renault 5 Turbo 3e from last year, the E-T16 Concept shows us that hatchbacks needn’t just be humble devices for running errands; they can excite, too. I’m not entirely sure about that multifunction steering wheel, though.
What if I need something bigger?
“But Jonathan, I don’t live a block from a metro station, and I need something a bit bigger to cope with my family,” you say. It is true that cars like the 2 CV or ID. Polo will be too small for some. This is true for Europeans as well, and both Renault and Fiat had something for these segments.

The styling was challenging for some, but it was a masterclass in space efficiency, seating six in two rows of three abreast. Rather than simply copying that, but with a slab of batteries under the cabin, the Fiat Multiplay explores the idea of a vehicle that’s adaptable, transforming from a three-row people carrier to a pickup. The front passenger seat can be reconfigured as a lounger, and there’s a “Petsenger” seat—a modular mounting point that allows you to swap in a pet bed, child’s car seat, storage compartment, or small table.

The original Renault Espace was very much loved and created the people-carrier segment out of thin air, at least in Europe. The familiar one-box shape remains for the new E-Space Concept, though with massive 23-inch wheels at the corners, the proportions are a little more Hot Wheels or Matchbox than the 1984 version. (Even in Europe, car designers are drawn to oversized wheels.)
There is a criminal lack of electric minivans on the market today, and the only one available here in the US is the VW ID. Buzz. And that sold so poorly that VW suspended imports for a model year. Which probably tells you how likely a US launch for a production E-Space would be.

articles.title: Grand Theft Auto 6's PC version will reportedly arrive 'in the first quarter of 2027' and fans are convinced Rockstar has moved the date up to avoid a potential PS5 emulator — 'GTA 6 will probably be emulator ready a month after launch'
articles.text:
GTA 6 will reportedly launch on PC in early 2027, and fans believe it's so Rockstar can avoid clashing with 'the PS5 emulator breathing down their necks'
Fans suggest an earlier PC release will allow Rockstar to get ahead of an emulator
- The PC version of Grand Theft Auto 6 will reportedly launch in early 2027, a few months after the console versions
- Some fans believe a 2028 release was possible, but Rockstar Games has moved the PC release up
- Fans speculate that Rockstar wants to get ahead of a potential PS5 emulator
A new report has claimed the PC version of Grand Theft Auto 6 will launch in early 2027, and fans believe Rockstar Games wants to get ahead of a potential emulator.
The news comes from GamesBeat, which reports that Rockstar plans to release the PC version of GTA 6 "in the first quarter of 2027," and that's according to "four industry sources familiar with the studio’s plans, all of whom requested anonymity to avoid damaging business relationships."
It's worth taking this report with a grain of salt, as Rockstar has yet to announce any PC edition; However, this is GTA 6 we're talking about, and fans are already theorizing over potential reasons a PC release could arrive mere months after the PS5 and Xbox versions, despite the PC version of GTA 5 arriving roughly two years after the console editions.
Many have speculated that Rockstar moved the PC release date up to anticipate a possible PS5 emulator, which would allow PC owners access to a "PC build" of GTA 6 without having to wait and pay for the official version. This would also allow users to avoid the "double dipping" scheme that many believe Rockstar is going for.
One redditor suggested Rockstar is "Not waiting a year with the PS5 emulator breathing down their necks." Some other fan wrote something similar, saying, "GTA 6 will probably be emulator ready a month after launch. It’s almost guaranteed at this point."
Some have also pointed out the more recent leaks from 'Cyberleek' (via GamesRadar) and suggest the studio wants to get ahead of the hacker.
"I actually believe this because of the leaks and emulator thing, they probably want the game out asap," a fan said on Reddit, as another wrote, "Im leaning heavily towards an original 2028 PC launch, but some exec has seen the speed that recomps are coming out and realised if they dont release it quick, everyone will be playing it for free."

Other fans think Rockstar hasn't announced the PC release date yet in order to maximise console edition sales; we've recently seen retailers hit with huge price hikes on the PS5 and PS5 Pro in anticipation of the game's launch.
"Not the first rumour we've heard like this," one fan said. "I find it believable - I strongly suspect the PC version is already pretty much done and the 'delay' is artificial from Rockstar to maximise the console release."
We'll have to wait for an official announcement from Rockstar, but in the meantime, PS5 and Xbox users don't have much longer to wait because GTA 6 launches next month on November 19.
In other news, new details have emerged ahead of the GTA 6's launch, which details even more gameplay features and immersive systems.

articles.title: AI causes uproar in mathematics as experts warn against sharing research with LLMs after OpenAI shares 722 manuscripts and proofs — professor argues that the field must focus on building community over raw solutions
articles.text:
AI causes uproar in mathematics as experts warn against sharing research with LLMs after OpenAI shares 722 manuscripts and proofs — professor argues that the field must focus on building community over raw solutions
Mathematics is a collaborative field, now disrupted by AI
Last week, OpenAI shared over 400 results for longstanding mathematical formulas that have troubled humans for decades; now researchers say it could take years for humans to validate and prove all the AI-driven work. But while analysts try to check the work of the unnamed OpenAI internal frontier model that found these alleged solutions, mathematicians argue this kind of AI-powered research and release threatens the field itself.
There's even the claim that by leaping from a prompt to a solution without a clear working in between, there is little benefit to these solutions in the first place. Mathematicians and the field itself may not be able to build on the results, as they don't know how they were achieved, nor has the development of such solutions produced new fields of mathematical understanding.
To make matters worse, there are suggestions that the growing confluence of mathematical and cybersecurity capabilities of frontier AI could bring into question the sanctity of cryptography itself. Alongside raising serious concerns for national security and modern digital systems, it could also put trillions of dollars worth of cryptocurrency at imminent risk.
Over 722 manuscripts dropped
The official count for OpenAI's maths solution release was 722 manuscripts, but with only 300 of the results formalized — digitizing human-readable formulas so they can be computer-verified — it's very difficult to know what's legitimate research. Some of the researchers The Verge spoke to found nonsense explanations within the reports, formulas that don't make sense, and some research that has already been completed by others.
The burden of proving the veracity of OpenAI and its model's claims is very much on the mathematical community, too. OpenAI didn't release the name of the model it used to generate these results, nor the prompts that generated them — despite those recommendations from the Advisory Group on Mathematicians and Artificial Intelligence (AGMAI).
OpenAI has at least published changelogs for its GitHub repository of the results, making it clearer where mistakes were made. But with several retractions and corrections already, it seems clear that it didn't check over the results in any great detail before releasing them.
It's this brashness, the pace of releases, and OpenAI's seeming disinterest in remotely slowing down its progress in the field that have so many mathematicians up in arms.
A looming threat becomes immediate
Mathematics isn't the first field to suffer a major upheaval because of AI. Writers first felt the looming threat with the release of ChatGPT in 2022, and both visual and musical artists faced the same concerns shortly after. Artificial intelligence is impacting almost every industry in some way, but while there are some potential benefits for its use in the field of mathematics, researchers within the field are concerned about the impact this may have on the collaborative nature of the field and how it might discourage future mathematicians from exploring it.
Speaking to Business Insider, mathematics professor at NYU, Tristan Buckmaster, said that OpenAI's release had upended the world of many early-career mathematicians, suggesting it had wiped out their whole research programs. Alongside their own research being invalidated by some of OpenAI's solutions, he suggested that some were now fearful that, by using AI tools, researchers had inadvertently contributed to the results, raising the potential of them not using advanced tools in the future and being less likely to talk about their research publicly.
This could cause huge problems for mathematics as a whole, argued mathematics professor at Northwestern University, Bryna Kra. Highlighting how collaborative maths is, with researchers sharing ideas, research data, and formulas, she is now extremely concerned that OpenAI has made mathematicians more secretive, reducing their ability to work together towards solutions and build on each other's research.
Professor of mathematics at the University of California, Terence Tao said on Mastodon that "many fewer seminars, workshops, collaborations, or other activities are being generated from these results compared to traditional breakthroughs." He argued mathematics may need to pivot to value "progress more holistically," by elevating the role of community building over raw solutions.
Researchers have described an atmosphere of extreme anxiety, that whatever they're working on could be invalidated overnight. That can undermine job applications, grant proposals, and those building the early components of their academic careers. Understanding and developing core mathematical capabilities at a high level can take years. AI dumps eradicating years of effort in such a haphazard fashion risk making it seem a near-pointless endeavour.
With swirling rumors of yet more releases from OpenAI, and potentially companion releases from other AI labs chasing the same headlines, the morale in many mathematical fields is extremely low.
Cryptography
With how much mathematics underpins key components of our digital world, it's no surprise that major changes in the pace of its development could have a domino effect elsewhere. One proposed potential minefield is the fertile ground of cryptography.
Associate professor of computer science at Johns Hopkins Whiting School of Engineering, Matthew Green, said on social media that he believes the congruence of mathematical developments and cybersecurity capabilities could result in AI that can defeat encryption as we know it.
While that raises potential concerns for all manner of fields that rely on encryption to protect the security of sensitive data, it could open up the cryptocurrency industry to wholesale theft, potentially impacting trillions of dollars of digital tokens.
Not everyone agrees with Green that this is an inevitability. British cryptographer — and one of the few people accused of being Bitcoin developer Satoshi Nakamoto — Adam Back, described these claims as nonsense and that there was little suggestion that just because AI can do certain mathematics now, that they'll be able to defeat encryption at some unnamed date in the future.
Ethereum creator Vitalik Buterin urged calm too, stating on Twitter/X that nobody should rush to move their tokens to a new wallet or panic over wallet security. However, he did argue that AI had the potential to one day be a far more dangerous threat to the sanctity of cryptocurrency than quantum computing.
While it doesn't appear that cryptography is a field AI is set to invalidate just yet, it's clear that it poses a potential threat to mathematical researchers and the core underlying 'way of doing things.' Much like it has just about everywhere else.
Researchers are adjusting to it, but the dust isn't likely to settle anytime soon, and in the meantime, OpenAI and its contemporaries may just move on to a new field to focus on as it continues to chase relevance and profitability.
Jon Martindale is a contributing writer for Tom's Hardware. For the past 20 years, he's been writing about PC components, emerging technologies, and the latest software advances. His deep and broad journalistic experience gives him unique insights into the most exciting technology trends of today and tomorrow.

articles.title: Estas versiones de Windows 11 se quedan sin soporte desde hoy: cómo te afecta y qué puedes hacer
articles.text:
A partir de hoy, Microsoft deja sin soporte a dos versiones de Windows 11 que todavía se utilizan en un gran número de ordenadores en todo el mundo. Esto significa que quienes las ejecuten ya no recibirán nuevas actualizaciones de características, ni tampoco parches de seguridad en el caso de detectarse vulnerabilidades. Nos referimos puntualmente a las ediciones Home y Pro de Windows 11 24H2.
La finalización del soporte de Windows 11 24H2 aplica a las mencionadas versiones de uso personal. Quienes las tienen instaladas en sus PC no podrán acceder a actualizaciones de seguridad extendidas, ni nada por el estilo. Distinto es el caso de las ediciones Education y Enterprise, que sí cuentan con un soporte más amplio que se extiende hasta octubre de 2027.
Que Microsoft deje sin soporte las versiones Home y Pro de Windows 11 24H2 no es una decisión deliberada ni que caiga por sorpresa. La compañía de Redmond lleva tiempo apegada a su estrategia de soportar estas ediciones por dos años, antes de continuar enfocando el soporte en las ediciones más recientes. No olvidemos que la firma viene de lanzar la actualización a 26H2 hace solo cuestión de días.
Para los usuarios de las variantes de Windows 11 24H2 impactadas, esto no es un baldazo de agua helada. Después de todo, quienes usan esta versión del software han recibido el aviso de su discontinuación con 90 días de anticipación. Por otra parte, Microsoft también está finalizando hoy el soporte para Windows 10 Enterprise LTSB 2016.
Windows 11 24H2 Home y Pro se quedan sin soporte hoy mismo
Si bien Windows 11 24H2 Home y Pro se quedan sin soporte hoy, eso no quiere decir que van a dejar de funcionar. Puedes seguir usándolos con absoluta normalidad, pero debes comprender los riesgos que ello representa a medida que transcurre el tiempo. Seguramente puedes vivir sin recibir nuevas actualizaciones de características, pero continuar un software que ya no recibe parches de seguridad puede volverse un problema con suma rapidez.
Hoy en día, la IA generativa está ayudando a que cada vez más fácil desarrollar y distribuir malware, explotando bugs y brechas que en muchos casos llevan años sin ser detectadas por hackers humanos. Por ello siempre se recomienda no dejar pasar mucho tiempo sin instalar las actualizaciones de seguridad más importantes.
También es una realidad que Windows 11 ha cosechado una merecida mala fama de romper muchas de sus funciones con cada actualización. Se comprende, entonces, que muchas personas no sean adeptas a instalar de inmediato la versión más reciente. En casos así, es importante tratar de encontrar una solución lo más equilibrada posible.
Si no quieres quedarte sin soporte, lo más sencillo que puedes hacer es actualizar a una versión de Windows 11 más nueva que la 24H2. Puedes ingresar en Configuración > Windows Update y ver qué edición tienes a mano para descargar. Es posible que no puedas dar el salto directo de 24H2 a 26H2, así que si pruebas 25H2 tal vez te encuentres con un software lo suficientemente estable y sin bugs como para no dar todavía el salto a la opción más reciente.
Además de Windows 11 Home y Pro 24H2 y Windows 10 Enterprise LTSB 2016, hoy también se quedan sin soporte todas las aplicaciones que forman parte de Microsoft Office 2021 LTSC.

								October 14th, 2026 -

Combining light-based components with traditional electronics is not straightforward. Conventional electronic design automation (EDA) workflows were never built to handle the complex physics and deep integration demanded by photonics. As optical and electronic technologies converge, engineers face tighter cross-domain coupling and unprecedented system-level complexity.
Addressing these challenges requires a new design paradigm: electronic photonic design automation (EPDA).
Driven by exploding bandwidth demands, power and latency constraints, and the rapid adoption of silicon photonics, EPDA is no longer optional — it is essential for delivering scalable, manufacturable electronic photonic systems.

articles.title: Applications open for 2026 Africa Energy Entrepreneurship Award - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
UK-based clean energy firm Octopus Energy has opened applications for the second edition of its Africa Energy Entrepreneurship Award, which offers grant funding, mentorship and support to early-stage startups expanding clean power access across the continent.
Run in partnership with the Sustainable Markets Initiative (SMI), and this year also supported by Nigerian solar company Salpha Energy, the Africa Energy Entrepreneurship Award will select three winners to receive a grant to scale product development and deployment, as well as access to a mentorship programme and resources and visibility aimed at helping them unlock follow-on funding.
The programme is open to startups based in Sub-Saharan Africa that are no more than five years old and have fewer than 20 full-time employees. Applications will be assessed on the uniqueness of the innovation, how it improves energy access, scalability, community impact, and the strength of the founding team. A panel of CEOs, founders and C-suite executives with experience in Africa’s energy transition will judge entries.
Last year’s winners were Nigeria’s Nimsy Agro Solar, which provides solar-powered irrigation pumps to smallholder farmers; PAM AI, which uses technology to optimise mini-grid energy; and KAMIM Technologies, which builds solar-powered cooling systems for farmers.
“With last year’s grant funding, we developed and piloted a first-of-its-kind solar irrigation reservoir in Giwa LGA in the Kaduna State in Nigeria,” said Onimisi Charles Atere, founder of Nimsy Agro Solar Concept. “The award has opened up new opportunities and networks, positioning us for greater impact and scale.”
Zoisa North-Bond, CEO of Octopus Energy Generation, said the company was proud to back early-stage startups delivering change through energy.
“We can’t wait to see this year’s applicants and hope this award continues to provide a launchpad for trailblazers to take their ideas to the next level,” she said.
Applications close on December 11.

articles.title: US Arrests Two in Crackdown on North Korean IT Worker Laptop Farms
articles.text:
Two US nationals were arrested in a new law enforcement operation targeting fraudulent North Korean IT worker schemes.
The suspects, Michael James Bostelle of Pennsylvania and Juan Cecilio Pena Carrillo of Texas, allegedly helped North Korean IT workers (ITWs) illegally obtain remote work at US companies.
According to a four-count indictment, the multi-year fraud scheme by Bostelle, Pena, and their co-conspirators generated over $3 million in fraudulent revenue.
As part of the scheme, which allegedly ran between 2019 and July 2025, the two housed and configured laptops issued by victim US companies so ITWs would appear to work from the US.
Using fake IDs and VPN and proxy infrastructure masking their real locations, the ITWs, aided by US facilitators, obtained employment at over 70 US companies in the communications, cyber support, healthcare, manufacturing, and retail sectors.
The indictment also charges China-based Sun Sheng Ming, Pei Li Guang, Weng Shou Cheng, Han Guo Bin, Wang Jian Jun, Sheng Zhang Kun, Zhang Wei Ping, Zhang Li Ping, Yu Yang, and Jin Long for participating in the scheme.
In a separate effort named Operation Lonestar Roundup, the FBI searched 40 locations in Texas suspected of operating as laptop farms for ITWs and seized 187 laptops and KVM devices used to commit fraud.
Famous Chollima
According to CrowdStrike, which tracks the fake IT worker scheme as Famous Chollima, operatives abroad employ various deception techniques to convince employers to ship company-issued laptops to farm locations.
Some of these include filing fraudulent police reports about stolen laptops to obtain replacements, claiming sudden relocation to divert shipments, rotating through multiple residential addresses, and using IT staffing firms during the hiring process, which allowed end-client devices to be quietly redirected to laptop farms.
At the farm, US facilitators install hardware and software that enable ITWs to remotely access them.
In response to recent defenses organizations have been implementing, Famous Chollima started hiding the remote access tools, spoofing device hashes, and using the same device identifiers across multiple organizations and personas.
“Laptop farms are vital to Famous Chollima’s revenue-generating operations because they solve three problems the adversary cannot easily overcome from abroad: physical, financial, and legal,” CrowdStrike notes.
The farms and facilitators provide a US footprint that includes a physical address, a legal identity, and a mechanism to satisfy regulation, but their disruption is expected to have a limited impact on Famous Chollima.
CrowdStrike also points out that Famous Chollima’s activity is sector-agnostic, targeting any organization that offers remote employment as a source of revenue.
“The dozens of victim organizations identified across the clusters disrupted in this operation span critical sectors including aerospace, energy, financial services, healthcare, cybersecurity, defense engineering, government technology, and consumer technology,” CrowdStrike notes.
An ‘identity in depth’ approach to detect ITWs
In a fresh alert, the FBI warns the general public that ITWs are increasingly using facilitators to evade detection, relying on the help of witting and unwitting US nationals to obtain employment in the country.
“ITWs are paying Americans for an expanding range of services to hide their own involvement in the scheme, including asking some to appear on camera, participate in job interviews or meetings, verify fraudulent identities, provide access to personal social media or professional networking accounts, ship packages, complete urinalysis tests or fingerprint submissions, or keep employment-related devices connected to the Internet from personal residences,” the FBI notes.
According to the Bureau, to identify ITWs reliably, organizations should look for multiple compounding behaviors and adopt an ‘identity in depth’ approach that involves layered access controls and detections throughout the employment lifecycle.
ITWs use remote desktop and remote monitoring and management (RMM) software, external hardware to control laptops, frequently download applications unrelated to their jobs, almost always exfiltrate data, tend to rotate through bank accounts and physical addresses, and forge verification documents for stolen identities to obtain employment.
“‘Identity in Depth’ — layered detections, access controls, and continuous identity verification throughout employment — avoids unreliable filters while enabling moderate, weak, or unavoidable signals to justify enhanced scrutiny when aggregated together. Evaluating identity-related fraud based on probabilistic behavioral data rather than easily bypassed rules provides defenders the resilience and flexibility necessary to counter North Korean ITWs and their ongoing tactical advancements,” the FBI notes.

articles.title: L’utilitaire le plus mignon de l’année : Citroën ressuscite au Mondial l'incroyable 2CV Fourgonnette !
articles.text:
Une 2CV peut visiblement en cacher une autre… Cela est déjà arrivé en 1951 quand une version Fourgonnette de la Deuche a débarqué sans prévenir, pour le plus grand bonheur des artisans. Citroën remet le couvert pour le XXIème siècle avec la 2CV Fourgonnette Concept qui dérive étroitement de la 2CV Concept fraîchement présentée. L’équation est simple : remplacer la partie arrière par une cellule en tôle pouvant engloutir n’importe quoi.
Vous obtenez ainsi une nouvelle fois l’un des utilitaires les plus mignons qui soient. Xavier Chardon, le PDG de Citroën, le confirme ouvertement : « la 2 CV Fourgonnette n’était pas seulement un outil de travail. Elle faisait partie de la vie. Simple, ingénieuse, accessible, elle avait surtout quelque chose que peu d’utilitaires ont : une âme. C’est cette idée que nous faisons revivre aujourd’hui. Parce qu’utile ne devrait jamais vouloir dire banal ».
Entre nostalgie et modernité : le coup de crayon parfait ?
La face avant est alors entièrement reprise à la 2CV Concept. Rien n’a changé et c’est possiblement la meilleure chose qui puisse arriver. On retrouve donc un regard absolument adorable formé par les feux circulaires et le pare-chocs proéminent lui conférant une bouille souriante. Le capot bombé est toujours au programme avec ses multiples rainures tirées du projet TPV préfigurant la première 2CV.
Le pare-brise vertical avec ses essuie-glaces apparents reste également de la partie, tout comme les portes avant dotées de poignées pivotantes. Les jantes pleines inspirées de la 2CV Fourgonnette originelle sont pareillement du voyage. Elles reposent néanmoins sur des pneus à flancs blancs contrairement à la 2CV Concept, qui se contentait de roues plus standard. Aussi, l’inscription 2CV au centre passe du jaune au rouge.
Un profil idéal… sans suite commerciale ?
C’est bien l’une des rares différences si l’on fait abstraction de la partie arrière. La Deuche s’équipe en effet d’une cellule de chargement carrée permettant d’optimiser au mieux la capacité d’emport. Les rainures jonchant les flancs singent sans détours la tôle ondulée du modèle original. On remarquera même côté droit la trappe de recharge imitant l’orifice du réservoir d’essence de l’ancêtre. C’est bien pensé et bien conçu.
La partie arrière, elle, se distingue par ses portes battantes noires dotées de vitres très discrètes. Ce n’est pas le cas du logo Citroën, largement mis en valeur sur la gauche. On notera enfin des feux à LED finement intégrés à l’horizontale. Cette étude de style aurait bien sa place sous le Berlingo Van en tant qu’alternative originale à l’ë-C3 Van. Prometteur. Sauf que la marque indique clairement qu’aucune mise en série de l’engin ne sera prévue. Snif…

articles.title: Ubitium raises $14M to build universal processor for machines that perceive, think and act - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Ubitium raises $14M to build universal processor for machines that perceive, think and act
Ubitium GmbH, a German semiconductor startup developing a universal processor for machines that perceive, think and act in the real world, today announced it has raised $14 million in additional seed funding led by Ibex Investors.
OpenOcean participated in the round alongside existing investors including KBC Focus Fund, Runa Capital and Inflection. Florian Seibel, co-founder and co-CEO of European defense technology company Quantum Systems, also joined the round. The new funding brings the total seed investment to $18 million since the company was founded in 2024.
Ubitium builds custom silicon for autonomous machines, otherwise known as physical AI, that do physical work, such as drones, robots, industrial equipment and self-driving vehicles. The company is building a single universal processor to replace today’s more specialized chips.
Autonomous AI machines rely heavily on three different things: signal processing for sensing, artificial intelligence inference and orchestration. These three foundational principles are generally stitched together across circuitry or silicon with wiring, allowing a machine to perceive, think, and act in the real world.
Today’s developers divide that work across a signal processor, a neural processing unit (or a graphics processing unit) and a central processing unit for control. The interconnection generates additional latency, data transfer time, coordination and engineering complexity.
Ubitium built a single processor using RISC-V technology and separate specialized logic as one array of programmable elements for signal processing, AI and real-time control.
“Physical AI machines bring a whole new set of computing challenges, and the inference isn’t the hardest one,” said co-founder and Chief Executive Hyun Shin Cho. “Sensing the real world and controlling the machine in it are just as hard, and today those still run on separate chips. We built one physical AI processor that does all three, proved it in silicon in a year, and this funding turns it into a product.”
The company built on RISC-V because it is a free, open-source architecture based on the reduced instruction set principle. It is open and royalty-free, unlike proprietary frameworks such as those from Intel Corp. and Arm Ltd. or, more importantly, CUDA, the standard that underpins Nvidia Corp.’s chipset.
Nvidia currently dominates the physical AI market by a wide margin, acting as the gravitational center by providing the hardware and software stacks. Estimates for the global market itself vary in scale, but it is projected to surpass $430 billion by 2030 and approach $1.6 trillion by 2040, according to a ResearchAndMarkets.com research report.
Ubitium’s first chip, the UB108 with 256 processing elements, manufactured on Samsung Electronics Co. Ltd.’s eighth-nanometer process, proved that the three processes could work together on a single silicon die. The company plans to roll out its first commercial processor, the UB410 with 4,096 processing elements, and deliver units for evaluation in 2027.

articles.title: Exclusive: Cambridge Heavy Industries has been quietly building a desktop fusion device | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Fusion power usually conjures images of massive industrial facilities laced with large lasers or magnets, but a startup in Cambridge, Massachusetts, has been quietly building a device that can fit on a tabletop.
The optics of the device were on display behind Yun Kai, co-founder and CEO of Cambridge Heavy Industries, while he chatted with me on a video call. The company has been operating in stealth out of a small lab near MIT, and Kai gave TechCrunch an exclusive look at the technology it has been developing.
“We purposely built a small modular reactor. It’s tiny, it’s benchtop,” he told me. “Because it’s small, it makes everything easier.”
The small size has allowed Cambridge Heavy to experiment and iterate quickly. “The small module nature can enable 50 to 80 experiments, 50 to 80 shots per day,” he said. Data from those experiments will feed simulations that use AI to optimize the design.
That nimble approach has attracted investor attention. The startup recently raised a $6.2 million seed round led by Azolla Ventures with participation from Overlay, Neta Foundation, P3A, MassCEC, and the Rothrock family.
Cambridge Heavy’s fusion reactor uses lasers to compress a fuel target, similar to the groundbreaking experiment that proved controlled fusion reactions could produce more power than they consume. But unlike other inertial confinement designs, Cambridge Heavy’s minimizes the number of lasers required to spark fusion.
The system uses two main lasers to drive ignition. One laser is split into multiple beam lines that deliver light in concentric rings. Those rings of laser light are timed to hit the flat, round fuel target successively, starting from the outside and working in. The first ring starts a compression wave within the target that starts traveling inward. The subsequent laser rings are timed to boost the wave at just the right moment to further compress the fuel.
As the shock wave reaches the center of the target, a laser fires on the target, generating heat and producing a magnetic field. With the right amount of pressure and heat, fusion occurs.
Cambridge Heavy’s design generates high pressures with relatively low laser power, Kai said. The concept emerged from the lab of Keith Nelson, a chemist at MIT. There, researchers used the laser pulses to study materials under extreme conditions. As they ramped up pressures, they realized they were approaching fusion-ready conditions.
In about a decade, Cambridge Heavy plans to develop a power plant from the concept, though that’ll require scaling up the design. It will be larger than the current benchtop prototype, though not quite as large as other fusion power plants. Kai said it should be about the size of two basketball courts, and it will test whether the approach can generate enough energy to support a power plant.
Before that happens, though, Cambridge Heavy plans to use its smaller-scale devices to make tritium, a rare isotope of hydrogen that will be used by nearly all fusion power plants in the works today. Tritium sells for around $30,000 per gram today.
Each power plant won’t need a lot of tritium — on the order of grams per year — but the substance is so rare that only about 40 kilograms exist today. One recent study predicts that without new sources, the fusion power industry will be short by about 28 kilograms in 2054. At current prices, that’s about $840 million worth of tritium.
Fusion startups are in the process of designing fuel systems that will help the reactors be largely self-sufficient when it comes to tritium supplies, though they may need occasional top-ups. But that process could take up to 10 years, Kai said, giving Cambridge Heavy years of potential revenue as it pursues its power plant.

articles.title: Datenleck bei Autohäusern: Mit diesen echten Details wollen Kriminelle dein Geld abgreifen
articles.text:
Datenleck bei Autohäusern: So erkennst du gefälschte Zahlungsaufforderungen
Ein Datenleck bei einer Software für Autohäuser könnte deutschlandweit besonders schwer zu erkennende Betrugsversuche bei Kunden nach sich ziehen. Weil die Täter dem Anbieter der Software zufolge Informationen wie Auftrags- und Rechnungsnummern, Liefertermine oder Kauf-, Zahlungs- und Finanzierungsbeträge erbeutet haben, könnten deren Nachrichten besonders echt wirken. Zuvor hatte die Mediengruppe Straubinger Tagblatt/Landshuter Zeitung über das Datenleck berichtet.
Die Polizei bestätigt auf Nachfrage, dass es einen Cyberangriff auf einen IT-Dienstleister im Raum Würzburg gab. „Nach derzeitigem Ermittlungsstand erfolgte der Zugriff über eine Drittanbietersoftware, welche zu dieser Zeit eine schwerwiegende Sicherheitslücke aufwies“, heißt es von dort. Zum genauen Umfang der entwendeten Daten und der Zahl der betroffenen Kunden könne man derzeit aber noch keine Angaben machen.
Bei den betroffenen Autohäusern handelt es sich dem Softwareanbieter zufolge vor allem – aber nicht ausschließlich – um solche, die Marken des VW-Konzerns führen. VW bestätigte zudem, dass die betroffene Software auch in der konzerneigenen Volkswagen Group Retail Deutschland genutzt wird, die rund 120 Autohäuser in Deutschland hat. Man habe die betroffenen Kunden zeitnah informiert und auf mögliche Risiken hingewiesen.
Echte Details machen glaubwürdig
Der Softwareanbieter hat nach eigenen Angaben vorsorglich alle von ihm betreuten Autohäuser informiert und warnt: „Kriminelle versuchen in solchen Fällen häufig, Käufer dazu zu bringen, offene Rechnungen auf fremde Konten zu überweisen. Dazu könnten sie sich mit den erbeuteten Angaben als Autohaus oder Verkäufer ausgeben, etwa mit gefälschten Zahlungsaufforderungen, angeblich geänderten Bankverbindungen oder Anrufen. Da die Täter möglicherweise echte Details aus dem Kaufvorgang kennen, können solche Nachrichten glaubwürdig wirken.“ Besonders vorsichtig sollten Käufer sein, wenn vor der Auslieferung ihres Fahrzeugs noch eine Zahlung von ihnen verlangt wird.
Weiter seien auch Phishing-Mails denkbar, die Verbraucher dazu bringen sollen, auf Links zu klicken oder weitere persönliche Daten preiszugeben, heißt es. Zu den Autohäusern, die die Software des Unternehmens einsetzen, gehören laut dessen Homepage auch einige der größten Handelsgruppen Deutschlands, die teilweise Umsätze im Milliardenbereich machen und zehntausende Autos pro Jahr verkaufen.
Kaufvorgänge bei Händlern in ganz Deutschland
Wie viele Kunden und welche Autohäuser genau betroffen sind, ist derzeit noch nicht endgültig klar. Es gehe aber um Kaufvorgänge bei Händlern in ganz Deutschland, heißt es vom Anbieter. Die Händler würden auf deren Kunden zugehen – insbesondere um diese davor zu schützen, offene Rechnungen auf falsche Konten zu überweisen.
Dazu raten der Softwareanbieter und die Polizei, im Zweifelsfall beim Autohaus anzurufen. Wichtig dabei: Nicht die Nummer aus der verdächtigen Nachricht verwenden, sondern aus einer sicheren Quelle. Außerdem solle man geänderte Zahlungsverbindungen kritisch hinterfragen, in E-Mails keine Links anklicken, keine persönlichen Daten eingeben und Warnhinweise der Bank ernst nehmen, wenn Empfängername und IBAN nicht zusammenpassen. Habe man das Geld bereits auf ein verdächtiges Konto überwiesen, solle man sofort die Bank anrufen, um die Zahlung zurückzuholen.

articles.title: The Download: faking blood and the future of batteries
articles.text:
The Download: faking blood and the future of batteries
Plus: The FBI has arrested an OpenAI engineer accused of snooping.
This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
The US military’s race to make fake blood
In February 2007, a US military helicopter carrying blood to a field hospital was shot down in Iraq, killing all seven crew members. The mission was a reminder of the risks of transporting blood, which has a limited shelf life and is often in short supply.
Now, a $73 million DARPA effort aims to create shelf-stable versions of plasma, platelets, and red blood cells. The idea is to develop dried blood products that can be stored for long periods and deployed quickly on the battlefield.
The project aims to have bags of dried blood products deployed in the field by 2029. But getting it all done will be tough, and researchers still have major questions about the safety and effectiveness of synthetic alternatives.
Discover how the military hopes to make blood last longer.
—Andrew Rosenblum
This story is from the next issue of our print magazine. Subscribe now to get your hands on a copy as soon as it lands on Wednesday, October 21!
10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch: WeLion New Energy and its semi-solid-state batteries
WeLion New Energy is one of MIT Technology Review’s10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch 2026, available exclusively to subscribers.
WeLion New Energy is on a quest to make safer, better batteries. The Chinese company’s liquid-solid hybrid cells aim to pack more power into electric cars, boats and drones, potentially improving safety and offering greater energy density than lithium-ion batteries.
In 2023, WeLion released a battery pack with EV-maker Nio that offered a range of over 1,000 kilometers. Now, the company is developing batteries with even higher energy density. But scaling up production and competing on cost remain major challenges.
Explore WeLion’s push to make safer, higher-capacity batteries.
—You Xiaoying
Subscribers can now access the full 10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch, spanning everything from geothermal power plants to carbon dioxide batteries.
MIT Technology Review Narrated: Weight-loss drugs show signs of slowing biological aging, say drugmakers
Popular weight-loss drugs may do more than help people shed pounds. They might also slow the aging process.
Drugmakers Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk say patients taking their GLP-1 drugs age less quickly, according to molecular “aging clocks” that track changes in DNA or levels of key proteins.
The findings add to speculation that GLP-1 drugs could be acting on basic causes of aging and might be true longevity treatments. But how much can we read into these results?
This is our latest story to become an MIT Technology Review Narrated podcast, which we publish each week on Spotify and Apple Podcasts. Just navigate to MIT Technology Review Narrated on either platform, and follow us to get all our new content as it’s released.
The must-reads
I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.

“It is like a thumb on the scale that we haven’t really ever seen.”
—Danielle Citron, a University of Virginia law professor, tells The Washington Post that Elon Musk’s ability to amplify conspiracy theories on X could give misinformation an unprecedented influence in the midterms.
One more thing
Is the Pentagon allowed to surveil Americans with AI?
The ongoing public feud between the Department of Defense and the AI company Anthropic has raised a deep and still unanswered question: Does the law actually allow the US government to conduct mass surveillance on Americans?
Surprisingly, the answer is not straightforward. More than a decade after Edward Snowden exposed the NSA’s collection of bulk metadata from the phones of Americans, the US is still navigating a gap between what ordinary people think and what the law allows.
Today, the legal complexity has a new edge: AI is supercharging surveillance—and our laws haven’t caught up. Here’s how the Pentagon’s use of AI has exposed legal gray areas.
—Michelle Kim
We can still have nice things

articles.title: Google ya permite crear apps para Android gratis y sin programar: así funciona la nueva herramienta con IA
articles.text:
Hasta hace unos meses, crear una aplicación para el móvil exigía conocimientos de programación y dominio de herramientas de desarrollo. La llegada de la IA y el "vibe coding" vinieron a cambiar todo y ahora cualquiera puede crear una app con unos cuantos prompts. Esto lo sabe Google y ha decidido lanzar una herramienta para crear aplicaciones para Android sin necesidad de escribir código.
De acuerdo con una publicación en el blog de la compañía, cualquier persona con una cuenta de Google gratuita puede crear una app. La herramienta convierte una simple instrucción en lenguaje natural (prompt) en una aplicación funcional que se ejecuta en tu móvil. Los usuarios solo requieren acceder a Google AI Studio para comenzar a construir la aplicación y probarla de forma local.
Las aplicaciones creadas con IA están separadas del catálogo público de la tienda, por lo que no habrá necesidad de marcarlas como privadas. Los usuarios pueden experimentar y construir las apps que quieran sin coste alguno, las cuales se pueden compartir con su círculo de amigos y familiares. En caso de que quieras ofrecerla al resto del mundo, necesitarás una cuenta de desarrollador profesional para publicarla en la Play Store.
Si optas por esto último, tu app tendrá que cumplir con los mismos lineamientos que se aplican al resto de aplicaciones de Android. Esto incluye las revisiones de Trust & Safety y el estándar de calidad con el que se mide el trabajo de otros desarrolladores.
Vale la pena mencionar que esta no es la primera vez que Google experimenta con este tipo de herramientas. AI Studio ya incluía un creador de apps con Gemini, pero estaba enfocado a cuentas profesionales y requería conectar el móvil a tu PC a través de la depuración USB. Ahora se puede instalar en el móvil con un clic y compartirla más adelante.
Android se prepara para recibir una oleada de apps creadas con IA
A primera vista, las apps creadas con IA parecen un paso lógico para Google. La compañía no solo tiene las herramientas y la plataforma, sino que busca recuperar el terreno perdido frente a OpenAI y Anthropic. La tecnológica está eliminando el requisito principal de una cuenta de desarrollador, permitiendo que cualquier persona con una cuenta gratuita pueda generar una aplicación desde cero sin conocimientos de programación.
Debido a que las aplicaciones se ejecutan de forma local, los usuarios pueden construir alternativas a apps que cumplen tareas sencillas. Por ejemplo, puedes generar una app que convierta divisas o una que te ayude con tus pendientes. Android ya ofrece miles o millones de estas aplicaciones, pero son lentas o imposibles de utilizar sin ver anuncios antes.
La herramienta para desarrollar apps de Android con Google AI Studio estará disponible a partir de hoy. Lamentablemente, el despliegue comienza en Estados Unidos con idioma inglés, aunque la compañía planea expandirlo a otros países en un futuro no muy lejano.

articles.title: Accelerating Advanced IC Package Design: A Methodology for Early and Iterative Optimization of Chiplet Integration
articles.text:
Optimizing chiplet integration, power integrity, and performance through early-stage IC package design and analysis.
Today’s multi-chip and chiplet solutions are leading the way for the “More than Moore” vision, with companies leveraging packaging technologies to create value and differentiate themselves from their competitors. Through-silicon via (TSV), wafer-level packaging (WLP), and 3D stacking technologies offer a wide range of packaging options for all form factors. Figure 1 illustrates a common example of 3D die/wafer stacking vs the traditional 2D system-on-a-chip (SoC).
Fig. 1: Common example for 3D die/wafer stacking. Source: Cadence
As semiconductor packaging technologies such as chip-on-wafer-on-substrate with redistribution layer (CoWoS-R) and local silicon interconnect (CoWoS-L) increase in complexity due to the rapid growth in the number of signals and the integration of high-bandwidth memory (HBM), high-speed interface areas are a key focus for design and analysis. This complexity challenges traditional design and analysis workflows, as importing large designs into analysis tools and managing redesigns can exceed project time constraints, making it difficult to meet deadlines.
This white paper presents a comprehensive methodology that enables early and iterative optimization of IC package designs. By integrating in-design analysis (IDA) directly into the design environment and leveraging scalable multiphysics simulation engines, IC package engineers can compress design cycles, reduce late-stage surprises, and achieve confident sign-off on complex advanced package designs.

articles.title: Microsoft October 2026 Patch Tuesday fixes 1,411 flaws, 3 zero-days
articles.text:
Today is Microsoft's October 2026 Patch Tuesday, with security updates addressing a record-breaking 1,411 flaws, including one actively exploited and two publicly disclosed zero-day vulnerabilities.
This Patch Tuesday addresses 70 "Critical" vulnerabilities, 57 of which are remote code execution, 11 are elevation of privileges, and 2 are spoofing.
The approximate number of bugs in each vulnerability category is listed below:
- 677 Elevation of Privilege Vulnerabilities
- 40 Security Feature Bypass Vulnerabilities
- 317 Remote Code Execution Vulnerabilities
- 254 Information Disclosure Vulnerabilities
- 73 Denial of Service Vulnerabilities
- 28 Spoofing Vulnerabilities
When BleepingComputer reports on Patch Tuesday security updates, we only count vulnerabilities released by Microsoft on Patch Tuesday itself.
Therefore, today's total excludes 348 flaws fixed earlier this month, including vulnerabilities in Azure API Center, Azure App Service, Azure Event Grid, Azure SRE Agent, Mariner, Microsoft Bookings, Microsoft Dataverse, Microsoft Exchange Server, and Microsoft Partner Center.
This is a record-breaking Microsoft Patch Tuesday as Microsoft continues to use artificial intelligence platforms to find and remediate security vulnerabilities in its products.
Microsoft announced today that Windows 11, version 24H2 Home and Pro, and Windows 10 Enterprise LTSB 2016 have reached end of support.
"Today, October 13, 2026, Windows 11, version 24H2 Home and Pro, and Windows 10 Enterprise LTSB 2016 have reached end of updates. The October 2026 monthly security update is the last update available for these editions," Microsoft said.
Earlier this month, Microsoft also said organizations running Windows 11 23H2 Enterprise, Education, and IoT Enterprise editions should upgrade to newer versions as they will no longer receive security updates starting next month.
To learn more about the non-security updates released today, you can review our dedicated articles on the Windows 11 KB5127648 & KB5126653 cumulative updates and the Windows 10 KB5126657 extended security update.
Microsoft patches 3 zero-days
This month's Patch Tuesday fixes one actively exploited and two publicly disclosed zero-day vulnerabilities.
Microsoft classifies a zero-day flaw as publicly disclosed or actively exploited when no official fix is available.
The actively exploited zero-day vulnerabilities addressed during this October 2026 Patch Tuesday are:
CVE-2026-96951 - Windows Shell Security Feature Bypass Vulnerability
Microsoft patched an actively exploited zero-day security bypass flaw that allowed attackers to bypass the Mark of the Web security feature.
"Improper neutralization of special elements used in a command ('command injection') in Windows Shell allows an unauthorized attacker to bypass a security feature over a network," warns Microsoft.
No details have been shared on how attackers exploited the flaw or who disclosed it.
The two zero-days that were publicly disclosed are:
CVE-2026-108398 - .NET Framework Security Feature Bypass Vulnerability
Microsoft has fixed a security feature bypass in the .NET Framework that can be exploited to run unauthorized applications.
"Untrusted search path in .NET Framework allows an authorized attacker to bypass a security feature locally," explains Microsoft.
Microsoft says this flaw could allow attackers to bypass Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) enforcement and run unauthorized applications.
"An authenticated attacker could place a specially crafted .NET assembly on an affected system and register it for loading by a protected process." Microsoft says.
"Successful exploitation could bypass Windows Defender Application Control restrictions and allow the attacker to execute code within the protected process. User interaction is not required."
James Forshaw of Google Project Zero discovered the flaw.
CVE-2026-92707 - MessagePack-CSharp Denial of Service Vulnerability
Microsoft fixed a denial-of-service flaw in MessagePack-CSharp.
"Improperly controlled sequential memory allocation in .NET allows an unauthorized attacker to deny service over a network," explains Microsoft.
Microsoft has not shared who disclosed the vulnerability.
Recent updates from other companies
Other vendors who released updates or advisories in October 2026 include:
- Adobe released security updates for numerous products, including Commerce, Substance 3D Samples, ColdFusion, Photoshop, Dimension, and Framework.
- Atlassian released security updates for a critical vulnerability (CVE-2026-21589) in multiple self-hosted Data Center products, including Confluence, Jira, and Bitbucket. Attackers soon exploited the flaw after a PoC was released.
- Cisco released security updates for numerous products, including critical vulnerabilities in its NX-OS data center network operating system that can let attackers run arbitrary code with root privileges on Nexus switches.
- Citrix released security updates for NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway flaws, with CVE-2026-88779 exploited in zero-day attacks before it was patched.
- Dell released security updates for critical vulnerabilities in the System Update (DSU) command-line interface (CLI) deployment tool and Container Storage Modules (CSM).
- Docker patched a critical flaw in DockerHub that lets attackers impersonate users and push images from others' repositories.
- Fortinet released security updates for numerous products, including a critical FortiMail vulnerability (CVE-2026-104286) that attackers exploited in zero-day attacks.
- GitLab released security updates for critical flaws in AI Gateway and CI/CD Regular Expression Compiler.
- Ivanti released security updates for an actively exploited zero-day vulnerability in the Ivanti Connect Secure (ICS) remote access gateway.
- Kiteworks released security updates for 126 vulnerabilities, including a max-severity flaw affecting its Email Protection Gateway (EPG) security solution.
- Progress Software released security updates for critical and high security vulnerabilities in MarkLogic Server.
- SAP released the October security updates, addressing 20 security flaws, including a maximum-severity OAuth2 SSRF vulnerability in Cloud SDK for Python.
- SonicWall released security updates for a critical SMA1000 server-side request forgery (SSRF) flaw, which attackers exploited within two days.
New risk cohorts help prioritize security updates
With this month's record-breaking number of vulnerabilities, Microsoft has also introduced a new method for organizations to prioritize security updates by grouping related flaws into what it calls "risk cohorts."
The new approach groups similar vulnerabilities together to help organizations better understand which security flaws pose the greatest risk to their systems and should be prioritized for patching.
For October 2026, Microsoft published 15 risk cohorts, including:
- 136 vulnerabilities affecting Windows filesystems, storage, and backup.
- 135 vulnerabilities involving Office documents and mail clients.
- 131 vulnerabilities affecting Windows graphics, media, and content processing.
- 109 vulnerabilities involving Windows core and kernel privilege boundaries.
- 103 vulnerabilities affecting Windows installation, deployment, and update services.
Microsoft stressed that these groups do not necessarily indicate which flaws are the most dangerous, as the actual risk depends on whether they are being exploited in attacks, their severity, and how an organization uses the affected software.
Microsoft says the new approach is still experimental and is meant to help organizations prioritize security updates, not replace its existing patching recommendations.
Microsoft has published a PDF mapping the October 2026 vulnerabilities to their respective risk cohorts.
The October 2026 Patch Tuesday Security Updates
Below is the complete list of resolved vulnerabilities in the October 2026 updates. Note, this report does include the flaws fixed earlier this month.

articles.title: SA's KhayaHR builds AI-first workforce platform for frontline economy - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
South African startup KhayaHR is building an AI-first workforce platform for the country’s frontline economy, and has already signed up more than 12,000 workers since launching in May.
Founded by Jacques Roux, KhayaHR gives workers a portable digital workforce passport. Employers can use it to find, assess, hire and then manage frontline staff in one place.
“Most recruitment technology assumes that candidates already have formal CVs, established digital histories and easily verifiable employment records,” Roux told Disrupt Africa.
“That assumption excludes many frontline workers. Their work experience may be informal, references fragmented, certificates stored as photographs or paper documents, and availability known only through personal networks or WhatsApp groups.”
The worker passport holds identity and right-to-work confirmation, skills, experience, references, employer recommendations, certificates, availability, and optional voice or video introductions. Workers cannot publish a profile until their identity and right to work in South Africa have been confirmed.
On the employer side, Khaya AI turns a natural-language hiring requirement into a structured search of the available workforce.
“An employer can describe the role, location and experience they need, and Khaya AI converts that into a structured search,” said Roux. “Employers can then assess real profile evidence, connect with suitable workers and manage employment through KhayaHR’s HR and payroll system.”
Khaya AI also works as an on-demand HR assistant for households and small businesses that do not have an internal HR department. It offers practical guidance on onboarding, contracts, leave, pay, UIF and managing workers correctly.
“This is an important part of the model – KhayaHR does not stop when a worker is found,” Roux said. “Once a worker is hired, many households and small businesses have no affordable HR support to help them manage contracts, leave, payroll, UIF and everyday employment questions correctly. We help smaller employers move from recruitment into responsible, structured employment.”
The platform also includes KhayaHR Academy, which offers short, mobile-friendly certificate courses. Certificates earned there are added automatically to the worker’s profile.
“That creates a direct link between learning, verified evidence and employability,” said Roux. “The longer-term objective is to create a complete workforce operating system connecting worker identity, skills development, recruitment, accessible HR support and ongoing employment management.”
KhayaHR is entirely self-funded and run by the husband-and-wife team. Roux leads product, technology and commercial strategy, while his wife manages most day-to-day operations and worker-facing activity.
“We have deliberately kept the team small while building and validating the platform,” he said.
Workers have taken to the platform quickly. KhayaHR now has a live, publicly discoverable workforce spanning all nine South African provinces and 50 occupations. It has also launched its first five Academy courses and an integrated HR and payroll platform.
“Worker uptake has been significantly faster than we initially expected,” said Roux. “The strongest demand has come from domestic work, housekeeping, cleaning, care, hospitality, retail, general labour and related frontline roles.”
KhayaHR competes with conventional job boards, specialist domestic-worker marketplaces, recruitment agencies, HR consultancies and standalone HR or payroll products. Roux said its point of difference is bringing everything together in one platform.
“Our distinction is combining the worker passport, identity and right-to-work requirements, AI-assisted discovery, on-demand HR guidance, the Academy and employment-management tools,” he said.
The startup earns revenue in several ways. Employers pay to unlock and connect with workers, and they subscribe to the HR and payroll platform on a per-employee basis. Workers can buy Academy courses, and larger employers can engage KhayaHR for targeted sourcing, readiness and placement programmes.
“We are generating early revenue, but the business remains in its initial commercialisation stage,” Roux said. “We are currently reinvesting in product development, verification, worker acquisition and employer adoption rather than optimising for short-term profitability.”
The rapid growth on the worker side has brought its own problems.
“The largest challenge has been balancing rapid worker adoption with employer demand,” said Roux. “Building a workforce supply base has proven faster than changing employer recruitment behaviour. The next commercial challenge is translating that worker adoption into consistent employer demand, successful placements and ongoing use of the HR platform at scale.”
Verification is also demanding work.
“Maintaining trust means reviewing identity, right-to-work and supporting evidence carefully rather than allowing every registration to become a public profile,” he said.
Designing for a mobile-first audience with different levels of literacy, data access and digital confidence has also shaped the product.
“This has required us to simplify onboarding, use WhatsApp extensively and continually rethink how workers complete profiles and learning content,” Roux said. “Making AI-supported HR guidance simple, useful and responsible is another important challenge. Small employers need practical answers in plain language, while the platform must still recognise when a matter requires professional or legal intervention.”
“As a self-funded two-person business, prioritisation is constant. We have had to build the technology, operate the platform, support workers and develop the commercial market simultaneously.”
For now, KhayaHR is focused on growing employer adoption and placements in South Africa. Once that is working, it plans to expand into selected Southern African markets.
“Once the model has repeatable employer demand and sustainable unit economics, we intend to expand through local partnerships,” said Roux. “We do not want to copy South African employment rules into other countries; identity, right-to-work and employment requirements would need to be adapted for each market.”

articles.title: Un italiano ha entrado en el Libro Guinness de los Récords al convertir un Fiat Panda en el coche más estrecho del mundo
articles.text:
Aparcar en un hueco imposible siempre ha sido la promesa de los coches pequeños, pero ningún fabricante se atrevió a tanto. El italiano Andrea Marazzi decidió llevar la búsqueda de aparcamiento al extremo más absurdo posible modificando un Fiat Panda de 1993.
Un récord Guinness sobre ruedas. Con su creación, Marazzi se ganó un puesto en el Libro Guinness de los Récords como creador del coche conducible más estrecho del mundo. La idea del proyecto surgió en 2024 cuando llegó un Fiat Panda en sorprendente buen estado al desguace de su familia. Marazzi decidió darle una segunda vida y, tras un año de trabajo, convirtió aquel utilitario en algo difícil de imaginar: un coche de tan sólo 50,2 centímetros de ancho.
Amor por un clásico popular. El Panda es un auténtico icono cultural en Italia. El propio Marazzi siente devoción por este modelo y suele acudir a la concentración anual "Panda a Pandino", cerca de la localidad de Pandino, donde los aficionados celebran su legado. Al tener un ejemplar a mano en el taller, vio la ocasión perfecta para experimentar.
Adelgazamiento extremo. Hay otro coche que presume de ser ultra estrecho. Es el Tango Hybrid Narrow Car (apareció en un episodio de la genial serie 'Silicon Valley') que mide 99 cm de ancho. Es muy estrecho, pero aún así es prácticamente el doble de la creación de Marazzi. También es más estrecho que la mayoría de motos. Por ejemplo, una Vespa Primavera 50 que no es especialmente grande ya tiene una anchura de 73,5 cm.
El Fiat Panda original mide 146 cm, por lo que consiguió reducirlo a casi un tercio de su tamaño. Lo bautizó como "Panda per Uno".
Cirugía de precisión milimétrica. Marazzi conocía al dedillo la estructura del Panda, lo que le daba una ventaja técnica fundamental para afrontar el reto. Para adelgazar el chasis, tuvo que retirar las puertas y las molduras laterales originales y después cortó la carrocería longitudinalmente por la mitad.
Tuvo que fabricar a medida los paneles exteriores, las lunas, el capó, el techo y el portón trasero. Pese al corte radical, logró crear el "Panda per Uno" con el 90% de piezas del coche original. En su perfil de Instagram mostró imágenes de todo el proceso.
Mecánica eléctrica a escala reducida. Con una carrocería tan estrecha era imposible meter el motor de gasolina original, así que lo sustituyó por un pequeño motor eléctrico que tan sólo alcanza los 15 Km/h, suficiente para validar su condición de vehículo operativo. Además, conserva un sistema de dirección adaptado a su nueva anchura y faros e intermitentes plenamente funcionales. Sin embargo, aunque se pueda conducir, evidentemente no está homologado para circular en carretera. De hecho, Guinness señala que el vehículo no es especialmente estable en las curvas. Por lo que sea.
La obsesión de Marazzi con el Fiat Panda no terminó ahí. En su siguiente proyecto decidió recorrer el camino inverso y transformó otro Panda en un auténtico monster truck dotado de neumáticos gigantescos.
