articles.title: The Tesla Roadster could have stayed vaporware
articles.text:
For a car that’s supposed to be one of the fastest ever made, the new Tesla Roadster certainly took its sweet-ass time getting here.
The Tesla Roadster could have stayed vaporware
It took nearly a decade for Tesla’s next-gen sports car to arrive, but it’s finally here. The timing couldn’t be worse.
The Tesla Roadster could have stayed vaporware
It took nearly a decade for Tesla’s next-gen sports car to arrive, but it’s finally here. The timing couldn’t be worse.
It’s been nearly a decade since Elon Musk made the surprise announcement about plans to build a next-gen Roadster. Now, the Tesla Roadster is finally expected to make its production-ready debut at an event in Waco, Texas — and the timing couldn’t be worse.
The new Roadster is set to arrive in an EV market beset by high energy prices, political turmoil, and consumer uncertainty. The tax-credit-fueled exuberance of the post-covid years has since given way to slower sales and fewer options. Automakers are scaling back their EV plans as sales stall in the US. Even Tesla, the market leader that has weathered its own share of chaos, is still struggling with shrinking demand and lowered expectations.
But the Roadster isn’t your average EV. It’s the ultimate status symbol, defined by its outrageous promises and elusiveness. Musk has said the Roadster can accelerate from 0–60mph in less than two seconds, will have a top speed over 250mph, and will come with an optional “SpaceX package” that adds cold-gas thrusters, enabling it to “fly a little.”
The Roadster isn’t a compelling product because it might be able to briefly hover (although that would be pretty impressive). In the years since it was first announced, it’s become defined by its unattainability. It’s vaporware in the extreme. After years of missed deadlines, it seemed likely that the Roadster would go the way of the solar roof tiles, battery swapping, robot charging, and other Tesla projects that were once promised but never delivered. Several reservation holders, like OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and YouTuber Marques Brownlee, canceled their orders under the assumption that the Roadster would fail to launch. For the average buyer, it was double-locked behind broken promises and an astronomical price tag.
Like a broken clock, Musk occasionally delivers on his outrageous promises — or at least a scaled-down version of the original promise. Tesla’s robotaxi service may not cover 50 percent of the US population, but dozens of its steering-wheel-less Cybercabs currently roam the streets of Austin, Texas. The Cybertruck may not be able to float in water, but it definitely exists. I’m told you can even buy one, though weak demand suggests few people want to.
It’s the ultimate status symbol, defined by its outrageous promises and elusiveness
Now that we know that some version of the next-generation Roadster is going into production, the question shifts to why it even exists. Musk, who has been pushing for Tesla to become less of a company that makes cars and more of a company that makes robots, has said that the Roadster will be the last Tesla vehicle built for human driving. Everything else will be autonomous. The company recently ended production of its original flagship models, the Model S and X, to make room for production of its humanoid Optimus robots. Musk is openly mulling the idea of merging Tesla with his other company, SpaceX, as a way to accelerate in the race for AI. The Roadster has been relegated to relic status before it even reaches a single customer.
The Roadster loses even more of its luster once you realize Tesla has already achieved some of its claimed performance goals. Tesla’s Model S Plaid was released in 2021 with a claimed 0–60mph time of 1.99 seconds (minus a 1-foot rollout), which was later confirmed by independent tests. When Tesla demonstrates its likely very quick Roadster on Thursday, some observers would be forgiven for feeling as if they’ve seen this movie before.
But Tesla watchers have been suffering from déjà vu all year. The company that used to reveal new products every year has since taken to rereleasing products it’s already shown off. This year saw the rereveal of the Cybercab (first announced in 2024), the Semi (2017), and now the Roadster (also 2017). In fact, the Cybertruck is the only new consumer vehicle Tesla has delivered in the last five years — and it’s been a noticeable flop.
Once it enters production, the Roadster will face fresh challenges. When the vehicle was first revealed, Tesla didn’t know that the electric hypercar market would be so chilly. Since then, there have been several automakers that have attempted to make two-door EVs at that price point and performance level, without any success. While hyper-EVs like the Rimac Nevera, Pininfarina Battista, and Lotus Evija achieved impressive engineering feats, they faced low sales volumes, severe production delays, and weak demand.
The Roadster has been relegated to relic status before it even reaches a single customer.
It turns out the super rich that can afford exotic cars that cost upwards of $1 million overwhelmingly prefer internal combustion engines. The appeal is rarely rooted in utility or straight-line 0–60mph numbers. Instead, it relies on brand loyalty, mechanical characteristics, engine noise, and manual or dual-clutch gear shifting. Bugatti CEO Mate Rimac has noted that despite setting dozens of world records with the 1,900-plus-hp Rimac Nevera, the company struggled to sell its planned run of 150 units. He compared high-end electric hypercars to high-tech smartwatches — capable of incredible feats, but lacking the emotional prestige of a handcrafted timepiece.
Ferrari opted for four doors when it designed its first EV and still faced near universal ridicule when the Luce was finally revealed. Porsche delayed pure-EV replacements for the 718 Cayman and Boxster multiple times. Even Lamborghini abandoned its planned pure EV in favor of an all-hybrid lineup.
It’s not even clear that the Roadster’s performance capabilities — 0–60 under two seconds, or even less than one second in certain configurations, if Musk is to be believed — will help bring in customers. When the original Tesla Roadster arrived in 2008, sub-four-second 0–60 times were reserved for high-end exotics. Today, the physics of electric motors make extreme straight-line acceleration relatively easy to achieve across different form factors. There are other limiting factors, like weight and thermal mechanics, that could blunt the Roadster’s ambitions. Two-door sports cars are built to be light, agile, and engaging around corners. But battery packs are heavy and can weigh down a sports car on twisty roads or racetracks.
The Roadster doesn’t need to be a huge success in order to be a win for Tesla. The company has had two generationally successful products — the Model 3 and Model Y — that will define its legacy going forward. The Roadster is likely to be a limited-run, ultra-high-end supercar where success is measured not by sales volume, but by scarcity. It may be the case that selling only a handful of Roadsters plays directly into to Tesla’s strategy.
While Tesla builds human-driven sports cars as a legacy afterthought, Musk’s eyes are fixed on low Earth orbit, where SpaceX plans to launch solar-powered orbital data centers to fuel his AI ambitions. Tesla has already moved on to AI and autonomous tech, rendering its own human-driven halo car obsolete before it launched. The last time a Tesla Roadster captured the world’s collective imagination was when Musk launched one into space in 2018. That car is still drifting millions of miles away with a dummy “Starman” astronaut in the driver’s seat.
Eight years later, the next-gen Roadster likely arrives as a grounded, earthbound artifact of a future Tesla has already left behind.

articles.title: Gemini 4 Argon begins rolling out in Gemini app and Antigravity, but only if you pay
articles.text:
Google revealed Gemini 4 Argon a few weeks ago, saying that it needed to move cautiously toward a full release because of the potential for nefarious use. Google seems to have worked all that out pretty quickly, though. Argon is beginning its wide rollout today, but it’s only coming to paying users at this time, and even those on lower-tier plans won’t have full access.
Nothing about Gemini 4 Argon’s capabilities has changed. Google still points to the benchmarks it published late last month as evidence of the model’s advanced reasoning and agentic coding capabilities. The model is supposedly trained to refuse malicious instructions, and an automated misalignment monitor can stop processing if it detects an unintended workflow. Google claims Argon needs that because it’s so capable.
The company has a few new examples of how Argon has helped inside Google, where it has been used by thousands of Googlers. Argon has reportedly been instrumental in making YouTube’s comment system more efficient. Argon identified redundant emoji rendering that, when eliminated, dropped server load by 45 percent. Engineers also turned Gemini 4 loose on the proprietary drone physics simulator used in Project Wing, and the AI found critical bugs that had been in the codebase since 2018. Google also notes that Argon has advanced its robotics program, showing a measurable step increase in embodied reasoning.

articles.title: The US military’s race to make fake blood
articles.text:
The US military’s race to make fake blood
DARPA is funding a redoubled effort to develop a shelf-stable substitute for what field medics and trauma doctors need most: more blood.
Its call sign was Morphine 1-2.
In February 2007, the hulking dual-rotor casualty evacuation helicopter had just flown three wounded soldiers to a field hospital in Balad, north of Baghdad, when another call came: an emergency mission to fly through an insurgent-controlled area in broad daylight. Typically, helicopters would be in a spot like this only at night, and with all lights turned off.
As it passed near the city of Karmah, in the eastern side of Al-Anbar province, an insurgent fired a portable missile launcher. The tail gunner, who likely saw the shot roaring in, yelled for the pilot to make an evasive move. But the missile had already locked on, and the ensuing blast started a fire on board. After the pilot battled the failing machine for 58 agonizing seconds, Morphine 1-2 plunged to the ground. All seven crew members were killed.
Why was the helo there in daylight? “It was getting blood and bringing it back. It was [on] what we call a ‘blood run,’ and [it’s] the highest of priorities besides casualty evacuation,” explains Lieutenant Commander Robert Murray, a Navy officer and program manager at DARPA, the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, who studied this incident as an intelligence officer.
Today, a chronic shortage of blood in both the military and civilian worlds is fueling a race to develop synthetic alternatives. About 90% of preventable battlefield deaths are due to hemorrhage—bleeding that happens when a blood vessel ruptures—and it’s the leading cause of maternal deaths worldwide. A study published in Transfusion in 2025 found that of 1.2 million trauma patients in the United States who potentially needed blood before reaching a hospital, just 1% received it. The shortage results in about 10,000 preventable deaths each year in the US, according to the American College of Surgeons. Globally, that figure is likely in the millions.
One reason for the shortfall is that blood has a storage problem. Whole blood lasts only 35 days when refrigerated, so banks separate out components to stretch the timeline. But that’s an imperfect solution. The platelets that help wounds clot are typically stored at room temperature and last for a week or less. Hospitals and the military freeze the red blood cells that carry oxygen, as well as the protein-rich plasma that restores volume and aids coagulation. Once thawed, though, both will spoil within days. “What happens if I don’t know when I’m going to be attacked? Well, thaw it and you let it expire, right?” Murray says.
 A JAMA study of combat injuries in Afghanistan suggests a magic number for someone who needs a transfusion: You have 36 minutes to get started.
That’s why Murray—who, in addition to his military experience, has a PhD in physiology—is leading a DARPA effort to address blood’s battlefield problems. He’s in charge of a new $73 million dollar program called RAPIID (for “resuscitation and prevention of ischemia-induced dysfunction”). Its goal is to create shelf-stable versions of the three major transfusion constituents: plasma, platelets, and red blood cells. As it gets underway late this year, RAPIID picks up on decades of work to synthesize blood or help it last longer. Most recently, that includes a prior $47.5 million DARPA project called FSHARP (for “fieldable solutions for hemorrhage with bio-artificial resuscitation products”), in which researchers have demonstrated promising results in animals.
With RAPIID trials for the different components occurring in parallel, the goal is to have bags of dried blood products deployed in the field by 2029. That puts Murray in the position of a conductor coordinating an orchestra of clinical trials with the FDA, while also sourcing the paraphernalia that goes along with transfusions—everything from combat-durable storage bags to tests that could check how much artificial blood a patient already has.
Getting it all done will be tough, but the military is feeling the pressure to address its shortage. Blood drives may not deliver in time after a mass-casualty event, and a JAMA study of combat injuries in Afghanistan suggests that if the injured person needs a transfusion, the magic number is 36 minutes. “If something is survivable—and generally we classify most all hemorrhage as survivable—[you’re] almost guaranteed to survive if you get the blood before that 36-minute mark,” Murray says. After that, the chance of survival “starts to drop precipitously.”
In the mission to make portable, shelf-stable blood components, plasma is the low-hanging fruit. Researchers have known how to isolate and freeze-dry plasma, the yellowish liquid that makes up 55% of whole human blood, since the late 1930s. On the battlefields of World War II, its mix of water, salts, and thousands of types of proteins helped restore blood volume in wounded soldiers—and to some degree controlled bleeding. In the 1960s, the US abandoned freeze-dried plasma because it carried a risk of transmitting hepatitis to recipients from infected donors. But screening, testing, and drying techniques improved, and starting in 2010, the US military launched a yearslong effort to rebuild its capacity for producing these products. Over the past two years, the FDA has allowed two types of freeze-dried plasma to be used in emergencies by the US military—and one can even be used by civilians.
As for platelets, efforts at extending their life date back to the 1950s, but they haven’t seen a ton of success. Bioengineers have, for example, attempted to attach the membranes of platelets to synthetic particles. The most successful project comes from a company called Cellphire, which freeze-dries actual human platelets. The product has shown safety and efficacy in humans in clinical trials, but its dependence on donors means it’s unclear whether this approach can scale.
Red blood cells have been similarly tough to preserve or mimic. Their most critical component is hemoglobin, which carries oxygen and comes encased in a cell membrane. For more than a century, researchers have been looking for ways to deliver hemoglobin without the immunological challenges created by this exterior, including the fact that donors’ and recipients’ blood types need to be compatible. Evolutionary pressure developed that wrapper for very good reason, though: “Naked” hemoglobin tends to break down quickly in the bloodstream, and that can cause organ damage. It also scavenges nitric oxide, our body’s natural mechanism for opening up blood vessels, and causes those channels to constrict.
This problem became all too clear in the 1980s and 1990s, when fears that transfusions could transmit HIV sparked interest in a class of membrane-free delivery mechanisms called hemoglobin-based oxygen carriers (HBOCs). One, named HemAssist, consisted of hemoglobin subunits linked together to avoid the rapid-breakdown problem. It had the added benefit of lasting roughly a year in cold storage (red blood cells last about 40 days)—but it didn’t solve the nitric oxide problem, so it constricted blood vessels. In a clinical trial, 24 of the 52 people who received HemAssist died, compared with eight out of 46 in the control group. The parent company terminated trials in 1998. A review of clinical studies published in JAMA in 2008 further solidified HBOCs’ fate, finding that they generally triple patients’ chances of heart attack and increase the risk of death by 30%.
More recently, researchers have tried to grow red blood cells in a lab using a technology called “blood pharming,” which involves making them from progenitors known as induced pluripotent stem cells. The stumbling blocks? Cost and yield. DARPA launched a pharming initiative in 2008, using stem cells from discarded umbilical-cord blood, but was unable to get the cost below tens of thousands of dollars per unit of red blood cells. They pulled the plug and offloaded the research to the Uniformed Services University. Even if the cost were lower, though, pharmed blood can’t be stored in a backpack. “These are still cells—they still require a refrigerator, they still require special handling,” Murray says.
It won’t be easy to solve all these challenges at once. “Each one of those projects individually is a massive undertaking,” says John Holcomb, a surgery professor at the University of Alabama at Birmingham, who was a combat surgeon in Mogadishu, Somalia, during the battle that inspired Black Hawk Down. “I think that they will probably be successful individually. How we use those individual products, or combine those products together, I think remains to be seen.”
Several years after DARPA gave up on lab-grown blood, Murray was stationed at a base on Okinawa, an island 400 miles southwest of the Japanese mainland, where he witnessed the vulnerability of the blood supply firsthand. The site houses a blood bank that serves the roughly 27,000 Marines commanded from the island—plus thousands more military personnel on the base and deployed within a 100-million-square-mile stretch of the Pacific called USPACOM, which ranges from western India to Hawaii and from Antarctica to the Arctic. “The blood center is right next to the hospital, which is about 200 meters from all of the satellite communications on that island,” Murray told me. A missile strike could take out all three.
Murray wondered: Is there a way to produce synthetic blood that could last longer? As he completed his PhD in physiology in 2018, the military was also awakening to the vulnerability of the Okinawa facility. The 2018 National Defense Strategy, which shifted military focus from terrorism to a potential ground war with China or Russia, showed war planners the risks of relying on a single site for blood runs covering all of USPACOM. DARPA then got serious once again about making fake blood and kicked off the FSHARP program in 2023. Murray came aboard as a deputy program manager in DARPA’s Biological Technologies Office in 2024 and was named a program manager in 2026, just a few months before RAPIID put out its call for proposals this past May.
Before he took the helm, related work had been underway for years. Aided by FSHARP funding, researchers at a company called KaloCyte continued testing a technique—originally developed by doctors who are now at the University of Maryland, Penn State, and the University of Pittsburgh—that “upcycles” hemoglobin from expiring donor blood. “We take that hemoglobin and then we package it in a lipid nanoparticle that functions like an artificial cell membrane,” explains CEO Elaine Haynes.
The product, called ErythroMer, is essentially a new kind of HBOC. The membrane prevents breakdown, limits dangerous scavenging of nitric oxide, and also helps the hemoglobin take up and release oxygen. Each ErythroMer cell includes a lipid called KC-1003, which acts like a sentry: In response to high pH in the lungs, it signals another small molecule within ErythroMer to move away, allowing oxygen in. Then, in tired tissue, where pH is lower, KC-1003 brings the small molecule back, releasing the oxygen.
Using a well-understood process called lyophilization, similar to one that World War II–era scientists used with plasma, the team freeze-dries its product to store at room temperature, where it can remain stable for two years. In a 2016 study of mice and rats with up to 70% of their blood removed, ErythroMer stabilized blood pressure and oxygen delivery—without the devastating constriction of blood vessels that sank HemAssist. FSHARP furthered that work, helping fund studies on how the HBOC interacted with plasma and platelets.
 Much like the handle of a Swiss Army knife, the synthetic platelet has specialized attachments—peptides that serve as the biological equivalents of a corkscrew or a nail file.
KaloCyte, though, still has plenty to figure out. Haynes says the company can source only about 1,000 to 2,000 units of expiring hemoglobin a month. So it has licensed a yeast strain that it aims to use to create its own hemoglobin in the lab.
Over a video call from her desk, Haynes showed me a sample of ready-to-use ErythroMer. It was encased in a heavy-duty storage bag with two chambers. One was full of scarlet powder—the hemoglobin product—and the other of sterile water to rapidly rehydrate it in the field. Eventually, she explained, under Murray’s master plan, “you’ll have another container with the synthetic platelet, and then a third container with the plasma.”
But achieving that vision depends on finding a synthetic platelet that works.
To do that, DARPA has turned to Anirban Sen Gupta, a bioengineering professor at Case Western Reserve University. “Traditionally platelets were thought of [as] blood cement, but it’s not that simple,” he explains. “They are, in my opinion, like drones, surveilling the blood vessel wall continuously, looking for signs of injury.” Sen Gupta’s team, which also includes collaborators at the University of Pittsburgh, used FSHARP funding to continue work on a product called SynthoPlate. Fabricated from a lipid nanoparticle that he likens to the handle of a Swiss Army knife, it has specialized peptide attachments—the biological equivalents of a corkscrew or a nail file. The first version has three: One binds to a chemical called von Willebrand factor, which helps platelets stick to the walls of injured blood vessels; another attaches to collagen, which acts as a scaffold for regrowing cells; and the third mimics a blood protein called fibrinogen, which acts like a Lego connector that allows the synthetic platelets to stick to real ones near a wound. Like ErythroMer, the product is freeze-dried and can be reconstituted with sterile water. It keeps for over a year at room temperature and at least three months at a desertlike 122 °F.
In a 2026 paper in Advanced Science, the researchers showed that SynthoPlate cut bleeding time and blood loss by more than half in mice with low platelet counts. In a separate study, they also safely injected the faux platelets into rats’ bone marrow—a more useful delivery site, given that a bleeding patient might not have an available vein. Sen Gupta and a colleague have spun this work out into a company called Haima Therapeutics.
The good news, as he sees it, is that the pharmaceutical industry excels at mass-producing millions of billions of lipid nanoparticles—witness Operation Warp Speed, in which these blobs of fat held delicate snippets of mRNA in covid shots. “The magic of the artificial platelet is in all those peptides that are decorating the surface of the particle, but the scalability of the platform is very well established,” he says.
Around the world, prospective blood alternatives abound. Researchers at Cambridge University in the UK are trying to pharm red blood cells for people with rare blood types or blood disorders like sickle cell anemia, and other researchers have also cultured platelets and red blood cells. Japanese scientists are already testing their own version of encapsulated human hemoglobin in human subjects.
Over the course of the next three years, RAPIID will move DARPA’s efforts closer to real life. In addition to ErythroMer and SynthoPlate, the agency in early October announced funding for five other companies working on blood components. Among them is a firm called Abioremedi that eschews hemoglobin for synthetic versions of other oxygen-carrying proteins such as cytoglobin, neuroglobin, and myoglobin encased in albumin—the most abundant protein in human plasma. Octapharma USA won the sole contract to supply plasma to RAPIID and will also be competing in platelets with an FDA-approved pair of clotting proteins it affixes to a disc-shaped nanoparticle.
With those players in place, the agency will focus for the next year on getting technologies through large FDA-regulated animal studies. Murray has set up a bit of a Hunger Games scenario: Each contractee working on blood components has only one year of guaranteed funding. He says he’s taking advantage of advancements in the field since FSHARP launched but is also hedging against any manufacturing or regulatory setbacks ahead of his 2029 deadline. Getting cut doesn’t mean the product is bad, just that the time frame was too demanding.
The second and third years will focus on human trials, overseen by the University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus. That will include using the products in situations where the risk of side effects is outweighed by the danger of doing nothing, such as with severely injured people in ambulances.
The possibility of fatal outcomes has invited second-guessing about DARPA’s choices. For Shibani Pati, who directs the Center for Research in Transfusion Medicine and Cell Therapies at the University of California, San Francisco, Murray could be making things too “DARPA hard” on himself by backing products like SynthoPlate and ErythroMer, which are previously untested in humans. “They need to make a very concerted effort to take what they’ve already developed and push it through to approval through the FDA,” she says. “Not start with moonshot projects that will take forever to get through.” For platelets, Pati thinks the RAPIID program would have done better to tap Cellphire, since its products have already received millions from the Pentagon and shown safety and efficacy in humans. (Murray notes that he can only select companies that apply, and Cellphire did not.)
She has similar qualms about ErythroMer. A different HBOC that sources hemoglobin from cattle, called Hemopure, has been approved for use since 2001 in South Africa, she notes. And though it hasn’t been approved by the FDA—it was part of the fateful 2008 JAMA study—US doctors are cleared to use it for patients who have bad immune responses or religious objections to conventional transfusions.
Holcomb, the surgery professor, worries the effort will run into issues with interactions between the products. He notes that individual blood components have more than one role: Red blood cells also help with clotting, platelets also are anti-inflammatory, and plasma helps tune coagulation. There’s no guarantee that the versions RAPIID helps develop will work in the same ways.
Murray says that FSHARP’s animal studies tested all the products together, using whole blood as a baseline, precisely because of such possible interactions. The cocktail met its program metrics in all but one area: The clotting was not quite as good, perhaps because negative charges in some molecules repel one another.
“I do not think they will replicate all the functions that whole blood does in our body,” Holcomb says. But, he admits, “you may not need to, right? When you get seriously injured and you lose 50% of your intravascular volume, you’re dead, right? So if you lose 30% and maybe you’re hanging on to life just barely, maybe you show up with all these different products, and you have enough whole blood left in you to do these other functions.”
Murray is determined to complete trials so that shelf-stable blood can be delivered in 2029. In addition to the storage bags, he’s already sourcing finger sticks for in-field blood testing and a battery-powered device to heat up the blood components.
The danger of blood runs—and, by extension, the vulnerability of millions in combat zones, maternity wards, and ambulances—drives his scientific daring. Knowing the stakes, he told his boss in 2024 that even if FSHARP failed, “we should invest 50 million more dollars in it and do it again.”
Andrew Rosenblum is a technology journalist and the author of the techno-thriller Stretch Goals.

articles.title: Google lanza Gemini 4 Argon, su IA más potente hasta ahora
articles.text:
Google ha lanzado Gemini 4 Argon, su modelo de frontera más poderoso a la fecha. Tras meses de retrasos y de ceder terreno a Anthropic y OpenAI, el gigante tecnológico contraataca con una nueva IA enfocada en flujos de trabajo completos. Gemini 4 llega con mejoras en razonamiento, programación y tareas de larga duración.
Si bien Google ya había anunciado Gemini 4 Argon a finales de septiembre, el modelo no se encontraba disponible. La tecnológica lo ofreció primero a un grupo de socios especializados en ciberseguridad para evaluarlo. La buena noticia es que el modelo de Google ya se puede usar en la app de Gemini.
De acuerdo con Google, Gemini 4 Argon está diseñado para proyectos de ingeniería de software, conocimiento empresarial en áreas como derecho y finanzas, así como también en defensa en ciberseguridad. La compañía coloca a esta versión como el comienzo de la próxima era de su inteligencia de frontera, un modelo que tendrá lo suficiente para medirse con Claude, ChatGPT y otras IA poderosas.
El cambio más notable con respecto a la versión anterior es que Argon responde de forma más directa y con menos titubeos. Gemino 4 dejará atrás los clichés y las respuestas con muchas repeticiones que no llevan a ningún lado, algo que veíamos en la generación anterior. En tareas de larga duración, la IA informará su progreso con más frecuencia para que sepas en qué punto va sin que tengas que preguntarle.
A diferencia de su predecesor, Argon tiene un límite de generación de 1 millón de tokens, lo que le permite razonamientos y flujos de trabajo más extensos en una sola ejecución.
Gemini 4 Argon es una bestia en programación y ciberseguridad
En las primeras pruebas de rendimiento, Gemini 4 Argon logra un buen puntaje en DeepSWE v1.1, un benchmark que mide el desempeño en tareas de desarrollo de software real. Google afirma que sus ingenieros lo usan a diario, desde tareas de depuración hasta migraciones de bases de código de gran tamaño. Entre los casos de uso destacados se encuentran la optimización de algoritmos para computación cuántica y la reducción del uso de memoria en centros de datos.
Fuera de la programación, Gemini 4 Argon tiene un enfoque marcado en la ciberseguridad defensiva. El nuevo modelo de Google puede encontrar, validar y corregir vulnerabilidades de software. En la prueba de CWE-bench v1, que mide la capacidad de la IA para remediar fallos de seguridad, Argon supera a Claude Opus 5.5 y comparte el primer lugar con GPT-6 Astra y Grok 4.7. La tecnológica menciona que ha trabajado con empresas como Wiz, que ya usa Gemini 4 en sus sistemas de defensa.
Otros hitos del nuevo modelo incluyen el descubrimiento de múltiples vulnerabilidades en bases de código complejas que abarcan 20 lenguajes de programación. Gemini 4 Argon es más eficiente que 3.8 Flash Cyber en descubrir la superficie de ataque, identificar vulnerabilidades y producir pruebas de concepto para validarlas.
Gemini 4 Argon ya está disponible para los suscriptores de Google AI Pro y Ultra a través de la app de Gemini para macOS.

articles.title: Why Heat Is Becoming A Bigger Chip Design Issue
articles.text:
Increasing complexity requires thermal, electrical, and mechanical effects to be analyzed together.
Key Takeaways:
Experts at the Table: Semiconductor Engineering sat down to discuss the growing thermal challenges and trade-offs as dies are stacked, vertically integrated, and harder to cool, with Lang Lin, director of product management at Synopsys; Jack Berg, vice president of business development at Silvaco; Satish Radhakrishnan, head of semiconductor and electronics at Vinci; Chris Mueth, director of new markets management at Keysight EDA; and John Ferguson, senior director of product management at Siemens EDA. What follows are excerpts of that conversation, which was held behind closed doors at the recent Design Automation Conference. To view part one of this discussion, click here. Part two is here.
L-R: Silvaco’s Berg; Synopsys’ Lin; Vinci’s Radhakrishnan; Keysight’s Mueth; Siemens’ Ferguson.
SE: One of the big trade-offs in advanced designs is voltage versus current. How do you balance that?
Lin: If you reduce the voltage, it will change your timing and reduce the performance. But it also reduces heat. If you keep running the chip fast, you will run into a lot of thermal problems. These are conflicting physics. You need to find the sweet spot for your chip. You need to try the real combination of, say, this voltage versus this timing budget. And you need to do a loop of timing, thermal, and supply voltage or power integrity co-optimization. You have to close this loop and run a couple different workloads to make sure there is not a failure or any other problems. We don’t have a tool yet to do this big loop, so the engineer may be asking how to solve their place-and-route problem while also running timing, thermal, and voltage. And then, they still have to make sure they can close the design.
Radhakrishnan: Along with thermal, you also have the resistance change because of the temperature. You need to understand the dynamics of a temperature-based transient. As you pass the current, the temperature rises and the resistance changes. Are you going to keep the same performance? Are you going to change the total current. How much power do you budget? That’s where the coupled nature of the entire simulation is going, and that’s where a lot of focus in the industry will be. As power rises, temperature rises, so you’re going to allow more cooling, and you’re going to push up the power. All of this is going to be coupled, probably starting next year.
SE: So given all these issues, is a full 3D-IC possible?
Mueth: It’s just a matter of time. We’ll solve a lot of the problems. That will require a lot of materials science, which needs more investment. For the aging problem, we will use specialized materials science types of solvers, which need to be extended to achieve that. There are exotic things you can do, like stacked intercoolers with fluid circulation. Of course, that means it’s going to be incredibly expensive to make those, and you’re only going to use them for high-performance applications. You’re not going to use them for everything else.
Radhakrishnan: People are already talking about 3D DRAM and 3D-IC. From a thermal view, there are different techniques like a cooled interposer, but the industry is going more toward a 3D-IC where everything is stacked together and you have optics coming in on the side. It will be more expensive, though, so maybe you need to start with a narrow application.
Mueth: One thing that hasn’t been mentioned yet is heterogeneous technology, and how you can bring that in to use the right modal technologies for the right application and integrate that stuff together. That can help if you have a super high-performance application and you need a small size. You can use that for a specialty application to integrate the different technologies together.
SE: This goes into orchestration, where it’s not just whatever you’re doing as a process, but also the materials that you use, as well.
Berg: Absolutely. The materials are extraordinarily important, and the time constant associated with thermal is different from the speed of electrons through a transistor. That disconnect needs to be consistently taken into account. But for 3D-ICs, it’s not a matter of if we’re going to do them. It’s a matter of when. It will happen.
SE: For full 3D-IC, or 2.5D or 3.5D?
Berg: Well, you can call a stack of 16 HBMs in a single package a 3D-IC. So, depending on your definition, we already have it. But that z-level scaling is going to be very important, and it will take a group of very intelligent materials scientists, and people with thermal and mechanical skills to make that happen.
Radhakrishnan: Hybrid bonding is enabling that. More innovation, like having nanometer-based TSVs, will allow that.
Ferguson: The whole discussion is interesting. It reminds me of the early days of Moore’s Law, where every time we went to a new process, somebody would say, ‘That’s it. We can’t do it. We’re never going to get to the next node.’ But we get there. Maybe we don’t get there exactly when we want, but we do get there. And then we say, ‘Well, that was great, but now I need it to be faster. Now I need better signal intent.’ Now, as we bring in the MCPs (Model Context Protocols), it’s not just bringing in the intelligent people. Intelligent MCPs can do this so much faster than we can, and we need the people to find and build the right MCPs. One of the things we need to think about in this industry is that we’re looking at each thing almost in isolation. Here we’re talking about thermal. What are the thermal impacts? But in the meantime, somebody else is looking at changing the chemistry of some of the materials. And if you didn’t know that, they’re going to come together at the wrong time. We’ve got to think about bringing the whole ecosystem together so we’re all communicating and we know exactly when things are going to fit correctly.
SE: We lost that with the end of the ITRS, and now we’re looking to AI to pick up the mantle.
Mueth: Yes, and I’ve been surprised at how much AI has advanced in the last year. It’s astounding. We had a hackathon a couple months ago. We were doing an amazing number of things with the tools we never thought were possible. If the customer knows the problems they have to solve, it’s our job as vendors to supply the tools to help them out. But in the end, because they know what they need to do, they’re going to want to drive the orchestration, and we need to enable them to do that.
Lin: This becomes a very interesting engineering regrouping, or upgrading of the organization time. In the old days, we would have thermal engineers solve the thermal problem, and the semiconductor team wouldn’t look at it. ‘Just send the data to the thermal team, and they will resolve any issues.’ But today, even the place-and-route engineer has the luxury to deal with the thermal problem because we have chip agents. So they can use natural language to tell an agent, ‘I want to see if this design passes thermal. Show me the Tmax. The agent will help you run the simulation and give you back the result.
Mueth: Traditionally, everyone trained on one discipline, so you had single-domain engineers. But they really need to do multi-domain problems now. How do you accomplish that? One way is through AI. Another is to dumb down the offerings of multi-physics, such that a person in a single domain can run those simulations. But AI would be a big help.
Radhakrishnan: AI is good, but it has to be accurate. That’s the most important thing, because while a designer can run it, if he’s going to make a decision using the AI and it’s wrong, it will lead to a wrong design. But I agree that it needs to go beyond just a specialized simulation team. It needs to involve other people, and you have to make it easy for them to get the geometry and simulate it very quickly so they can get the design right. And, of course, it needs to talk to other teams where mechanical, electrical, and everything else are combined. This has to be done correctly, accurately, and together.
SE: As we move toward agentic AI, you need more than just GPUs. You need CPUs, and probably different types of accelerators. Does that add to the thermal issues, or does it make it easier to manage them because they’re just one more variable rather than trying to make this a single thing?
Mueth: It’s hard to manage two different technologies, obviously. But what you’re gaining is that you’re pushing multiple technologies to gain efficiencies. If you gain efficiencies, you gain thermal performance, and hopefully electrical performance. So it’s a trade-off of design complexity against performance of an electrical circuit — and the thermal performance, as well.
Berg: I generally agree. Having multiple solutions at this point for both training and inference is important, and it’s an important consideration to make things a bit more effective and cost-effective.
Lin: For traditional EDA tools, we’re typically running CPU-based acceleration. But when we go into the multi-physics domain, we see GPUs playing an important role because there is a lot of 3D solving. You can parallel the matrix solver with a GPU kind of load. That’s another important use of GPUs — to accelerate the tool simulation. This is runtime improvement and parallel processing.
SE: So massively parallel systems?
Lin: Yes, with thousands of GPUs running all together to solve partition-based design of your 3D-IC. The CPU is going to be orchestrating and doing some kind of reasoning, and then driving the process.
Berg: In order to create synthetic data with multiple physics solvers that are cross-coupled together, you need a very large bank of GPUs. Once you have that synthetic data, you’re capable of coming up with surrogate models that can be run on CPUs on somebody else’s PC to take a look at ‘what ifs.’ The key is ensuring that your multi-physics is calibrated to data, and that it is also capable of ensuring that you have boundaries where interpolation is occurring, versus extrapolation.

Rising power density and chiplet complexity drive thermal considerations earlier in the design process.
Thermal Complexity Grows With AI Chips And Photonics
Increasing power density makes heat, stress, and aging harder to predict, and more critical to address earlier in the design flow.

articles.title: Endeavor Catalyst closes $320m Fund V - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Endeavor Catalyst, the venture capital arm of global entrepreneur network Endeavor, has closed its oversubscribed Fund V at US$320 million, taking its total assets under management past US$850 million.
Endeavor Catalyst invests exclusively in companies led by Endeavor Entrepreneurs, co-investing alongside leading venture capital and growth equity firms. Across its five funds, it has already backed 437 companies in 44 markets, deploying more than US$500 million across 469 investments.
Africa makes up seven per cent of both the portfolio and Catalyst capital, with 29 companies backed across five African markets, including the likes of Flutterwave, Moniepoint, MAX and Moove. Six of these are valued at US$1 billion or more. A decade ago, the fund had made no African investments.
Fund V has already backed 30 companies and deployed more than US$55 million, with a further US$25 million to US$30 million expected to be invested before the end of 2026.
“For the founders we have yet to welcome into the Endeavor community, it sends an important signal: world-class capital is looking for ambition, wherever that ambition is being built,” said Ireayo Oladunjoye, managing director and CEO of Endeavor Nigeria.

articles.title: Citrix, Fortinet, Ivanti Patch 29 Vulnerabilities Across Their Products
articles.text:
Security updates released on Tuesday resolve 29 vulnerabilities across Citrix, Fortinet, and Ivanti products, including multiple critical-severity bugs.
Citrix published three advisories detailing nine security defects impacting Workspace App for Windows, XenServer 8.4 and XenServer 9, and UniconOS.
Successful exploitation of the flaws could allow attackers to execute arbitrary code, cause denial-of-service (DoS) conditions, leak information, compromise or crash the host from within the VM, elevate privileges, execute arbitrary commands, and read arbitrary files.
Fortinet released 10 advisories dealing with 13 bugs, including two critical-severity issues in FortiSIEM and FortiSandbox GUI that could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute arbitrary code (CVE-2026-106173) and bypass authentication (CVE-2026-107656).
It also resolved four high-severity SQL injection vulnerabilities in FortiAnalyzer, FortiAnalyzer Cloud, FortiManager, and FortiManager Cloud, and another in FortiMail webmail. All five could allow authenticated attackers to execute arbitrary code or commands.
Ivanti rolled out patches for seven security defects in Connect Secure, Neurons Patch for Intune, and Xtraction.
The Connect Secure update deserves special attention, as it resolves CVE-2026-104935, an exploited zero-day that covers two underlying bugs chained together to compromise patched VPNs.
In Neurons Patch for Intune, Ivanti resolved CVE-2026-109412, a critical flaw that could allow attackers to leak sensitive authentication information.
The Xtraction update fixes five issues, including a critical bug (CVE-2026-106042) that could allow attackers to redirect application-generated requests and capture EPMM connector credentials.

articles.title: Apple tiene 12 flamantes nuevos productos para el hogar y Europa no va a disfrutar al completo ninguno de ellos
articles.text:
Confieso que llevaba unos días esperando la presentación de Apple del 13 de octubre. Aunque avisaron oficialmente de que mostrarían algo, realmente ya estaba todo el pescado vendido. Mark Gurman ya había hablado prácticamente sobre todo lo que presentarían y sabíamos que veríamos nuevos altavoces, el HomeView (que es el desembarco de Apple en los altavoces con pantalla) y el nuevo Apple TV.
Resulta que también han terminado llegando un montón de dispositivos inteligentes como cerraduras, sensores o cámaras, y todos con una cosa en común: en Europa pagaremos lo mismo que en otros sitios, pero no podremos aprovecharlos al máximo.
¿El motivo? Siri AI.
Hace unos años, Huawei comenzó a mover la idea de una estrategia llamada 1 + 8 + N. 'N' son infinitos dispositivos para el hogar como enchufes, cámaras, bombillas y ese tipo de cosas; '8' hacía referencia a coches, auriculares, ordenadores, tablets, pantallas inteligentes, altavoces y gafas y, en el centro de todo, estaba el smartphone como centro de control de absolutamente todo lo demás.
Era su idea del ecosistema, pero aunque Huawei, Samsung o Xiaomi tienen ecosistemas sólidos, la facilidad que da Apple para integrarlo todo de forma nativa los pone un paso por delante (sumado a su imagen de marca, que tampoco se puede obviar). Por eso, lo presentado ayer es tan interesante.
Apple ya vendía dispositivos para el hogar dentro de su propia tienda, pero no dejaban de ser dispositivos de otras marcas como Nuki, Eve o Aqara. Lo que los hace "dignos" de venderse en la Apple Store es que tienen compatibilidad con la app Home, pero si algo nos enseña el interior del iPhone es que Apple prefiere controlarlo todo y ahí entra la Apple Home Collection.
Se trata de un conjunto de cámaras, sensores, termostatos y una cerradura inteligente que son fabricados por LG y Schneider Electric, pero con Apple, esta vez sí, muy metida en el proceso de desarrollo. Algo importante: de momento, aunque estos dispositivos funcionan con Home, no se venden en Europa por el momento.
Sin Siri Ai, la casa de Apple no funciona
Luego está el HomePod Mini 2 y las dos joyas de la corona: el HomeView y el Apple TV 4K. Y aquí es donde las cosas se empiezan a poner interesantes ya no por una cuestión de precio (349 euros el Apple TV 4K, gracias a la crisis de componentes que atravesamos, y 169 euros el HomePod Mini 2 cuando el anterior costaba 99), sino porque ese Apple TV no tendrá la función más importante en Europa y el HomeView, directamente, ni se venderá en la UE.
El porqué ya te lo he comentado: Siri AI. Desde que anunciaran la renovación del asistente en junio de este año, avisaron de que la disponibilidad del mismo en la Unión Europea se retrasaría debido a la Ley de Mercados Digitales.
Desde entonces ha existido un cruce de acusaciones entre la empresa y la UE y, aunque han ido diciendo que estaban acercando posturas, meses después seguimos con dispositivos que son objetivamente peores que en otros países fuera de la UE, pero al mismo precio. iOS 27 es un ejemplo de hasta qué punto da igual una nueva versión del sistema cuando la ligas tanto a una función que no tira en tu país.
Cuando nos metemos en la página estadounidense del HomePod Mini 2, HomeView o Apple TV 4K, vemos que Apple no ha escatimado en dejar claro que Siri AI es la principal característica de los tres. Su renovado asistente lleva años dándoles dolores de cabeza, provocando una vergüenza pública y haciendo que retrasen planes de lanzamiento de algunos productos (se estimaba que el Apple TV debería haber llegado hace meses).
Porque Siri AI era la justificación para nuevas generaciones de productos y líneas nuevas como el HomeView y, sin ella, es evidente que estos dispositivos pierden gran parte de la gracia.
En la web española, tenemos un apartado de Siri, pero es tan anodino como el limitarse a decir "puedes hablar con Siri estés donde estés", básicamente como podemos hacer desde hace años con el HomePod Mini. Y en el Apple TV 4K más de lo mismo, las menciones habituales a una Siri que ya se podía usar en la anterior generación.
El caso del Apple TV 4K me parece especialmente sangrante porque si el anterior costaba 169 euros, este se va hasta los 349 euros. 200 más por un chip que sí, es mejor, pero por unas funciones que ya estaban en el anterior. Porque ya tenía conexión con los dispositivos de Home, ya podíamos conectar los HomePod como altavoces y ya era 4K. Vale que la crisis de componentes no ayuda, pero es un dispositivo más caro porque integra una tecnología nueva que, de nuevo, no podemos usar como usuarios europeos.
Y luego, repito, está ese HomeView que no se lanza porque su uso está ligado a un iPhone con Siri AI.
Al final, como europeos podemos comprar esas nuevas cámaras, sensores, termostatos, el altavoz o el Apple TV, pero es evidente que Apple quiere que todo lo que se han gastado en Siri AI dé frutos más pronto que tarde y en los países en los que no tengamos disponible el nuevo asistente, la experiencia se queda muy coja.
El iPhone sigue siendo el centro de control de todo, pero ahora ya no basta con tener un iPhone, sino que ese iPhone debe tener Siri AI sí o sí. De hecho, visto lo visto, en un símil con esa estrategia 1 + 8 + N, en el caso de Apple ese '1' estaría compartido entre el iPhone y Siri AI.
Los de Cupertino han invertido muchísimo en Siri AI y si empieza a ligar ciertos dispositivos a esa tecnología, más vale que arreglen las cosas con Bruselas porque pagar el mismo dinero que un estadounidense cuando el dispositivo carece de la única función que justifica su existencia es algo que seguro nos alejará a más de uno.

articles.title: Apple lance 9 objets connectés pour la maison avec LG : vous pourrez en acheter 0
articles.text:
Neuf produits, et pas un seul logo Apple. Ce mardi 13 octobre, à l’occasion de l’événement « Welcome Home » organisé à New York, Apple a levé le voile sur l’Apple Home Collection, une famille d’objets connectés pensés pour accompagner son nouvel écran, le HomeView. La firme de Cupertino ne les fabrique pas elle-même : c’est LG et Schneider Electric qui s’en chargent, sous leur propre marque.
Le procédé n’est pas nouveau chez Apple. La marque l’avait déjà appliqué aux écrans LG UltraFine, dessinés avec Cupertino puis vendus par le constructeur coréen. Cette fois encore, les produits ont été conçus avec Apple mais portent la marque de ses partenaires. Ils seront toutefois vendus directement sur le site et dans les boutiques d’Apple. « Nous avons conçu chaque accessoire pour qu’il fonctionne parfaitement avec Apple Home », assure Matthew Costello, vice-président de l’ingénierie matérielle chez Apple. Schneider Electric complète le tableau avec son propre thermostat et un capteur de température et d’humidité.
Sonnette, serrure, caméras : ce que contient la gamme
Une bonne partie de ces produits avait fuité avant l’annonce, à travers les documents déposés par LG auprès de la FCC, le régulateur américain des télécoms, et les visuels publiés par le leaker pdfu.
Côté sécurité, LG proposera une sonnette vidéo filaire (LG Video Doorbell Wired) et trois caméras : une intérieure, une extérieure et une à projecteur (LG Indoor Cam Plug-In, LG Outdoor Cam Plug-In et LG Floodlight Cam). Pour le confort, on trouve un thermostat à écran rond (LG Smart Thermostat), compatible Wi-Fi, Thread et Bluetooth, et un capteur de température et d’humidité (LG Temperature Sensor) qui fonctionne sur pile. Enfin, la serrure connectée (LG Smart Deadbolt Lock) est alimentée par quatre piles AA.
Une serrure qui reconnaît votre iPhone à l’approche
La pièce la plus intéressante de la gamme est sans doute la serrure. Elle utilise l’ultra-wideband (UWB), la technologie de localisation précise qu’Apple exploite déjà dans les AirTag et les iPhone, pour savoir à quelle distance vous vous trouvez. Avec une clé de maison enregistrée sur un iPhone ou une Apple Watch compatible, la porte se déverrouille d’elle-même quand vous arrivez devant, sans sortir votre téléphone de la poche. On peut aussi l’ouvrir d’un geste avec l’iPhone ou la montre, via le pavé numérique intégré, ou avec une clé de secours cachée. La serrure détecte si la porte est ouverte, fermée ou forcée, et prend en charge Matter ainsi qu’Aliro, le nouveau standard de contrôle d’accès. Ses fonctions essentielles tournent en local et continuent donc de marcher sans connexion Internet. Comme pour tout le reste de la gamme, un simple contact avec l’iPhone suffit à l’installer, sans application ni compte supplémentaire.
Les thermostats, eux, s’appuient sur l’iPhone pour savoir si quelqu’un est à la maison, s’apprête à dormir ou est absent, et ajustent la température en conséquence, sans programmation manuelle. Côté vidéo, LG décline trois caméras (intérieure, extérieure et à projecteur) et une sonnette, de quoi aller chercher Ring, la filiale d’Amazon, et Google Nest sur leur terrain.
Toutes filment jusqu’en 2,5K et reconnaissent les personnes, les visages familiers, les animaux, les véhicules et les colis. La sonnette embarque deux caméras, dont une tournée vers le sol pour garder un œil sur les colis, tandis que la caméra intérieure s’incline automatiquement vers le bas pour cesser de filmer dès qu’un membre du foyer rentre. Les vidéos sont conservées dix jours dans iCloud+, sans abonnement supplémentaire, et chiffrées de bout en bout : ni Apple, ni LG, ni Schneider ne peuvent y accéder.
Ni HomeView ni Home Collection en France
Le HomeView, comme le nouveau HomePod mini et l’Apple TV 4K, a été pensé autour de Siri AI, toujours bloqué en Europe. Apple l’assume désormais noir sur blanc : le HomeView ne sera pas vendu dans l’Union européenne, faute de Siri AI sur iOS. Les accessoires LG et Schneider n’ont pourtant pas ce problème. La serrure, les thermostats et les capteurs sont compatibles Matter, le standard commun à Apple, Google, Amazon et Samsung, et tous les produits prennent en charge Thread. Ils fonctionnent avec l’app Maison et un produit Apple existant, qu’il s’agisse d’un HomePod, d’un HomePod mini ou d’une Apple TV 4K. Pas besoin de Siri AI pour verrouiller une porte ou régler le chauffage.
Sur le papier, la gamme aurait donc pu arriver en France sans attendre Bruxelles. Mais Apple ne la commercialisera, au moins dans un premier temps, qu’en Amérique du Nord et au Royaume-Uni. Les caméras et la sonnette arrivent aux États-Unis, au Canada et au Royaume-Uni, tandis que la serrure, les thermostats et les capteurs se limitent aux États-Unis et au Canada.
Prix et date de sortie
L’Apple Home Collection sera disponible à partir de décembre sur le site et dans les boutiques d’Apple, certains accessoires n’arrivant qu’au début de 2027. La caméra intérieure LG démarre à 199,95 dollars, la sonnette à 249,95 dollars, la caméra extérieure à 299,95 dollars et la caméra à projecteur à 399,95 dollars. La serrure LG est affichée à 349,95 dollars. Les thermostats de LG et de Schneider coûtent tous deux 199,95 dollars, et leurs capteurs 39,95 dollars.

articles.title: New tech order will be built from Karnataka: Priyank Kharge
articles.text:
New tech order will be built from Karnataka: Priyank Kharge
The Karnataka government has initiated numerous programmes to create a talent pool that meets the demands of emerging technologies, said the Minister for Home, IT, BT & E-Governance, Government of Karnataka, at Techsparks 2026.
The new tech order will be built from Karnataka, said Priyank Kharge, Minister for Home, IT, BT & E-Governance, Government of Karnataka, at the ongoing Techsparks 2026 summit in Bengaluru.
In a fireside chat with Shradha Sharma, Founder & CEO, YourStory and The Bharat Project, the minister said the state government is focused on building the skill sets required to cater to the needs of the global market.
The minister elaborated the various measures taken by the Karnataka government to expand the skills base in the state. “We have to come up with a programme of ensuring that we build skill sets by the industry, for the industry, of the industry to ensure that people unlearn and relearn technologies that are going to be relevant for the next decade or so.”
The plan will not be limited to the technology sector and also focus also on blue-collar jobs in sectors such as manufacturing, he said.
The minister said that, in the last nine months, the state has attracted close to $4.9 billion investments just from the technology sector. Karnataka’s capital Bengaluru is already the fourth largest technology cluster in the world.
“Forty-three per cent of all tech investments in India come to Karnataka, and this speaks volumes about the availability of talent here,” the minister remarked.
Kharge also highlighted how the talent in the state is engaged in the various centres of excellence (CoE) that the government has created. These CoEs span multiple sectors including agriculture, aerospace, IoT, and AI. The minister said these CoEs have created more than Rs 10,000 crore in market valuation and added that these are run professionally by the industry, with minimum interference from the government.
The Karnataka government's ELEVATE programme provides equity-free grants to startups, and this has now been extended to deeptech startups under ELEVATE Nxt.
As part of Elevate Nxt, the state government provides Rs 1 crore of equity-free grant to deeptech startups focused on solutions for problems faced by citizens. It also provides market access programmes with 40 countries.
“We will be ensuring that we do everything in our capacity to ensure that you succeed as an entrepreneur,” the minister said.
The overall goal is to ensure IP creation, CoEs, state government grants, and local accelerator programmes drive the economic growth of Karnataka.
Edited by Swetha Kannan

articles.title: Microsoft releases Windows 10 KB5126657 extended security update
articles.text:
Microsoft released the Windows 10 KB5126657 extended security update, which includes this month's record-breaking October 2026 Patch Tuesday fixes and a few bug fixes and changes.
If you are running Windows 10 Enterprise LTSC or are enrolled in the ESU program, you can install this update like normal by going into Settings, clicking on Windows Update, and manually performing a 'Check for Updates.'
After installing this update, Windows 10 will be updated to build 19045.7807, and Windows 10 Enterprise LTSC 2021 will be updated to build 19044.7807.
What's new in Windows 10 KB5126657
Microsoft no longer releases new features for Windows 10, and the KB5126657 update mainly includes security updates and bug fixes.
The update also includes fixes released as part of today's record-breaking October 2026 Patch Tuesday, which fixed a massive 1,411 vulnerabilities across Microsoft's products, including one actively exploited zero-day flaw.
The complete list of fixes and changes in KB5126657 is listed below:
- [Time and Date]
  - This update enables permanent Daylight Savings Time (DST) support for British Columbia and Alberta starting in November 2026.
  - This update introduces the new time zone Manitoba Standard Time "(UTC-5:00) Manitoba".
- [ReFS security] This update adds auditing and optional policy controls for ReFS volumes on externally attached storage devices. Auditing is enabled by default, while enforcement controls remain disabled by default to give administrators time to evaluate and prepare for future security hardening changes. To learn more, see KB5130741.
- [Storage Spaces] Addresses an issue that might cause some Storage Spaces Direct virtual disks to remain offline after installing a Windows update. This issue occurs when valid tiered storage metadata is incorrectly identified as invalid during recovery, preventing affected virtual disks and dependent workloads from coming online.
- [File History (known issue)] Fixed: This update addresses an issue where File History might fail to back up or restore files to an external drive or network location. Affected devices might incorrectly display a "Reconnect your drive" message even when a compatible backup drive is connected and working properly.
- [Secure Boot] This update continues the deployment of updated Secure Boot certificates using the latest high-confidence targeting data to identify eligible devices that are ready to automatically receive the new certificates. Deployment through Windows Update remains ongoing across supported device.
Microsoft says the update has a known issue affecting some USB Audio Class 1.0 devices after installing the September 2026 Windows security updates.
Affected devices may fail to start with a Code 10 error in Device Manager, stop producing audio, or experience unresponsive volume controls and sound settings. Some devices may also work in standard stereo mode but fail when using 8-channel or 3D audio configurations.
Microsoft partially fixed the issue in an emergency out-of-band update released on September 14, which addressed problems with 8-channel and 3D audio modes.
However, other audio issues remain unresolved, and Microsoft says it is working on additional fixes.

articles.title: Le sol s’enfonce sous certaines grandes villes, jusqu’à 21 cm par an : nos satellites ont aussi ausculté Paris
articles.text:
Le sol s’enfonce sous certaines grandes villes, jusqu’à 21 cm par an : nos satellites ont aussi ausculté Paris
Neuf ans d'images radar, 465 villes passées au crible : une équipe de l'université de Pékin publie une carte mondiale des sols urbains qui s'affaissent. Au sommet, Medan, Bandung et Mexico. Et Paris dans tout ça ?
Le bitume sous nos semelles n'a rien d'immuable. Publiée le 12 octobre 2026 dans la revue Nature Cities, une étude pilotée par Shengli Tao et Xie Hu, chercheurs à l'université de Pékin, a mesuré entre 2014 et 2023 les mouvements verticaux du sol dans 465 villes de plus d'un million d'habitants, réparties sur 107 pays. Le phénomène porte un nom, la subsidence : un tassement lent qui lézarde les façades, tord les canalisations et aggrave les inondations. Les auteurs revendiquent la première évaluation planétaire menée avec une méthode homogène, là où les travaux antérieurs juxtaposaient des études locales aux protocoles disparates.
Medan, Bandung, Mexico : les villes où le sol descend le plus vite
À l'échelle d'une agglomération entière, Medan, en Indonésie, détient le triste record avec une vitesse médiane d'environ 33 mm par an, devant Bandung (22 mm), Torreón au Mexique (17 mm) et Ispahan en Iran (11 mm). Mexico affiche une médiane plus modeste, 8 mm, mais certains de ses quartiers plongent d'environ 217 mm chaque année. Plus de 21 cm. Le pompage intensif des nappes phréatiques figure parmi les grands coupables : privées d'eau, les couches de sédiments se tassent comme une éponge qu'on essore.
Un autre satellite confirme l'ampleur du phénomène. Lancé en juillet 2025 par la NASA et l'agence spatiale indienne, NISAR a vu plusieurs secteurs de la capitale mexicaine perdre plus de 2 cm par mois entre octobre 2025 et janvier 2026.
The ground beneath Mexico City is slowly sinking, and now, the NISAR satellite can track it from space. 
New data shows parts of the city (in blue) that sank more than half an inch (more than 2 cm) per month from Oct. 2025 to Jan. 2026. pic.twitter.com/5uDM1B9Mwx
— NASA Earth (@NASAEarth) April 29, 2026
L'Asie du Sud-Est et de l'Est offre un tableau contrasté. Nombre de villes y ralentissent leur descente, signe selon les auteurs que des mesures d'atténuation d'envergure portent leurs fruits, tandis que de vastes zones urbaines de ces mêmes régions continuent d'accélérer. La carte fait aussi émerger des territoires longtemps délaissés par la recherche, en Afrique, en Amérique du Sud et en Russie.
Sentinel-1 en vigie, Paris sur la terre ferme
La prouesse repose sur l'interférométrie radar (InSAR) appliquée aux images de Sentinel-1, la constellation du programme européen Copernicus. D'un passage à l'autre, le décalage de phase des ondes réfléchies trahit des variations millimétriques, cartographiées avec une résolution de 40 mètres.
Ce tour du monde porte une signature chinoise, mais il s'appuie sur des yeux européens. Pilotés par l'Union européenne et l'Agence spatiale européenne, ces satellites livrent leurs images gratuitement aux chercheurs du monde entier. La flotte vient d'ailleurs de rajeunir : Sentinel-1C a rejoint l'orbite en décembre 2024 à bord d'une Vega-C, suivi de Sentinel-1D en novembre 2025, propulsé par Ariane 6 depuis Kourou.
Bonne nouvelle pour l'Hexagone : dans les données publiées par l'équipe, Paris, Lyon et Marseille bougent de moins d'un millimètre par an, une valeur à la limite de ce que la méthode sait distinguer, comme Londres ou Tokyo. L'Italie mérite davantage d'attention. Florence et Rome descendent de 2 à 3 mm par an en médiane, et leurs secteurs les plus instables dépassent 15 mm, selon le même indicateur qui attribue 217 mm à Mexico.
Les 465 villes de l'étude se consultent sur le portail interactif GUS, mis en ligne par les chercheurs. Ceux-ci reconnaissent leurs angles morts : des mesures relatives, bornées aux limites administratives des villes, et moins fiables là où les stations GPS au sol se font rares. Pour le reste de la France, l'EGMS, le service européen de surveillance des mouvements du sol, exploite ces mêmes radars Sentinel-1 pour cartographier le continent au millimètre près, quartier par quartier.
