articles.title: Microsoft Patches Record 1,413 Vulnerabilities, Including Exploited Windows Zero-Day
articles.text:
Microsoft’s October 2026 Patch Tuesday updates fix a record-breaking number of vulnerabilities, including a Windows zero-day exploited in the wild.
According to Microsoft, the latest updates resolve 1,413 CVEs, including 1,102 affecting Windows, 134 in Office, 61 in developer tools, and 36 in SharePoint Server. Exchange Server, Azure, Defender, and other products also received security patches.
This month alone, Microsoft patched more vulnerabilities than it did in all of 2025. The surge, largely driven by AI, has pushed the number of flaws fixed so far in 2026 past 4,000.
The exploited zero-day is tracked as CVE-2026-96951 (CVSS score 8.8/10). Microsoft describes it as a Windows shell security feature bypass flaw that enables an attacker to evade Mark of the Web (MotW) defenses.
MotW tags internet-downloaded files, signaling security mechanisms like Defender SmartScreen and Office Protected View to restrict automatic execution. Bypassing MotW allows malicious files to launch without triggering warnings.
“In an email or instant message attack scenario, the attacker could send the targeted user a specially crafted file that is designed to exploit the vulnerability,” the tech giant explained in its advisory. “In any case an attacker would have no way to force a user to view attacker-controlled content. Instead, an attacker would have to convince a user to take action.”
The issue was independently reported to Microsoft by researchers at Fujitsu, Anthropic, and an independent expert. No information has been shared about the zero-day attacks, but threat actors often exploit these types of MotW bypass vulnerabilities in their campaigns.
CISA added CVE-2026-96951 to its KEV catalog on Tuesday and instructed federal agencies to address it by October 16.
Two of the newly patched vulnerabilities were publicly disclosed before Microsoft made fixes available. One of them is CVE-2026-108398, which allows an attacker to bypass Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) enforcement. Microsoft believes this flaw is unlikely to be exploited.
The second, which Microsoft has not assessed for exploitability, is CVE-2026-92707. It’s a DoS vulnerability affecting the MessagePack-CSharp component in Visual Studio and .NET.
Microsoft also announced on Tuesday the introduction of ‘risk cohorts’ to help users prioritize security updates.
“A risk cohort is a group of CVEs that require a similar customer assessment. The CVEs may not share a root cause or a CVSS score. What they share is a question about the customer environment that can inform prioritization,” Microsoft explained in a blog post.
It added, “Risk cohorts are a starting point, not a final decision. Customers should continue to review each CVE for active exploitation, severity, attack vector, user interaction, and product-specific guidance.”
Related: Ivanti Zero-Day Chain Gave Attackers Root Access to Fully Patched VPN
Related: Adobe Patches 176 Vulnerabilities Across 11 Products
Related: SAP Patches Critical NetWeaver, S/4HANA Vulnerabilities
Related: Microsoft Patches 18 Vulnerabilities in AI, Cloud Products

articles.title: Workday is using TypeSafe's Jev to build user interfaces on the fly
articles.text:
Workday is using TypeSafe’s Jev to build user interfaces on the fly
Workday on Tuesday made Sana, its AI assistant, the new home screen for its HR, finance, and IT software. If you’re not an HR pro, that may not be all that exciting for you, but the way the team built this is maybe one of the most interesting use cases of Jev, TypeSafe’s decision model. Workday is building the user interface on the fly — and all of that is managed by Jev.
In a demo during a press briefing ahead of the announcement, a question about a paycheck brought up a card with the amount hidden behind a click, for example, while a request for time off produced a date picker, with Sana filling in the rest of the form.
Sana, which Workday bought for $1.1 billion last year, is available now, and admins can roll it out to their users without making it the default.
Picking components instead of writing them
Joel Hellermark, Workday’s chief AI officer and Sana’s founder, said in a press briefing that the usual approach to generative UI, in which a model generates the full interface, is “quite slow.”
“If you use a classification model instead and you just give it all of the design components to pick from, you can literally do it instantly,” he said.
Workday gave Jev every atomic component in its design system and hard-coded none of the selection logic, Hellermark said, though the team also had to get data preloading right. In the demo, the paycheck card appeared before he finished typing, for example.
TypeSafe claims Jev answers in 70 to 500 milliseconds, which makes it ideal for this kind of real-time use case.
In many cases, Hellermark said, AI that works through real interface elements does significantly better than pure back-and-forth chat.
A model built to choose
According to TypeSafe, developers send Jev application data and a set of typed questions, and it returns a pick from a list of up to 255 options, a score, or a yes-or-no answer, each with a probability attached. It doesn’t generate text.
TypeSafe launched Jev on Sept. 15 with a $40 million seed round led by DCVC. On Friday, it said it raised an $870 million Series A, led by Andreessen Horowitz, at a $7.5 billion valuation. TypeSafe says a third of the Fortune 500 already use Jev but hasn’t named them. Andreessen Horowitz’s own announcement puts the figure at 25 percent, and TypeSafe’s only published case study features Jack & Jill, an AI recruiting marketplace.
There is no dearth of competition in this field, of course. OpenAI, Amazon, Cloudflare, and Perplexity have already shipped their decision models too, with Microsoft following on last week.
A pattern developers are already testing
Using Jev and similar models for building user interfaces isn’t completely new, though. CopilotKit, an open source framework for adding AI copilots to apps, published a recipe in which Jev picks which prebuilt panel to show, with an OpenAI model as the fallback.
Vercel Labs is testing a Jev mode in json-render, its framework for rendering AI-generated UIs from developer-defined components.
Andrew King, who leads solutions architecture at app developer Very Good Ventures, wrote last month that handing every closed question (one with a fixed set of answers) to Jev cut his generative dashboard’s median render time to 3.8 seconds, from 29 seconds with a frontier model composing it. His tests ran on synthetic data.
“A shape nobody anticipated cannot appear on screen,” King writes. Anything Jev answers with less than 50 percent confidence goes to a language model instead, a setup he calls “a cage with a door.”
In a test on OpenRouter’s blog using the Banking77 intent-classification set, Jev answered in a median 175 milliseconds and scored 81 percent accuracy. Claude Opus 5 scored 84.4 percent but took 2.3 seconds and cost about 22 times as much.
TypeSafe’s own documentation says Jev struggles with counting, arithmetic, and dates, leans toward whichever option is listed first, and doesn’t treat injected content as hostile by default.
Workday hasn’t said how large its design system is or what Sana does when no combination of components fits. King wrote in September that he was keeping client data off Jev because the vendor was “weeks old with no published security certification yet.” TypeSafe now offers a SOC 2 Type II report on request.
What leaves Workday
Workday recently added TypeSafe to its list of subprocessors, the outside companies that can process customer data (the ones you only think about when a SaaS service you subscribe to emails you about a change of subprocessors that you promptly forget). This entry, it’s worth noting, covers all of Workday’s product lines, not just Sana, for natural language processing, intent classification, and confidence scoring.
According to TypeSafe, Jev runs only on its hosted API and processes data in the U.S., and the company offers zero data retention to enterprise customers.
Staying inside Workday
Hellermark also showed Sana working inside Anthropic’s Claude. That’s an AI-to-AI integration, Gerrit Kazmaier, Workday’s president of product and technology, said in the briefing, and users lose the Jev-driven interface and some context along the way.
Workday’s May partnership with Google Cloud already covers A2UI, Google’s spec for agents to describe interfaces that host apps then render. MCP Apps, a Model Context Protocol extension, brings interactive UI into Claude and ChatGPT. Neither shows up in Workday’s announcements this week, so for now, it seems, employees who reach Sana through Claude get the conversation without the date picker.

articles.title: Un micro caché dans du papier toilette chez OpenAI : un ingénieur saoudien arrêté par le FBI
articles.text:
Un enregistreur branché sur un port USB derrière un téléviseur et dissimulé dans… du papier toilette. C’est le dispositif découvert le 30 septembre dans une salle de réunion d’OpenAI, à San Francisco, a annoncé la firme sur X. Un endroit où se discutent des informations confidentielles sur les recherches, les futurs produits et la stratégie du créateur de ChatGPT.
L’affaire a été rendue publique le 13 octobre 2026 par les autorités américaines. Quatre jours plus tôt, le FBI avait arrêté Abdulrahman Alfozan, un ingénieur saoudien de 35 ans employé par OpenAI depuis juillet 2025, soupçonné d’avoir installé l’appareil. L’entreprise affirme que ses propres modèles d’intelligence artificielle l’ont aidée à remonter jusqu’à lui.
Un micro derrière le téléviseur, un autre dans un sac
Selon le communiqué de presse de la justice américaine, OpenAI situe l’installation du dispositif autour du 28 septembre. Les données stockées sur l’appareil étaient chiffrées.
Des images de vidéosurveillance montreraient l’ingénieur à proximité de la salle à plusieurs reprises avant la découverte de l’enregistreur, alors qu’il n’était autorisé ni à y accéder ni à participer aux réunions. Selon l’accusation, ces échanges portaient notamment sur des recherches confidentielles, les futurs produits et les avancées techniques d’OpenAI, mais aussi sur ses relations avec les pouvoirs publics et ses partenaires commerciaux.
Le 5 octobre, l’ingénieur aurait également été filmé regardant derrière le téléviseur. Ce même jour, les équipes de sécurité ont retrouvé un second enregistreur similaire dans un sac laissé sans surveillance, qui contenait également ses papiers d’identité.
Abdulrahman Alfozan a comparu devant la justice fédérale le 13 octobre. Il est poursuivi pour interception ou tentative d’interception de communications orales et reste présumé innocent.
À ces découvertes s’ajoutent des recherches effectuées avec des outils numériques. Selon les autorités, l’ingénieur s’était renseigné sur les salles et les lieux des réunions de dirigeants à l’aide d’un « outil de productivité ».
Un compte de chatbot associé à son épouse, partageant plusieurs identifiants et caractéristiques avec son propre compte, aurait également posé des questions sur la fabrication et la dissimulation d’un enregistreur, l’écoute à distance et le chiffrement de son stockage. Certaines requêtes mentionnaient même l’adresse MAC, un identifiant réseau propre à l’appareil retrouvé. Le communiqué ne précise pas quel chatbot était utilisé.
OpenAI met en avant le rôle de ses IA
L’intelligence artificielle aurait aussi servi à enquêter. Dans son message publié sur X, OpenAI explique avoir mobilisé ses modèles pour comprendre le dispositif et son origine, contribuant à identifier l’employé. L’entreprise présente l’affaire comme un exemple de la manière dont ses technologies peuvent aider à traiter des menaces de sécurité.
Difficile, toutefois, de savoir quelle place leur accorder dans la résolution de l’affaire. OpenAI ne précise ni les modèles utilisés, ni ce qu’ils ont permis de découvrir. Les éléments présentés par les autorités comprennent aussi des indices très concrets, des images de vidéosurveillance au deuxième appareil retrouvé dans le sac.
Le FBI donne à l’affaire une portée plus large. Son directeur, Kash Patel, présente la protection des technologies d’IA américaines comme une priorité de contre-espionnage. Aucun lien avec un État n’est cependant établi dans les éléments rendus publics. La nationalité du suspect ne permet donc pas de conclure à une opération menée pour le compte de l’Arabie saoudite.
OpenAI affirme enfin n’avoir aucun indice, à ce stade, d’accès indu ou d’exfiltration des paramètres de ses modèles, de son code source ou des données de ses clients. L’entreprise indique avoir licencié l’ingénieur. S’il est reconnu coupable, il encourt jusqu’à cinq ans de prison et 250 000 dollars d’amende, ainsi que trois ans de liberté surveillée.

articles.title: ZCS Command Injection via SNMP Handlers Enables Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution
articles.text:
A critical remote command execution vulnerability affecting the Zimbra Collaboration Suite mail platform has come under active, widespread exploitation, allowing adversaries to harvest complete mailbox archives and persistent authentication credentials without prior system access.
The defect, tracked as CVE-2026-73570, carries a CVSS score of 8.9 and stems from improper input sanitisation inside the platform's SNMP notification subsystem. When paired with public-facing mail transfer agents, the pipeline permits unauthenticated remote attackers to inject arbitrary operating system commands that execute under the context of the underlying Zimbra operating system user account.
Maintainer Synacor initially addressed the vulnerability quietly in Zimbra Collaboration Suite version 10.1.20 on July 20, 2026, but delayed public disclosure until August 13, 2026. During this multi-week disclosure lag, adversaries reverse-engineered the binary changes and launched scanning campaigns against public instances. Telemetry captured by Microsoft and Polish national cybersecurity agency CERT Polska confirmed that threat groups actively probed enterprise mail infrastructure throughout late July and August, deploying backdoors before most operations teams recognised the severity of the patch.
At the protocol level, the flaw sits within the path where Postfix and upstream mail services hand off operational status alerts to the internal Simple Network Management Protocol daemon. Zimbra installs an optional telemetry service package, designated as zimbra-snmp, which runs the swatchdog log monitoring utility to scan log lines and dispatch snmptrap alerts. When inbound SMTP transactions parse user-controlled header parameters, specifically crafted envelope fields are logged directly into local syslog targets without shell argument sanitisation.
The swatchdog daemon watches these logs using regular expression pattern rules. Once matched, it interpolates the captured text variables into an unquoted string passed directly to a system shell execution call. Because characters such as semicolons, backticks, and pipes remain intact through the log parsing process, the external caller can append commands directly into the operating system trap execution string.
Image Source: Microsoft Blog Post
Observed exploitation begins with lightweight recon sweeps, where threat actors dispatch SMTP packets carrying shell logic designed to invoke out-of-band network calls via curl or nslookup. These callbacks confirm command execution before heavier payloads arrive. Once verification succeeds, attackers inject base64-encoded strings that write JSP web shells directly into web-accessible server directories, such as the Jetty application server root (/opt/zimbra/jetty/webapps/zimbra/).
With arbitrary file write and execution established within the Jetty container, operators execute zmprov command-line utilities natively available to the zimbra Unix user. This yields administrative LDAP tokens, authentication keys, and database credentials, unlocking access to export full user mailboxes into encrypted staging archives before exfiltration to external cloud buckets.
POST /zimbra/public/jsp_shell.jsp HTTP/1.1
Host: mail.target-enterprise.com
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
cmd=zmprov+getAllAccounts+-v+domain.com
zmmailbox -z -m user@domain.com getRestURL "//?fmt=tgz" > /tmp/backup.tgz
Remediating CVE-2026-73570 requires updating nodes to Zimbra version 10.1.20 or newer, which replaces shell-concatenated string execution within the monitoring subsystem with direct parameter arrays passed safely to system execve routines. For organizations unable to perform an immediate binary migration across multi-node clusters, maintainers recommend disabling the SNMP service package entirely to eliminate the vulnerable swatchdog loop.
su - zimbra
zmcontrol stop snmp
zmprov ms `zmhostname` -zimbraServiceEnabled snmp
Disabling SNMP halts outbound telemetry and automated performance trapping, which degrades central monitoring pipelines and cluster observability dashboards. However, operational intelligence from the Shadowserver Foundation indicates that approximately 274 compromised production instances were observed following disclosure, while roughly 10,000 public-facing Zimbra deployments remain exposed to scanning scripts. Systems teams running exposed mail gateways must treat unpatched servers as compromised, review Jetty deployment directories for unauthorized JSP files, rotate all LDAP and zimbra service account credentials, and restrict administrative endpoints to internal jump hosts.

articles.title: Sosh annonce une augmentation de prix sur un forfait : attention, vous pouvez refuser — Frandroid
articles.text:
La manœuvre est devenue un grand classique des opérateurs low cost. Vous vous abonnez à un prix très compétitif, sans limite apparente de durée pour votre offre, puis l’opérateur augmente discrètement le prix de votre forfait en ajoutant des options que vous n’avez pas demandé.
Red by SFR, B&You chez Bouygues Telecom ou encore Sosh pour Orange, ils sont tous devenus experts du sujet. Sosh vient d’en donner un nouvel exemple.
3 euros de plus par mois, refusable
Sosh a envoyé un email à certains abonnés pour les prévenir. Intitulé « Important : votre forfait évolue », l’opérateur y annonce : « vous avez un forfait Sosh qui envoie déjà du lourd, mais on vous en propose plus à un tarif exclusif qui vous est réservé ».
Dans le mail reçu par la rédaction, Sosh propose de passer d’un forfait 100 Go en 4G à un forfait 130 Go en 5G, pour 3 euros de plus par mois, soit 14 euros par mois.
L’augmentation sera effective le 15 décembre 2026, et Sosh permet de refuser le changement avant le 15 novembre 2026.
Pour cela, vous devez vous connecter sur votre espace client Sosh, et indiquer votre refus de l’augmentation.
Selon le dernier observatoire de l’Arcep, publié le 8 octobre, un client mobile consomme en moyenne 19,3 Go par mois. Les 100 Go actuels couvrent déjà plus de cinq fois cette moyenne : les 30 Go supplémentaires ne serviront qu’aux très gros consommateurs, et la 5G qu’aux abonnés équipés d’un smartphone compatible.

articles.title: Menacée de fermeture, la célèbre plateforme Character.AI dépose le bilan
articles.text:
Character.AI s’est placé sous la protection du Chapter 11 aux États-Unis et cherche désormais un repreneur. Disney a posé une première offre à 20 millions de dollars sur certains actifs, mais la plateforme pourrait disparaître si la procédure n’aboutit pas à une solution permettant de poursuivre son activité.
Le service de chatbot IA fonctionne toujours, abonnements payants compris, mais son avenir se joue désormais devant un tribunal américain. En effet, la société vient d’engager une procédure de restructuration sous Chapter 11 et prévoit une vente de ses actifs qui devrait se conclure entre fin novembre et début décembre prochains.
Faute d’une offre de reprise permettant de maintenir le service, la plateforme pourrait tout simplement fermer. Un scénario assez spectaculaire pour l’une des premières start-up à avoir popularisé les conversations avec des personnages alimentés par l’IA.
Disney ouvre les enchères sans racheter Character.AI
Le groupe propose 20 millions de dollars pour une licence perpétuelle et non exclusive sur une partie de la propriété intellectuelle de Character.AI ainsi que certains droits détenus par l’entreprise. L’accord prévoit également des services de transition assurés avec d’anciens salariés de la start-up recrutés par Disney.
Il ne s’agit donc pas d’un rachat de la plateforme pour 20 millions de dollars. D’autres candidats peuvent présenter une offre supérieure, et Character.AI cherche également des repreneurs susceptibles d’acquérir la totalité ou l’essentiel de ses actifs. Le tribunal devra encore approuver les modalités de l’enchère puis la transaction retenue.
Disney retrouve un ancien dirigeant de Character.AI
Cette proximité ne sort pas de nulle part. Disney a récemment nommé Karandeep Anand au poste de directeur technique. Avant de rejoindre le groupe, il avait dirigé Character.AI pendant un peu plus d’un an et accompagné son virage vers les microdramas.
Les relations entre les deux entreprises n’ont pourtant pas toujours été paisibles. Disney reprochait à Character.AI d’héberger des chatbots utilisant sans autorisation certains de ses personnages et lui avait adressé des mises en demeure pour défendre sa propriété intellectuelle.
La start-up avait déjà perdu une partie importante de ses forces en 2024. Google aurait à l’époque versé environ 2,7 milliards de dollars dans le cadre d’un accord de licence technologique accompagné du recrutement des cofondateurs Noam Shazeer et Daniel De Freitas ainsi que d’autres membres de l’équipe.
Character.AI évoquait depuis des difficultés juridiques, réglementaires et opérationnelles, alors que plusieurs procédures avaient également relancé les débats sur la sécurité de ses chatbots.
Les utilisateurs peuvent déjà sauvegarder leurs données
Dans l’immédiat, rien ne change pour les abonnés. Character.AI continue de fonctionner normalement et la facturation reste active. L’entreprise prévoit de prévenir ses abonnés à l’avance si la procédure entraîne une modification des fonctions payantes.
Les utilisateurs gardent la possibilité de supprimer leur compte ou d’exporter leurs données depuis le site et l’application. Ceux qui souhaitent conserver certaines conversations ont donc intérêt à les sauvegarder dès maintenant…

articles.title: The unfinished business of a startup's collapse
articles.text:
First published on October 11, 2026
Image Source: TechCabal
Koko Networks raised more than $100 million from international investors to sell subsidised clean cooking stoves, relying on carbon credit sales to help cover their costs. Copia Global raised $123 million to bring e-commerce to smaller towns. Both businesses built sizeable operations around costly problems in African markets. When they collapsed, the question became how much money was left to repay those who had financed their growth.
In February 2026, the administrators of Copia estimated the realisable value of its assets at KES 206.6 million ($1.6 million), while its liabilities were considerably greater than that figure. Similarly, Koko Networks (UK) Limited had accumulated significant debt as a result of regulatory and commercial problems that had disrupted its carbon credit business.
The two failures expose a less visible side of venture capital. Raising millions and reaching customers does not guarantee that a business will have enough cash or saleable assets to meet its obligations. When the money runs out, investors are not the only ones who lose. Suppliers, employees and lenders must pursue claims against what remains, often through lengthy court proceedings that determine who gets paid and how much.
Read smart insights about Francophone Africa’s tech ecosystem—weekly.
When growth does not leave enough behind
Copia entered administration in May 2024 after struggling to sustain its agent-based e-commerce model. The company allowed customers in smaller towns to order goods through local agents. Its operations required warehouses, logistics, inventory, and working capital to move products from suppliers to customers.
The model addressed a real distribution problem, but it also carried costs that persisted when sales or funding weakened. Suppliers still expected payment, inventory needed financing, and logistics infrastructure required money to operate.
On September 17, 2026, the High Court in Nairobi ordered Copia into liquidation, appointing its existing KPMG administrators, Julius Mumo Ngonga and Anthony Makenzi Muthusi, as joint liquidators. Copia had KES 206.6 million ($1.6 million) in estimated realisable assets, against KES 169.5 million ($1.3 million) in creditor claims and administration costs, before preferential claims and other costs.
Koko, on the other hand, sold subsidised bioethanol stoves and fuel to households that might otherwise rely on charcoal or kerosene, using revenue from carbon credit sales to help cover the cost.
The model depended on selling credits generated by its Kenyan operations in international markets. Access to higher-priced compliance markets required government authorisation. Kenya did not grant the required approval, cutting off a route to market that Koko needed to support its financial model.
Koko Networks (UK) Limited reported turnover of £39.8 million ($50.5 million) in 2024, up from £1.8 million ($2.3 million) a year earlier. It still recorded a £14 million ($17.8 million) loss and accumulated deficits of £104.6 million ($132.8 million), according to its accounts.
The UK entity entered administration in February 2026, with PwC appointed as administrator. Its administrators later struggled to find a buyer for the company’s carbon credits, which were valued at £274,992, according to Business Daily.
Copia struggled to sustain a costly distribution network, while Koko’s revenue depended on regulatory approval and international carbon markets. Their failures show why funding, customer numbers and commercial reach cannot compensate for weak margins, insufficient working capital or exposure to risks a company cannot control.
Who gets paid when a startup fails?
Insolvency proceedings determine whether a distressed company can be rescued or whether its assets should be sold to repay creditors. When liquidation becomes necessary, the proceeds are distributed according to legal priorities. Secured creditors can claim against assets covered by their security, while certain employee and tax claims may receive preferential treatment. Ordinary unsecured suppliers generally rank further down the repayment queue.
Copia’s liquidation proceedings show how the process can become contentious. Tuffsteel Limited, an unsecured creditor, told the High Court it was owed KES 13.3 million ($103,000) for supplies. Jastan Traders Limited, which provided transport services, claimed KES 793,022 ($6,100).
Both challenged aspects of the proposed liquidation process. Tuffsteel sought additional safeguards and an independent forensic investigation into the company’s affairs, including asset transfers and related-party transactions. The creditors also questioned the reported transfer of Copia’s brand, intellectual property and transactional data to US-registered Copia Holdings.
These were creditor concerns, not judicial findings that assets had been improperly transferred. Justice Rhoda Rutto of the Kenya High Court dismissed the applications for additional orders and appointed the existing administrators as liquidators. The ruling allowed the liquidation to proceed under the existing practitioners.
The dispute shows why insolvency involves more than selling assets. Creditors also want to know what the company owns, how assets have been handled and whether the process protects their interests. The court must weigh those concerns against the costs and delays further proceedings can create.
Suppliers that extended credit or delivered goods on the expectation of payment under ordinary commercial terms can be left recovering only a fraction of what they are owed when a customer collapses.
When a corporate structure complicates recovery
Technology groups often operate through several legal entities, with one owning intellectual property, another running local operations and a third borrowing money or selling products internationally. Although the group may function as one business, its assets and liabilities remain legally separate.
Koko’s UK company relied on carbon credits generated by its Kenyan operations, leaving it exposed when regulatory barriers disrupted access to international markets. Its administration and the Kenyan insolvency proceedings remained separate legal processes despite their commercial links.
Copia’s creditors, meanwhile, questioned the transfer of intellectual property and customer data to Copia Holdings. The court dismissed their request for additional safeguards, but the dispute raised questions about asset ownership and creditor recovery.
Creditors cannot automatically claim assets held by another company in the same group. Guarantees, security arrangements and intercompany obligations may provide routes to recovery, but these depend on the relevant agreements and law.
The separation can leave creditors with limited prospects for recovery, even when the wider business holds valuable intellectual property, customer relationships, or other assets. Creditors can recover assets held elsewhere in the group only where the relevant legal arrangements allow it.
The cost of venture-backed failure
Copia and Koko expose distinct weaknesses in businesses built to solve costly problems, from Copia’s need for sufficient margins and working capital to Koko’s dependence on carbon-credit revenue and regulatory approval.
Their failures also spread losses across investors, employees, suppliers and lenders, with each group facing different prospects of recovery. Employees may pursue unpaid entitlements, suppliers can be left with unpaid invoices, and lenders may seek repayment from secured assets or companies that guaranteed the debt.
Creditors’ recoveries depend on the assets realised, the costs of insolvency, the validity of their claims and their legal priority. Neither company’s proceedings establish how much every creditor will ultimately receive.
These cases raise questions about how venture-backed growth distributes risk. Investors finance expansion, while suppliers and employees help sustain it, yet the latter may have far less protection when a company runs out of money.
The two startups show how the risks built into a startup’s business model can fall on creditors when the company fails. Founders and investors may drive expansion, but suppliers, employees and lenders can end up absorbing losses when margins prove too thin, working capital runs short or regulatory approval fails to materialise.

articles.title: Microsoft closes a worrying Windows 11 account bypass hack — all it took was one click
articles.text:
Microsoft closes a worrying Windows 11 account bypass hack — all it took was one click
'Learn more' account bypass hack fixed
- Clicking 'Learn more' would skip Microsoft account demands when setting up Windows 11
- It now shows user data policies, so you'll have to sign in with your account (or create one)
- Having an account can make certain things easier, but it's one less choice for consumers
Microsoft has finally fixed one of the easiest ways for attackers to bypass its account requirements when installing Windows 11, but it's bad news for anybody who didn't want to sign in with – or create – a Microsoft account during setup.
Previously, users only had to click the 'Learn more' hyperlink on the sign-in screen to be taken to a local account creation screen.
Ultimately, it marks another step in the company's ongoing efforts to make Microsoft accounts mandatory during the initial setup of Windows 11 on consumer PCs.
Microsoft wants you to use an account to activate Windows 11
Before the fix, users could click the 'Learn more' link and be taken to a screen that allowed them to enter a local username, create a password, configure security questions and complete Windows 11 setup without ever entering their Microsoft username or password.
Instead, the link now opens a page that explains how the company managers user data.
The change "has been recently quietly patched server side," Bob Pony said in a Bluesky post after revealing that "a new method for skipping the mandatory Microsoft Account login in Windows 11 Home Edition has been discovered" just one month ago.
Local accounts remain supported to a certain degree, but creating them either requires technical knowledge to use a third-party tool or command-line methods, or enterprise versions of Windows rather than consumer-grade operating systems.

articles.title: The traditional PC layout might not be the best: unusual GPU placement cuts temperatures by 17°C
articles.text:
In a nutshell: PC builders have long tried to find the most optimal cooling setups for their components, moving around fans, cables, etc. to find the best configurations. A YouTube channel decided to try something a little different: moving the components themselves. This included shifting the GPU next to a case's side-intake, which resulted in a 17-degree drop in temperatures.
The experiment was carried out by TrashBench, which used an Asus ROG Strix RTX 3080 inside a dual-chamber case. The cooling came from three side-intake fans, a rear exhaust, and a top-mounted 360mm CPU AIO.
The idea was to change component placement without moving the case fans. PCIe riser cables were used so the graphics card could be moved away from its usual slot on the motherboard.
Testing involved looping 3DMark Time Spy alongside 7-Zip running on 12 CPU threads. All fans stayed at fixed RPMs, with each configuration tested for ten minutes and temperatures averaged over the final five.
The GPU's first position was on the case floor, which required the removal of the bottom mesh because it touched the card's fans. GPU temperatures barely changed, but the CPU and motherboard VRM dropped around 4°C and 7°C, respectively. Conventional vertical mounting slightly worsened GPU temperatures while modestly improving everything else.
However, placing the card directly against the side intake made all the difference. GPU core temperatures fell 16.7°C, the hotspot dropped 19.3°C, and VRAM cooled by 14°C. Motherboard VRMs also dropped around 8°C, while the CPU warmed just 1.1°C.
Moving the card behind those intake fans, into the rear chamber, improved on stock temperatures but couldn't match the previous arrangement.
Next came the CPU. Relocating its radiator would have introduced another variable, so TrashBench placed the GPU back in its usual position and reversed the radiator fans from exhaust to intake. CPU temperatures dropped about 6°C, but the graphics card suffered from the radiator's warm exhaust.
Combining the intake radiator with the GPU beside the side intake improved both components over stock. It led to a 3.3°C reduction in CPU temperature and a 14°C cooler GPU hotspot, sacrificing some GPU cooling for a better overall balance.
TrashBench acknowledges that the experiment wasn't rigorously scientific, and different cases, fans, and fan positions will likely change the results. But as the channel points out, it illustrates how the normal PC layout might not be the best one.
TrashBench carries out lots of experiments like these. Last year, it strapped dual CPU tower coolers to an RTX 2060, cutting temperatures by 31°C.

articles.title: Cisco's OCP message: The network is now AI's critical path, and openness is the price of admission - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Cisco’s OCP message: The network is now AI’s critical path, and openness is the price of admission
For most of its history, Cisco Systems Inc. won by building vertically integrated network products and asking customers to buy all of it. The company did very well with that model. Security, meanwhile, was something Cisco sold as a separate product line rather than something that was inherent to its infrastructure. Patching a core switch meant scheduling a maintenance window, crossing your fingers and hoping nothing broke.
Under Chief Product Officer Jeetu Patel, Cisco has moved away from that model and embraced openness. That’s why I found Cisco’s announcements at this week’s Open Compute Project Global Summit in San Jose more interesting for what they reveal about the company than for the products themselves.
As Mike Wheatley outlined in his SiliconANGLE post, Cisco rolled out a new pluggable optics form factor with Nvidia Corp., shipped its first Silicon One G300 systems, introduced the G302 top-of-rack chip and a new out-of-band management platform, and brought its Live Protect runtime security capability to SONiC. His post detailed the announcements, but it’s worth a deeper look at why these matter for artificial intelligence and what they say about a Cisco trying to be both open and secure, neither of which were strengths before Patel.
The network is now in the critical path of AI
During the event’s pre-briefing, Cisco Senior Vice President of Engineering Will Eatherton discussed the problem the company is trying to solve. A few years ago, a large training run used hundreds of graphics processing units. Today, the largest clusters use hundreds of thousands of GPUs. Cisco cited Epoch AI data showing that projects that once fit in one or two buildings now span campuses, metros and regions, largely because that’s where power and real estate are available.
This changes the role of the network. In a traditional data center interconnect, the wide-area network carries many small, independent flows, and a network hiccup affects a single application or user. In large-scale deployments, the network needs to “scale-across” and carry a small number of massive, synchronized flows between accelerators working on the same job.
As Rakesh Chopra, Cisco Fellow and senior vice president of silicon and systems architecture, explained on the call, scale-across puts the long-haul network “directly in line with the workload performance.” If a link slows down, GPUs sit idle, and idle GPUs are the most expensive waste in information technology today.
That’s the context for Cisco’s OCP news. The Ultra-Dense Small Form Factor Pluggable, or USFP (pictured), is the first pluggable module designed for 400-gigabit-per-lane signaling, delivering up to 12.8 Tbps and about four times the bandwidth density of today’s leading modules. The key word is pluggable.
Cisco’s optics team made a fair point on the call: the competing XPO approach requires liquid cooling, which no optic in the industry needs today, and it creates real headaches when handling, replacing and validating modules. Keeping the operational model familiar while doubling the lane rate is the kind of pragmatic engineering that speeds adoption.
Equally important, USFP is being standardized as a multisource agreement with TE Connectivity and Amphenol. Optics is one of the highest cost and supply-chain constraints in AI buildouts, and a multivendor spec should drive higher volumes, greater competition,and lower prices.
Open at every layer is a big shift for Cisco
Cisco used the phrase “open at every layer of the stack” throughout the briefing, and Eatherton was clear that this “is not just a SONiC story.” That spans P4 programmability at the chip level, Nvidia Reference Architecture compliance in systems, OpenZR+ in optics, a choice of SONiC, FBOSS, a custom NOS, NX-OS, or IOS XR, third-party controllers, and the CNCF-governed Cilium ecosystem at the Kubernetes layer.
Eatherton called SONiC a first-class network operating system at Cisco and admitted that is “unusual for Cisco in the context of our 20- or 30-year history.” SONiC was once viewed within Cisco circles as a threat, a way for hyperscalers to commoditize switching. Now Cisco offers community builds, custom builds using its software development kit, and a turnkey Cisco-validated version under the Nexus One controller. Though this may seem inconsistent with Cisco’s past strategy, it aligns with Patel’s commitment to make Cisco unrecognizable from what it was two years ago.
The openness also extends to Cisco. Intelligent Collective Networking, the G300 capability that detects remote congestion and link failures and signals back to the ingress leaf in hardware time, is being standardized by the Internet Engineering Task Force rather than kept proprietary. Five years ago, I’m not sure Cisco would have given away something it considers a competitive advantage.
Why the change? Because the customers driving AI infrastructure spending will not accept lock-in. Hyperscalers have built their own operating systems and controllers, and the more mature neoclouds are now closely examining SONiC. Cisco is betting it can win on silicon, optics, systems engineering and support while letting customers choose what runs on top. Microsoft running Silicon One P200 systems in production and Alibaba deploying its in-house router on the P200 at massive scale suggest that bet is paying off.
Being open doesn’t hurt Cisco; it expands its addressable market. A Cisco that requires its full stack can sell only to customers that want it. A Cisco that is open at every layer can sell silicon to one customer, optics to another, and validated SONiC to a third.
Security that keeps the network running
The announcement I believe is most underappreciated is Live Protect for Cisco SONiC. Cisco cited data showing that the mean time to exploit a vulnerability has dropped from about nine months to roughly 10 hours. Eatherton noted that attackers now feed newly published CVEs into large language models and attempt exploits within hours.
That creates an impossible situation for AI network operators. Patching a switch typically requires a reboot, and rebooting a switch in a fabric running a multiweek training job across thousands of GPUs is not something anyone wants to do on short notice. So operators either risk an outage or a breach.
Live Protect addresses this by applying a “shield,” a compensating control, to the live system at the kernel level without downtime or rebooting. The switch is protected immediately, and the patch can be applied during a planned window. Cisco has had this capability in NX-OS for about a year and is bringing it to Cisco-validated SONiC on Nexus One, with availability targeted for the second quarter of 2027.
There are two important aspects to this. First, it reflects Cisco’s move to build security into the infrastructure rather than bolt it on, a shift the company has long discussed but often struggled to deliver, and now appears to be delivering. Second, it brings Cisco’s security engineering to an open operating system.
One criticism of SONiC has been its lack of enterprise-grade security and support, and closing that gap makes SONiC viable beyond the largest hyperscalers. With line-rate, quantum-resilient encryption built into the P200, Cisco now has a security story for AI infrastructure it simply didn’t have a few years ago.
Final thoughts
AI infrastructure is being built under conditions that punish both lock-in and downtime. Cisco’s OCP announcements address both issues and show that the company understands the AI market won’t be won the way the enterprise campus was.
For infrastructure leaders building AI capacity, my advice is to evaluate the network on job completion time and GPU utilization, not port speeds alone; to require open interfaces at the operating system and controller layers so you keep your options; and to ask every vendor how it will protect production fabrics during the hours between a CVE disclosure and a maintenance window.
Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

articles.title: German robotics unicorn NEURA launches Neuron AI to advance Physical AI and humanoid robotics | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Metzingen-based NEURA Robotics today introduced Neuron AI, its multimodal foundation model for Physical AI – combining 3D vision, touch, audio, robot state and language with memory – enabling their robots to act on information beyond what the camera sees and even retain context when it disappears from view.
This comes off the back of their previously announced a Series C of up to €1.2 billion in June 2026, following its €120 million Series B in 2025, to support the development and deployment of cognitive robotics, shared intelligence infrastructure and Physical AI systems such as Neuron AI.
“An intelligent robot needs a brain that brings its senses together and remembers what happened,” says David Reger, Founder and CEO of NEURA Robotics. “With Neuron AI, we are building the brain of the physical world: Physical AI that turns human expertise and physical experience into capabilities robots can learn and apply. Developed in Germany, built for the world.”
This AI launch follows a series of European investments in Physical AI and industrial robotics during 2026.
In Germany, Stuttgart-based Sereact secured €93 million to expand its AI-powered robotics platform, while Munich-based RobCo raised €89.2 million for industrial automation.
Elsewhere, London-based Humanoid raised €133 million, Barcelona-based THEKER secured €73 million, and Norway- and US-based Trener Robotics announced €26 million, bringing the total relevant funding in Europe across 2026 to approximately €414.2 million (not including Neura’s funding).
Neuron AI was developed and trained in-house in Metzingen, Germany. Founded in 2019, NEURA brings together the robots, hands, sensing technology, data infrastructure and AI development needed to connect model training with physical performance.
Germany’s industrial base provides an important setting for this work: complex manufacturing processes, specialised expertise and demanding operating environments. Data partnerships with industrial companies including Schaeffler and Bosch complement training in the NEURA Gyms.
The NEURA Gyms connect data collection, skill training and benchmarking before deployment. Training data and skills developed in the Gyms inform subsequent model releases.
For NEURA, this proximity connects the development of Physical AI with the knowledge and practical requirements of the industries it is intended to serve.
Rather than treating each sensor as a separate input, Neuron AI encodes 3D vision, tactile and force data, audio, robot state and language, aligns them in one shared space over time, and turns them into a single stream of action.
The company explains that multisensory perception matters most for tasks that cameras cannot solve on their own. When a robot opens a lock, only sound and touch confirm that it is really open. With touch, a robot can grasp objects it cannot see. The additional senses also improve tasks that vision can already handle: in welding, for example, the quality of a seam can be judged from the sound of the process.
In addition, Neuron AI has a memory function. To act in the physical world, a robot needs a sense of cause and effect and object permanence, the ability to remember objects when they are out of sight, which humans acquire in their first two years of life.
Unlike purely digital AI, a robot acts in a continuous physical world and must keep track of objects and the consequences of its own actions over time, often without seeing them. NEURA adapted the model’s architecture specifically to introduce memory and trains it on dedicated datasets that make use of it.
Neuron AI is trained on three complementary sources of physical experience:
- Real-world robot data: Robots across different embodiments perform tasks in NEURA Gyms, NEURA’s training infrastructure for cognitive robots and Physical AI and real-world environments, generating synchronised vision, touch, force, audio and movement data.
- Simulation-amplified data: NEURA’s Data Amplifier and simulation stack expand training data through simulated variations of tasks and environments.
- Human demonstration data: People wearing sensor-equipped data suits capture human movements and task demonstrations, bringing practical expertise into the training pipeline.
Together, these pillars combine real physical interactions, simulated variation and human know-how to train a shared foundation across five NEURA robot embodiments, with different grippers and hands.
NEURA will demonstrate its humanoid robot 4NE1 (“For Anyone”) at NVIDIA GTC Berlin 2026 performing an eleven-minute laundry-handling sequence with the current version of Neuron AI.
The sequence includes sorting laundry, loading a washing machine, closing and reopening it, unloading it and transferring the laundry to a dryer, without human intervention.

articles.title: Gana diamantes y skins gratis en Free Fire canjeando los códigos disponibles el 13 de octubre de 2026
articles.text:
Garena habilitó una nueva serie de códigos para Free Fire que permite reclamar diamantes, skins de armas, trajes y otros objetos dentro del videojuego. Los beneficios están destinados a jugadores que tengan una cuenta registrada y vinculada con alguna de las plataformas autorizadas.
Como ocurre cada día, la difusión de estas combinaciones alfanuméricas concentra la atención de miles de usuarios. Los códigos tienen un número limitado de usos y su disponibilidad puede variar según la región, así que conviene validarlos antes de que expiren o alcancen el límite de canjes.
Cuáles son los códigos de Free Fire disponibles hoy 13 de octubre
Los códigos publicados para este 13 de octubre de 2026 combinan letras y números. Cada jugador debe ingresarlos sin alterar las mayúsculas ni cambiar el orden de los caracteres, porque un error puede impedir la validación del premio.
La lista difundida para la jornada incluye más de 20 alternativas. Los jugadores registrados pueden probar los siguientes códigos en el sistema oficial de recompensas de Free Fire:
- FM6N1B8V3C4X.
- FT4E9Y5U1I3O.
- 4N8M2XL9R1G3.
- FU1I5O3P7A9S.
- BR43FMAPYEZZ.
- FFCBRAXQTS9S.
- B1RK7C5ZL8YT.
- F7F9A3B2K6G8.
- UPQ7X5NMJ64V.
- H8YC4TN6VKQ9.
- FA3S7D5F1G9H.
- FFR4G3HM5YJN.
- 6KWMFJVMQQYG.
- FF6YH3BFD7VT.
- FZ5X1C7V9B2N.
- FQ9W2E1R7T5Y.
- 4ST1ZTBZBRP9.
- FP9O1I5U3Y2T.
- FE2R8T6Y4U1I.
- S9QK2L6VP3MR.
- FK3J9H5G1F7D.
En qué página hacer el canje de los códigos en Free Fire
El canje se realiza en el portal oficial de recompensas de Garena. Allí, el usuario debe iniciar sesión con una cuenta vinculada a Google, Facebook, Apple, Huawei o VK antes de introducir la combinación correspondiente.
Las cuentas de invitado no pueden participar del sistema. Una vez que el código fue aceptado, los artículos se acreditan en la cuenta del juego y suelen estar disponibles en un plazo de hasta 24 horas. El mensaje “código inválido o expirado” indica que la clave dejó de estar vigente o ya alcanzó su límite de uso.
Qué premios pueden obtener los jugadores de Free Fire
El sistema de canje de Garena contempla incentivos de distinto tipo. Entre los artículos que pueden aparecer figuran los diamantes, una de las monedas internas más solicitadas por los usuarios, además de atuendos, skins para armas, accesorios y objetos coleccionables.
Los diamantes permiten acceder a contenido dentro del juego, mientras que otros premios pueden modificar el aspecto del personaje, del equipamiento o de determinados elementos de la partida. Las recompensas dependen de cada código y no todos los usuarios reciben los mismos artículos.
Asimismo, en algunas fechas, los códigos habilitan artículos que no suelen formar parte de la tienda virtual. Es el caso de trajes temáticos, accesorios vinculados con celebraciones y objetos de edición limitada.
Cuáles requisitos y cuidados deben seguir los usuarios
Para acceder a los códigos es necesario contar con una cuenta formal de Free Fire vinculada a uno de los servicios autorizados. El videojuego debe estar instalado desde las tiendas oficiales: Google Play Store en dispositivos Android o App Store en equipos con sistema operativo iOS.
El teléfono o la tableta debe disponer de espacio de almacenamiento suficiente y una conexión estable a internet. Una interrupción durante el inicio de sesión o el envío de la clave puede impedir que el sistema complete la verificación.
Garena sugiere utilizar únicamente sus canales oficiales para descargar el juego y gestionar las recompensas. Las aplicaciones modificadas o instaladas desde sitios no autorizados pueden comprometer la seguridad de la cuenta y exponer información personal.
Qué riesgos implican el uso de aplicaciones piratas
Los programas descargados fuera de las tiendas habilitadas pueden contener modificaciones no verificadas. Ese tipo de archivos puede facilitar el robo de credenciales, el acceso a perfiles o la instalación de malware.
Las versiones ajenas a los canales oficiales tampoco reciben actualizaciones de seguridad de forma regular. Esto aumenta la exposición a errores corregidos en la aplicación legal y puede afectar tanto el funcionamiento del juego como la protección de los datos asociados a la cuenta.

articles.title: Wanze im Konferenzraum: FBI nimmt OpenAI-Mitarbeiter wegen Spionageverdachts fest
articles.text:
Wanze im Konferenzraum: FBI nimmt OpenAI-Mitarbeiter wegen Spionageverdachts fest
Ein Mitarbeiter des ChatGPT-Entwicklers OpenAI steht unter Verdacht, ein Abhörgerät in einem Konferenzraum der Firma platziert zu haben, in dem oft Geschäftsgeheimnisse besprochen werden. Der 35-jährige saudische Staatsbürger wurde festgenommen, wie die KI-Firma und das US-Justizministerium mitteilten. Die US-Bundespolizei FBI ermittelt zu dem Fall.
Das vor zwei Wochen entdeckte Aufnahmegerät war den Ermittlern zufolge etwa zwei Tage zuvor in dem Konferenzraum in San Francisco platziert worden. Es steckte demnach in der USB-Buchse eines Fernsehers, eingewickelt in Toilettenpapier. Der festgenommene Mitarbeiter wurde nach Angaben des Ministeriums Ende September von Sicherheitskameras in der Nähe des Konferenzraums gefilmt, zu dem er eigentlich keinen Zutritt hatte. Die Ermittler veröffentlichten auch ein Bild, auf dem zu sehen ist, wie er später versucht, hinter den Fernseher zu schauen.
OpenAI-Mitarbeiter hatte vorher KI-Chatbot befragt
Laut dem Ministerium wurden über einen Chatbot-Account der Ehefrau des OpenAI-Mitarbeiters Anfragen zu Aufnahme-Vorrichtungen gestellt. Im Chatverlauf fanden sich demnach auch Merkmale des im Konferenzraum entdeckten Abhörgeräts. Dem Mitarbeiter drohten bei einer Verurteilung bis zu fünf Jahre Haft und eine Strafe von bis zu 250.000 US-Dollar (etwa 225.000 Euro).
US-Geheimdienstkoordinator Jay Clayton betonte in der Mitteilung, der Fall zeige, wie wichtig es für die nationale Sicherheit der USA sei, den Wettlauf bei der Entwicklung Künstlicher Intelligenz zu gewinnen. Clayton war von Präsident Donald Trump auch mit einer zentralen Rolle bei der KI-Aufsicht betraut worden. Erst vor kurzem hatte ein nun als Whistleblower auftretender KI-Forscher die Vermutung geäußert, dass chinesische Spione die großen KI-Labore von OpenAI und Anthropic unterwandert hätten. Belege dafür präsentierte er nicht.

articles.title: The Download: open model trade-offs and geothermal power’s promise
articles.text:
The Download: open model trade-offs and geothermal power’s promise
Plus: A cyberattack overheated fridges at hundreds of French supermarkets.
This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
Open models have real benefits. Do they outweigh the risks?
Anthropic recently released a report arguing that a powerful new model released by the Chinese company Z.ai, poses a major cyberattack risk. Its core concern was that it is freely available for anyone to download and modify.
The warning was the latest flashpoint in a debate over whether frontier AI models should be open or kept behind the doors of frontier labs. Safety advocates warn that open models can be misused by bad actors, while supporters argue they could prevent a handful of companies from controlling this powerful technology.
Here’s why the debate over open AI is more complicated than it seems.
—Grace Huckins
This story is part of MIT Technology Review Explains, our series untangling the complex, messy world of technology to help you understand what’s coming next. Read more from the series here.
10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch: Fervo Energy and its plan to streamline geothermal power
Fervo Energy is one of MIT Technology Review’s10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch 2026, available exclusively to subscribers.
Fervo Energy wants to expand geothermal power beyond the handful of places where it has traditionally been practical. The company uses horizontal drilling and hydraulic fracturing to open pathways through underground rock, potentially making geothermal development possible in far more places.
Now, Fervo is betting that AI’s power boom will help scale up enhanced geothermal energy. With a $2.2 billion public offering and an expanded agreement with Google, it plans to build larger plants and drive down costs. But can its approach work beyond Utah and Nevada? Read the full story to find out.
—Eshan Raul

articles.title: IA tem menos regras que uma caixa de leite, diz Microsoft • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
IA tem menos regras que uma caixa de leite, diz Microsoft
Presidente Brad Smith compara IAs a produtos cotidianos, enquanto CEO Satya Nadella defende um “freio de emergência” para interromper modelos.
As inteligências artificiais estão sujeitas a menos exigências de segurança do que produtos cotidianos, como máquinas de lavar e caixas de leite. É o que afirma o presidente da Microsoft, Brad Smith, que defendeu regras mais rígidas e a criação de normas de monitoramento e responsabilização das empresas por acidentes.
Em entrevista à BBC, Smith disse que “toda caixa de leite que você vê na mercearia passa por regras de segurança e inspeção” e que, por isso, “sabemos que ele é seguro”. Para ele, é esse tipo de confiança que a indústria precisa gerar para a IA.
Entre as medidas que possibilitariam isso estão notificações de pessoas afetadas por incidentes e avaliações independentes de sistemas avançados antes da liberação pública. A defesa de regras mais rígidas também se soma à posição do CEO da Microsoft, Satya Nadella, favorável à criação de mecanismos para pausar ou desligar modelos de IA que apresentem comportamentos inesperados.
Em uma publicação no X, Nadella afirmou que as empresas precisam considerar a possibilidade de seus sistemas serem comprometidos e garantir que pessoas autorizadas possam interromper suas operações. “Devemos presumir que um modelo está comprometido e contê-lo desde o início”, escreveu o CEO.
“Pense nisso como um freio de emergência. Qualquer pessoa autorizada deve ser sempre capaz de pausar ou desligar um modelo no meio de uma tarefa. Modelos mais avançados exigirão tecnologias de contenção mais avançadas que precisamos padronizar.”
– Satya Nadella, CEO da Microsoft
O mecanismo, conhecido como kill switch, permitiria interromper uma tarefa caso o sistema representasse algum risco. Nadella também defende separar o modelo de IA dos mecanismos responsáveis por coordenar e executar suas ações, além de padronizar tecnologias de contenção.
A cobrança contrasta com a preferência do governo de Donald Trump por uma abordagem mais favorável à autorregulação do setor. O presidente dos Estados Unidos reuniu no fim de setembro representantes de gigantes da tecnologia, incluindo OpenAI, Anthropic, Google e Meta, para a assinatura de um compromisso de segurança que prevê colaboração com mecanismos de supervisão e auditorias.
Smith elogiou a iniciativa, mas afirmou que compromissos voluntários não são suficientes para garantir que todas as empresas adotem práticas responsáveis.
“É um bom passo, é um passo necessário… Mas não acho que seja suficiente por mais tempo […] as empresas boas farão o que você pede. São as companhias que não são responsáveis que devem nos preocupar.”
– Brad Smith, presidente da Microsoft
OpenAI, Anthropic e Meta estiveram entre as desenvolvedoras de IAs que afirmaram ter tido problemas com modelos em treinamento “fugindo” de ambientes de testes, acessando a internet e inclusive hackeando sistemas de terceiros, como no caso do repositório Hugging Face.
As revelações acabaram promovendo, ainda que indiretamente, as capacidades agênticas de alguns modelos e deram mais força aos críticos das práticas de segurança das empresas.

articles.title: Niobia takes the guesswork out of some of tech's most expensive mistakes | TechCrunch
articles.text:
San Francisco-based startup Niobia is betting big on a critical but often overlooked part of battery and chip making: helping engineers understand how and why things go wrong. Its AI software flags production defects and lets engineers ask a chatbot what caused them, aiming to deliver answers in minutes rather than days.
How it works (broadly): The company’s customers place AI agents on their production lines to look for defects, then loop in human engineers to work out what might cause a product to fail. The agents run on self-contained GPUs mounted directly on manufacturing equipment, much like a sensor. They can spot pinhole-sized flaws such as scratches. Niobia’s AI also gathers all the data in one place so engineers can ask a chatbot what went wrong and dig deeper into the cause.
Speed is so critical because chips and batteries are some of the world’s most important products, while also increasingly in short supply. As manufacturers continue to develop and improve their technologies, things inevitably go awry during research and development. Engineers then spend days or longer figuring out a fix before they can restart production. Each flaw or mistake can prove costly — sometimes running into the millions of dollars — and set back manufacturing timelines.
Niobia co-founders Gaurav Jha and Harveen Kaur both have PhDs in chemistry and have worked at chipmakers and battery manufacturers, giving them firsthand experience with the challenges within the industry. In a call ahead of TechCrunch Disrupt 2026, where the company is a Battlefield finalist, Jha explained that while what Niobia does is specialized, it serves a multibillion-dollar market that includes some of the biggest battery and semiconductor makers today.
“It’s extremely niche; maybe people will never know about it,” said Jha, speaking of the battery and chip manufacturing market that his company aims to serve. “But it’s like behind the scenes, this is powering everything… we just don’t see it in the regular world.”
“Every product around you, like glasses or shoes, slippers, wallets, and headphones — these processes touch every single part of it,” added Jha.
Niobia’s agents run on open source models that the company trains further with battery and chip research and other data. That training is what lets them identify pinhole-sized defects. Jha said that Niobia chose open source models largely because its customers don’t want their highly sensitive company information going into a public AI cloud where it might be used to train the model.
“None of our customers want their proprietary data to go to the cloud, even if we tell them it’s safe,” said Jha. The startup also outlines how it approaches cybersecurity, given the high-stakes race among adversarial nations to innovate in the battery and chip space. Niobia, for instance, lets its customers hold their own encryption keys so that the startup cannot decrypt the customers’ data.
Jha said that the company’s priority for now is to focus on three specialties, such as film coating, electroplating (which is coating a surface with metal using an electric current), and fluidized bed reaction (a chemical process where solid particles are suspended in a gas or liquid).
He said that the company also wants its technology to become more autonomous, with the eventual aim of building out a fully self-driving factory for its customers.
If you’re curious to learn more, Niobia will present onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt this afternoon in San Francisco. Join us to catch the company and the 19 startups against which it’s competing as part of our storied Startup Battlefield competition, happening today, Tuesday, through Thursday, October 15.

articles.title: Apple’s first smart display is the 7-inch HomeView for $299
articles.text:
Apple opened preorders for the HomeView smart home hub today.
The HomeView is a 7-inch smart display and speaker that aims to be a central access point for up to six members of a family to access and control Apple’s ecosystem of devices, apps, and the Siri generative AI chatbot that’s currently in beta.
Users can speak to HomeView to control smart home devices, such as, for example, telling Siri to close the smart blinds or activate smart locks. HomeView can also show a livestream for up to nine video feeds simultaneously.
“With a supported iCloud+ subscription, HomeView works with compatible cameras to deliver intelligent, end-to-end encrypted recognition of people, familiar faces, pets, packages, and vehicles, notifying the household the moment someone arrives at the front door. With video descriptions for HomeKit Secure Video footage, HomeView helps users quickly understand what happened in a video clip without even watching it,” Apple’s announcement said.
Competing with devices like the Amazon Echo Show, HomeView uses its integrated camera to identify who’s using it and show them their profile, which users can personalize with their preferred apps and widgets. Users can connect their HomeView profile to their Apple Intelligence-supporting iPhone or iPad and use the hub to access their Messages, Calendar, Reminders, and FaceTime.
“With an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad, Siri AI does more for each person—taking action across apps and surfacing relevant information from Messages and Calendar, playlists on Apple Music, and more by drawing on their personal context,” Apple’s announcement says.

articles.title: Fairphone’s latest repairable earbuds are smaller, lighter, and longer-lasting
articles.text:
Repairable, ethical phone brand Fairphone has released its second pair of earbuds. The Fairbuds 2 are just as repairable as the first generation, but deliver improved audio and almost twice the battery life. The Fairbuds 2 are out now in the UK and Europe from £99 / €119, and a US launch at $119 will follow on November 2nd.
Fairphone’s latest repairable earbuds are smaller, lighter, and longer-lasting
The Fairbuds 2 are just as repairable as the first pair, and are launching in the US.
The Fairbuds 2 have been redesigned from the ground up, moving to a stemmed design, available in black or green, and a case that’s 37 percent smaller than the first generation. Despite that shrinking hardware, Fairphone has almost doubled the buds’ battery life, which now totals 40 hours without active noise cancellation, with eight hours on the buds alone, dropping to six with ANC on. Charging is over USB-C, and takes a couple hours for a full top-up. Sadly Qi wireless charging isn’t supported — though it isn’t on Apple’s $129 AirPods 5 either.
I never used the original Fairbuds, but sound should be improved here thanks to new bio-cellulose dynamic drivers, though still at the same 11mm size, plus refined ANC and new support for the LDAC codec. Multipoint connectivity supports two devices at once, and a five-band EQ in the app lets you fine-tune audio.
I’ve been using the Fairbuds 2 for a couple of weeks, and while I wouldn’t say they’re the most polished or premium earbuds you’ll find for $120, I’ve got no real complaints either. They look great, the simple touch controls work well, and audio quality is good, if a little muddy at times, lacking the expansive sound stage of some other buds. The ANC has impressed me too, cancelling out most background noise I’ve wanted rid of.
Of course, the main reason to buy Fairbuds is the repairability, which remains relatively unique — though European legal changes will force other manufacturers to catch up soon. Here, Fairphone has concentrated on matching what it offered in the first Fairbuds, but that’s still impressive: the battery in each earbud can be removed in less than a minute without any tools, while a single T5 screw is all that’s between you and the cell in the case. Spare parts will be sold on Fairphone’s site, with a total of seven user-replaceable parts, including the eartips and sleeves. An IP54 rating guarantees some additional measure of protection against rain and sweat, though not complete waterproofing, and a three-year warranty should deliver a little extra peace of mind.
The other side of Fairphone’s promise is transparency about its production and materials. The company says that 49 percent of the materials in the Fairbuds 2 are “fair and recycled,” including recycled plastics and rare earth minerals, and cobalt, gold, and silver sourced with fair mining credits. It also says the buds themselves are assembled under fair working conditions.
Photography by Dominic Preston / The Verge

articles.title: Confirmado el regreso de 'The X-Files' con una nueva serie del director de 'Black Panther' y 'Sinners'
articles.text:
The X-Files, la icónica serie de FOX, prepara su regreso con una nueva versión de la mano de Ryan Coogler. Hulu ha dado el visto bueno a una nueva producción creada por el director de Black Panther y Sinners, que funcionará como una suerte de reboot del título original.
La nueva serie de The X-Files no tendrá a David Duchovny y Gillian Anderson como protagonistas, pero tampoco pondrá a nuevos actores en la piel de los icónicos Fox Mulder y Dana Scully. Esto significa que el proyecto presentará a dos nuevos personajes originales interpretados por Himesh Patel y Danielle Deadwyler.
De acuerdo con la sinopsis oficial de la nueva serie de The X-Files, Patel y Deadwyler darán vida a dos agentes del FBI muy diferentes, pero con una química muy especial, que son asignados a una división que lleva mucho tiempo cerrada y que se encarga de casos relacionados con fenómenos no explicados.
A primera vista, es lógico pensar que la serie de Ryan Coogler intentará replicar la dinámica original de Mulder y Scully. Sin embargo, no está claro si la nueva serie de The X-Files será un reboot total o si tomará algunos elementos del título original y lo reimaginará para un público más actual. Tampoco se sabe si Duchovny y Anderson pueden llegar a tener alguna participación invitada o si se busca hacer borrón y cuenta nueva a nivel argumental.
The X-Files tendrá nueva serie en Hulu
Además de Patel y Deadwyler, se espera que la nueva serie de The X-Files incluya a otras varias figuras de renombre en su reparto. Tales los casos de Steve Buscemi, Ben Foster y Amy Madigan, por solo citar algunos. Ryan Coogler no solo oficia de productor ejecutivo del proyecto, sino que también ha estado a cargo de escribir el guion y de dirigir el episodio piloto. El cargo de showrunner está en manos de Jennifer Yale.
Coogler se ha reconocido fanático de The X-Files, por lo que este proyecto guarda un lugar especial en su portfolio. "Lo que creó Chris Carter es algo especial, y quisimos honrar todo aquello que hizo que la serie original conectara con tanta gente, al tiempo que encontrábamos nuestra propia manera de adentrarnos en ese mundo. Danielle e Himesh, junto con el resto del reparto, han aportado perspectivas e interpretaciones sumamente originales a estos personajes, y ver cómo todo ello ha cobrado forma ha sido una de las partes más gratificantes de la experiencia", remarcó el cineasta.
Todavía no se sabe cuándo se lanzará la nueva serie de The X-Files. Lo que sí es un hecho es que se trata de una producción de Hulu, de modo que a nivel internacional su distribución estará disponible a través de Disney+.

articles.title: Workday makes Sana its new home for AI-driven HR and finance - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Workday makes Sana its new home for AI-driven HR and finance
Enterprise management software company Workday Inc. today announced that it wants to turn its existing knowledge of people, money and business rules into an operational foundation for agentic artificial intelligence tools.
At Workday Rising, the company’s annual global conference, the company said Sana, an agentic experience that brings together tasks, experiences, decisions, meetings and agent activity in one place, is becoming the new Workday Home. Employees will now work directly with Sana to get everything done.
The company also introduced Sana Concierge, a new service agent for human resources and information technology teams, which can resolve employee requests. It can handle onboarding, leave and password requests without passing these tedious twenty-minute tasks that can be automated to people, so they can focus on issues that require actual intuition.
The company also said Sana now adapts to each employee with a “Home” experience that can tailor itself to each employee role. This includes a user interface that can generate interactive applications using Jev, a cutting-edge model from TypeSafe AI that can create forms, calendars, approval cards, visualizations and interactive experiences in real time.
“AI is the new UI,” said Chief AI Officer Joel Hellermark. “Users shouldn’t have to decide which agent to use, just as they shouldn’t have to click between dozens of different systems. We’re giving our customers an agentic experience that opens up a whole new way to work.”
Included in this new experience, Workday’s executives demonstrated a shift from “copilot to autopilot” during a press briefing. This follows an industry trend alongside agentic automation, where many enterprises are giving employees access to AI agents that can act behind the scenes without needing to be touched and can be triggered when data changes or comes their way, instead of needing a chat interface.
For example, a recruiter autopilot agent prepares for a user’s day by checking open requisitions without waiting for the recruiter to log in, prepares outreach and surfaces candidates. Then the employee reviews outreach and chooses whether to advance candidates from the Sana interface; interview scheduling then runs autonomously. When the interview happens, the agent joins to listen in, prepare notes and uses recruiter feedback to influence future recommendations.
Work Intelligence and Decision Intelligence
As more teams begin to incorporate AI agents, models and tools, Workday announced two new platforms that help teams interact with AI experiences: Work Intelligence and Decision Intelligence.
Work Intelligence helps businesses build for AI by showing enterprise teams how AI tools and agents change work. Workday said AI rarely changes a whole job at once; it can change tasks, and as those tasks change, the underlying skills that matter also change. Every worker that interacts with AI is a data point for how the company can grow.
“Work Intelligence gives leaders the data to thoughtfully redesign roles, build careers and help people grow into what’s next,” said Vice President of Talent Management and Insights Nikki Helmer.
Workday said it can use its deep understanding of skills, delivered through its Skills Cloud, which is now used by more than 3,450 customers and built on an ontology of more than 75,000 canonical skills, to help leadership plan how to grow people as work changes. AI won’t just change existing roles; it will create new ones too.
Decision Intelligence lets HR and finance teams operate in the same space without curating and trading information across clunky communication channels, which often rely on dry reports pulled on a periodic basis. Too often, hiring decisions and procurement are based on analyst-produced reports that slowly go out of date; with an AI analyst on hand, those decisions are based on real-time business data. When the HR or finance team needs to look over a hiring plan, explain shifts in margins or respond to changes in business, they need trustworthy workforce and financial data but this data is often siloed.
As a result, Decision Intelligence performs analysis for both HR and Finance, allowing them to make “decisions,” thus the name, and compare using actionable, real-time data based on business needs.
For example, if HR wants to hire 50 people, it can ask whether the business still needs 50 based on the current workforce makeup. Decision Intelligence can look at the composition, skills that exist, roles that can be filled and how the hiring plan affects costs. Hiring managers and leadership can look at current workforce data instead of staring at a static report.
C1.ai joins Workday
In addition to the Sana updates, Workday announced that it agreed to acquire ConductorOne Inc., also known as C1.ai, an agentic identity platform for people and agents.
C1.ai provides a platform that governs people and agents so that they have the right access at the right time. This means that when a new agent or person is onboarded, they receive the roles they need, and only the roles they need, to get the job done, and then when they no longer need those permissions, they are turned off. This removes the stress of constantly monitoring every part of the system for potential rogue activity.
Without these kinds of controls, AI agents can become lawless, creating security and compliance risks across the entire enterprise.
“Today’s companies run on a combined workforce of people and AI agents,” said Workday President of Product and Technology Gerrit Kazmaier. “With C1.ai, we’ll help secure that workforce by managing and enforcing exactly who – and what – has access to connected apps and systems…”
C1.ai will combine with the Workday Agent System of Record, which already provides a place to see and manage agents. It will go beyond registering agents to also govern what they can access across Workday and other enterprise systems.
