articles.title: Mira el impactante tráiler de 'Narnia: El sobrino del mago', lo nuevo de Greta Gerwig
articles.text:
Greta Gerwig, la directora que logró aclamación mundial por Barbie, está de regreso con Narnia: El sobrino del mago. La nueva película de la saga Las crónicas de Narnia acaba de lanzar su esperado tráiler, revelando los primeros detalles de lo que veremos una vez que llegue a los cines (y luego a Netflix).
El primer tráiler de Narnia: El sobrino del mago nos permite conocer un poco más sobre la tónica que le imprimirá la cineasta a esta adaptación de la obra literaria de C. S. Lewis. Si bien ya habíamos visto algunas primeras imágenes de la producción a través de la revista Empire, faltaba ver realmente cómo se plasmaría la visión de Gerwig en el plano audiovisual.
La realidad es que Narnia: El sobrino del mago promete generar reacciones de lo más divisivas. Ya sucedió en el último tiempo cuando Greta Gerwig reveló que su idea para esta adaptación era la de crear una ópera rock con guiños a artistas icónicos como The Who y David Bowie. Lo mismo, cuando se anunció que la voz del león Aslan está a cargo de Meryl Streep. El primer tráiler llega con Stairway to Heaven de Led Zeppelin para generar gran impacto.
Si bien Narnia: El sobrino del mago será la cuarta película basada en los trabajos de Lewis, servirá como reinicio de la franquicia. Tengamos en cuenta que el libro El sobrino del mago es el primero de la saga en orden cronológico, aunque fue el sexto (y penúltimo) en publicarse en la década de 1950. A continuación puedes ver el tráiler de la adaptación cinematográfica.
Narnia: El sobrino del mago se estrenará en cines, y luego en Netflix
Si bien Netflix se encuentra detrás del desarrollo de Narnia: El sobrino del mago, la película llegará a los cines antes que a la plataforma de streaming. Esto se debe a un acuerdo de distribución que la empresa ha firmado con Columbia Pictures y Sony Pictures International.
Según la sinopsis oficial de Narnia: El sobrino del mago, al tocar un anillo mágico dos niños son transportados al antiguo mundo de Charn. Allí, por error despiertan a una poderosa y malvada hechicera de su sueño eterno. Sedienta de poder, ella no dudará en destruirlo todo y a todos a su paso. Pero el gran león Aslan hará despertar con su canción una nueva esperanza, un nuevo mundo: Narnia. Un lugar donde todo es posible.
El elenco de Narnia: El sobrino del mago incluye a David McKenna (Digory Kirke), Beatrice Campbell (Polly Plummer), Emma Mackey (Jadis), Meryl Streep (Aslan), Carey Mulligan (Flora Kirke) y Daniel Craig (Andrew Ketterley), por citar solo a algunos.
Narnia: El sobrino del mago se estrenará en cines el 12 de febrero de 2027, mientras que el 2 de abril se añadirá al catálogo de Netflix.

articles.title: Priyank Kharge on Karnataka’s plans to drive tech growth beyond Bengaluru
articles.text:
Priyank Kharge on Karnataka’s plans to drive tech growth beyond Bengaluru
At TechSparks 2026, Priyank Kharge, Minister for Home Affairs, IT, Biotechnology, and E-Governance, Govt. of Karnataka, highlighted the state’s Beyond Bengaluru policy.
Karnataka’s strategy to ease pressure on Bengaluru is to bring investment to where talent already exists, rather than making talent come to where the investment is, Priyank Kharge, Minister for Home Affairs, Information Technology, Biotechnology, and E-Governance, Govt. of Karnataka, said.
The minister was speaking on the sidelines of TechSparks, YourStory’s flagship startup and technology event. In a fireside chat with Shradha Sharma, Founder & CEO, YourStory and Bharat Project, Kharge spoke about the government’s plans to create opportunities for startups and talent beyond Bengaluru through targeted policies, infrastructure and region-specific centres of excellence.
“Because of the government’s constant push on its Beyond Bengaluru Mission and local economic acceleration programmes, Mysuru is today delivering close to Rs 4,000 crore in IT exports, Mangaluru close to Rs 3,500 crore, and Hubballi-Belagavi-Dharwad close to Rs 3,000 crore,” the minister highlighted.
He said manufacturing units and global capability centres (GCCs) have come up across the state, and that one of Apple’s supply chain partners operates out of Belagavi, doing precision manufacturing. The state has also announced a Bioeconomy Mission covering biotech and agritech, along with related schemes.
Kharge said the state runs dedicated entrepreneurship programmes for startups outside Bengaluru and cited recent deals to emphasise the state’s Beyond Bengaluru policy.
He said NTT acquired two Udupi-based startups for an undisclosed sum. There have also been acquisitions involving semiconductor design companies in Belagavi and Mangaluru.
He added that the founders involved are only 23 or 24 years old.
The government is setting up centres of excellence matched to each region’s strengths, Kharge said. “Wherever there is innovation possible, wherever we are able to ensure that the demography or the talent is good, we are tailor-making policies for that region, and we are ensuring that we accelerate growth,” he said.
“The government is extremely serious about this, which is why we are building centres of excellence based on each region’s geography and demography. We have an AI centre of excellence at IIIT Dharwad and another at IIIT Raichur. We have an agritech centre in Kalaburagi, and we are setting up a horticulture centre in Bagalkot. Wherever innovation is possible and talent is strong, we tailor policies for that region to accelerate growth,” he added.

articles.title: Roborock amplía su catálogo de aspiradoras en seco y húmedo: así son las nuevas F25 BX Gen 2 y F25 LT Gen 2
articles.text:
El mercado de las aspiradoras escoba capaces de aspirar y fregar al mismo tiempo sigue sumando alternativas de gama alta. Roborock, conocida popularmente por sus robots aspiradores, ha anunciado la llegada a España de su nueva familia de dispositivos de limpieza en seco y húmedo con el lanzamiento de los modelos Roborock F25 BX Gen 2 y Roborock F25 LT Gen 2. Ambas apuestas aterrizan en el mercado con ofertas de lanzamiento temporales activas hasta el próximo 1 de noviembre.
roborock F25 Bx Gen 2 Aspiradora-Fregona Sin Cable, Diseño Plano de 180°
roborock F25 LT Gen 2 Aspiradora en seco y en húmedo, Diseño Plano de 180°
Potencia bruta y diseño reclinable para llegar a cualquier rincón
Los dos nuevos modelos comparten gran parte de sus especificaciones de rendimiento estructural, destacando por incorporar una potencia de succión de 20.000 Pa y una velocidad de cepillado de 4500 revoluciones por minuto, acompañadas de una presión constante de 20 N sobre el suelo para ayudar a desincrustar la suciedad.
Uno de los apartados técnicos más reseñables es la evolución de su diseño para facilitar el acceso a zonas bajas. La tecnología FlatReach 2.0 permite reclinar el cuerpo de la aspiradora hasta 180 grados, quedándose a una altura reducida (de 12,5 cm en el caso de la versión BX) para limpiar con total comodidad por debajo de camas, sofás y muebles bajos sin perder capacidad de succión.
También incorpora el sistema de antienredos JawScrapers, que combina rascadores de presión constante y elementos en forma de diente de tiburón para evitar que el cabello se enrolle en el rodillo durante el uso.
Además, otra de las cosas por las que destaca es por ofrecer limpieza de bordes. Su diseño permite aproximarse a menos de 1 mm de paredes y zócalos, reduciendo los puntos ciegos en las esquinas de tu hogar.
Diferencias clave entre la F25 BX Gen 2 y la F25 LT Gen 2
Aunque comparten la base tecnológica, cada modelo orienta sus prestaciones a diferentes necesidades y presupuestos.
Roborock F25 BX Gen 2
- Autonomía: ofrece hasta 60 minutos de funcionamiento continuo en modo ECO, lo que permite cubrir superficies amplias de hasta 480 metros con una sola carga.
- Autolimpieza avanzada: incorpora el sensor inteligente DirTect, que monitoriza el nivel de suciedad en tiempo real para adaptar la potencia. Su base realiza un lavado de rodillo con agua y un flujo de aire caliente a 90 °C, automatizando gran parte del mantenimiento higiénico.
- Precio y oferta: su precio oficial recomendado se sitúa en los 399 euros, pero cuenta con un precio promocional de lanzamiento de 249 euros hasta el 1 de noviembre.
roborock F25 Bx Gen 2 Aspiradora-Fregona Sin Cable, Diseño Plano de 180°
Roborock F25 LT Gen 2
- Enfoque en ligereza y maniobrabilidad: configura su sistema antienredos mediante un peine de 141 dientes y un rascador flotante, situando además el depósito de agua limpia en una posición más baja para equilibrar el centro de gravedad y hacer que el manejo diario resulte más ligero.
- Mantenimiento y secado: cuenta también con autolimpieza a 90 ºC y un proceso de secado rápido por aire caliente asistido por un sistema que previene la humedad residual en los conductos.
- Precio y oferta: su precio de salida recomendado es de 349 euros, rebajado temporalmente a 219,99 euros hasta el 1 de noviembre.

articles.title: 👨🏿‍🚀TechCabal Daily – Microsoft closes a Window in Nairobi
articles.text: In partnership with Lire en Français اقرأ هذا باللغة العربية Good morning. Before you scroll, one quick favour: help us make TC Daily better. Tell us what you love, what you skip, and what you want more of. Share your thoughts here . Let’s dive in. Read smart insights about Francophone Africa’s tech ecosystem—weekly. Subscribe Microsoft shuts down Nairobi hub UK fintech Wise secures Category Two status iOCO profit jumps 39% CashAfrica, Chicken Republic partner World Wide Web 3 Events Big Tech Microsoft is closing its Nairobi engineering centre after seven years Image Source: Tenor In 2019, tech giant Microsoft made a big promise to Africa’s tech talent that they could build products for the world without leaving home. Seven years later, that promise is coming undone. What happened? Microsoft is winding down its Africa Development Centre (ADC) in Nairobi, Kenya, putting nearly 400 jobs at risk. Microsoft employees in Nairobi were called to a meeting on Monday and told to meet their managers by October 16 to discuss exit options, including severance terms, according to two employees who spoke to TechCabal. The company has not disclosed how many employees will leave. Why are they doing this? Microsoft said the proposed changes are part of its global restructuring, but insists it remains committed to Kenya and will continue employing people in the country. William Kabogo, Kenya’s ICT minister, met a Microsoft delegation on Monday and said the company had briefed him on its evolving operations. The two sides agreed to develop an action plan, though it remains unclear whether that could change the outcome. Explain like I’m new here : Microsoft launched its Africa Development Centre in Nairobi and Lagos in 2019, pledging more than $100 million to develop African tech talent . The idea was to recruit local engineers to work on products for global markets, rather than limit African offices to sales and customer support. By 2022, the Nairobi centre employed more than 450 engineers , meeting Microsoft’s original hiring target ahead of schedule. Cracks began to show: In March 2023, Microsoft cut jobs at the Nairobi centre when it laid off 10,000 employees globally. Then, in 2024, it shut down its Nigerian engineering centre in Lagos, Nigeria. At the time, Microsoft said the changes in Nigeria would not affect its Kenyan operations. Now, Nairobi faces a possible wind-down. In July, the company cut roughly 2.1% of its global workforce , following about 15,000 job cuts in 2025 . What happens to the talent? During the expansion of its engineering hub in Kenya, Microsoft recruited experienced workers from banks, telecom companies, and local tech firms. Now, that skilled talent is available for poaching in the local market. Microsoft spent seven years building an engineering team capable of developing products for global markets from Kenya. If the centre closes, Kenya will have to ensure that the talent and experience built in those seven years do not leave with it. Happy customer service week. Your success and ours are the same story. Happy Customer Service Week. This year’s theme is The Extra Mile, and it’s the only way we know how to do this. Visit: fincra.com . Fintech Wise is building its South African foothold Image source: Tenor Wise, the UK remittance fintech, has spent the past year entering South Africa without actually launching the full Wise experience there. It secured conditional regulatory approval in December 2025, then signed a deal in April 2026 to power international payments for tier-1 bank Capitec’s 25 million customers. Now it has its own local regulatory footing. What happened? On October 5, the South African Reserve Bank (SARB) confirmed it has appointed Wise Payments South Africa as a Category Two Authorised Dealer in foreign exchange (FX) with limited authority. The categorisation allows Wise to handle certain FX transactions, including transfers under South Africa’s R2 million ($120,000) annual discretionary allowance , and to offer remittance services through external money-transfer operators. Explain like I’m new here: Wise has been selling the plumbing before opening the shop. Its April partnership with Capitec gave it distribution through South Africa’s largest bank by customer numbers. The new licence gives Wise its own regulated position inside the country’s FX system. It still is not a bank. South Africans also cannot yet open the full Wise account available in markets such as the UK. Between the lines: Compare that with Revolut, another UK remittance fintech and Wise’s competitor. Revolut applied for a full South African banking licence in September 2025 and wants the country, where it has since hired a chairman to supervise its operations, to become its first African banking market. By June 2026, the fintech said its local waitlist was approaching 100,000 people . The two companies are entering Africa from opposite ends. Wise is starting with cross-border payments, infrastructure and bank partnerships. Revolut wants the broader banking relationship. Zoom out: In March 2026, Wise has also received conditional approval to expand into Nigeria. Global fintechs are no longer content to move African money from offshore. They are seeking local licences, partners, and customers, putting them in direct competition with local fintechs and banks already fighting for those transactions. Don’t miss Moonshot 2026 for anything in the world! True scale demands moving beyond surface-level integrations to robust execution. We’ve filtered the noise out of Moonshot 2026, optimising the conference strictly for high-calibre connections between startup founders, global financial operators, enterprise leaders and individuals rewiring Africa’s technical frameworks. Join us on October 28 & 29, 2026. Get your ticket . Companies iOCO’s profit jumps, but growth is still doing less of the work Image Source: Tenor iOCO, the South African technology services group formerly known as EOH, made more profit in its latest financial year. The interesting part is where that jump came from. What happened? The company’s profit rose 39% to R357 million ($21.6 million), while adjusted earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA) climbed 21% to R624 million ($37.8 million). Revenue, however, grew just 2.7% to R5.73 billion ($347.5 million). Most of the improvement came from spending less. Employee costs fell by R288 million ($17.5 million), finance costs dropped 30% as debt came down, and iOCO paid a lower effective tax rate after recognising previously unused tax losses. Between the lines: iOCO is becoming more profitable before it becomes much bigger. Services, still its largest revenue line, fell 6.6% to R3.9 billion ($236.5 million). Hardware sales jumped 50%, while software and licence revenue grew 20%. iOCO is making more money, but its biggest business is still shrinking. Cash gives another clue. Operating cash flow fell 44% to R239 million ($14.5 million), even though cash generated before working capital movements improved. The difference was timing: customers released a large amount of cash in the previous year as receivables fell, while receivables rose slightly this year. State of play: iOCO also cut its debt and returned some cash to shareholders. Interest-bearing debt fell to R607 million ($36.8 million), within its lender limits. The company spent R69 million ($4.2 million) buying back 16.8 million shares. iOCO has already squeezed more profit from roughly flat revenue. To keep earnings growing, it now needs revenue to do more of the work, especially services, which still make up most of the business. Zoom out: The company is starting to spend for growth again. It bought Dyner AI in May, its first acquisition in eight years, and followed that with a deal for Astraia Technology in July. With services revenue still falling, those acquisitions now have a clear job: help iOCO grow the top line. Fintech CashAfrica brings tap-to-pay to Chicken Republic outlets CashAfrica and Food Concepts team at partnership launch in Lagos. Image source: CashAfrica Chances are you have seen someone in a Hollywood movie pay for coffee by tapping their phone or card and walking away. CashAfrica, a Nigerian fintech providing contactless payment infrastructure, wants to make that the new checkout routine at Chicken Republic, the Nigerian quick-service restaurant (QSR) chain run by Food Concepts. What happened? CashAfrica has partnered with Food Concepts to introduce mobile tap-to-pay across 350 outlets run by the restaurant chain. Customers with compatible phones, such as those with near-field communication (NFC) tech, and supported banking or fintech apps will be able to tap their devices at PalmPay’s point-of-sale (PoS) terminals. CashAfrica provides the contactless technology, while ChamsSwitch, a Nigerian payment switching company, routes transactions between financial institutions. The rollout will begin in Lagos before expanding to Abuja and other locations. Explain like I’m new here: Nigeria has been moving towards digital payments for years, but tapping a phone—or card—to pay is not yet the default. In 2022, the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) introduced a plan to facilitate contactless payments, later noting that over 12 million contactless payment cards were in circulation by November 2025. Why aren’t Nigerians tapping everywhere already? Most Nigerians pay with bank transfers, cash, or the familiar card-and-PIN method. Even where contactless payments are possible, there has been little concerted effort to make tapping a familiar option at checkout. Tap-to-pay technology needs Near Field Communication (NFC)-enabled devices—a wireless technology that lets two devices placed close together exchange information. NFC-enabled PoS terminals and compatible phones already exist in Nigeria. The hard work is in getting banks and fintechs to support the service, giving merchants a reason to offer it, and making customers aware they can tap to pay in the first place. What’s different now? CashAfrica has already learnt that getting the technology to work is only part of the challenge. The company said earlier integration discussions with PalmPay, AltBank, and Sterling Bank stalled amid extended due diligence and regulatory concerns. Financial institutions needed assurance that the infrastructure met their compliance requirements before integrating it. Can Chicken Republic instil the habit? With more than 350 outlets, the restaurant chain gives the company a chance to put tap-to-pay in front of customers during everyday transactions. However, if CashAfrica wants the service to catch on at scale, customers need access through the banking and fintech apps they already use. They also need to know the option exists, which means user awareness. Tap-to-pay needs to work safely and reliably, protecting merchants from fraudulent chargebacks and giving customers an authenticated way to request refunds when a transaction goes wrong. Get those basics right, and CashAfrica has a better chance of making tapping a habit rather than a novelty. articles.title: Apple dévoile le HomePod mini 2 : voici ce qui change
articles.text:
Ce 13 octobre, Apple a tenu sa conférence estampillée « Welcome Home ». Comme ce slogan l’indique, il a été question d’un événement centré sur les nouveaux produits domotiques d’Apple. Nous avons pu découvrir la nouvelle Apple TV 4K, le HomeView (un hub domotique équipé d’un écran), ainsi qu’un partenariat exclusif avec LG. Mais l’entreprise à la pomme en a aussi profité pour dévoiler le HomePod mini 2, soit la nouvelle génération de son enceinte connectée sortie en 2020. Spécificités, prix, date de commercialisation, voici tout ce qu’il faut savoir.
HomePod mini 2 : pas de révolution du design, mais des gains de performances
Au niveau du design, autant dire que nous ne sommes pas face à une révolution. Le HomePod mini 2 présente la même forme sphérique, le même type de tissu maillé et plus ou moins les mêmes dimensions que son prédécesseur. Notons en revanche la présence d’une fonction baptisée Sound Glow : le dessus du HomePod mini « se transforme en une toile visuelle qui s’illumine et pulse au rythme de la musique, réagissant en temps réel aux basses et aux aigus ».
C’est plutôt dans ses entrailles que des changements sont à noter. En effet, l’appareil intègre une puce S10, soit un processeur que l’on retrouve notamment dans l’Apple Watch Ultra 3. Notons également la présence d’une puce Ultra Wideband de deuxième génération et de la puce réseau N1 d’Apple, compatible avec le Wi-Fi 7, pour une connexion plus stable et performante, ainsi qu’avec Thread, un protocole de communication sans fil conçu pour les objets connectés de la maison.
Côté qualité audio, Apple promet « un son immersif » à 360°, ainsi que « l’expérience home cinéma la plus immersive jamais conçue » par l’entreprise, lorsque l’enceinte est connectée à la nouvelle Apple TV 4K. Par ailleurs, les utilisateurs peuvent créer une expérience sonore surround à quatre haut-parleurs avec l’Apple TV 4K (4e génération) et le HomePod mini 2.
Siri AI au cœur de l’expérience, mais toujours indisponible en Europe
Sans surprise, Apple met Siri AI au cœur de l’expérience d’utilisation du HomePod mini 2. L’utilisateur peut ainsi faire appel à l’assistant IA d’Apple à tout moment pour notamment poser des questions, envoyer des messages, contrôler la maison connectée, définir des rappels et gérer les contenus multimédias. La puce S10 devrait d’ailleurs permettre à l’IA d’exploiter pleinement ses capacités sur l’appareil.
En réalité, le HomePod mini 2 est en grande partie pensé autour de Siri AI. Il s’agit d’un produit centré autour de l’intelligence artificielle, soit une expérience bien plus avancée que celle offerte par Siri sur le HomePod mini lancé en 2020. Siri AI peut notamment comprendre un contexte pour adapter ses réponses et anticiper les besoins de l’utilisateur, tout en prenant en charge plusieurs requêtes. Mais nous avons une mauvaise nouvelle : Siri AI est toujours bloqué en Europe. Les utilisateurs européens devront donc se contenter d’une enceinte dotée d’une puce plus performante et d’un meilleur son, mais sans Siri AI.
Le HomePod mini 2 sera commercialisé à partir du 30 octobre prochain au prix de 149 $. L’enceinte est proposée en cinq coloris : noir, blanc, rose, vert et bleu. Les précommandes seront ouvertes dès maintenant.

articles.title: They war-gamed dimming the Sun. It went even worse than you think.
articles.text:
When it comes to deciding the fate of the planet, Colleen Golja always thought science and reason would have a seat at the table. That was until one morning last September in London, when the climate researcher took part in the first in a series of war games. The goal: to prevent an uncontrolled global race to develop a technology aimed at cooling the planet but that comes with vast, unknown risks that could reshape life on Earth.
“I thought that would be such an easy thing. Like, we can all agree to do ethical research and make sure it’s for the better of all humans,” she told WIRED. “And boy, was I wrong.”
The simulation, titled Exploring Geopolitical Tipping Points and Climate Cooling Strategies, saw a couple dozen foreign-relations experts, scientists, military personnel, and former government officials from across the world convene in a meeting room at Queen Mary University of London. After making introductions over coffee and little yogurts, they sat at tables arranged in a square with the name of the country or organization each person was playing: national governments, climate NGOs and nonprofits, indigenous groups, and tech companies. Golja was assigned to provide technical advice to help participants make scientifically literate decisions.
The point of the game was to stress-test the world’s response to a group of prospective technologies known collectively as solar radiation modification. These technologies promise to reverse global warming by reflecting away a portion of the sunlight reaching Earth, for example by spraying particles of sulphur dioxide or some other manufactured substance into the atmosphere. The cooling effect of this kind of solar geoengineering is widely accepted. It would mimic the well-known impacts of large volcanic eruptions, which temporarily cool the planet by half a degree or more. But the fallout is less certain—and less equal. Some regions will suffer: Models predict drying in sub-Saharan Africa and more intense tropical storms in the Atlantic. The cooling effect would also last only as long as the geoengineering continued; after that the global temperature could shoot back up with wild and hard-to-predict effects.
Until recently, the idea of solar radiation modification was a speculative niche of climate science. That has changed fast. Private firms are exploring solar geoengineering as a commercial opportunity: Last year, a US-Israeli startup called Stardust Solutions raised $60 million, and in May it released details of a suite of new inventions it claims would give humans the ability to dial down the global temperature as desired. In August, Elon Musk, whose company SpaceX might be a candidate for delivering geoengineering interventions, threw his voice behind solar geoengineering, writing on X: “Space satellites to control temperature and massive geo-engineering will be needed or it will be game over.”
The world is going to have to make decisions about how to govern this technology much sooner than most policymakers imagine, Cynthia Scharf, a former UN advisor, told WIRED. “It’s not 15 years from now; it’s in the next decade, easily.”
It was against this backdrop that Danielle Young, an assistant professor in international relations at Leeds University, arranged the war game. Its setting was a hastily convened UN committee charged with coordinating the international response to developments in solar geoengineering. The game unfolded over simulated meetings set at three points in time: the present, September 2027, and September 2028. Each step ratcheted up the stakes, with the game creators introducing new advances in sunlight-reflecting technology. As in real life, no one knew all the facts, and players had to respond to events that were bringing the world closer to a full-scale attempt at deploying solar geoengineering tech, even when they may not have a full picture of what had truly occurred—or what any of the others were up to.
The first session set the tone. Distrust and disinformation dominated. As participants discussed rules governing outdoor experiments in an attempt to agree an international deal, players representing both the US and China told the group they could not sign a deal that constrained their pursuit of research considered to be in their “national interest.” Nor could they accept a deal that would see their superpower rival taking the lead technologically. Speaking to WIRED, Jeffrey Nielsen, a major in the US Army who played the role of a US national security attaché, summarized the position as “worse than no deal at all is any deal that favors China.”
Tensions escalated when the team running the simulation handed the Russian delegates an “intelligence report” indicating they had found a plane near the Bering Strait believed to be involved in a US geoengineering research program. The US team—which was indeed flying research missions—accused Russia of disinformation.
Meanwhile, the US became convinced China was also conducting research and developing its own program. Beijing’s representatives had tried to insert language into a mooted deal that would ensure no retroactive punishment for past experiments. Then, China approached a player representing SpaceX to float the idea of a technology-sharing program. In a private discussion away from the group, the SpaceX player immediately reported the Chinese approach to the US team. The US demanded an international investigation. The finger-pointing continued, and countries abandoned the talks. The Canadian representative called it a “humiliating defeat.”
At the end of the session, Nielsen was pumped. He’d busted China and derailed any prospect of a global deal. In the context of the game, he told WIRED, it was a “humungous victory” for the Americans. But Young, the researcher who designed the scenario, said the Chinese were not, in fact, conducting experiments in the game. Mutual suspicion meant all parties left the room believing the others were moving as quickly as possible to build their own geoengineering capability.
What played out in the first session reflected “the likelihood, in my opinion, of the geoengineering arms race,” says Nielsen, who clarified he was speaking to WIRED in a private capacity and not representing the views of the actual US government. Most experts agree it would take a superpower’s reach to ensure the safe passage of planes needed to deliver payloads of dust to the stratosphere in a geoengineering exercise. But neither the US nor China would lightly cede control over the global thermostat, says Nielsen, and distrust and poor communication are a significant risk: “Any action related to the issue by one actor can be perceived as malintent by the other.”
The threat of falling behind a rival is “a very strong driver of research and development of capability,” a former British diplomat with a background in national security told WIRED. “But that’s not at all the same thing as deployment.” There are similarities with nuclear arms dynamics—though solar radiation management, unlike nukes, has more obvious benefits as well as downsides, many of which are poorly understood. “There is an interdependence here,” says the former diplomat, who was not involved in the game and spoke on condition of anonymity to preserve relationships. “It’s not an inherently zero-sum game.”
Scharf, who represented the US government alongside Nielsen in the game, told WIRED a “scientifically transparent international collaboration” between China and the US “might be the best we can do in terms of fending off a very dangerous competition between the two. But I certainly cannot imagine that happening under the Trump administration.”
Compounding the problem is a lack of information. Geoengineering has historically been viewed with suspicion and often ignored by the scientific mainstream. One researcher told WIRED he’d experienced ostracization and barriers to academic progression owing to his interest in the technology; he no longer works in the field.
This lack of scientific interest greatly frustrated Golja, who spent much of the game watching as a bystander while political posturing dominated. Given the low level of knowledge around solar radiation modification and its side effects, she was one of very few experts who could help the participants understand the climate impacts of what they were discussing—yet she was largely ignored.“I was just so surprised about how little anyone actually cared about the science,” she says.
In the next sessions, the organizers tried in vain to nudge the talks back toward the realities of climate change. The participants received frequent notifications of climate disasters. These barely registered. Golja had prepared an “emulator,” a real-world demonstration of the best available science on how solar radiation management might affect weather patterns in different regions. It was ignored. If country representatives asked her anything, it was usually a leading question looking for data that would serve their ends or frame a rival’s proposal as reckless.
Then, during the last day, players were trying to find a way to respond to reports that a major plume of aerosols had been detected. In the game, this had been caused by a joint US-Saudi test of Stardust’s technology, though not everyone knew this. Finally, scientific advice was at a premium. Countries needed to know how to establish a monitoring network of satellites and other observational tools in order to prevent tests like this from happening in secret. A player representing an NGO called the Climate Futures Cooperative approached Golja, offering her money to fund such a scheme.
“Great. Fabulous. Why wouldn’t I do that?” she recalls thinking.
But it soon came out that the Climate Futures Cooperative was actually backed by the fossil fuel industry. The organizers had recognized that fossil fuel companies and major producing countries like the US and Saudi Arabia would have a clear interest in removing barriers from the development of a technology that could combat climate change without having to immediately stop burning coal, oil, and gas. The shadowy NGO spent the game subtly wrecking the vibe and carping about process—though mostly they just sat back and let it burn. Some players—Russia, the US, SpaceX and Stardust—figured out the CFC was not what it seemed, says Young. “But they assessed it was to their benefit and didn’t draw attention to it.” Then the CFC chose its moment to offer money to Golja, only to crater her credibility, isolating and fragmenting the voice of science in the room.
“It was a whole mess,” says Golja.
That final lesson in fossil fuel realpolitik was about all Golja could endure. By the end of the last day, she was in tears.
At no point did the countries in the game agree to a deal, despite multiple proposals being put forward. European countries and Canada tried to build support for safeguards and open scientific research, but the talks constantly got bogged down by delay tactics and veered into tense showdowns over duelling strategic interests. In their final report, the researchers running the simulation—whose work was sponsored by the UK government-funded Advanced Research and Invention Agency—concluded that “strategic competition and state sovereignty drove the simulations, not climate concerns.”
Simulations like this one are not supposed to predict the future. The outcomes depend on the design of the game and the relative personalities and experience of the players. Many of those in the room lacked first-hand diplomatic and national security experience. The UN forum, which organizers selected as the game’s setting, may also not be as effective as talks between smaller groups of major countries. But the experiment in London echoed and refracted through the real world, during and after the months it was running.
In March, two papers from conservative US think tanks urged the Trump administration to take the lead on solar radiation modification and counter China’s threat. One memorably invoked a new, MAGA-coded term: “Weather sovereignty.” This month, the Observer newspaper in London revealed that the UK Ministry of Defense had paid a deep tech security consultancy to conduct research into sunlight reflection. Then, last week, the British government released its first official policy paper on the field, backing further research but stating firmly that it did not support deployment and “does not plan to do so.” Stardust has continued its lobbying of the US and governments around the world; CEO Yanai Yedvab told WIRED its job was getting easier as, unlike before, “the majority of policymakers … are already aware of this technology.”
Stardust has always maintained that it will not conduct large-scale outdoor experiments, let alone full deployment, before global governance is in place. “We are developing a very powerful tool,” Yedvab says. “When you develop this kind of powerful technology—and you have many precedents—national interests will play out. We’re not naive about it.”
Meanwhile, drivers of the climate crisis are intensifying. During the time span of the game, efforts to curtail the use of fossil fuels were being undermined by rising energy costs and political hostility. Week after week, an incredible summer of drought and heat pounded Europe. In the final week of August, the collapse of a glacier on the Tibet-Nepal border fulfilled the prophecies of decades of climate scientists, killing more than 1,450 people.
In the months since the simulation ended, Golja has reevaluated many things. On a corkboard behind her desk, she has pinned up a note to herself, laying out a vision for life in a world ruled by narrow geopolitical self-interest rather than science, evidence, and reason. Her answer: She plans to return to the small coastal town where she grew up in Connecticut and use her expertise to help local climate groups build the seawalls and coastal erosion buffers they will need to cope with the inevitable. “To try and make a difference where it feels like I actually have traction,” she says. After what she saw, pursuing science in the hope of informing global decisions no longer held as much appeal. “Now it feels a little bit more personal.”
Wired.com is your essential daily guide to what's next, delivering the most original and complete take you'll find anywhere on innovation's impact on technology, science, business and culture.

articles.title: Adenocarcinoma de pulmão: o que é a doença detectada no Papa Leão XIV
articles.text:
O Papa Leão XIV passou por uma cirurgia na terça-feira (13) para retirar um nódulo do pulmão direito. Os médicos detectaram um adenocarcinoma pulmonar, o tipo mais comum de câncer de pulmão.
O tumor costuma crescer mais lentamente do que outras formas da doença e se desenvolve na região periférica dos pulmões. Quando identificado precocemente, há mais chances de tratamento antes que se espalhe para outros órgãos.
O que é o adenocarcinoma de pulmão
O adenocarcinoma surge nas células glandulares que produzem muco e, na maioria dos casos, se forma nos alvéolos, estruturas responsáveis pelas trocas gasosas nos pulmões. Ele faz parte do grupo dos cânceres de pulmão de não pequenas células (CPNPC).
Em comparação com outros tumores desse grupo, tem maior probabilidade de ser detectado antes de atingir outros órgãos. Embora o tabagismo seja a principal causa do câncer de pulmão, o adenocarcinoma também afeta pessoas que nunca fumaram e é mais frequente entre mulheres e jovens.
Fatores de risco e sintomas
Além do cigarro, a exposição ao fumo passivo, ao radônio, aos gases de escapamento de motores a diesel e a substâncias como amianto, alcatrão, níquel, cromo e berílio pode aumentar o risco de desenvolver a doença.
O adenocarcinoma pode evoluir sem sinais claros no início. Quando aparecem, os sintomas podem ser confundidos com os de outros problemas de saúde. Entre as manifestações possíveis estão:
- Sintomas respiratórios: tosse persistente, falta de ar, chiado no peito e rouquidão;
- Outros desconfortos: dor no peito, dificuldade para engolir e cansaço frequente;
- Sinais adicionais: tosse com sangue, perda de apetite, emagrecimento sem explicação e inchaço no rosto ou nas veias do pescoço.
Esses sintomas não significam necessariamente câncer, mas devem ser avaliados por um médico quando surgirem.
Diagnóstico e tratamento
A investigação pode incluir exames de sangue e urina, além de exames de imagem, como raio-X e tomografia computadorizada. Se houver suspeita de tumor, o médico pode solicitar uma biópsia, que consiste na retirada de uma amostra de tecido para análise.
No caso do papa, o nódulo foi identificado durante exames de rotina e removido. Após a confirmação da doença, outros exames permitem determinar o estágio do câncer e verificar se ele permanece localizado ou se atingiu outras partes do corpo.
A possibilidade de cura é maior quando o tumor é descoberto cedo, ainda pequeno e sem comprometimento dos gânglios linfáticos. O tratamento depende do estágio e das características do câncer e pode incluir cirurgia, quimioterapia, radioterapia, imunoterapia ou terapias-alvo, que atuam sobre características específicas das células cancerígenas.
Valdir Antonelli é jornalista com especialização em marketing digital e consumo.

articles.title: Apple’s HomeView ad is confusing to everyone except parents
articles.text:
Apple’s ad introducing its new HomeView smart display is a little unusual. It’s fast-paced and unruly, depicting a family of five as they rush through the morning routine. There’s yelling and mess, misplaced keys and discarded eggshells. Apple’s typical vibe is clean, simple, orderly; this commercial is chaos.
Apple’s HomeView ad is confusing to everyone except parents
The chaos is surprisingly real for an Apple commercial.
But the spot has parents — those with teen children in particular — feeling seen.
I’ll admit that it stressed me out the first time I watched it, too. Mornings getting my five-year-old out the door are a special breed of chaos, and usually culminate in us playing whatever ad-libbed game will get him to put his shoes on. But it’s not quite as intense as this one, which features dad making French toast, mom losing and finding keys in her pocket, a proxy battle over the thermostat, a teenage boy helping himself to whipped cream from a can, and an unexpected video call. There’s also a microdrama about the daughter’s ride to school with a boyfriend nobody knew about that ends with everyone gathered around the HomeView watching the security camera feed of the two of them departing the porch. It’s a lot for just over three minutes of screentime.
If I know anything, though, I know to trust my colleague Jen Tuohy, senior reviewer and parent to two teens, on matters of the home. Her take? “The most unrealistic part of the video is that no one is holding an iPhone.”
Other parents of teens shared similar reactions on Threads. When tech analyst Benedict Evans posted about the ad feeling stressful and confusing, CNET editor at large Bridget Carey chimed in to defend it, saying “It was exactly what my morning is like and it was the most real ad I’ve ever seen from Apple.” Others agreed, saying it “accurately captured” real life and that it “hit home,” no pun intended, at least I think.
Even if Apple didn’t need to do much to heighten the stakes of a family getting out the door, there is of course plenty of sleight of hand at work when it comes to making the HomeView appear so essential. The family has seemingly drilled a hole directly into the middle of their kitchen island to accommodate the charging cable, for one. And what sibling is going to check a text message from a secret boyfriend on the communal kitchen screen with their brother sitting at arm’s length? I don’t believe any teenager trusts Apple’s privacy features that far.
The confusion about the commercial is understandable. This is a far cry from the quiet luxury lifestyle everyone seems to enjoy in Apple’s Vision Pro ads. There’s also Evans’ observation that the HomeView doesn’t really solve any of the problems that come up throughout the course of the video. In the case of a spontaneous FaceTime call from the grandparents, the screen in the middle of the kitchen seems to make things worse.
But maybe morning chaos isn’t the problem that’s being solved. If the alternative is five people all interacting with their own phones, then the HomeView presents a different picture where everyone gets the essential information they need from one shared screen and stays more present.
A screen that makes you be more present is a lovely idea, but the real test will come when it’s in real households. Is the HomeView going to be enough to convince families to put their personal devices down? Will everyone just ignore it and keep scrolling on their own iPhones? These are questions worth answering before you start drilling holes in your kitchen island! In any case, an ungovernable morning routine is probably a feature of a busy household, not a bug. Just ask a parent.

articles.title: Exclusive: Rivian's startup Mind Robotics hires former Ford EV chief Doug Field | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Doug Field has worked on EVs at Ford and Tesla, the not-so-secret car project at Apple, and was employee No. 1 at Segway. Now the executive is turning his attention to Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe’s latest project: Mind Robotics.
Field has been hired as president of Mind Robotics, an industrial AI and robotics venture Rivian created last year. The news, shared onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 (taking place October 13-15 in San Francisco), is another sign that Mind Robotics is getting ready to scale up its early operations just one year after its founding.
Scaringe will still be involved with Mind Robotics, but the day-to-day aspects of the business, including product, engineering, and operations, will be handled by Field.
Mind Robotics, which has already amassed more than $1 billion in backing from Accel, Andreessen Horowitz, Eclipse, Kleiner Perkins, and the venture arms of Volkswagen and Salesforce, is building a full stack for industrial manufacturing. The purpose-built robots will run on foundation models with a goal of automating industrial and manufacturing tasks at scale.
Unlike the humanoid robots being developed by Tesla and others, Scaringe says Mind Robotics won’t attempt to mimic all the biomechanics of a human. The startup is also using Rivian as “a live, high-volume manufacturing environment for model training and deployment,” with Rivian being Mind Robotics’ first customer.
Scaringe said on the Disrupt Stage Tuesday that he wanted someone like Field to help run Mind Robotics, and so he called him up to ask for a recommendation.
“Him and I then really began digging into how important it is that we really think deeply and very intentionally about how we develop robotics and deploy robotics into our society, into our economy, and we found such alignment in how we thought about this from the overall mission of the business, but even more important, we found really deep alignment just in how we both work and how we build teams,” he said.
Field left Ford in April after five years shaping the automaker’s electric vehicle and technology strategies. His departure was part of a wider reorganization of the automaker’s leadership. Prior to Ford, Field led Apple’s Project Titan, the electric, autonomous car project that was canceled in 2024. He also served as senior vice president of engineering at Tesla, where he oversaw development of the Model 3 and got the sedan through “production hell.”
“Integrating AI and robotics is one of the most important — and difficult — engineering challenges of our time,” Field said in a statement. “Mind has assembled an exceptional team and has a unique advantage: the ability to deploy and learn inside a real, high-volume factory from day one. I’m thrilled to join RJ in building a team, culture, and technology that will redefine what we can make in America.”
Mind Robotics is the second company that Scaringe created outside of Rivian, following Also, a micromobility play that’s starting with high-end e-bikes. Like with Field and Mind Robotics, Scaringe is involved as chairman at Also but has tapped someone to run the day-to-day: Chris Yu, the former chief product officer of Specialized.
Mind Robotics and Also operate as stand-alone companies, but Rivian has minority stakes in both. The company reported owning about a third of each startup as of June 30, 2026.

articles.title: On theCUBE Pod: IBM competes for AI's operating model - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
On theCUBE Pod: AI doubters get loud, and IBM seeks competitive advantage
Americans have big concerns about artificial intelligence, but that hasn’t stopped OpenAI Inc., Nvidia Corp., IBM Corp. and others from charging ahead.
Last week saw shares of Nvidia, CoreWeave Inc., Oracle Corp. and Nebius Group N.V. decline amid reports that OpenAI’s annualized net revenue was approximately $50 billion, roughly $20 billion below previously reported figures. Despite the ongoing public pushback against AI, John Furrier (pictured, right), research executive analyst at theCUBE Research, sees the uproar as temporary.
“This is an AI freakout moment,” he said. “It’s funny to watch knowing what’s happening on the inside. We talk to all those suppliers, whether it’s Nvidia, the chip side … the neoclouds or the AI infrastructure clouds. This new AI layer is a system; the data center as a system is now the computer. Rack scale is changing. Companies like Marvell, Broadcom and others are creating chips to create more efficiencies.”
On the latest episode of theCUBE Pod, Furrier and Dave Vellante (pictured, left), chief analyst at theCUBE Research, discussed takeaways from the recent IBM Analyst Council. They also explored chipmaker Marvell Technology Inc.’s growth and the industry shift toward inference.
IBM bets on commodity models
Big Blue’s recent meeting provided insights into the legacy company’s position in the AI era. As Vellante sees it, customers are increasingly spending on the infrastructure and models needed to produce intelligence before turning to IBM to put that intelligence to work, presenting a challenge for the company as the AI market matures.
“The alpha is going to be in your data, your processes and your operating model,” Vellante said. “This is [IBM’s] opportunity. That AI operating model is going to be the new source of competitive advantage. It’s not going to come from Palantir; it’s not going to come from models. It’s going to come from your own proprietary data, how you apply that data, how you streamline your processes and how fast you can get products and services to market.”
IBM has promoted a four-part architecture composed of agents, data, automation and hybrid infrastructure, with an orchestration layer that can integrate agents from different vendors. Rather than relying exclusively on proprietary models, IBM is positioning itself as a provider of hybrid AI operating infrastructure for enterprise customers, building on Red Hat’s open-source foundation.
“Their bet is the commoditization of the models,” Furrier said. “Having a nice model management capability will be good for IBM; but when you have a commoditization bet, you better be right. IBM doesn’t need its own proprietary operating system [because] … they have a valuable abstraction control layer around open infrastructure through Red Hat. Red Hat gets paid a lot of money to manage that open abstraction. That’s an opportunity: IBM could run all the agents.”
The question remains whether IBM’s bet on commodity models and open-source solutions will pay off. Customers trust IBM. but they don’t see the company as an innovator in the current AI landscape, according to Vellante. However, if IBM can establish itself as a provider of the operational infrastructure around AI models and agents, then it could own “the scarcity around the abundance.”
“They’ve got to play in both camps,” Vellante added. “In other words, they’ve got to have the IBM version of Oracle’s Red Stack. Last year, we asked [IBM’s CCO] Rob Thomas, what is the platform? And the answer came back: Red Hat. I agree. Let’s build a solution around Red Hat to simplify the adoption of AI. It’s unclear to me what that solution is. It’s clear to me they got all the piece parts.”
AI market enters the inference stage
In the chip world, Marvell Technology Inc. is drawing attention with an ambitious revenue target of $70 billion to $90 billion for fiscal 2031. Earlier this year, the company, which makes custom AI processors and optical networking technology, announced a partnership with Nvidia’s NVLink Fusion.
“What impressed me about Marvell is that they had a 10-year vision,” Furrier said. “Their mission statement that they put up from 10 years ago … they didn’t have factories. It wasn’t in the dialogue. But back then … they made the argument that AI research is becoming a connectivity problem as much as a compute problem. And they’re not wrong. You’ve got a semiconductor company talking about economics. They’re talking about real value.”
Furrier doesn’t believe the AI market is approaching a bubble, while Vellante sees the breaking point as being farther away than many might expect. As the enterprise world shifts its focus from training to inference, companies such as Marvell and the neoclouds stand to benefit financially as spending on AI infrastructure increases.
“A year ago, 90% of the workloads — we saw this at CoreWeave — were training,” Vellante said. “Today, it’s like 60-40 training-inference. The expectation is that it’s going to flip to 10-90. Why is that? Because they’re driving revenue; they’re making money off of inference. That’s where you talk about this all the time. You go to college for training, and then you go make money and you continually learn.”
Watch the full podcast below to find out why these industry pros were mentioned:
Ray Dalio, chief investment officer of Bridgewater Associates
Matt Calkins, CEO of Appian
David Lazovsky, EVP and GM of the Data Center Networking Business Group at Marvell Technology
Arvind Krishna, chairman and CEO of IBM
Rob Thomas, SVP of software and chief commercial officer at IBM
John F. Akers, former CEO of IBM
Prith Banerjee, SVP of innovation and member of the executive leadership team at Synopsys
Matt Murphy, partner at Menlo Ventures
Charlie Kawwas, president of Broadcom
Donald Trump, 47th president of the United States of America

articles.title: Ce chauffage connecté Philips perd 20 % sur Amazon, avant les premiers froids
articles.text:
Mi-octobre, la période est souvent inconfortable. Le thermomètre baisse le matin et le soir, mais rallumer le chauffage de tout le logement semble encore exagéré. Un chauffage d’appoint permet de réchauffer une seule pièce, comme le bureau où vous télétravaillez ou une chambre exposée au nord, sans faire grimper la consommation de toute la maison.
Philips vend justement un modèle connecté pour cet usage, la colonne CX5120/11 de sa Série 5000. Amazon la propose aujourd’hui à 79,99 € au lieu de 99,99 €. Cela fait 20 € de remise, soit 20 % de moins que le prix public de Philips, qui vend ce modèle 99,99 € sur sa propre boutique.
C’est quoi, ce chauffage Philips Série 5000 ?
Le CX5120/11 est une petite colonne de 58 cm de haut pour 2,4 kg, que l’on déplace facilement d’une pièce à l’autre. C’est un chauffage soufflant : un ventilateur pousse l’air sur un élément chauffant en céramique PTC. Ce type de céramique limite naturellement sa puissance quand sa température monte, ce qui évite la surchauffe. Sa puissance se règle sur deux niveaux, 1 200 et 2 000 watts, et Philips le recommande pour les pièces de 20 m² au maximum. Selon la marque, l’air chaud arrive en 2 secondes. Il peut aussi osciller sur 60° pour mieux répartir la chaleur.
Il se connecte au Wi-Fi, mais uniquement en 2,4 GHz. Il se pilote ensuite depuis l’application Philips Air+, avec Alexa ou avec Google Assistant. L’application permet d’allumer le chauffage, de planifier des plages horaires ou de programmer un minuteur de 1 à 12 heures. Pratique si vous voulez trouver un bureau tiède en vous installant le matin. Le thermostat se règle entre 1 et 37 °C.
Philips met en avant son mode Eco AI. Cet algorithme tient compte de la température de la pièce et de vos habitudes pour ajuster la chauffe. La marque annonce jusqu’à 50 % d’économies d’énergie par rapport à un chauffage soufflant classique,en fonction de la pièce, de son isolation et de votre usage. Côté sécurité, Philips liste cinq protections, dont un système anti-basculement, une coupure en cas de surchauffe (à partir de 85 °C) et un arrêt automatique après 24 heures d’inactivité. Niveau bruit, Philips annonce 55 dB à pleine puissance, et 40,5 dB au plus bas.
À ce prix, le Philips CX5120/11 est-il une bonne affaire ?
À 79,99 €, ce Philips intéresse surtout celles et ceux qui veulent programmer leur chauffage d’appoint depuis leur téléphone. À puissance égale, un chauffage soufflant non connecté produit autant de chaleur. Le supplément paie la programmation, le pilotage à distance et le mode Eco AI. À ce tarif, il reste tout de même une très bonne affaire pour s’équiper d’un chauffage d’appoint connecté sans faire exploser son budget.
Ce modèle sert à dépanner, pour réchauffer ponctuellement un bureau en télétravail ou une chambre. À 2 000 watts, il consomme 2 kWh par heure à pleine puissance, soit environ 0,40 € au tarif réglementé d’EDF (0,2001 € le kWh en option Base depuis le 1er août 2026). Programmer des plages courtes dans l’application évite de le laisser tourner pour rien, et c’est là que le côté connecté sert vraiment.

articles.title: Pour défier le FSD de Tesla, BYD lance sa conduite autonome God's Eye en Europe dès 2027 — Frandroid
articles.text:
La guerre bat toujours son plein entre les différents constructeurs automobiles, qu’ils soient chinois ou non. Elle se joue sur plusieurs terrains, que ce soit le prix, l’autonomie ou encore les technologies. La conduite autonome en fait évidemment partie. Si Tesla avait lancé le mouvement au cours des années 2010, la firme américaine s’est depuis largement fait rattraper, notamment par les constructeurs chinois. On pense par exemple à BYD, qui avait dévoilé en 2025 sa propre technologie concurrente.
Baptisée God’s Eye, elle se décline en plusieurs versions, selon le niveau d’automatisation. Mais jusqu’alors, elle était uniquement réservée à la Chine. Cela va désormais changer, puisque le constructeur a confirmé que cette conduite semi-autonome débarquerait bientôt en Europe. BYD l’a annoncé cette semaine au Mondial de l’Auto de Paris, et on sait déjà quelle sera la première voiture à inaugurer cette technologie en Europe. Il s’agit de la nouvelle Denza Z9 GT, que nous avions récemment pu essayer.
Le break électrique de 1 156 chevaux, vendu à partir de 115 000 euros en France, sera donc le tout premier modèle du groupe chinois à avoir droit au God’s Eye en Europe. Il faudra en revanche patienter jusqu’en 2027 pour en profiter. Pour l’heure, aucune date plus précise n’a été confirmée par la marque. Pour mémoire, cette technologie est une conduite semi-autonome de niveau 2, qui ne permet pas encore de quitter la route des yeux.
Les clients qui ont déjà acheté une Z9 GT en profiteront aussi. Selon Denza, le matériel nécessaire est monté de série depuis le lancement européen de la voiture, en avril, et la fonction arrivera par une mise à jour à distance (OTA). Le logiciel est encore en phase de calibration, avant l’homologation selon le règlement R171 de l’ONU, obligatoire pour sa commercialisation.
Une conduite semi-autonome pensée pour la ville
En revanche, ce système sait gérer la conduite en ville, sous la surveillance du conducteur. Denza assure qu’il peut s’arrêter aux feux rouges, céder le passage à l’entrée des ronds points ou contourner une voiture garée en double file. Pour le moment, la réglementation européenne autorise uniquement la conduite semi-autonome dans des conditions très précises.
C’est le cas seulement sur les voies rapides séparées par un terre-plein central, et jusqu’à 130 km/h. En ville, il faut passer par une homologation spécifique, que Tesla a obtenue le 10 avril 2026 aux Pays-Bas pour son FSD supervisé. Denza vise de son côté une homologation selon le règlement R171 de l’ONU. Mais la vice-présidente exécutive de BYD, Stella Li, est déjà très enthousiaste à ce sujet.
Dans le communiqué de Denza, elle affirme que « cette technologie contribuera à rendre la conduite en ville moins stressante, des embouteillages aux intersections et ronds-points encombrés ». La technologie God’s Eye existe en trois versions, avec ou sans capteur LiDAR. La Z9 GT européenne a droit à la variante B (aussi appelée DiPilot 300), avec un LiDAR, 11 caméras, trois radars et 12 capteurs à ultrasons, tous montés de série. Pour l’heure, la Z9 GT sera la seule auto dotée de ce système, mais Stella Li a annoncé son déploiement sur toute la gamme Denza.
BYD a aussi présenté son Atto 8 au salon parisien, premier modèle de la marque BYD à recevoir la recharge flash en Europe. La marque n’a en revanche pas confirmé l’arrivée du God’s Eye sur ce grand SUV électrique à sept places. Plus tard, d’autres modèles du groupe devraient aussi s’offrir cette technologie, qui vise à concurrencer Tesla. La firme d’Elon Musk cherche de son côté à étendre son FSD (Full Self-Driving) supervisé au-delà des Pays-Bas, mais son homologation dans le reste de l’Europe s’annonce plus complexe que prévu, et la France ne l’autorise toujours pas.
BYD n’est pas le seul constructeur chinois à viser la conduite assistée en ville. Xpeng prévoit d’apporter son système NGP en Europe au premier trimestre 2027, d’abord sur les modèles équipés de sa puce Turing, comme la berline P7+ ou le SUV G9L. Les deux marques devraient donc arriver à peu près en même temps sur ce terrain.

articles.title: L’aspirateur-robot laveur Lefant M5 Pro passe sous la barre de 400€ grâce à cette petite astuce à connaître chez Amazon
articles.text:
L’aspirateur robot laveur Lefant M5 Pro est un modèle adapté à l’entretien quotidien des petits logements. Sur Amazon, il est actuellement possible de l’acquérir pour 399,98 € au lieu de 999,99 € grâce à l'association d'une remise immédiate et d'un coupon de réduction.
Tous les aspirateurs-robots laveurs avec station d’autonettoyage n’affichent pas un prix à quatre chiffres. Le Lefant M5 Pro est une référence de milieu de gamme adaptée aux petits logements sur un niveau, et il coûte actuellement 399,98 € au lieu de 999,99 € chez Amazon. Pour obtenir cette remise de 60%, il ne faut pas oublier d’activer le coupon de réduction de 50 €, présent sur la fiche du produit et valable jusqu’au 21 octobre 2026.
L’aspirateur-robot laveur Lefant M5 Pro revient à 399,98 € chez Amazon grâce à une remise immédiate et à un coupon de réduction.
Pourquoi choisir le Lefant M5 Pro ?
- Pour son rouleau de 20 cm : il est alimenté en eau propre pendant le nettoyage, tandis qu’une raclette récupère les saletés et l’eau usagée.
- Pour sa station automatique : elle collecte la poussière et lave le rouleau à l’eau chaude jusqu’à 75°C après chaque cycle.
- Pour sa gestion des tapis : le robot les détecte et relève son rouleau de 8 mm pour limiter leur contact avec l’humidité.
Un système de lavage adapté aux sols durs
Le Lefant M5 Pro est un aspirateur-robot laveurparticulièrement adapté aux logements dotés d’une majorité de sols durs, comme du carrelage, du linoléum ou encore du parquet. Néanmoins, pas d’inquiétude si vous avez des tapis, puisque l’appareil est capable de relever son rouleau de 8 mm pour éviter de trop les mouiller. Le rouleau-brosse qui équipe le robot est raclé et alimenté en eau propre en permanence, ce qui optimise grandement le nettoyage des sols. Au retour à la base, le rouleau bénéficie d’un nettoyage à l’eau chaude et d’un séchage à l’air froid. La poussière et l’eau sale sont automatiquement stockées respectivement dans un sac et dans un bac dédiés, présents dans la station.
Une station pratique, avec quelques concessions
La station multifonction qui accompagne le Lefant M5 Pro automatise certaines tâches d’entretien, ce qui s’avère pratique. Néanmoins, la capacité des réservoirs d’eau propre et d’eau sale est plus limitée que sur d’autres modèles d’aspirateurs plus haut de gamme, il faut donc intervenir manuellement plus souvent.
✅ Les points forts
- Rouleau lavant de 20 cm alimenté en eau propre.
- Lavage du rouleau avec une eau à 75°C.
- Collecte automatique de la poussière.
❌ Les limites
- Séchage du rouleau à l’air froid.
- Relevage de 8 mm peu adapté aux tapis épais.
Pour obtenir le Lefant M5 Pro à 399,98 €, pensez à cocher le coupon avant de passer commande.
L’aspirateur-robot laveur Lefant M5 Pro affiche un bon rapport qualité-prix pour les logements essentiellement composés de sols durs sur un seul niveau. Sa station multifonction permet de réduire les besoins d’intervention manuelle.
En revanche, si vous possédez beaucoup de tapis, c’est un modèle un peu moins adapté. Il faut aussi penser à acheter des sacs à poussière de remplacement afin d’en changer de temps en temps.

articles.title: NVIDIA plans minority investments in four French startups as European tech commitment nears €9 billion | EU-Startups
articles.text:
NVIDIA, the US-based chipmaker behind the AI infrastructure buildout, has announced planned minority investments in four French startups: Doctolib, Entalpic, Genesis AI and Pigment.
These startups are striving to solve challenges across healthcare, materials discovery, physical AI and business planning. The US chipmaker has been deepening its commitment to building Europe’s artificial intelligence ecosystem. The announcement comes as NVIDIA’s total commitment to the European technology ecosystem reaches nearly €9 billion ($10 billion).
“[These investments] launch the artificial intelligence revolution in Europe,” said Jensen Huang, President and CEO of NVIDIA.
Huang revealed NVIDIA’s further investment in Europe’s AI ecosystem at a reception held at Place Vendôme in Paris, attended by French Economy Minister Roland Lescure and representatives from French technology companies.
The four new investments build on NVIDIA’s past investments, including Alice&Bob, Gradium, and Scintil Photonics. The four French startups backed by NVIDIA are innovating to solve challenges across healthcare, materials discovery, physical AI, and business planning.
Doctolib, a French HealthTech unicorn, builds agents that free up healthcare professionals to deliver better care, while providing patients with a digital health companion that improves access to care and supports preventive, continuous medicine. The company had earlier confirmed that NVIDIA agreed to buy a minority stake, without revealing the size or value.
Entalpic, a Paris-based startup, accelerates the engineering of advanced materials at the atomic scale. Its expertise lies in surfaces and interfaces for semiconductor manufacturing and next-generation electronics.
Genesis AI is a global robotics company developing general-purpose robots with frontier intelligence and capabilities through its foundational models, data collection systems, simulation infrastructure, and robot hardware. “We are excited that NVIDIA is a strategic investor in Genesis AI,” the company said in a statement.
Pigment, a Paris-based enterprise software company, is building a planning platform that helps businesses forecast performance, model scenarios and make decisions across finance, sales, workforce, and operations. In April 2024, the company announced a €133 million Series D funding round, led by ICONIQ Growth. It announced its €80 million Series C funding in June 2023.
The investments also underscore France’s rise as Europe’s leading hub for AI technology companies. The country has seen major progress in scaling AI companies, driven by the AI Action Summit in February 2025 and the Choose France Summits in 2025 and 2026, which brought major compute commitments to French soil.
NVIDIA says its open Nemotron models are in production across French organisations that require sovereign, trustworthy data, while French AI startup Mistral introduced, under private preview,e Mistral Large 4 with state-of-the-art open weight performance in cyber defence, manufacturing, finance, and multimodal tasks.
The ecosystem has gradually moved from ambition to application, and the four French startups can see immediate impact with other investors and potential partners thanks to NVIDIA’s backing.
NVIDIA’s GTC Berlin event will take place on 20–22 October, with Huang delivering a live keynote at the Tempodrom on 21 October.

articles.title: Agentic video startup Clueso raises $10M in Series A funding round
articles.text:
Agentic video startup Clueso raises $10M in Series A funding round
The startup founded by IIT Madras alumni plans to use the funding to scale its enterprise go-to-market reach, deepen its agentic layer, and expand editing capabilities.
Clueso, the agentic video platform for business founded by IIT Madras alumni, has raised $10 million in a Series A round of funding led by Dharana Capital, with Founders Future and Neotribe Ventures joining as new investors.
The round also saw participation from Y Combinator and f7 Ventures. This round brings the total fund raised to $12 million.
Founded in 2023 by Akash Anand, Prajwal Prakash, and Neel Balar, Clueso is based out of California and Bengaluru. It plans to use the funding to scale its enterprise go-to-market reach, deepen its agentic layer, and expand editing capabilities.
The startup says more than 1,000 companies use its platform to create videos for functions such as marketing, customer success and education, onboarding and training. Customers include Atlassian, Zendesk, Gainsight, GlobalPartners, Seismic, and Ironclad. Clueso claims that users have reported productivity gains of over 5x and an 80% reduction in video production costs.
Clueso's co-founder & CEO Akash Anand noted that the company started out by helping customer-facing teams create product tutorials faster. “We quickly saw the same problem across marketing, sales, training and internal documentation. That made us realise the opportunity was much bigger. Today, Clueso acts as an AI video production team that anyone or any team in the organisation can rely on, handling the work of creating, editing and maintaining videos as the business moves.”
Clueso is building AI agents that understand a company’s products, processes, brand and context, and then use that knowledge to create and maintain video across the organisation.
Vamsi Duvvuri, Founder and Managing Partner at Dharana Capital said, “With AI, video is evolving from static media files into living, context-aware assets that continuously adapt as business processes and products change. Clueso is building the infrastructure powering this shift.”
Edited by Swetha Kannan

articles.title: Microsoft: Windows 11 24H2 Home and Pro reached end of support
articles.text:
Microsoft announced today that devices running Windows 11 24H2 Home and Pro editions have reached the end of support and will no longer receive monthly security and non-security preview updates.
However, according to Microsoft's lifecycle policy, Windows 11 24H2 Enterprise and Education editions remain under mainstream support until October 12, 2027.
"Today, October 13, 2026, Windows 11, version 24H2 Home and Pro, and Windows 10 Enterprise LTSB 2016 have reached end of updates. The October 2026 monthly security update is the last update available for these editions," Microsoft said in a message center update.
"Devices running these editions will no longer receive monthly security and non-security preview updates containing protections from the latest security threats."
Microsoft advises users to upgrade to Windows 11 26H2, the latest Windows 11 version, also known as the Windows 11 2026 Update, which is now rolling out in phases to eligible Windows 11 devices where the "Get the latest updates as soon as they're available" option has been enabled.
Windows 11 26H2 became generally available in September 2026 as an enablement package and will reach end of support for consumers in October 2029.
"Windows 11, version 26H2 rollout is phased and will expand over the next few months," it added. "If the update is ready for your device, it will download and install automatically, and a single restart will complete the process."
Last week, Microsoft also reminded customers that systems running Windows 11 23H2 Enterprise, Education, and IoT Enterprise editions will also stop receiving security updates in 30 days, after Windows 11 23H2 Home and Pro editions reach end of support in November 2025.
Earlier this year, it extended the free Windows 10 Extended Security Updates (ESU) program for home users and announced that Windows Server 2022 also reaches the end of mainstream support today (but will remain under extended support until October 2031).
More recently, on Thursday, it warned customers to upgrade devices running unsupported versions of Windows as they will stop receiving security updates after next year's Windows Update certificate rotation.
More information about Windows 11 servicing dates is available on the Windows Lifecycle FAQ page or using the Lifecycle Policy search tool.

articles.title: Al cobrar impuestos por cada puerta y ventana abierta durante 126 años, Francia empujó a los ciudadanos a transformar sus casas de una manera que aún hoy es visible
articles.text:
Durante más de un siglo, Francia convirtió algo tan cotidiano como abrir una ventana en una cuestión fiscal. En 1798, el Estado decidió cobrar impuestos por cada puerta y ventana de las viviendas, desencadenando una reacción inesperada: propietarios que tapiaron huecos, eliminaron elementos arquitectónicos y modificaron sus casas para pagar menos. La medida sobrevivió 126 años y dejó una herencia extraordinaria: algunas de aquellas decisiones tomadas para escapar de Hacienda todavía pueden reconocerse en las fachadas francesas.
Un impuesto que cambió las casas. La historia comenzó el 24 de noviembre de 1798, cuando el Directorio francés aprobó una contribución sobre las puertas y ventanas de los edificios. Lo que inicialmente se planteó como un tributo anual terminó prolongándose durante casi 127 años, hasta su desaparición efectiva en 1926.
Durante todo ese tiempo, el número de aberturas de una vivienda influyó en lo que pagaban sus propietarios, creando un incentivo económico para transformar físicamente los inmuebles. El resultado fue una intervención indirecta del Estado en la arquitectura doméstica, cuyas huellas siguen presentes en determinadas calles y edificios históricos.
Contar ventanas desde la calle. El impuesto fue impulsado por Dominique Ramel, ministro de Finanzas del Directorio, en un contexto de graves dificultades económicas posteriores a la Revolución francesa. Su funcionamiento era sencillo: los recaudadores contabilizaban las puertas y ventanas que daban a calles, patios o jardines, utilizando elementos visibles como indicadores de riqueza.
Según las tarifas iniciales recogidas por los registros históricos, cada abertura podía costar 0,20 francos en municipios de menos de 5.000 habitantes y 0,60 francos en ciudades de al menos 100.000 habitantes. Las puertas cocheras y las de los comercios soportaban una tributación doble. El sistema permitía calcular el gravamen sin entrar en las viviendas, respetando formalmente la privacidad de sus ocupantes.
La arquitectura contra Hacienda. Como era de esperar, los propietarios encontraron distintas maneras de reducir la factura, algunas de ellas tan surrealistas como levantar muros donde antes había ventanas. Las tradicionales ventanas renacentistas divididas por parteluces también sufrieron modificaciones, porque determinadas configuraciones podían contabilizarse como varias aberturas y encarecer el impuesto. Eliminar esas divisiones permitía reducir la cantidad gravada.
Algo parecido ocurrió con las grandes puertas cocheras, que algunos propietarios sustituyeron por accesos ordinarios. En Montmort-Lucy, en el departamento de Marne, se conserva un ejemplo de esa transformación. También aparecieron falsas ventanas pintadas o representadas mediante trampantojos para mantener la simetría de las fachadas sin añadir nuevas aberturas sujetas al tributo.
El precio de la luz natural. No solo eso. Las consecuencias llegaron también al interior de los edificios. Reducir el número o el tamaño de las ventanas significaba limitar la entrada de luz solar y dificultar la circulación del aire, especialmente en las viviendas más modestas. El impuesto terminó ganándose el sobrenombre de "tributo sobre el aire y la luz", y recibió críticas de quienes denunciaban sus efectos sobre la higiene y la salud pública.
La legislación contemplaba algunas excepciones: graneros, establos, bodegas y otras construcciones no destinadas a vivienda quedaban exentos, al igual que determinadas aberturas pequeñas, como tragaluces y respiraderos. Estas diferencias fiscales pudieron influir en las soluciones arquitectónicas elegidas para iluminar ciertos espacios.
Una idea con antecedentes. Francia había tomado como referencia la Window Tax británica, introducida en Inglaterra y Gales en 1696, que también utilizaba las ventanas como indicador de la capacidad económica de los propietarios. El principio respondía a una preocupación característica de la fiscalidad de aquella época: encontrar señales exteriores de riqueza que permitieran establecer impuestos sin conocer los ingresos reales de cada ciudadano.
En Francia, la contribución pasó a formar parte de los cuatro grandes impuestos directos heredados de la Revolución, conocidos posteriormente como las quatre vieilles. Aquella reforma pretendía extender las obligaciones fiscales bajo el principio de igualdad tributaria, aunque sus consecuencias prácticas terminaron siendo muy diferentes según las características de cada inmueble.
El final de una anomalía. Las críticas de los movimientos higienistas, el desarrollo de nuevas formas de tributación y el solapamiento con otros impuestos inmobiliarios fueron debilitando la justificación de la medida. Finalmente, la ley del 19 de julio de 1925 estableció su supresión, efectiva en 1926, cuando la contribución apenas generaba unos 60 millones de francos anuales. Francia cerraba así un capítulo fiscal iniciado durante el Directorio, mientras consolidaba un sistema tributario en el que el impuesto sobre la renta había adquirido un papel creciente desde 1914.
Hoy, las ventanas tapiadas que todavía se observan en algunas fachadas recuerdan aquella época. Si se quiere también, la historia dejó una lección particularmente visible: que una decisión tributaria puede alterar el aspecto de las ciudades mucho después de que desaparezca la ley que la provocó.
