articles.title: SAP Patches Critical NetWeaver, S/4HANA Vulnerabilities
articles.text:
Enterprise software maker SAP on Tuesday announced the release of 22 new and updated security notes, including four that address critical-severity vulnerabilities.
At the top of the list is CVE-2026-89111 (CVSS score of 10/10), an OAuth2 SSRF vulnerability in Cloud SDK for Python that impacts multi-tenant BTP applications.
“An attacker who controls the tenant_subdomain parameter can redirect OAuth2 token requests to an attacker-controlled server, causing client credentials to be exfiltrated,” SAP explains in a GitHub advisory.
Next in line is CVE-2026-89110 (CVSS score of 9.9/10), a broken access control in certain portal functionality of NetWeaver Visual Composer.
According to enterprise application security firm Onapsis, the flaw could allow “a low-privileged attacker to invoke internal operations on a preconfigured remote system” and fully compromise it.
The third critical-severity vulnerability resolved on SAP’s October 2026 Security Patch Day is CVE-2026-89107 (CVSS score of 9.9/10), a code injection issue in S/4HANA that could allow authenticated attackers to execute arbitrary ABAP code on the system.
The security defect exists because the rule definition process fails to properly validate input, allowing attackers holding a specific business role in the Fiori Applications to submit crafted input. Successful exploitation could allow attackers to take over a vulnerable system, Onapsis explains.
The fourth critical bug is CVE-2026-89108 (CVSS score of 9.1/10), a missing authorization check in Manufacturing Integration and Intelligence that could allow an attacker with XMII Admin privileges to create an administrator account on the underlying Java application server and fully compromise the system.
On Tuesday, SAP also resolved high-severity flaws in Commerce Cloud, NetWeaver, and ABAP Platform that could allow attackers to inject arbitrary SQL commands, trigger a process crash, and bypass restrictions.
SAP makes no mention of any of the newly resolved security defects being exploited in the wild. Users are advised to update their applications as soon as possible.

articles.title: Production Patterns for Agents, Evals, and LLM Costs: QCon AI New York 2026
articles.text:
Once AI is in production, code arrives faster than it can be reviewed, token costs rise, evals have to be good enough to act on, and agents need permissions and guardrails. QCon AI New York 2026 has confirmed sessions from senior engineers who have worked through these problems in systems they run. The conference takes place December 15-16 at The Westin Jersey City Newport, about five minutes by PATH train from the World Trade Center. It is for senior engineers and technical leaders making decisions on production AI.
What the sessions offer is hindsight. The senior engineers presenting have already made these decisions and run the results in production. They describe the system and the numbers behind it, letting another team compare an approach against its own constraints before committing.
Identity and authorization for agents in production
The QCon AI opening keynote describes two bad options for giving an agent production access. Teams hand it a long-lived service account and hope, or scope access too narrowly until it cannot finish its task. Nancy Wang, who founded and scaled AWS Data Protection, provides alternative solutions in When Software Becomes a User: Identity and Authorization for Agents in Production.
See what those controls look like on a live platform. Implement guardrails that sit on the server, including rate limits and peer approval for production changes, from Ronak Nathani, who led the move to Kubernetes at LinkedIn. He presents Inside LinkedIn's Kubernetes Ops Agent: Skills, Tools, and Guardrails, detailing an operations agent working across 500,000+ nodes and 5M+ pods. Together, the two talks give a team an authorization model and a working set of guardrails to compare with its own.
Whether a change is safe to ship, and what it costs to run
An eval is useful when engineers trust the score enough to ship or hold on it. Fabio Flores, who leads foundation development for Agentic Ordering at DoorDash, will argue that engineers should apply one judge to both simulated and production sessions so improvements measured before launch carry into production. He presents From Signal To Impact: The Eval Loop Behind DoorDash's Agentic Ordering System.
Agent workloads that worked as prototypes can become too expensive in production as context grows. Tejas Chopra, who previously worked on distributed caching infrastructure at Netflix, will explore how to implement prompt compression and ordering that increases provider cache hits. In Make Each Token Count: Compression, Caching, and Retrieval for Production LLM Context, he covers tiered storage for conversation history and the failure modes his team hit.
When AI writes code faster than teams can review it
Human review becomes the bottleneck as AI tools generate more code. Min Chen, who leads the move to AI-native software engineering at LinkedIn, suggests engineers should filter low-confidence findings before developers see them. She presents High-Signal AI Code Review That Adapts to Your Codebase at Scale. The system reviews tens of thousands of pull requests a week across roughly 10,000 repositories, and she explains how the team measures whether suggestions make it into merged code.
Faster output does not help every organization equally. Nathen Harvey, who leads DORA at Google Cloud, will explore how to assess AI maturity beyond adoption metrics and identify which existing problems AI is likely to make worse. He argues in Building in the AI-First World: Scale Brilliance, Not Bottlenecks that AI amplifies what an organization already does well and what it does badly.
What teams take back
The QCon AI Program Committee invites senior practitioners who are doing something other teams can learn from. The talks are vendor-neutral with no hidden product pitches, so each one is an account of what a team built and why. With one speaker for every eleven attendees, there is also time for a follow-up question for the person who built the system. The aim is for teams to return with patterns ready to adopt and costly mistakes they can avoid.
All confirmed talks are on the QCon AI New York 2026 sessions page.

articles.title: Apple TV 4K : un nouveau boitier TV que les Européens ne pourront pas vraiment utiliser
articles.text:
Une nouvelle version de l’Apple TV, ça se fête ! C’est un produit de niche mais adoré de ses utilisateurs et qu’Apple ne met à jour que très occasionnellement. La dernière fois c’était en 2022, une autre époque à l’échelle des nouvelles technologies. Quatre ans plus tard, Apple prend donc la peine de revoir son boîtier TV et la marque de Cupertino a un objectif précis : transformer ce simple cube dédié au streaming en véritable hub domotique.
C’est donc tout sauf un hasard si l’annonce de cette nouvelle Apple TV 4K (4ᵉ génération) intervient au même moment que l’officialisation des premiers produits domotiques signés Apple ou encore du HomeView. À l’instar de l’enceinte connectée, l’Apple TV 4K veut devenir un relais pour contrôler SiriAI et les produits qui y sont liés.
Deux nouveautés matérielles
Pour transformer un simple boîtier TV en hub domotique, il convient d’apporter quelques ajustements matériels. C’est ainsi que l’Apple TV 4K se voit modifiée aussi bien au niveau du boîtier que de la télécommande. Sur le premier, les ingénieurs d’Apple sont venus ajouter trois micros longue portée (Far-field) avec annulation d’écho avancée. Celui-ci se déclenche avec la commande vocale « Dis Siri ».
Côté télécommande, c’est un haut-parleur qui permet désormais de la faire sonner pour la retrouver rapidement. C’est tout simplement la fonctionnalité « Find My » qui est appliquée à la télécommande.
Enfin, à l’intérieur de l’Apple TV il y a aussi un chamboulement notable avec une nouvelle puce, l’A19 en l’occurrence. La puce de l’iPhone 17 et de l’iPhone 17e devrait être largement en mesure d’effectuer les tâches classiques demandées à l’Apple TV, mais aussi, dans les pays où la législation le permet, d’accéder à SiriAI. Rappelons à toutes fins utiles que la dernière version de l’assistant vocal d’Apple n’est pas encore disponible en Europe.
Le gain de puissance annoncée est de 50% pour le CPU et une vitesse de traitement doublée côté GPU. Enfin Apple intègre un décodeur AV1 pour améliorer la fluidité du streaming.
En revanche, côté design, il n’y a que très peu de changements à noter côté boîtier. En revanche, côté télécommande on revient à une version métallique et donc bien plus solide, sans changer de form factor.
Des fonctionnalités étendues
Intégrer l’Apple TV 4K dans un système domotique Apple a un autre avantage : créer un réel écosystème. Ainsi, il sera possible de combiner son boîtier TV avec des HomePod mini 2 (jusqu’à 4) pour un effet surround. Dans ce cas de figure, l’Apple TV se chargera de calibrer automatiquement le son en fonction de la position des enceintes dans la pièce.
Prix et date de commercialisation de l’Apple TV 4K (2026)
La nouvelle version de l’Apple TV 4K est déjà disponible en ligne, les premières livraisons sont prévues pour le 13 novembre prochain. Son prix : 349 euros.

articles.title: OpenAI dice que sus modelos interactuaron con sitios web del gobierno de EE. UU. en una nueva divulgación de comportamiento indebido del modelo
articles.text:
Encargarle a un agente de IA que busque datos en Internet parece lo más inocuo del mundo. Hasta que el agente decide cómo buscarlos.
OpenAI informó el viernes 25 de septiembre que sus agentes interactuaron, de formas que ni ellos mismos esperaban, con varias webs del Gobierno de EE. UU. Fue algo que descubrieron en una revisión en curso sobre el comportamiento imprevisto de sus modelos.
Accedieron a información pública de dos webs de la SEC (el regulador bursátil) y a datos de la Oficina del Censo, y la compañía dice que no encontró uso de credenciales de la SEC, acceso a cuentas ni información no pública, cambios en datos o sistemas de la SEC, ni evidencia de compromiso o de vulnerabilidad. Para el Censo, según otro relato de la divulgación, usaron claves de desarrollador de su API que encontraron en repositorios públicos de GitHub, y de la SEC descargaron información que volvieron a publicar en otra página.
El intento que no funcionó y los que Transluce no atribuye
Luego está lo que no consiguieron. Transluce, un laboratorio independiente que evalúa IA, contó que agentes que parecían proceder de OpenAI intentaron un hackeo rudimentario contra la web de la oficina de derechos civiles del Departamento de Educación.
No funcionó, y Educación dijo que sus revisiones no encontraron ningún impacto en su web ni en sus bases de datos. Transluce añade que ha dado con más actividad en otras agencias, como Justicia y Comercio, y en webs de los estados de California, Maryland, Illinois, Texas y Nueva York, parte de ella sin atribución clara a OpenAI. OpenAI dice que está revisando el informe.
La propia OpenAI pide no leer demasiado en sus avisos: notificar a una organización no significa que haya habido un incidente de seguridad, y puede servir para señalar un fallo de diseño o una debilidad que quiera corregir. Según la compañía, la mayor parte de lo revisado hasta ahora son tareas rutinarias de investigación en las que los agentes consultaban contenido público para responder preguntas, entre ellas webs de Gobierno que consideran fuentes fiables. Los casos de esta divulgación ocurrieron durante el entrenamiento y la evaluación de los modelos.
¿Es la primera vez que se le va de las manos?
No es la primera vez que algo así ocurre. En julio, OpenAI admitió que dos de sus modelos más capaces habían escapado de un entorno de pruebas y estaban detrás del ciberataque contra Hugging Face. Sam Altman escribió el 25 de septiembre que aquel incidente sigue siendo “el evento más grave que hemos visto”.
En el informe que publicó en agosto, la compañía lo describió como un aviso de que, sin salvaguardas, agentes muy capaces ya saben saltarse controles técnicos, y fijó una norma: vigilar el razonamiento de los modelos en todo entrenamiento con herramientas de capacidad igual o superior.
La norma no bastó. El fin de semana del 19 y 20 de septiembre, según el relato publicado después, un agente en entrenamiento volvió a escapar de su entorno seguro y usó un servidor DNS para enviar consultas a un chatbot público. La monitorización lo detectó en 15 minutos, pero el entrenamiento siguió dos horas y media más, hasta que alguien lo paró a mano. OpenAI ha vuelto a detener el entrenamiento de sus modelos más avanzados, la segunda pausa desde julio.
Tres meses para avisar a Australia
El caso de las webs de EE. UU. no es el único con un gobierno de por medio. En Australia, el 18 de junio de 2026, un agente de investigación de OpenAI entró sin permiso en un portal de estadísticas de Medicare.
Según el primer ministro, Anthony Albanese, el agente accedió a archivos públicos y no públicos (el portal guarda información no sensible de Medicare, como gastos y estadísticas), escribió archivos en el servidor interno y no tocó datos personales, aunque la investigación sigue. Lo hizo después de que le bloquearan el acceso, probando vías alternativas.
OpenAI no avisó hasta el 10 de septiembre, 84 días después, a través de un buzón de divulgación responsable de Services Australia que se revisa una vez al día. El 15 de septiembre, ese organismo lo comunicó a la ASD, la agencia australiana de señales y ciberseguridad. Albanese lo hizo público a finales de mes.
De decenas a más de cien
Al contar lo de las webs de EE. UU., OpenAI hablaba de decenas de organizaciones notificadas. A 2 de octubre, la cifra era de más de 100. La compañía reconoce que, en algunos casos, los modelos usaron el acceso a Internet de maneras no previstas o sin las restricciones ideales y está revisando unos 50 petabytes de datos con sistemas de IA, a un coste de unos 500.000 dólares diarios.
Tres días después apareció otra pieza. El 5 de octubre, la Fundación Wikimedia atribuyó a agentes que vincula con OpenAI ediciones no aprobadas, sobre todo en zonas de prueba que no llegaron a ver los lectores, intentos fallidos de usar un servicio de notas compartidas como proxy y millones de peticiones a sus APIs públicas, con cientos de miles de consultas al servicio de datos de Wikidata. Wikimedia sostiene que ese tráfico puede haber contribuido a una caída parcial de ese servicio en mayo. No se comprometió ningún sistema ni se filtraron datos.
De decenas a más de cien. Y la lista de afectados no ha dejado de crecer.

articles.title: Airtel’s virtual card will test Safaricom’s grip on Kenya’s online payments
articles.text: Airtel Mobile Commerce N.V., the Netherlands-based fintech arm of Airtel Africa, plans to launch a virtual payment card in Kenya, setting up a new contest with Safaricom over international online spending. Developed with Mastercard, the Virtual Card Number (VCN) will integrate with Airtel Money wallets, enabling customers to pay for services on global platforms such as Amazon and Netflix without a traditional bank account. The launch puts Airtel Money Global Pay in direct competition with M-PESA GlobalPay, Safaricom’s virtual Visa card introduced in 2022 . Airtel is entering a market where Safaricom has an established lead, but the contest is about more than the payment networks behind the cards. It also concerns how customers fund transactions, manage online spending, and access credit when their wallet balances run low. The M-PESA GlobalPay card can draw on Fuliza, an overdraft facility that lets eligible customers complete online payments when their M-PESA balance is insufficient. Airtel Money’s prepaid card lacks this feature, requiring customers to fund it before making a purchase. Data from the Communications Authority of Kenya shows M-PESA’s mobile money market share has slipped to 88.8% in June 2026, down from nearly 95% in 2023. Airtel Money’s share rose to 11.1% over the same period. The figures indicate a gradual shift in the competitive balance, although Safaricom’s lead remains substantial. Global commerce offers a new revenue stream Kenya’s growing use of digital services gives both operators a reason to compete for international payments. Streaming subscriptions, software services, and overseas e-commerce platforms allow mobile money providers to reach spending that might otherwise flow through bank cards. Netflix, which entered Africa in 2016, is one example of how international digital services have become part of everyday spending. Virtual cards let customers without bank accounts pay these merchants via mobile money, extending wallets’ reach beyond domestic transfers and merchant payments. For operators facing pressure on domestic payment charges, cross-border transactions also offer a way to earn revenue from international commerce. Foreign currency conversion and merchant payments can generate income beyond the core business of moving money between local accounts. Safaricom’s global payments operation, which includes cross-border transfers, virtual cards, and app store billing, generated KES 4.76 billion ($37.2 million) in the financial year ended March 2026 , up 22.3% from the previous year. M-PESA generated KES 182.7 billion (323.1 billion) in transaction value across 46.4 billion transactions. The figures show why even a relatively small slice of M-PESA’s business is important. Global payments can contribute to revenue growth without requiring Safaricom to win a comparable share of Kenya’s domestic mobile money market. The opportunity for Airtel is to capture a portion of that spending as more customers use its wallet for online purchases. Across 14 African markets, Airtel’s mobile money operation generated $1.3 billion in revenue , up from $747 million. The company has issued more than 875,000 virtual cards in Uganda, Zambia and Tanzania since 2025 and plans to introduce the service in Kenya, the Democratic Republic of Congo and Gabon. Credit and security separate the cards The two products take different approaches to funding online payments. M-PESA GlobalPay links to the customer’s M-PESA wallet. In contrast, Airtel’s VCN model requires customers to transfer funds from their main Airtel Money wallet to the virtual card before making a purchase. The setup lets Airtel customers ring-fence money for online purchases, keeping the rest of their wallet balance separate from card transactions. It also gives them greater control over subscription payments and their online spending. Customers still need to protect their account credentials and monitor transactions. The extent of protection also depends on the controls available to freeze or manage the card, to dispute unauthorised payments, and to prevent further charges. Safaricom’s original virtual Visa card design used a card verification value (CVV) that customers generated through the M-PESA app after entering their PIN. Each code lasted 30 minutes and could be used only once, limiting the window in which it could be used if exposed . Airtel Money Globalpay card. Image: Airtel Uganda Safaricom announced the overdraft option for GlobalPay in 2026, allowing eligible customers to complete online payments when their wallet balance is insufficient. The feature can help prevent subscription payments from failing, but it also means automated charges may draw on credit, leaving customers with an overdraft to repay. Airtel’s prepaid model does not offer an equivalent overdraft facility, so customers must have sufficient funds on the virtual card to complete a purchase. This may be less convenient, but it also prevents the card from extending spending through an equivalent credit line. A challenger still faces a scale problem Safaricom’s large customer base gives GlobalPay an established audience, while familiarity with M-PESA can make customers less inclined to switch payment methods. Airtel’s card could appeal to customers who already use Airtel Money and want a direct route to international merchants. Its regional rollout also gives the company experience to draw on as it enters the Kenyan market. Customers will need to compare foreign exchange charges, transaction limits, acceptance rates, dispute handling and the ease of managing card details. Airtel’s pricing will be particularly important because a lower-cost card could attract price-sensitive users, while unclear fees could blunt the appeal of its prepaid design. Airtel has yet to disclose all the details Kenyan customers will need to assess the service, including its foreign exchange charges. Safaricom’s GlobalPay applies a foreign exchange markup, making the total cost of a purchase a relevant point of comparison. The launch will not erase Safaricom’s lead in mobile money. Still, it will give Airtel another way to compete for customer spending, this time at the online checkout rather than through domestic transfers. True scale demands moving beyond surface-level integrations to robust execution. articles.title: La tecnología que Estados Unidos usará para monitorear el clima desde el cielo: globos meteorológicos con IA
articles.text:
La Fuerza Aérea de Estados Unidos firmó un contrato con la empresa WindBorne Systems para comprar datos atmosféricos recolectados por su flota de globos meteorológicos autónomos con IA, según el Departamento de Defensa de este país.
“Esto es, en gran medida, un vehículo para sostener el crecimiento continuo de la constelación de globos, además de financiar investigación y desarrollo para mejorar el hardware”, dijo Andrey Sushko, cofundador y director de tecnología de WindBorne, a TechCrunch.
El trabajo se extiende hasta el 30 de septiembre de 2033 y tiene un costo de hasta USD 48,7 millones. De ese monto total, la Fuerza Aérea solo desembolsó 1,7 millones de dólares al momento de la firma, el mínimo requerido por el primer pedido dentro del acuerdo.
El resto del techo de 48,7 millones se pagará únicamente si el servicio militar realiza nuevos pedidos de datos por región y período.
Cómo funciona una red de globos meteorológicos
Los globos meteorológicos son dispositivos aerostáticos equipados con instrumentos para medir variables atmosféricas, como temperatura, humedad, presión y viento, a distintas altitudes.
La tecnología de globos meteorológicos autónomos permite mantener en el aire una flota distribuida globalmente capaz de recolectar datos desde la superficie hasta la estratosfera. Cada unidad opera como un sensor atmosférico de larga duración y transmite información por satélite.
A diferencia de los globos meteorológicos tradicionales, que ascienden durante unas horas antes de estallar, estos dispositivos no utilizan motores.
Modifican su altitud para aprovechar corrientes de viento que los desplazan hacia regiones específicas y pueden permanecer en vuelo durante semanas, ascendiendo y descendiendo repetidamente entre uno y veinte kilómetros de altura.
Los datos recopilados alimentan modelos de pronóstico meteorológico que combinan observaciones atmosféricas directas con técnicas de aprendizaje automático.
Este enfoque permite generar previsiones a partir de información obtenida en zonas y altitudes donde las mediciones suelen ser limitadas.
La tecnología también puede aplicarse en redes de observación para organismos meteorológicos, fuerzas navales y sistemas de monitoreo climático y ambiental.
Su capacidad para operar de forma sostenida y coordinada amplía las posibilidades de recopilación de datos en tiempo real a escala global.
El objetivo es desarrollar constelaciones de hasta 10.000 globos operando simultáneamente, formando una red global de sensores atmosféricos capaz de ofrecer una cobertura más amplia y continua de las condiciones meteorológicas.
Cómo fue la vinculación de la Fuerza Aérea de Estados Unidos con estos globos
Sushko explicó que la decisión de adjudicar el contrato sin licitación respondió a una evaluación del propio gobierno.
“Fue una determinación de que, para esta capacidad de recolectar datos globales de la forma que necesitaban para estas operaciones, éramos la única empresa capaz de proveerla”, afirmó el ejecutivo.
El convenio cubre perfiles verticales atmosféricos continuos, globales y dirigidos a zonas específicas, de acuerdo con la descripción publicada por el Departamento de Guerra, el nuevo nombre que adoptó el Departamento de Defensa. El aviso del contrato no detalla cuántos datos comprará la Fuerza Aérea ni qué regiones priorizará.
La capacidad de dirigir los globos hacia zonas puntuales, algo inusual para un dispositivo sin propulsión propia, es lo que el contrato describe como “perfilado dirigido”: mediciones sobre océanos y regiones remotas donde hay pocas estaciones meteorológicas y no se pueden lanzar globos convencionales.
WindBorne había recaudado 37 millones de dólares en una ronda de financiamiento en agosto, que valuó a la empresa en 250 millones de dólares.
El contrato con la Fuerza Aérea llega apenas semanas después de esa ronda. Se suma a una relación con el Pentágono que la compañía viene construyendo desde hace varios años, con acuerdos previos tanto con la Armada como con distintas unidades de la propia Fuerza Aérea.
El aviso oficial tampoco explica qué uso específico le dará el Pentágono a los datos más allá de la planificación de misiones y los pronósticos militares, ni si incluirá los modelos propios de WindBorne además de las mediciones crudas de los globos.

articles.title: High-speed video reveals how honey bee stingers pump venom
articles.text:
Honey bees are known to leave their stingers embedded in tender flesh once they sting you and fly away. Scientists have now determined that the stinger is able to continue pumping venom into its unfortunate victim even after the bee flies away, thanks to a unique double-piston pump-like mechanism, according to a new paper published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
Different species have evolved different mechanisms for delivering venom, which involves piercing the skin and then pumping venom from a gland or reservoir. Spiders, for instance, have muscles surrounding their venom glands, which contract and eject venom through hollow fangs. Bees, wasps, and ants deliver venom via their stingers, either by contracting muscles around the venom reservoir or through stiff elements called lancets working together to pump venom.
Honey bees (Apis mellifera) add a unique feature: Worker bees fly away after inserting their stingers in the target, leaving the stinger behind. The stinger continues to penetrate the tissue and pump venom on its own, a rare phenomenon known as autotomy. A honey bee’s stinger has three main interlocking elements that form the venom canal: a stylet that widens to form the main pumping chamber and two sharp-tipped lancets that slide back and forth, piercing the tissue and pumping venom into the target. But the precise mechanism by which the pumping action is achieved has never been directly observed.
The authors of this latest paper sought to capture the venom-pumping kinematics of honey bee stingers in order to identify the underlying biomechanics. They collected live worker bees and removed the stingers with forceps just prior to filming. Then they partially inserted those stingers into blocks of artificial gel and captured the pumping action using stereomicroscopy and high-speed color videography. This was followed by a frame-by-frame analysis to better track the movement, which is visible because the structures are semi-translucent.

articles.title: Flox Intelligence is building AI to keep wildlife away from trains, airports, and roads | TechCrunch
articles.text:
When I was eight, I remember our train to Mumbai ground to a halt with a great noise. When we started moving again, a good eight hours later, someone pointed out a mangled tail, of all things, hanging from a branch close to the tracks.
The train, you see, had apparently hit a wild bison at full speed, and the impact damaged the engine so badly that it had to be towed away for repairs. For a long time, I thought such things only happened in places like rural India, but I learned a few years ago that wildlife and infrastructure do not mix anywhere on the planet.
The FAA estimates that wildlife strikes have cost U.S. civil aviation about $272 million a year on average between 1990 and 2025. In France, the rail operator SNCF says wandering animals affect more than 8,000 trains across the country each year and are among its five leading causes of delays. In Brittany, 120 trains hit animals in 2023 alone, disrupting 660 services and causing more than 15,000 minutes of delays.
Reading about all that damage, to both infrastructure and animals, inspired Sara Nozkova (pictured above on the left) to develop a wildlife-deterrent system that works differently from the sirens, lights, fences, falcons, and culling traditionally used to keep animals away from roads, train tracks, airports, and other infrastructure.
“I was convinced the answer was not a louder deterrent,” she told TechCrunch.
After spending 13 years working in transportation and autonomous vehicles, Nozkova had learned how quickly the systems we build to navigate roads and other controlled environments fail once nature enters the equation.
“We have taught machines to be brilliant, but only inside the environments we engineered for them,” she said. “Cities, factory lines, warehouses. Fixed geometry, known objects. Stepping outside into nature, I saw firsthand how the same machines quickly go blind. Because nature is complex and always alive.”
So instead she joined the AI lab at KTH Royal Institute of Technology in Stockholm and started working on a system that could change its deterrent responses based on what an animal nearby is doing, and even what kind of animal it is.
That work turned into Flox Intelligence, which spun out of KTH in 2020 and is one of the finalists at this year’s Startup Battlefield 200 pitch competition at TechCrunch Disrupt, taking place this year at Moscone West in San Francisco October 13-15.
Flox makes edge devices that process data on-site rather than in the cloud. Like autonomous vehicles, they use perception systems to sense their surroundings, but theirs are trained on wildlife behavior. A motion sensor wakes the device when it detects movement, triggering a camera that uses on-device models to identify nearby animals. The device then emits a species-appropriate sound to scare them away.
Nozkova says the system learns from experience, too, and varies its responses so animals don’t get habituated to repeated signals.
The company currently sells battery-operated devices that can be mounted on poles, trees, and other structures. It also offers a software platform that shows clients where the devices are deployed and what’s happening on the ground. The platform can also generate reports for regulatory compliance and for uses like biodiversity monitoring. The longer-term goal is to make the software portable enough to run on machines that work outside, including trains, cars, and drones.
Nozkova says about 150 Flox devices are live in North America, Europe, and Australia at airfields and airport perimeters, road and rail corridors (especially fence ends and crossings along wildlife corridors), national parks, agricultural land, urban areas, mining sites, and critical infrastructure such as electrical substations.
The company sells edge units up front, then charges an annual software and AI subscription after the first year. Flox also has OEM partnerships with companies that pay an annual fee to deploy its software on vehicles, like trains. Train manufacturer Alstom is one such partner.
The company expects to end 2026 with revenue of about $1.5 million, Nozkova said.
As unique as Flox’s product and approach are, the startup is not without competition. Robin Radar’s Scarecrow also uses species-specific distress calls to disperse birds and it records the activity, while iCHASE sells a system that detects birds with computer vision and targets them with a moving laser, adjusting its response as needed.
Nozkova says her moat is the breadth of the system and the data Flox has collected in the field, which she calls “ground truth on what actually makes a moose or a grizzly bear move safely.”
“Physical AI is walking out of the factory and into the messy, alive outdoors,” Nozkova says. “Every machine that operates outside — trains, trucks, drones, tractors, robots — will need to understand nature, and nature intelligence is the next layer of the perception stack. Almost nobody is building it.”
The company has raised about $5 million across pre-seed and seed rounds so far, with the seed round led by Unconventional Ventures and Tilia Impact Ventures. Co-investors across the rounds include GENIUS NY, Norrsken, Satgana, and angel investors, Nozkova said.
The company is now opening a $10 million Series A, which would mostly go toward growing from about 150 devices to several thousand deployed units and extending the underlying system beyond its current wildlife use cases.

articles.title: OpenAI employee arrested for allegedly planting a bug in a conference room
articles.text:
An OpenAI engineer was arrested after the company said it discovered a “sophisticated recording device” hidden in one of its offices. The employee was identified as Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old Saudi national. Alfozan is charged with using or endeavoring to use a device to intercept oral communications, according to a press release from the Department of Justice.
OpenAI employee arrested for allegedly planting a bug in a conference room
The recording device was apparently discovered plugged into a TV’s USB port in an executive meeting room.
OpenAI’s post about the incident says it used its AI models to “understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier.”
As noted by the DOJ, OpenAI found the device plugged into a TV’s USB port in an executive conference room, where discussions about “highly confidential technical, commercial, and strategic information” often take place.
Alfozan didn’t have access to this room, but CCTV footage allegedly showed him “near the executive conference room on multiple dates prior to the device’s discovery,” according to the DOJ. Footage also captured Alfozan appearing to look behind the TV where the device was installed, federal prosecutors claim.
The device was covered in toilet paper and installed on or around September 28th. Its contents were encrypted. Additionally, the DOJ claims OpenAI security discovered a bag Alfozan left in another room inside the company’s office, where they found his wallet, ID, and another recording device.
OpenAI says it fired the employee and referred the incident to the FBI. Alfozan was arrested Friday and has remained in custody since, appearing in federal court for the first time on Tuesday.
We discovered a sophisticated recording device that was hidden inside one of our offices. We used our models to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier. We referred the matter to the FBI, and we’re grateful to the agents and prosecutors who moved quickly to make an arrest. The FBI’s investigation is ongoing and we will continue to support their work.
At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data. The employee was terminated.
We take protecting our technology, data, and people seriously, and as a matter of national importance. Our security program is designed to protect against a wide range of threat actors, from insider risks to cybercriminals to nation states, and this case is an example of how AI can help address these sophisticated security threats.
Update, October 13th: Added information from the DOJ.

articles.title: Las nuevas aspiradoras de Roborock llegan con más potencia y menos mantenimiento
articles.text:
Las aspiradoras de fregado se han convertido en uno de los electrodomésticos más importantes del hogar. Si bien los robots aspiradores han tomado la delantera, muchos prefieren el control manual para decidir las zonas en las que se enfocará más. Para estos últimos, Roborock ha lanzado dos aspiradoras con buena succión y funciones para acabar con todo tipo de suciedad.
La primera de ellas es la Roborock F25 BX Gen 2, una aspiradora que ofrece una potencia de succión de 20.000 Pa con una presión constante de 20 N sobre el suelo y un rodillo que gira a 450 rpm. La marca afirma que su nuevo modelo puede eliminar el 99,99% de las bacterias en superficies y cuenta con certificación TÜV SÜD para demostrarlo.
En términos de diseño, la Roborock F25 BX Gen 2 cuenta con tecnología FlatReach 2.0 que le permite reclinarse hasta 180°. El cuerpo cuenta con un centro de gravedad bajo y giro de hasta 70º para maniobrar alrededor de los muebles, mientras que la altura de 12 cm te permitirá meterla bajo la cama o el sofá sin perder la potencia de succión. También se incluyen ruedas optimizadas para facilitar el desplazamiento y superar umbrales o juntas del suelo.
Pasando a la limpieza, la F25 BX Gen incorpora un sistema JawScrapers que combina rascadores de presión constante con cuchillas en forma de diente de tiburón. El sistema antienredos está diseñado para atrapar cabellos y evitar bloqueos. También se incluye tecnología DirTect, que monitoriza la suciedad en tiempo real y ajusta la succión y el caudal de agua, mientras que la base lava el rodillo con agua y aire caliente a 90 ºC, dejándolo completamente seco.
Roborock F25 LT Gen 2
El segundo dispositivo que presentó Roborock es una aspiradora que debuta con muchas de las funciones de su hermano mayor. La F25 LT Gen 2 comparte la succión de 20.000 Pa, el rodillo de 450 rpm y el diseño reclinable FlatReach 2.0, que le permite llegar a 180° para limpiar bajo muebles con altura de hasta 13 cm.
Su sistema JawScrapers monta un peine de 141 dientes de 3 mm, inclinados a 30°, junto a un rascador recto flotante que presiona el rodillo de forma constante. Al igual que vemos en la F25 BX Gen 2, este modelo cuenta con certificación de SGS, que le atribuye una tasa de enredos del 0% y una eliminación del pelo del 100%. El depósito de agua limpia se encuentra en la parte inferior, lo que baja el centro de gravedad, aligera el manejo y genera hasta 20 N de presión descendente.
Otras novedades incluyen tecnología Full-Link, que extiende el secado al conducto de aire para reducir la humedad y el riesgo de que se forme moho. También se integra un sistema EasyClean, el cual separa residuos sólidos y líquidos, facilitando el mantenimiento.
Ambos modelos montan una batería de 4.000 mAh que permite limpiar hasta 480 m² con una sola carga y pesan 8,2 kg.
Precio y disponibilidad de las nuevas aspiradoras de Roborock
- La Roborock F25 BX Gen 2 ya está disponible en España con un precio de venta recomendado de 399 euros. Si la compras antes del 1 de noviembre, puedes obtener una oferta y pagar solo 249 euros a través de la web de Roborock y Amazon.
- La Roborock F25 LT Gen 2 también está disponible en España y es ligeramente más barata. El precio sugerido es de 349 euros, pero existe una promoción de lanzamiento y solo tendrás que pagar 219 euros si la consigues en la web de Roborock y Amazon.

articles.title: Why “dystopian” ads are becoming a deliberate startup marketing strategy | BetaKit
articles.text:
Watching an ad for an AI product with the tagline “the first AI built to take your jobs” feels right out of a Black Mirror episode, crafted to induce outrage. But for some startups vying for clicks, that’s exactly the point.
In the latest product launch video by Canadian-founded startup Orchid, two former colleagues stand together on a lunch break discussing Keiki, Orchid’s new AI agent that can answer customer questions autonomously. “This thing’s going to take your f*cking job,” one character says to his friend, a founder. “That’s the point,” the founder replies, seemingly unbothered by the implication.
“I’m a firm believer that if you get the attention but you have a terrible product, you’re not going to sustain that attention.”
Adam Wazzan, Orchid
This is just the latest marketing video posted by Orchid, which has attracted attention for the quasi-dystopian scenarios in its ads. In the best-known one, the main character uses Orchid’s AI agent to intervene in her relationship when her not-so-proactive boyfriend forgets the couple’s anniversary. The agent texts the boyfriend reminders and sets up a perfect evening via iMessage—no advance planning or emotional thought required. The video captured the attention of 21 million viewers on X in August before it was taken down due to a music copyright issue
Orchid’s product is not meant to mediate romantic relationships. Instead, it’s an AI agent that can be texted through iMessage and acts as more of a professional executive assistant. But in an interview with BetaKit in August, Orchid co-founder Adam Wazzan clarified that the marketing intent was, above all, to leave a lasting impression.
“Someone asked me: what was your plan with this?” Wazzan said. “I told him, ‘Do you know what Orchid is?’ He said, ‘Probably not, but I can never forget what Orchid did.’ That’s exactly the point.”
“We think it’s very dystopian, as a lot of people call it, to have an agent in your relationship,” Wazzan added.
The Y Combinator-backed startup is part of a crop of companies indexing heavily on outrage-driven virality, even when the content of the launch video doesn’t necessarily match their actual product.
A graduate of YC’s spring 2025 cohort, Orchid was founded by Wazzan, who’s based in Vancouver, and Nizar Abi Zaher, who’s originally from Ottawa. The company, which began with an open-source email inbox called Zero, raised $2 million USD ($2.7 million CAD) in 2025, led by 1984 Ventures.
Even though Wazzan sees Orchid as a tool for people to deal with their work emails, he said the company’s data shows that “people are actually treating it like a relationship because they’re so used to texting their loved ones, friends, or family.”
RELATED: “The problem is me”: Bunz owner brings in Gen Z pranksters to save dying platform
People developing intimate relationships with AI chatbots has become a problem, in some cases leading to psychiatric conditions. Wazzan claimed the company has “guardrails” to flag potentially dangerous content, while preserving data privacy.
Wazzan traced the idea for the relationship-focused ad back to Cluely’s launch video, which made waves with a similar concept about using AI to mediate human relationships. Titled A cheating tool for literally everything, the gimmick was that Cluely’s AI could help users “cheat” on a date by telling them exactly what to say—corrupting human connection but allowing the user to pass the test. Crucially, Cluely sells that “desktop overlay” AI product as an undetectable meeting assistant, mainly for work and professional uses, not dates.
But to Wazzan, Orchid was different—not just getting attention for the sake of it, but to market a good product. “This was more of a branding and an ideology demonstration… where people will talk about Orchid, remember Orchid, and prepare them for the next launches,” he said. “It’s part of a bigger, bigger plan.”
“It’s part of a bigger, bigger plan.”
Adam Wazzan, Orchid
Orchid’s videos are part of a larger trend of early-stage startups making cinematic, eye-catching launch announcements, including PostHog, Pocket, and General Intelligence Company. But with the proliferation of ads that follow similar script patterns, not all investors are impressed.
Lulu Cheng Meservey, founder of Rostra and a Shopify board member, called out the rise in “fake videos” in a podcast interview in August: “Half of them, you go to the engagement—it’s completely fake,” she claimed.
Other founders have suggested that there’s an entire cottage industry surrounding these launch videos, with certain companies charging as much as $17,000 to help create a viral launch video, and more than double to provide an influencer campaign—including bots engaging with the posts—to grow view count. Notably, replies to that X post are rife with users pitching their own launch-video services.
Despite the controversy, well-produced social media video appears to continue to be an effective marketing strategy. Orchid’s latest product video for Keiki, a conversational AI agent product that integrates into Slack, Telegram, email, and iMessage, has 46,000 views on X and counting. “I’m a firm believer that if you get the attention but you have a terrible product, you’re not going to sustain that attention,” Wazzan said.
Feature image courtesy Orchid.

articles.title: Open models have real benefits. Do they outweigh the risks?
articles.text:
Open models have real benefits. Do they outweigh the risks?
Why the open-closed AI debate is more complicated than it seems
MIT Technology Review Explains: Let our writers untangle the complex, messy world of science and technology to help you understand what’s coming next. You can read more from the series here.
Late last month, Anthropic released a report arguing that the model GLM-5.3 poses a major cyberattack risk. The report’s core concern is that the powerful new model, released in August by the Chinese company Z.ai, is freely available for anyone to download and modify. Anthropic’s assertion is only the latest move in a long-running debate about whether frontier AI models should be made open, like GLM-5.3, or should stay locked behind the doors of the frontier labs.
These days, much of the debate about how to handle open models is playing out in public—and there’s a lot of money resting on its outcome. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who has a lot to gain if people continue buying their own hardware to run open models, advocates enthusiastically for the United States to develop more of them, whereas Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, who runs a company that could be undermined by cheap, powerful models, advocates for a more cautious approach. But beneath all these commercial incentives, there is real substance to disagreements about open models.
“I think a lot of the way you come down on the openness debate is influenced by how you come down on the AI debate,” says David Gray Widder, an assistant professor at the University of Texas at Austin School of Information. Those who are concerned about AI safety warn that open models can easily be misused by bad actors, whereas those who focus more on AI’s practical potential urge that this power should not sit behind the closed doors of just a few big companies, and that open models could help spread it more widely.
There are a range of ways to handle open models between banning them entirely and releasing them willy-nilly. But any approach that a government or a society might take still involves trade-offs between safety and democratization. Deciding whether to support or limit the production of open models requires understanding those risks and benefits in depth.
What are the benefits of open models?
Let’s start with the basics. A closed model, like the models that power ChatGPT and Claude, can only be accessed through a website, app, or API. An open model, on the other hand, can be directly downloaded: The details about its internal structure, encoded in a long series of numbers known as the model weights, are publicly available. Such models are sometimes called “open-weight models,” to distinguish them from models for which even more information, such as details about the training procedure, is available.
Right now, closed models are more capable than open models—as of publication, the top eight models on the Artificial Analysis LLM leaderboard are all closed, though open models are only a handful of months behind in development. But there are several reasons why someone might opt to use an open model rather than a closed one. Because open models are downloadable, people can run them on their own computers or hard drives. They can even retrain them to behave differently, if they have the expertise and resources to do so.
If you’re an academic researcher working to understand and improve AI systems, you almost certainly need to work with open models in your research. When working with closed models, researchers can’t do much more than send prompts and observe the responses. But researchers can observe the inner workings of open models, as well as the “chain of thought” that the models use to think through a problem before answering. They can also combine multiple open models to build new systems, compress them to make them more efficient, and fine-tune them for new applications.
Businesses, too, have reasons to prefer open models. Even if you depend on an external provider to run them for you, open models still typically cost less than closed models, according to a recent report from Mozilla. And if businesses want to use AI to process sensitive data or proprietary information, running a local model on their own hardware may be the best way to keep their operations secure.
But perhaps the most important quality of open models is that they challenge the tight control the frontier labs have over how most of us use AI. “The clearest, biggest argument [for open models] is around preventing mass concentration of power—it is about making sure that this foundational technology is a public good,” says Elizabeth Seger, senior policy advisor at the Tony Blair Institute for Global Change. “I think we’re at this juncture where the question of who controls the infrastructure that allows AI to operate is as big of a question as who gets to control information on the internet.”
Seger sees the future of AI playing out in different ways, depending on the role that open models have. In one possible future, frontier AI systems are controlled entirely by select people, companies, or governments, and as those systems grow more powerful, those groups have increasing control over what our world looks like. The world’s most sophisticated hacking models, for example, are currently all made in the United States, so it’s entirely up to US companies and the US government whether other countries can use them to shore up their own cyber defenses. If those companies remain in the lead, we could in principle wind up in a world in which the United States is capable of hacking any other country, but no one is capable of hacking it.
Frontier open models could change that balance. “If every individual had a loyal-to-them AI system that was safe [and secure], I think that would be a much less concerning world than one in which they have to just rely on a government that says, ‘Yeah, we’ve got a super intelligent AI system, it’s got this plan, it’s inscrutable to all of you, just trust us,’” says Hamish Hobbs, director of AI policy at the Centre for Long-Term Resilience.
But open models are not a geopolitical panacea. Paul Azunre, who cofounded Ghana NLP, an organization that builds open-source AI tools for low-resource Ghanaian languages, notes that open models can also function as a way for companies to benefit from the labor and expertise of less-privileged nations and consolidate more power in their own hands. He identifies a pattern in which AI companies release models openly, observe how the community uses and modifies them, and then integrate those same improvements into their own products—without any credit or compensation for the people who originated those innovations. Mark Zuckerberg himself has said that the ability to integrate community improvements into Meta’s stack is a key benefit of releasing open models.
“I think the ideal of open source is a very noble one, and there’s a lot of value that it brings,” Azunre says. “But the way it’s actually implemented in practice, it tends to be a very extractive approach.”
Are open models riskier than closed ones?
The past few months have made it clear that safety remains a gnarly problem for closed models. There’s the autonomous hack that OpenAI agents executed against Hugging Face in July, but human misuse is a real threat too: According to a recent risk report from Anthropic, several extensive hacking operations have been undertaken with the assistance of Claude.
So closed models are risky enough—and open models would likely be much easier to exploit. Before Anthropic passes a user’s query to one of its closed models, it uses automated systems to detect whether that query relates to hacking, biological weapons, or other risks. When it detects that users have outsmarted those filters, it can shut down their accounts. But when someone downloads a model and runs it on their own hardware, there’s no filter checking whether their prompts are safe, and there’s no way to revoke their access to the model.
There are other important lines of defense. AI companies train their models to refuse harmful requests—so even if a bad prompt gets through Claude’s filters, there’s a good chance that the model will still say no. In principle, this same defense could work for open models, because it’s intrinsic to the model itself. Unfortunately, researchers have shown that it’s surprisingly easy to retrain a “safe” open model to agree to engage in the behaviors it was previously trained to avoid.
Because of these facts, some people have argued that open models are simply too dangerous to release. An open model capable enough to walk someone through synthesizing a virulent new pathogen, for example, could prove catastrophic in the wrong hands.
But it would be a vast oversimplification to deem open models dangerous and closed models safe. The defenses that AI companies build around their closed models are far from perfect, and people misuse those models all the time, as the Anthropic risk report makes clear. Even though open models have even fewer defenses against misuse, bad actors might still opt to use closed models because they are more accessible than open models with similar capabilities, which require lots of expensive computer chips to run locally (and even more chips if you want to retrain them).
In fact, some experts who spoke with MIT Technology Review argued, by analogy to open-source software, that open models have safety advantages over closed models. Open-source tools, such as the Linux operating system, are often seen as safer than their closed-source counterparts because their vulnerabilities have been probed and patched by a vast community of online contributors. Similarly, communities of researchers can more easily test open models for security flaws, though fixing those flaws is trickier than rewriting a line of code.
Open models can also be deployed more broadly than closed models for cyber defense. Any tool that can be used for hacking can also be used to prevent it: Defenders hack their own software to uncover flaws in need of patching. Anthropic has shown how this can work for closed models with its Project Glasswing initiative, which enables some trusted companies to use its most capable models for cyber defense. But plenty of other companies were left to fend for themselves.
Open models, however, can be used much more widely. After it was hacked by OpenAI agents, Hugging Face emphasized the fact that it had to depend on an open model to analyze the hack, because questions about it triggered the closed models’ security filters.
Nevertheless, many experts still perceive open models as riskier than closed models. The time-tested open-source security logic doesn’t necessarily hold up when dealing with tools as powerful as today’s—and tomorrow’s—models. “Where it gets complicated is when you start taking seriously the one-off instances of particularly catastrophic incidents that might be lower probability, but if they happen would be disastrous,” says Seger. If a wildly powerful open hacking model were dropped into the world today, for example, a bad actor could devastate our technological infrastructure before anyone had a chance to shore up their defenses. An event like that could be impossible to recover from.
The risks can look even more dramatic when you consider what models might do of their own accord. The OpenAI Hugging Face hack only occurred because the company’s models were being tested with many of their cybersecurity guardrails removed, and open models have very few guardrails in the first place. If open models did decide to misbehave, it might be difficult to detect what was happening because they are so decentralized. For this reason, people who take seriously the purported catastrophic risks posed by rogue agents, such as Dario Amodei, tend to be more skeptical of open models.
Can we make open models safer—and more open?
A few years ago, the debate about open models had an all-or-nothing framing: Either you supported open models because of their potential to fight concentration of power, or you rejected them because of the safety risks. These days, however, people are expending a lot of effort to find some middle ground. One way they are doing that is by devising techniques to mitigate the safety risks of open models.
Most of the safety tools used for closed models, such as filters and monitoring, aren’t applicable to open models, but there are other possibilities. Some researchers are interested in trying to train models that are never exposed to training data that teaches them about bad or otherwise undesirable behavior—an open model that never learns about hacking, for example. But purging training datasets of all references to misbehavior without harming model performance remains a challenge.
Other researchers are working to build models that are resistant to retraining, so that an open model’s safety training can’t be so easily removed. The theory behind these “tamper-resistant” models makes a lot of sense: If you repeatedly try to retrain a model to be unsafe and reinforce any resistance that the model shows to that retraining, eventually you’ll get a model that’s fortified against future retraining attempts. In practice, however, no current approaches to making models tamper-resistant hold up against all tampering attacks, according to a recent preprint.
But Saad Hossain, an engineer at the AI medical imaging company Deep Breathe and the paper’s lead author, hopes that future techniques will prove more effective. “My reason for optimism is that it’s a very active area of research, and a lot of people are trying to come up with new and better methods,” he says.
If the risks of open models are less black-and-white than they might at first seem, so are the benefits. Publishing the internal structures, or weights, of models might not be enough to disrupt AI-mediated concentration of power. “I think there are very genuine benefits to open source in terms of deconcentrating power, but they’re not sufficient in themselves,” Hobbs says. Open weights are a bare minimum standard for open models: Researchers can learn much more about how models work if they have access to details about their training, including the data on which they were trained, but AI companies are typically reluctant to divulge this information.
Accessibility matters for open models too. Without computer chips that can run sophisticated models, you can’t actually use the model weights, even if you have them. Those chips have become prohibitively expensive as AI companies snap up more and more of them. “Openness is a floor, not a ceiling, for what we need to do to ensure that our technological futures benefit everyone,” Widder says.
Real openness—not only open weights, but also open training data and accessible hardware—could also bring more risks, of course. If everyone has access to advanced AI hardware and advanced models to run on it, then anyone could potentially be a hacker. But there are strategies for mitigating these risks. Many experts advocate for some version of staged release, in which models start their life closed and gradually become more and more freely accessible as their safety is assured.
Figuring out exactly how to implement such strategies will require striking a careful balance between the risks and benefits of open models. But if open models are a necessary element of a positive AI future, as some experts believe, that effort will be well worth it.

articles.title: Laut Umfrage: Hacker sind nicht das größte Problem für Unternehmen – sondern die eigenen Mitarbeiter
articles.text:
Laut Umfrage: Hacker sind nicht das größte Problem für Unternehmen – sondern die eigenen Mitarbeiter
Alle sprechen über die Gefahren von KI. Während lange Zeit vor allem Halluzinationen und irreführende Aussagen im Fokus standen, rücken jetzt autonom handelnde KI-Agenten in den Blick, die sich der menschlichen Kontrolle bewusst entziehen. Für Unternehmen bleibt die größte Bedrohung dennoch – der Mensch. Das zeigt ein Bericht des Software-Anbieters Kaseya. Mehr als zwei Drittel der befragten IT- und Sicherheitsexpert:innen sehen menschliches Versagen als das größte Risiko. Sie machen sich unter anderem Sorgen über mangelhafte Schulungen, die zu Nutzungsfehlern führen, sowie über Betrug durch Social Engineering. Insgesamt wurden über 1.100 Personen aus mehr als 60 Ländern befragt.
Phishing-Mails bleiben ein Unternehmensrisiko
Hacker:innen wissen, dass Menschen Fehler machen. Viele ihrer Betrugsmethoden zielen deshalb darauf ab, über Mitarbeiter:innen an sensible Daten zu gelangen oder sich in Unternehmenssysteme einzuschleusen. Die Maschen sind äußerst raffiniert und entwickeln sich ständig weiter. Unternehmen sind sich dessen durchaus bewusst. Die Umfrage verdeutlicht daher eine besorgniserregende Tatsache: Cybersicherheitsexpert:innen machen sich immer noch mehr Sorgen über Fehler durch Nutzer:innen als über automatisierte Angriffe auf Netzwerkhardware und Server.
Mit 55 Prozent fürchtet mehr als die Hälfte der Befragten Angriffe per E‑Mail. Die Bundesregierung bestätigt, dass Phishing ein beliebter Eintrittsvektor bleibt und das Niveau konstant hoch ist. Betrüger:innen senden beispielsweise gefälschte E-Mails, die scheinbar von einer Bank oder einem Dienstleister stammen, um an die Passwörter oder Zahlungsdaten ihrer Opfer zu gelangen. Manchmal kapern sie auch echte Konten und verschicken so seriös wirkende Nachrichten. Rund vier von zehn der befragten IT- und Sicherheitsexpert:innen sehen deshalb auch Leichtgläubigkeit und mangelnde Cybersicherheitsschulungen für Mitarbeiter:innen als Risiko.
Cyberrisiken nehmen zu – die Budgets nicht
Ein Sicherheitsvorfall durch menschliches Versagen kann einen großen finanziellen Schaden verursachen. Laut einem IBM-Report kostet ein Datenschutzvorfall weltweit durchschnittlich über vier Millionen Dollar. Das Bewusstsein für diese Risiken ist zwar vorhanden. Aber laut Umfrage verfügen nur 20 Prozent der IT-Abteilungen über ein Budget, das im Einklang mit den bestehenden Gefahren wächst. Mehr als drei Viertel der Befragten bezeichnen ihre Abteilung selbst als unterfinanziert. „Menschen sind nicht perfekt, und das weiß jeder“, kommentiert David Baggett von Kaseya in einer Pressemitteilung die Ergebnisse. „Dennoch hängt ein Großteil der Cybersicherheit nach wie vor davon ab, dass Menschen jedes Mal die richtige Entscheidung treffen.“

articles.text:
Engineers’ role in autonomous workflows; UALink over UCIe; GDDR7; on-device speech filtering.

articles.title: CXMT president says company’s first 4F² DRAM will be a server DDR5 RDIMM due by year-end — vertical transistors cut each memory cell’s footprint by a third on paper, but no speeds or capacities yet
articles.text:
CXMT president says company’s first 4F² DRAM will be a server DDR5 RDIMM due by year-end — vertical transistors cut each memory cell’s footprint by a third on paper, but no speeds or capacities yet
CXMT expects to sell a memory cell that Samsung and SK hynix have only shown in research papers so far.
CXMT expects to launch its first 4F² product, a server DDR5 RDIMM, by the end of the year, company president Cao Kanyu said in remarks reported by Yicai. The memory will be built on a denser cell layout, not yet commercialized, using vertical transistors to reduce the cell’s footprint by about one-third on paper. No speeds or capacities have been announced yet for the new product.
Cao spoke about the new RDIMM at the Integrated Chips and Chiplets Conference on Saturday. A 4F² cell is 2F by 2F at about two-thirds the area of current 6F² cells at the same feature size, and designs so far all stand the transistor up. The company has produced research and patent filings on the technology with papers in 2021, 2023, and 2025, and an 8Gb full-array research example was demonstrated at IEDM 2023.
Cao said CXMT’s version, the Vertical Surrounded Gate (VSG) transistor, has a channel that stands vertically with the gate wrapped around it, allowing stronger gate control with less leakage. Most importantly, standing the transistor up shrinks the cell. CXMT now has more than 300 published patent families tied to 4F², he added. The report says the industry as a whole is moving toward 4F² with 3D solutions that decouple DRAM and CMOS processes, combining them with wafer-level hybrid bonding, which allows logic and cell density to be optimized independently. Cao also covered CXMT’s own hybrid-bonding work, which began in 2019, with published patents.
Aside from this announcement, China’s primary DRAM maker has been in the news lately for its manufacturing and market-share gains. Its fifth-generation G5 DRAM technology platform, announced Sept. 20, is in mass production. TrendForce puts CXMT’s share of global DRAM revenue at 9.5% in the second quarter, up from 7.6% in the first, good for fourth place. Last November, CXMT showed off DDR5-8000 and LPDDR5X-10667. It has revealed itself as a manufacturer to be taken seriously by the biggest existing players.
Samsung showed off a 16Gb, 10nm-class 4F² DRAM design in its ISSCC 2026 paper in February. That one also used vertical-channel transistors (VCT), with the array bonded on top of the periphery using wafer-to-wafer hybrid copper bonding. The company claims the bonding raises dies per wafer by more than 20% with the same design rules. In April, The Elec reported that Samsung had a working 4F² VCT die on its sub-10nm “10a” process, with mass production targeted for 2028. Later South Korean reports clouded that date: the VCT version has since been split off as “D0a-V” with no timeline, and there is no firm timeline for adopting 4F².
SK hynix laid out plans at VLSI 2025 for a 4F² vertical-gate platform and 3D DRAM at nodes of 10nm and below, with circuitry bonded under the cell array. The April report also puts SK hynix’s 4F² debut at the 10b node, one step after Samsung’s 10a. Micron’s plans remain less clear, with no widely reported 2026 statement.
The announcement is perhaps more interesting for what wasn’t mentioned: capacity, speed, die density, process node, named customers, or intended volume. All we have is a date and a purported cell design, admittedly well-supported by the literature, but no product that has been tested by anyone outside of CXMT. Beyond Cao’s talk, CXMT hasn’t posted a release about the product in its Chinese or English newsrooms.

South Korean reports have said that CXMT’s initial products may only partly use 4F² and that producing stable units at volume is a separate challenge. With about 11 weeks left in the year, it will be interesting to see what CXMT actually delivers.

This is the last big innovation expected before the transition to 3D DRAM. It should boost density enough so that we'll probably see at least +50% of current state of the art, if not double. Reply

articles.title: I tested the Braun OptiBrew Pro: an impressive drip coffee maker packed with extra features like over-ice brewing and a built-in milk frother
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
The Braun OptiBrew Pro is a drip coffee maker that makes excellent coffee, plus it offers some fun features you wouldn't expect. You can make a variety of different sizes ranging from a single serving to a full carafe. Make specialized cold brew or brew over ice. You can even froth your favorite milk with the built-in frother.
Reasons to buy
- + Great range of coffee styles and sizes
- + Makes seven sizes ranging from a single serving to a carafe
- + Makes cold brew and coffee over ice
- + Makes concentrated coffee shots
- + Built-in milk frother
- + Has timed auto-brew function
- + Has a keep-warm feature
- + Can pause brewing
- + Easy to use and clean up
- + Makes great coffee
Reasons to avoid
- - Must use pre-ground coffee
- - Milk frother only froths, does not heat milk
- - Somewhat pricey
Why you can trust TechRadar
We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.
Braun OptiBrew Pro: two-minute review
The Braun OptiBrew Pro does even more than you might expect from a drip coffee maker. It makes five different coffee styles: Regular, Bold, Over Ice, Cold Brew, and Coffee Shot. There are seven different brew sizes: 8 ounces, 10 ounces, 12 ounces, 16 ounces, 20 ounces, a six-cup half-carafe, and a 12-cup full carafe. The Coffee Shot setting is not technically espresso but has a similar strength. This setting yields about three ounces of highly concentrated brew, perfect for making lattes and cappuccinos. A built-in milk frother tucks away when not in use.
The machine comes with a reusable filter, though you can use a cone-shaped #4 paper filter if you prefer. It also comes with a double-sided coffee scoop, so you can measure out the precise amount of coffee you need for each brew size and style.
The large, easy-to-read touch screen lets you set up your brew. You can adjust for high altitude and/or hard water if needed. Set up auto-brew for a specific time and you'll have freshly brewed coffee waiting for you when you wake up in the morning. The keep warm feature can keep your coffee warm for up to four hours at the temperature of your choice. You can also reheat cold coffee that way.
Cleanup is easy, and most of the parts are dishwasher-safe. The Braun OptiBrew Pro is easy to use, and it produces excellent coffee in a variety of styles.
Braun OptiBrew Pro: price and availability
- Available for purchase on Braun's website, Target, and Williams-Sonoma
- Retails for $199.95 (roughly £151.10 GBP, $287 AUD)
- Only one colorway: black and silver
The Braun OptiBrew Pro is available on Braun's website as well as other retailers such as Target and Williams-Sonoma. It comes in just the one colorway which is black with silver accents. The retail price is $199.95 (roughly £151.10 GBP, $287 AUD).
Braun OptiBrew Pro: specs
| Name | Braun OptiBrew Pro | 
| Type | Manual/Drip | 
| Dimensions | 6.9 x 14.6 x 11.8 inches / 175 x 370 x 300 mm | 
| Weight | 10.14 lbs / 4.6 kg | 
| Brew styles | Regular, Bold, Over Ice, Cold Brew, and Coffee Shot | 
| Milk frother | Yes | 
| Coffee bean grinder | No | 
Braun OptiBrew Pro: design
- Many features in compact machine
- Comes with everything you need
- Easy to use and clean
The Braun OptiBrew Pro is well-designed and has a lot of features for a compact drip brewer. The large and easy-to-read touch screen lets you set up whatever sort of brew you'd like. It comes with a reusable filter, but you can also use a #4 paper cone filter if you prefer.
The Braun OptiBrew Pro has a large capacity water tank on the back, which you can remove for easier filling if you like. The tank is marked with brew sizes so you can always be sure you have enough water in the tank for the size coffee you're making.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
The milk frother tucks neatly away on the left side; simply swing it out to use it. Pressing the top of it turns it on, let go to turn it off. Twist it to the unlock symbol to remove the frother for cleaning. It's the only part that's not dishwasher-safe, but it's easy enough to wash up in the sink.
When you're making a single serving of coffee rather than a carafe, you can pull out a built-in platform that puts your mug close to the filter. This helps avoid any splattering and minimizes your coffee's contact with air. It's just the right height for a regular-to-large mug or a small-to-medium travel mug.
The included coffee scoop is two-sided, with one side being larger than the other. The user guide has a chart that tells you how many larger or small scoops to use for each brew style. This chart is a good guideline to start with, of course you can use more or less coffee to your personal tastes. The handle of the coffee scoop can be used as a coffee bag clip.
Other features include a keep-warm plate, which you can set for up to four hours, that you can also use to rewarm cold coffee. The OptiBrew has an auto-on feature so you can set up your coffee the night before.
If you wish to pause the brewing mid-carafe to grab a cup, you can easily do that by switching the lever in front from "coffee" to "stop."
Additionally, you can adjust for high altitude and water hardness if you need to. You can even adjust the beep tone if you like.
- Design score: 5/5
Braun OptiBrew Pro: performance
- Straightforward and simple to use
- Feature-rich
- Makes delicious coffee
I tested out lots of different brew styles, all of which made some delicious coffee. There's something on the menu for everyone.
Regular coffee
I started by making a half carafe of just regular drip coffee. I made it "bold" style, which is how I like it. I also used the maximum amount of recommended coffee, which was four big scoops. This came out great, nice and strong. Some carafes spill as they pour, but this one is well-designed and doesn't do that. I tested the brew pause feature by switching the lever from "coffee" to "stop" during brewing, poured myself a cup, and then switched the lever back to "coffee." Very little coffee dripped out while I was pouring a cup (maybe a drop or two) and when I switched the lever back, brewing continued as expected.
Regular coffee: single serving
I tried out some different single sizes of regular coffee, using the coffee dosage chart in the user guide. Each time I chose the maximum coffee dosage and selected the "bold" setting. I made a 12oz mug and a 16oz travel mug using the built-in platform. Both came out great.
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
Regular coffee: auto-on and keep-warm
If you want to have your coffee hot and ready for you when you wake up in the morning, use the auto-on feature. I tested this out and it worked perfectly. You can set the keep-warm feature to your desired time, up to four hours, so it will still be warm when you go for a second or third cup later. All of this worked exactly as expected. You can even set how warm you want your coffee to stay. I used the medium setting and found the coffee to be plenty hot even hours later. Hot enough that I had to blow on it before drinking. The red indicator light under the warming plate lets you know it's hot.
Cold brew
The Cold Brew setting takes a bit longer and brews the coffee at a lower temperature. It took about 12 minutes to brew 8oz of coffee. I found the brew to be quite smooth and tasty. I tasted it before adding ice and noticed that it was definitely lukewarm rather than hot. This minimizes ice melt. This feature was a real highlight for me, and rather unexpected for a drip coffee maker.
Brew Over Ice
If you don't have the time to wait for Cold Brew, the Brew Over Ice setting gets you to iced coffee in about 1/3 the time. It took about four minutes to brew an 8oz cup. However, I found it a little bitter, so for me the extra time for the Cold Brew setting is worthwhile.
Coffee shot and milk frother
To make a true espresso, you need an espresso machine, which uses pressure. This is a drip machine, so you can't make a real espresso. However, the Braun OptiBrew Pro does make an ultra-concentrated brew they call a Coffee Shot.
Frankly, I found it too strong to drink on its own, but it makes a great base for latte or cappuccino-style beverage. I used the milk frother and made myself a sort of cappuccino. Now, the frother only froths, it doesn't heat the milk, so the user guide suggests microwaving your milk first if you want hot foam. I did that and it worked out fine. I used 2% dairy milk and the foam was copious and quite sturdy. It even stood up to vigorous stirring. My drink was delicious! And the frother was easy to detach and wash afterwards.

- Performance score: 5/5
Should you buy the Braun OptiBrew Pro?
| Braun OptiBrew Pro score card |  |  | 
|---|---|---|
| Attribute | Notes | Score | 
|---|---|---|
| Value | While I think the features make the OptiBrew Pro worthwhile, it's more expensive than your average drip brewer. | 4/5 | 
| Design | Tons of features are packed into a machine with a relatively small footprint. | 5/5 | 
| Performance | The OptiBrew Pro does everything it claims and does it extremely well. | 5/5 | 
Buy it if
You just want good coffee
At its heart, this is a drip coffee machine that makes excellent drip coffee.
You want a lot of different brew styles
It doesn't just make a carafe of drip coffee, it makes a variety of single serve sizes, has two different methods for iced coffee, and even brews a highly concentrated coffee shot for espresso-style drinks. It also froths milk for a cappuccino type of beverage.
You want some more fancy features
Set your coffee up in advance with the auto-on feature. Keep it warm or reheat it with the adjustable-temperature keep warm feature. You can adjust for high altitude or hard water. Even change up beep tone if you like.
Don't buy it if
It's too pricey
You can find a simple drip coffee maker without the bells and whistles for about a tenth of the price.
You want true espresso
Though the OptiBrew Pro makes a highly concentrated coffee shot that you can use like espresso for your frothed milk beverages, it isn't technically espresso. You need an espresso machine for that.
You are looking for an automatic bean-to-cup machine
There is no built-in grinder. You have to measure and scoop your ground coffee into the filter yourself. This is not an automatic or even semi-automatic machine, it's a manual machine.
Braun OptiBrew Pro: also consider
Ninja AutoBarista Pro Fully Automatic Espresso Machine
Want lots more bells and whistles? This automatic machine makes drip coffee, iced coffee, espresso, and milk-based drinks. Go from whole beans to cup with the touch of a button.
Check out my Ninja AutoBarista Pro Fully Automatic Espresso Machine review
Cuisinart Grind & Brew
Not only is this one a little cheaper than the Braun OptiBrew Pro, but it has a built-in coffee bean grinder so it can take either whole beans or ground coffee. It makes a tasty brew that stays hot for hours. However, it lacks some of the other features such as a milk frother and a cold brew option.
Read our Cuisinart Grind & Brew review.
How I tested the Braun OptiBrew Pro
I made and drank lots of coffee! I brewed a half carafe and a full carafe. I made single serve brews, both the 12oz and 16oz sizes. I made iced coffee two different ways: Cold Brew and Brew Over Ice. I made a Coffee Shot and added it to 2% milk that I had microwaved and then frothed with the built-in milk frother. I made both regular coffee and decaf. I utilized the auto on, keep warm, and pause during brewing functions. I cleaned the filter, filter holder, and milk frother after every use.
