articles.title: 15 startups selected for Google for Startups Accelerator: South Africa programme - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Fifteen startups have been selected for the Google for Startups Accelerator: South Africa, a three-month programme designed to support growth-stage, AI-driven startups with equity-free funding, technical mentorship and access to Google’s advanced AI technologies.
The programme forms part of Google’s plan to support 50 South African startups between 2024 and 2028. Each selected startup receives up to ZAR1 million (US$60,000) in equity-free funding, allowing founders to retain full ownership of their business while using the capital to accelerate growth.
They also gain direct access to Google’s AI tools, cloud infrastructure and models, including hands-on access to Gemini, helping them strengthen their products and enhance their technical capabilities.
Applications for the latest cohort opened in July, and received over 1,000 expressions of interest. From that, 15 South African-led, revenue-generating startups have been selected for the 2026 cohort.
They include Ambani Africa, an African language learning app that helps children connect with their mother tongue; Anvaya Legal AI, an AI legal assistant that speeds up research, drafting and document review; Boleka Africa, a community-based fintech helping underbanked adults access fair credit, savings and payments; Bro, a mobility platform connecting passengers with affordable transport; and Buddy Learning, an AI tutor on WhatsApp that delivers low-data, multilingual tutoring.
Also selected are Daedalis, which builds verified data infrastructure and enterprise AI for supply chains; Dataseka, an AI analytics platform that turns scattered business data into usable insights; Fly n Pay Later, a travel fintech that lets people book flights and pay in manageable installments; Kasicoach, an AI mentorship platform on WhatsApp and Telegram for township and rural youth; and Muna Africa. infrastructure that helps retailers run circular fashion resale programmes.
The cohort is completed by Propela Health, a marketplace connecting African healthcare professionals with global employers; Scale, which lets startups launch and issue card products; Thuto, an ed-tech building AI tools to improve learning outcomes; Tradeflow, an AI platform that automates supplier invoicing and ordering for restaurants; and Zumii, a WhatsApp platform that sources, packs and delivers school stationery to parents.

articles.title: Trellix Wise for Private Cloud runs AI security operations inside customer environments - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Trellix Wise for Private Cloud runs AI security operations inside customer environments
Cybersecurity company Trellix today launched Trellix Wise for Private Cloud to let enterprises run its artificial intelligence engine for security operations entirely inside their own environments.
The new release targets the main reasons large organizations have held back from handing security operations center work to AI agents. David Soto, Trellix’s chief information security officer, said those holdouts “aren’t resistant to the technology, but to the tradeoffs.” He described the tradeoffs as sending sensitive security telemetry to a public cloud, “absorbing unpredictable token costs” and working without visibility into how AI decisions are made.
Every outcome from the private cloud edition comes with a confidence level, and Trellix said each one is explained in plain language so it can be audited for governance purposes. Customers are not billed by the token. Trellix Wise first appeared in May 2024 as generative AI investigation features in the company’s extended detection and response platform.
Soto’s comments come from the latest edition of Trellix’s “Mind of the CISO” report, released alongside the product. Research firm Vanson Bourne Ltd. polled 600 chief information security officers on insider risk for the study in August and September. One of the report’s recommendations is that companies consider on-premises or private cloud deployments for sensitive workloads so data stays inside their own security boundary.
Respondents told Vanson Bourne that AI-driven or autonomous systems were behind 28% of the insider incidents they dealt with over the past year, on average. Ninety-nine percent still expect AI and automation to be critical or very important to managing insider risk within two years. Asked what stands in the way, 40% named a lack of trust in automated decision-making.
The average organization in the survey took seven hours to spot an insider incident. Responding took eight more, a window Soto described as an invitation to attackers who use AI to speed up every stage of an attack.
Companies that do not govern AI agents with the same rigor they apply to human employees are “operating with an unmonitored insider at scale,” Soto argued in the report.
The report also found 98% of respondents see a role for governments or regulators in helping them manage insider risk. One U.S. chief information security officer at a financial operations provider told interviewers that fragmented state rules were “a nightmare” and called for a “unified matrix of regulations” so companies can “safely use AI for legitimate business purposes.”
Trellix, formally named Musarubra US LLC, was formed in 2022 by Symphony Technology Group following STG’s acquisition of McAfee Enterprise and FireEye.

articles.title: Building agents that transact with Anchor Browser and AgentCore payments | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Building agents that transact with Anchor Browser and AgentCore payments
AI agents increasingly need to access web resources that are priced per request. For example, premium datasets charge by the query, research APIs meter by the call, and paywalled publishers gate content behind payment. When an AI agent encounters one of these resources, the server returns HTTP 402 Payment Required. The agent has no built-in payment mechanism, no budget attached to the session, and no programmatic way to satisfy the request. The task stalls and requires manual intervention.
Anchor Browser with Agentic Payments handles machine-to-machine payment workflows on behalf of the agent. Developed in collaboration with the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center Partner Agent Factory, it’s now available on AWS Marketplace. This post covers how Anchor Browser integrates with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore payments so that AI agents can pay for x402-protected pages and APIs autonomously. The x402 protocol is an open standard for HTTP-based machine-to-machine payments. A server responds with 402 Payment Required along with the amount, accepted payment methods, and payment address that the agent uses to complete the transaction.
Anchor Browser is a cloud-based browser automation solution purpose-built for AI agents. Each agent session runs inside a managed browser environment that maintains authentication state, handles navigation, captures network requests, and provides a live view of page interactions.
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore provides capabilities to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore payments is a fully managed capability within AgentCore that AI agents can use to discover, access, and pay for APIs, Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, and web content autonomously. AgentCore payments manages wallet connectivity, enforces configurable spending limits at the infrastructure layer, and processes payments through the x402 protocol. It also provides observability into payment attempts, approvals, denials, and settlements through Amazon CloudWatch.
When an agent running in Anchor Browser encounters a 402 response, AgentCore payments authorizes and completes the transaction within the configured budget. The workflow continues without interruption.
Challenges
When an autonomous agent encounters an x402-protected resource, the workflow stalls. The agent makes a request, such as fetching a premium research report or calling a paid data enrichment API, and the server responds with HTTP 402 Payment Required. Without a mechanism to pay, the task that was supposed to run autonomously now requires human intervention.
Today, developers must build the entire payment stack. This effort spans four categories of complexity:
Payment protocol handling
- Detecting and parsing the 402 challenge from the HTTP response, and distinguishing payment-required responses from other 4xx errors.
- Constructing the correct payment header with the cryptographic proof in the exact format the merchant expects.
- Supporting multiple payment schemes (exact, upto, and protocol variants) without hardcoding vendor-specific logic into the agent.
- Maintaining compatibility across x402 merchant implementations that might vary in challenge format, supported stablecoins, or settlement timing.
Security and key management
- Storing a private key to sign payments, requiring secure key storage within an environment exposed to untrusted inputs.
- Managing wallet lifecycle operations, including key rotation, credential refresh, and provider failover.
Operational resilience
- Resubmitting the original request with the payment header while preserving session state, cookies, and request context.
- Providing idempotency, which is essential for wallet operations.
- Enforcing per-session and per-transaction spend limits with real-time budget tracking across concurrent agent executions.
Observability and compliance
- Capturing every payment attempt, approval, denial, and settlement in audit logs for compliance and reconciliation.
Without a managed payment service, the agent must internalize the entire payment stack. On every x402-protected call that returns a 402 response, the agent must orchestrate the full payment flow internally, including:
- Signing the proof.
- Attaching the correct header.
- Retrying the request.
- Settling the transaction.
- Logging the result.
Each of these steps requires custom code that developers must build, secure, and maintain. Figure 1 illustrates this architecture. The agent contains eight tightly coupled components (Wallet, Private Keys, Budget Controls, Sign Proof, Attach Header, Retry Logic, Settle Payment, and Logging). The agent connects to an x402 API with a 402 challenge flowing back and a retry flowing forward.
The security considerations extend beyond the engineering effort.
Uncontrolled spending. Without hard spending limits enforced at the infrastructure level, a bug, retry loop, prompt injection, or inadvertent access can trigger unintended payments. An agent retrying a paid endpoint in a loop continues to authorize payments until manual intervention occurs.
Key exposure. When private keys reside inside the agent runtime, they share an execution environment with untrusted web pages, third-party tools, and external dependencies. These vectors might inadvertently disclose the credentials that control real funds.
Signing flow exposure. If the signing infrastructure is accessible from the runtime, a threat actor can attempt to access the key or redirect payments to an address under unauthorized control. Effective mitigation requires that the key doesn’t enter the runtime in the first place.
Browser-based agents introduce an additional constraint: the payment must occur within the same browser session. Otherwise, session recordings and live view no longer match what actually executed.
Solution
Anchor Browser and AgentCore payments address this complexity by moving the entire payment stack into managed infrastructure.
Unlike a stateless tool call, Anchor Browser provides a real cloud browser with persistent identity, repeatable and deterministic workflows, and the session context needed to log in, navigate, and finish tasks reliably. Authentication, navigation, network requests, recordings, and live view happen inside the same browser session. When a payment is required, the transaction happens within that session. The recording captures the full sequence from request to 402 to payment to content delivery. Anchor agents include a built-in x402 tool that handles paid API calls natively within the browser context. The built-in tool requires no changes to existing Playwright, Puppeteer, or Chrome DevTools Protocol-based workflows.
AgentCore payments serves as the payment layer. At the center of the service is the Payment Manager, the top-level resource that coordinates payment operations for the AWS account. Creating a Payment Manager requires specifying an authorizer type and an IAM role. AgentCore then provisions a corresponding workload identity in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity.
The remaining components connect the Payment Manager to external wallet infrastructure:
- A PaymentConnector integrates the Payment Manager with an external wallet provider, either Coinbase Developer Platform (Coinbase CDP) or Stripe Privy.
- A PaymentCredentialProvider stores wallet provider credentials securely in AgentCore Identity.
- A PaymentInstrument identifies the specific wallet address from which funds are drawn.
Anchor Browser sets up wallets through AgentCore payments using a supported wallet provider, without placing wallet secrets or private keys inside the agent runtime. AgentCore payments handles wallet operations through the configured provider. For endpoint discovery, AgentCore provides a curated Coinbase x402 Bazaar MCP server through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, so agents can discover available pay-per-use x402 endpoints programmatically.
AgentCore payments restructures the payment architecture. Sensitive operations move out of the agent runtime and into a managed service layer. The Anchor Agent holds only two payment-related components: a budget session and the x402 tool. The infrastructure, including authentication, wallet secrets, payment limits, observability, and payment proof signing, resides in the AgentCore payments layer. Figure 2 shows the Anchor Agent connecting to the AgentCore payments managed layer, which handles wallet provider integration with Coinbase CDP or Stripe Privy.
How the payment flow works
The following steps describe what happens end to end, from the moment a browser session encounters an x402-protected resource to the moment the agent receives the response and continues the task.
- Anchor Browser creates a dedicated AgentCore PaymentSession for the browser session. When the session starts with x402 turned on, Anchor Browser provisions a PaymentSession through AgentCore payments, linking the browser session to a configured payment instrument and budget.
- The browser receives an HTTP 402 Payment Required response. The agent navigates to a URL or makes a fetch or XMLHttpRequest (XHR) request. The merchant responds with a 402 challenge specifying the amount, accepted payment methods, and payment address.
- The browser selects a compatible payment method. Anchor Browser reads the 402 challenge payload and matches the requested payment method against the instrument linked to the PaymentSession.
- AgentCore verifies the session budget and generates the cryptographic payment proof. AgentCore payments validates that the payment amount falls within the session spending limit. The service then signs the transaction using the configured wallet provider (Coinbase CDP or Stripe Privy) and returns the cryptographic proof. No key material enters the browser or agent runtime.
- The browser retries the original request with the payment header. The browser attaches the signed proof as PAYMENT-SIGNATURE for x402 v2 or X-PAYMENT for x402 v1, then retries the original request exactly once.
- The merchant verifies and settles the payment, then returns the protected resource. The merchant validates the cryptographic proof, settles the transaction on-chain, and serves the content. The agent continues the task.
Wallet credentials remain with AgentCore and the configured wallet provider throughout this flow.
Prerequisites
Before you begin, make sure that you have a valid Anchor Browser API key (ANCHOR_API_KEY). To create one, see the Anchor Browser Quick Start guide.
Setting up automatic x402 payments
Setting up agentic payments for Anchor Browser requires one session property. Set session.x402 to true. The property defaults to false. When enabled, the browser session can automatically access x402-protected websites with payments signed by AgentCore payments and retried inside the same browser session. Enabling session.x402 authorizes the browser to make real payments from the configured payment instrument.
The following examples show how to create a payment-enabled session for Anchor Browser using cURL and JavaScript:
cURL
JavaScript
After connected through Chrome DevTools Protocol, the agent navigates normally. You don’t need to include a wallet key or payment header in your automation code. The browser handles 402 challenges, payment signing, and retries transparently for document navigation, fetch, and XHR requests.
Payment session limits and behavior
Anchor Browser enforces the following guardrails at the session level through AgentCore payments integration. Each payment-ready browser session operates within configured spending and time constraints. For specific limits, refer to the Anchor Browser technical documentation.
If the merchant response is malformed, no compatible network is offered, the budget is exhausted, or AgentCore payments rejects the payment, the browser returns the original 402 response to the page unchanged. Your automation code can then handle the 402 as a standard HTTP error.
The x402 session property controls payments to third-party resources only. The property doesn’t replace Anchor credits and doesn’t pay for the browser session.
Automation code for Anchor Browser
Your automation code for Anchor Browser remains unchanged. The following example demonstrates that no payment-specific code is required:
No wallet logic, no payment header construction, and no retry code. The agent navigates to the URL. If the server returns 402, Anchor Browser coordinates with AgentCore payments to sign the payment proof, retries the request with the appropriate payment header, and delivers the content to the page. Your automation code receives the final rendered page with no indication that a payment occurred.
This pattern applies uniformly to paywalled journalism, licensed financial data, gated API documentation, metered research databases, and other resources that gate content behind a 402 challenge.
Using the built-in x402 tool for API calls
Paid resources aren’t limited to web pages. Many are APIs that expect POST, PUT, or other HTTP methods. Common examples include data enrichment services, premium inference endpoints, and licensed content APIs. For these use cases, Anchor Browser agents include a built-in x402 tool that you call like a standard HTTPS API within the browser context.
Your agent makes the API call through fetch or XHR. If the server returns a 402 challenge, the browser coordinates payment signing through AgentCore payments and retries the request with the signed payment header. Your code receives the response as though the endpoint were free. The tool isn’t tied to a specific vendor, model, or framework. Payment operates as a session-level capability beneath your existing tooling, and no changes to agent code are required.
Your automation code doesn’t receive wallet credentials. Automatic payments are available only when session.x402 is set to true and remain subject to the spending and expiration limits described in the previous section.
Key benefits
This integration moves payment from application code to the infrastructure layer:
No payment infrastructure to build. No wallet SDK to integrate, no 402 response parser to write, no retry loop to implement, no header construction logic to maintain, and no custom audit logging to build. AgentCore payments manages the entire payment stack.
No changes to existing tooling. Playwright scripts, Puppeteer automations, Chrome DevTools Protocol commands, and agent flows in Anchor Browser continue to function exactly as before. Payment is a session capability attached to the browser, not a modification to agent logic, prompts, or tool definitions.
Private keys don’t enter the runtime. Signing and settlement happen inside AgentCore payments. The service communicates with Coinbase CDP or Stripe Privy through secure credential storage in AgentCore Identity. The agent runtime doesn’t have access to key material that can move funds.
Budgets are enforced at the infrastructure level. Every session operates within defined spend limits that AgentCore enforces before authorizing a payment. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Observability provides full payment audit trails through Amazon CloudWatch. When a session reaches the spending limit, AgentCore payments denies the payment.
Paid tasks complete successfully. Paid GET pages load. Paid API calls return responses. The agent completes the workflow rather than stopping at a 402 response and requiring manual intervention.
Billing is consolidated. Anchor Browser settles third-party x402 charges in credits on the same invoice as browser session time. There’s no separate crypto custody to manage, no USDC balance to monitor, and no on-chain settlement for the finance team to reconcile.
Conclusion
Anchor Browser, integrated with AgentCore payments, equips AI agents to handle x402 payment challenges autonomously for paywalled web pages and paid API endpoints. Wallet credentials stay out of agent code, and no custom payment infrastructure is required.
As more of the web moves to per-request pricing, agents that lack a payment mechanism can’t complete tasks involving paid resources. This integration addresses that gap: agents complete paid workflows end to end, operating within defined budgets, with full observability through AgentCore Observability, and without cryptographic key material in the runtime.

articles.title: AI labs are buying data from dead startups to train their models
articles.text:
AI labs are buying data from dead startups to train their models
Most startups fail. A new industry is giving their data an afterlife in AI.
When Keelan Miskell began winding down his crypto startup this year, he didn’t think its data was worth much: the users were anonymous, the company just a few years old. But he’s since turned the firm’s digital archives into real money. He’s netted roughly $25,000 for his code base and a still-pending amount (likely around $15,000) for the workspace data in Google, Notion, Figma, and Slack. “At least all that stuff we were doing for two and a half years is worth something to someone somewhere,” he says.
The sale was brokered by a company called SimpleClosure, part of a new growth sector in tech: businesses catering to dying startups. Estimates from Carta and AngelList show shutdowns rising between 26% and 56% annually in recent years, and an end-of-life ecosystem—including coaches, “death doulas,” and firms that help handle the legal, tax, and operational headaches of going belly-up—has emerged. Now tech undertakers are selling the data remains to AI labs.
SimpleClosure added data sales to its services in April. Its Asset Hub platform helps founders sell their code and workspace data—emails, chats, documents. Buyers include foundation AI labs, vendors that construct simulated workspaces for AI training, and mature tech companies building their own models. Asset Hub has handled over 150 deals and expects to return over $10 million to startups by the end of 2026. CEO Dori Yona has seen these transactions, once rare and “somewhat taboo,” become increasingly routine, with 47% of SimpleClosure deals now including code or data sales.
And it’s got company. Industry rival Sunset also has a rapidly growing data resale business. Founder and CEO Brendan Mahony says Sunset values a dying client’s assets by head count, years in operation, volume of data, and how the team used its tools. Particle board, he says, is a good analogy: “This operational exhaust data is like the wood shavings that everyone thought had no value, but it actually has a ton.”
Demand for defunct companies’ data emerged suddenly last year, as AI training labs hit the limits of public and synthetic datasets. Surge AI, for example, buys data to build “reinforcement-learning gyms” where clients’ AI agents practice tasks—think debugging a complex IT architecture or drafting appellate briefs. Nick Heiner, who leads the company’s work on these environments, says he seeks data archives reflecting a range of situations, from disagreements to tricky judgment calls. Heiner explains that one company’s Slack history, if it captures conversations with variety and depth, can be worth more than another’s Slack, email, and calendars combined.
Real archives avoid common errors in synthetic worlds, such as references to dates that don’t exist, but the extent of performance gains remains unclear. No company has yet released tests comparing results of real-world data training with the alternatives. Pricing reflects this uncertainty: Buyers quote wildly different numbers, Heiner says, because valuations are based on “research theses” estimating how many useful tasks come from, say, 100,000 lines of code.
That hasn’t stopped bigger deals from happening. This past August, as part of Spirit Airlines’ bankruptcy, Google outbid the AI data company Mercor to buy the carrier’s decades of data, including 100 million emails, 500 million Teams messages, and 176,000 employee records. The price tag: $10 million. And Bloomberg reported in September that SpaceX’s AI unit is weighing buying data from struggling startups.
Legally, this all could get iffy. Spirit’s flight attendants’ union objected to the sale on privacy grounds, and Greg Ewing, an attorney who advises AI startups, has called such data “legally radioactive.” Suppliers employ data scientists to scrub personally identifiable information and exclude HR records, and buyers say they scrub too. But Ewing points out some of the private details that lurk in emails and calendars: doctor appointments, school pickup arrangements, date-night plans. He describes a “Wild West of AI training” that is only starting to give way to proper licensing agreements and vetted use.
There’s also the question of who profits from these windfalls. The proceeds typically flow to senior creditors and investors—not employees. To Ifeoma Ajunwa, a law professor at Emory University and author of The Quantified Worker, this represents a form of “captured capital.” Legal precedent allows for monitoring to help workers do their jobs, but once a firm is out of business, that justification vanishes. “Employers should have express consent before selling workers’ data,” says Ajunwa, but she adds that there’s no federal law banning such sales.
While many see this new market as a chance for failing businesses to recover some value, these wind-down sales also have limitations. Founders have little to no visibility into who is buying the data and what they plan to do with it. Plus, there’s little assurance they’re getting a fair offer. Data prices will likely stabilize in the coming year, though, unless an AI bubble pops first. Either way, tech’s new undertakers will be there to appraise what’s left.
Matthew King is a technology and environmental journalist based in Baltimore.

articles.title: UK Housing Ombudsman Service investigates 'security incident'
articles.text:
The U.K. Housing Ombudsman Service is investigating a third-party IT security incident that impacted its case management system on Tuesday.
Established under the Housing Act 1996, the Housing Ombudsman is an executive non-departmental public body sponsored by the Ministry of Housing, Communities, and Local Government.
The watchdog settles disputes between social housing residents and social landlords in England, including housing associations, landlords, managers, and letting agents.
On Tuesday, the service added an alert to its official website, warning that it's working with the affected service provider to assess the incident's impact and said social housing residents cannot file new complaints until systems are back online.
Those who must raise new complaints are advised to call the Housing Ombudsman's phone line or email the watchdog at info@housing-ombudsman.org.uk.
"The incident has been contained, and we are working with our external supplier to establish the full facts, including the extent of the data involved," the service said. "We are continuing to investigate whether any personal information has been affected and will provide further updates as soon as we are able. "
The Housing Ombudsman service has also notified the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) of the incident and advised tenants and leaseholders to be wary of potential scams when receiving unsolicited messages.
"As a precaution, we recommend that individuals continue to exercise their usual caution when responding to unexpected communications," it added. "Do not disclose personal information unless you are confident of the identity of the requester and report any suspicious activity to the relevant organisation or authorities. "
The watchdog is working to restore its services "as quickly as possible" and will share further updates on the investigation as soon as they're available.
In March, the British government agency Companies House, which operates the registry for all U.K. companies, was also forced to take its WebFiling service offline to fix a security flaw that had exposed companies' information since October 2025.
Two months earlier, in January, the United Kingdom announced a new cybersecurity strategy, backed by more than £210 million ($283 million) and aiming to boost cyber defenses across government departments and the wider public sector.

articles.title: Srinath Ravichandran and Suyash Singh on overcoming failure in spacetech
articles.text:
Srinath Ravichandran and Suyash Singh on overcoming failure in spacetech
At TechSparks 2026, AgniKul’s Srinath Ravichandran and GalaxEye’s Suyash Singh share how frugal innovation, perseverance through failure, and strategic policy shifts are shaping India’s emerging private space technology sector.
The rise of private spacetech in India is frequently celebrated through triumphant headlines, but behind every successful rocket launch or satellite deployment lies a gritty reality defined by hundreds of investor rejections, acute supply chain bottlenecks, and the constant threat of orbital failure.
Speaking with Shradha Sharma, Founder and CEO, YourStory and The Bharat Project, at the 17th edition of YourStory’s flagship tech-startup event, TechSparks, Srinath Ravichandran, Co-founder and CEO of AgniKul Cosmos, and Suyash Singh, Co-founder and CEO of GalaxEye, shared practical insights into the complex task of building aerospace ventures in an emerging market.
When AgniKul started in 2017, the Indian regulatory framework for private space technology was still evolving, and local venture capital for deeptech was nearly non-existent. Ravichandran faced 275 investor rejections before securing initial backing. Singh encountered similar headwinds at GalaxEye, facing roughly 100 rejections. Their early survival required breaking down ambitious goals into manageable steps rather than relying on rigid long-term master plans.
“The first thing to do is to get started, one way or the other... break it down into smaller milestones and start doing something... patience building was the big thing for me at least,” Ravichandran said.
This pragmatic mindset also reshaped how both founders approached business models. In Western nations, legacy aerospace programmes often require half a billion dollars in capital before generating revenue. In contrast, AgniKul focused on a pay-per-kilogram transportation model for small satellites, effectively operating as a cargo carrier to orbit, aiming for commercial viability at the $50 to $60 million mark.
Explaining this frugal approach, Ravichandran noted, “It is more like you give me $500 million and then I will start giving you money back. That is not how India works. That is not how I am also built.”
Following a successful test launch in May 2024 using 3D-printed engines and a mobile launchpad, AgniKul is now preparing for orbital customer flights while testing rocket stage reusability, bringing hardware safely back to Earth to lower launch costs.
While launch providers handle transportation, satellite makers face distinct operational challenges. GalaxEye developed OptoSAR, a patented, world-first technology combining optical cameras with synthetic aperture radar to view the Earth through clouds and darkness.
However, hardware in space remains unforgiving. Just 30 days after launching India’s largest private liquid satellite to global praise, GalaxEye lost communication with the spacecraft.
Reflecting on the setback, Singh emphasised, “Whatever journey we are going through is dealing with those kinds of failures is also going to be very very important for the space industry.”
Despite such risks, market demand is expanding rapidly. Surging geopolitical conflicts across the globe have made space-based Earth observation indispensable.
“Geopolitics is hotter, and space based surveillance is not an option. It is mandatory. So I think defence is one of the largest markets,” Singh explained.
Yet, scaling space ventures in India reveals persistent structural friction. Growth-stage capital and funding checks of $100 million or more remains scarce as institutional investors slowly adapt to deeptech return profiles, where heavy upfront research and development precedes long-term gains.
Supply chains also present difficulties. Startups frequently encounter high minimum order quantities, the smallest number of custom components a manufacturer agrees to supply, forcing founders to rely on European vendors for specialised light sensors when domestic equivalents remain too heavy.
Despite these hurdles, both founders remain optimistic about human capital. Strict foreign visa regulations in Western aerospace sectors are encouraging top Indian engineers to stay or return home. Combined with employee stock option schemes that offer real wealth creation, deeptech in India is gaining prestige, pushing the nation’s private spacetech ecosystem to mature.
“I left technical engineering to go into finance... realised my heart is in engineering, so I came back... Equity is the only way to really get rich... with ESOPs people are starting careers,” Ravichandran noted.

articles.title: Todos los productos que ha presentado Apple para el hogar siguen dependiendo de una misma cosa: el iPhone
articles.text:
En el anuncio del HomeView, una familia de cinco intenta salir de casa por la mañana entre tostadas, llaves perdidas y discusiones por el termostato. Nadie tiene un iPhone en la mano, pero todos lo llevan encima. Lo sabemos porque, sin eso, la pantalla de la cocina no podría saber quién es cada uno.
Ese detalle resume perfectamente lo que Apple presentó ayer: ninguno de sus nuevos productos para la casa tiene un sentido completo por sí solo. Todos dependen del iPhone.
Una pantalla que no sabe nada sin tu iPhone. El HomeView es una pantalla de 7 pulgadas con altavoz que cuesta 299 dólares en Estados Unidos, pero no se puede comprar en la Unión Europea. Reconoce hasta seis caras y muestra a cada persona sus mensajes, su calendario y sus recordatorios. Pero no lo hace de forma autónoma:
UN VISTAZO A...
- No tiene Face ID. Para reconocer tu rostro necesita verte, pero también que tu iPhone esté en la misma red WiFi y se haya desbloqueado hace poco.
- No guarda tus datos. Los consulta en tu iPhone cada vez que le preguntas algo personal.
- Sus apps de terceros funcionan con la misma tecnología que CarPlay. Es decir: muestran las compatibles que tenga tu iPhone, pero nada de ir a una App Store a descargar nada específico.
El resto funciona igual. Incluyendo el Apple TV 4K y el HomePod mini 2, que sí llegan a la Unión Europea.
- Apple TV 4K: para usar Siri AI con información personal, el propietario de la casa necesita un iPhone con Apple Intelligence. Sin Siri AI, sus novedades son menores.
- HomePod mini 2: Siri AI llegará más adelante, y para activarlo hará falta ese iPhone. Sin Siri AI, es un modelo casi idéntico al HomePod mini original, de 2020.
- Apple Home Collection: los accesorios desarrollados con LG y Schneider Electric se configuran acercando el iPhone. Es la parte más comprensible: no dejan de ser accesorios como tal.
Apple no ha lanzado una gama para el hogar. Ha lanzado accesorios del iPhone para el hogar. Es lo que John Ternus anticipó hace un mes al definir el teléfono como un "hub personal inteligente" en la intro de la keynote de septiembre.
Mientras tanto en España. El HomeView no se venderá en la Unión Europea porque Siri AI no está disponible en iOS en Europa. Es la prueba más clara de esta tesis: si el iPhone no tiene Siri AI, el HomeView no tiene razón de existir.
El Apple TV 4K y el HomePod mini 2 sí llegarán, pero sin aquello que mejor los justifica fuera de Europa:
- HomePod mini 2 (169 euros): colores nuevos, un chip más rápido, la opción de usarlo como altavoz del Mac y Sound Glow, unas luces que imitan la portada del disco y que también llegarán al modelo actual.
- Apple TV 4K (349 euros): chip A19, soporte para AV1, un mando localizable y sonido envolvente con cuatro HomePod. Sus micrófonos para hablarle sin mando no funcionarán en español.
Son mejoras razonables, pero propias de una renovación al uso. Y por la RAMaggedon o no, llegan con subidas notables: el HomePod mini costaba 99 euros en 2020, y el Apple TV 4K de 2022 partía de 169 (189 en su versión equivalente, con Ethernet y 128 GB). Son subidas de un 70%/85% y un 106% en seis y cuatro años respectivamente.
En resumen. Lo que Apple ha presentado no es una estrategia para la casa. Es una estrategia para que el iPhone siga siendo el centro de todo, incluso cuando no lo tienes en la mano.
Por eso en el anuncio nadie sostiene un iPhone, y por eso todo funciona. En España, de momento, seguiremos sujetándolo.

articles.title: Employee Arrested After Listening Device Found in OpenAI Conference Room, FBI and the Company Say
articles.text:
An engineer at OpenAI has been charged with secretly installing a recording device inside a conference room in what officials said Tuesday was an effort to capture sensitive conversations about the company’s technology.
The employee, identified as a 35-year-old Saudi national named Abdulrahman Alfozan, was arrested Friday, a week after the ChatGPT maker discovered an audio recording device hidden in the conference room, according to a criminal complaint filed in federal court in San Francisco.
The complaint did not identify the company, but the company confirmed in a separate statement that it had discovered a “sophisticated recording device that was hidden inside one of our offices,” reported the finding to the FBI and fired the employee.
“We used our models to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier. We referred the matter to the FBI, and we’re grateful to the agents and prosecutors who moved quickly to make an arrest. The FBI’s investigation is ongoing and we will continue to support their work,” an OpenAI spokesperson said.
“At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data. The employee was terminated,” the statement said.
The complaint does not detail what Alfozan might have wanted to do with any captured communications.
Alfozan made his first court appearance Tuesday on a charge of using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications. It was not immediately clear if he had a lawyer who could speak on his behalf.
The recording device was found September 30 concealed in toilet paper and inserted into a USB port on the back of a television in the conference room, according to the complaint.
Though the conference room where the recording device was found did not have a camera at the time it was installed, closed-circuit television footage inside the company’s offices revealed that Alfozan was near the conference room on a half-dozen occasions last month despite not having any authority to access the space, the complaint says.
The company subsequently added a camera to the room that last week captured Alfozan entering and checking behind the television where the recording device was installed, according to the FBI.
The complaint also he also used a productivity tool to make multiple inquiries about the company’s building addresses, meeting rooms, meeting-room capacities and calendars.
Before his arrest last week, the complaint says, Alfozan left an unattended bag in a different room in the building that included his wallet, identification and another recording device.

articles.title: Some AI researchers are taking up smoking because they believe artificial intelligence will cure cancer
articles.text:
WTF?! The promise that AI is going to cure cancer has failed to materialize, but some AI researchers are so sure it'll happen one day that they've taken up smoking. That's according to Palantir CTO Shyam Sankar, who says this comically bad idea is a sort of flex to show others how much faith they have in the technology.
Sankar made his claim during an interview on CBS's Face the Nation on Sunday. The exec talked about Pascal's quote of how there is a God-shaped vacuum, or hole, in the heart of every person, and how many AI workers in Silicon Valley had filled that hole with the machine god that is AI (or AGI, as he calls it).
As an example of this unwavering faith in their Warhammer 40,000-like machine god, Sankar claims that many AI researchers have started smoking as a way of signaling to other researchers how much they believe in AI.
"'I believe so much in AI that it's going to cure cancer. So I will – I'm showing you my chips are all in.' So there is kind of this mass psychosis social delusion around it," the Palantir executive said.
Assuming this is true, and it very well may be, given some people's fetishism of AI, it's very stupid and a bit sad. Even if AI did help scientists develop effective treatments for some cancers, smoking can cause several different types of the disease.
Moreover, there's the time it takes to test these treatments in clinical trials, and let's not forget the numerous other non-cancerous but still potentially fatal conditions smoking can cause. So maybe think twice before deeply inhaling those tar-filled toxins into your spongy lungs.
Despite being filled with health-obsessed types like Bryan Johnson, there have been several recent articles about how smoking is making a comeback in certain tech circles, so maybe some of what Sankar says is true. Or perhaps in these uncertain times we live in, the smokers think there might not be a future to worry about – ironically, a big part of that is driven by the threat from rogue AI.
While not on the level of curing cancer, an AI-generated drug was reported last month to have shown signs of a different breakthrough: slowing the aging process. There were some caveats, of course, the big one being that changes in aging markers don't prove we'll soon be living to 150 or older.

articles.title: Homeview-Hub, Thermostate und Türschloss: Apple zeigt neue Smarthome-Produkte – doch es gibt einen Haken
articles.text:
Homeview-Hub, Thermostate und Türschloss: Apple zeigt neue Smarthome-Produkte – doch es gibt einen Haken
Das „Welcome Home“-Event von Apple hat es mit seinem Namen schon verraten: Der iPhone-Konzern plante geraume Zeit eine neue Offensive im Smarthome-Sektor. Jetzt hat Apple sein Portfolio deutlich aufgestockt. Im Zentrum des neuen Smarthomes steht dabei ganz klar der neue Homeview-Hub, der vom Homepod Mini und zahlreichen anderen smarten Gadgets unterstützt wird. Doch für deutsche Apple-Fans gibt es einen großen Haken.
Homeview-Hub: Deutsche Apple-Fans gehen leer aus
Beim Homeview-Hub handelt es sich um ein 7‑Zoll-großes Display, das auf einer stationären Halterung samt integriertem Lautsprecher befestigt ist. Wer will, kann das Display aber auch in einer Wall-Mounted-Version kaufen und es stattdessen an der Wand anbringen. Mit an Bord sind Mikrofone, eine Kamera sowie Siri AI. Über die Kamera kann der Homeview-Hub verschiedene User:innen im Haushalt erkennen und ihnen personalisierte Homescreens anzeigen lassen. Bis zu sechs Personen kann sich der smarte Hub dabei merken.
Wie bei vielen anderen smarten Hubs mit Display können über das Gadget auch Videoanrufe per Facetime geführt, Musik abgespielt und eben dein Smarthome gesteuert werden. Die Steuerung erfolgt dabei über Touch-Eingaben oder per Sprachsteuerung und Siri. Smarthome-Dashboards werden dabei in neun Kacheln auf dem viereckigen Display unterteilt. Mit ausreichend kompatiblen Geräten können sich User:innen also auch neun Videofeeds von Überwachungskameras gleichzeitig auf dem Homeview-Hub anschauen.
Gerade in Verbindung mit einem iPhone, auf dem Apple Intelligence aktiviert ist, soll Siri AI auf dem Homeview-Hub ihre Stärke demonstrieren. Dann kann die KI das Smartphone nach Nachrichten und Kalendereinträgen oder etwa Playlists bei Apple Music durchsuchen, um personalisierten Kontext über die Nutzer:innen zu erfahren. Wer kein iPhone mit Apple Intelligence nutzt, soll dennoch von Siris neuem Wissen, Konversationsfertigkeiten und „verbesserter Musiksuche“ profitieren.
Siri AI ist auch der Grund, warum deutsche und europäische Apple-Fans im Allgemeinen einen Dämpfer hinnehmen müssen. Im Kleingedruckten der Ankündigung des Smarthome-Hubs steht, dass das Gadget vorerst nicht in der EU erscheinen wird. Da Siri AI nicht in iOS in der EU verfügbar ist, bleibt auch das Gadget vorerst vom Markt fern. Wann sich das ändern wird, ist nicht klar. In anderen Märkten startet der Homeview-Hub zum Preis von 299 US-Dollar.
Homepod Mini mit integrierter Siri
Der neue Homepod Mini der zweiten Generation lässt sich aber hierzulande problemlos vorbestellen. Apple bietet den smarten Speaker für 169 Euro in Grün, Weiß, Blau, Pink und Schwarz an. Die Auslieferungen sollen ab dem 30. Oktober 2026 starten. Wie schon der Homeview-Hub unterstützt auch der Homepod Mini 2 Siri AI.
So kann ebenfalls ein iPhone mit Apple Intelligence verknüpft werden, um personalisiertere Antworten zu bekommen. Allerdings wird die KI erst per Update nachgereicht. Selbiges wird hierzulande dann wohl ausgesetzt. Wer den Homepod Mini 2 kauft, muss also auf die intelligentere Version von Siri verzichten und stattdessen mit dem regulären KI-gestützten Sprachassistenten vorliebnehmen.
Abgesehen von den KI-Neuerungen liefert der Homepod Mini der zweiten Generation jetzt nicht nur allein 360-Grad-Sound, sondern kann auch als Stereopaar und an einem Mac genutzt werden. In Verbindung mit dem neuen Apple TV 4K sind sogar vier Speaker gleichzeitig möglich, die einander im Raum erkennen und so den Sound der TV-Wiedergabe optimieren.
Neu ist auch das sogenannte „Sound Glow“. Auf der Oberseite des Homepod Mini 2 zeigt das Gerät eine Visualisierung des wiedergegebenen Sounds. Der smarte Speaker reagiert in Echtzeit auf Bässe und Höhen und nutzt für die farbliche Abstimmung die Cover-Farben von den gespielten Alben. Zu guter Letzt kann der Homepod Mini 2 natürlich auch ins Smarthome integriert werden, um Geräte per Spracheingabe zu steuern und Benachrichtigungen laut im Raum abzuspielen.
Neues Apple TV 4K mit alter Siri
Ebenso sieht es beim neuen Apple TV 4K aus. Das Gerät funktioniert dank Matter-Untertützung ebenfalls als Smarthome-Zentrale. Das war aber schon beim Vorgänger der Fall. Neu sind ein schnellerer Prozessor, der mehr Rechenleistung und dank eines Decoders qualitativ hochwertiges Streaming bei niedriger Bandbreite ermöglichen soll. In der Theorie war das neue Apple TV 4K damit auch fit für Apple Intelligence oder vorrangig Siri AI. Dass die Box darauf ausgelegt ist, zeigen die drei integrierten Fernfeldmikrofone, mit der man das Apple TV freihändig bedienen können soll.
In der Praxis schaltet Apple die neue Version von Siri in tvOS 27.2 jedoch nur in sieben Ländern frei. Deutschland gehört nicht dazu. Die Mikrofone lassen sich zwar nutzen, allerdings nur mit der alten Version von Siri. Vorbestellen lässt sich die Streaming-Box ab sofort. Ausgeliefert wird ab dem 13. November. Der Preis liegt bei 349 Euro.
Smarte Türschlösser, Klingeln und Thermostate von Apple und LG
Zu guter Letzt hat Apple die Home Collection vorgestellt. Dabei handelt es sich um eine Reihe von Gadgets von Thermostaten über Temperatursensoren bis zu smarten Türschlössern. Diese sind in Zusammenarbeit mit LG Electronics und Schneider Electric entstanden. Apple verspricht, dass sie sich allesamt mit nur einem Fingertippen mit Apple Home verbinden und nutzen lassen. Die Steuerung erfolgt über die Home-App und benötigt keinerlei Anwendung von Dritten. Neben Apple Home unterstützen die Geräte auch Matter, um sie in andere Systeme wie Home Assistant integrieren und vernetzen zu können.
Im Bereich der Eigenheimüberwachung bietet Apple eine LG‑Videotürklingel mit 2,5-K-Auflösung (250 Dollar), eine Flutlichtkamera mit Bewegungsmelder (400 Dollar) sowie eine Outdoor-Kamera mit Nachtsicht (300 Dollar) und eine Indoor-Kamera (200 Dollar) an. Alle Kameras funktionieren mit iCloud Plus, wodurch User:innen auf die Aufzeichnungen der vergangenen zehn Tage zugreifen können. Apple Intelligence kann dabei sogar die Aufnahmen durchsuchen und zusammenfassen, was darin passiert.
Daneben gibt es noch ein smartes Türschloss, für 350 Dollar, das Nutzer:innen und deren Apple-Produkte über Ultra-Breitband erkennt und automatisch die Tür öffnen kann. Wer die automatische Erkennung nicht nutzen will, kann iPhone oder Apple Watch aber auch an den integrierten Scanner halten oder einen PIN‑Code eingeben. Zudem bietet das Türschloss ein „verstecktes Backup-Schlüsselloch“.
Zu guter Letzt gibt es zwei Thermostate für je 200 Dollar, eins von LG, eins von Schneider Electric. So sollen Apple-User:innen die Wahl haben, welches Gerät mehr zu ihrem Smarthome-Ökosystem passt. Die Thermostate können dabei mit separat erhältlichen Temperatursensoren (je 40 Dollar) gekoppelt werden oder die Temperaturfühler nutzen, die im Homeview-Hub, dem Homepod oder Homepod Mini enthalten sind. Sämtliche Produkte der Collection sollen ab Dezember 2026 bei Apple verfügbar sein.

articles.title: 'GTA 6' llegaría a PC mucho antes de lo que todos pensábamos
articles.text:
La espera por GTA 6 en PC podría ser mucho más breve de lo que todos imaginábamos. Según reporta GamesBeat, Rockstar Games planea lanzar la versión para ordenadores apenas meses después de su debut en PS5 y Xbox Series X|S. Si esto se confirma será un auténtico bombazo, considerando que hasta aquí el estudio ha dado pistas prácticamente nulas de que la llegada del nuevo Grand Theft Auto podría darse en un plazo tan acotado.
De acuerdo con el citado medio, GTA 6 se lanzará en PC durante el primer trimestre de 2027. La información fue supuestamente ratificada por cuatro fuentes relacionadas con los planes de Rockstar y Take-Two Interactive. De ser cierto, el debut del título en ordenadores se dará, a más tardar, en marzo del próximo año.
Claro que la información debe tomarse con pinzas y no hay que dar nada por hecho. Por lo pronto, los responsables de GTA 6 no han realizado anuncios oficiales sobre una versión para PC. De hecho, cada vez que se les ha consultado sobre el tema han brindado respuestas evasivas. Y si bien todos esperaban que el juego llegara eventualmente a Windows, nadie en sus cabales pensaba que podría llegar a darse tan rápido.
Después de todo, suponiendo que la información es certera, GTA 6 estaría llegando a PC apenas 4 meses después de su debut en consolas, considerando marzo de 2027 como fecha más tardía. Esto pondría patas arriba cualquier especulación previa respecto de la expansión del juego más allá de su disponibilidad inicial en PlayStation y Xbox.
GTA 6 podría llegar a PC a más tardar en marzo de 2027
Desde que GTA 6 lanzó su primer tráiler a finales de 2023, Rockstar Games ha evitado ofrecer cualquier tipo de mención a una posible versión de PC. Las únicas referencias a su potencial llegada a la plataforma han sido de Strauss Zelnick, el CEO de Take-Two Interactive, la casa matriz del estudio. Desde 2024 hasta la actualidad, el ejecutivo ofreció referencias sobre el tema (algunas más crípticas que otras), dando a entender que una edición para ordenadores llegaría tarde o temprano, pero que no sería prioridad.
Recién en mayo de este año, Zelnick brindó una respuesta más directa sobre por qué todavía no se había anunciado GTA 6 en PC. El empresario argumentó, simplemente, que la mayoría de los jugadores de Grand Theft Auto estaban en consolas, y que por ese motivo preferían enfocarse primero en servir a su base de usuarios más amplia.
"Rockstar siempre empieza en consola porque creo que [...] se te juzga por cómo atiendes a tu público principal. Es decir, realmente atender a tu consumidor principal. Si tu consumidor principal no está ahí, si no se le atiende primero y de la mejor manera, no llegas a tus otros consumidores", explicó por entonces.
Pero esa parecía ser solo una parte de la historia. John Ricchio, histórico productor de Rockstar con pasado en GTA 5, Red Dead Redemption y Max Payne, explicó que también existía una justificación técnica. Según su experiencia, optimizar GTA 6 basándose en las limitaciones técnicas de la PS5 y las Xbox Series X|S haría mucho más fácil el proceso de portear el juego a PC.
"Siempre es mejor empezar por las limitaciones y luego ampliar, porque reducir es mucho más difícil que ampliar. Es mucho más difícil lograr un buen rendimiento en un juego que simplemente pensar: 'Oh, tenemos espacio extra, genial, podemos desoptimizar algunas cosas o hacerlas más llamativas'", comentó.
Considerando los antecedentes, el consenso general era que GTA 6 posiblemente se demorara unos dos años en llegar a PC. Pero si lo que reporta GamesBeat es certero, la historia esta vez podría ser muy diferente. Esto despierta un gran interrogante: ¿Por qué Rockstar cambiaría de estrategia ahora?
El citado reporte plantea dos opciones:
- Por un lado, la necesidad de capturar a cuantos jugadores sea posible para recuperar sus bestiales costes de desarrollo. GTA 6 habría costado unos 2.000 millones de dólares, y llegar temprano a los jugadores más casuales en PC podría agilizar la amortización.
- Por el otro, implementar una estrategia basada en mods, la creación de contenidos por parte de los usuarios y el role-playing. En tal sentido, se menciona que la compra de CFX.re por parte de Rockstar en 2023 podría jugar un papel clave en esta historia.
También se especula con que lanzar la versión para PC de GTA 6 apenas meses después de su llegada a consolas podría estar relacionada con ampliar la base de GTA Online desde el primer día. Según el CEO de Twitch, Rockstar planea lanzar el componente multijugador online del nuevo Grand Theft Auto en 2027. Por ende, ya hay teorías de que el arribo temprano del juego a los ordenadores podría estar relacionado con esto. Por lo pronto, no hay que dar nada por hecho, pero seguiremos atentos a cualquier novedad.

articles.title: It looks like Apple Music is getting a new icon
articles.text:
Apple Music’s iconic red app icon has reportedly been replaced with a black-and-white version in the latest iOS 27.2 beta, 9to5Mac reports. The eighth note on the icon also appears to have a slightly sharper angle than the original. A new Apple Music logo was also spotted last month on the Apple Music Hall website, so the company could be refreshing its app icon to match.
It looks like Apple Music is getting a new icon
Apple Music might be going monochrome.
Apple Music might be going monochrome.
According to 9to5Mac, the new icon is a black music note on a white background in light mode, or the opposite in dark mode. The icon’s not the only thing that’s been drained of color, either — 9to5Mac also says Apple Music widgets now have black backgrounds and the app now uses a splash of blue in the tab bar to show the active tab.
A user on X shared images of the new icon in the different color modes, including the tinted version. So if the new monochrome version of the app makes it to a public iOS release, you might be able to use the tinted homescreen option to make it look a bit like the previous red version again.

articles.title: Google backs launch of cross-Canada cybersecurity training hubs | BetaKit
articles.text:
A Brampton-based cybersecurity training hub has received a $3.5-million contribution from Google.org, the search giant’s philanthropic arm, to help Canadian organizations develop a cybersecurity game plan while giving budding cybersecurity experts real-world training.
“Cyber clinics give learners the opportunity to tackle current cybersecurity challenges under expert supervision, while providing smaller organizations with support they may not otherwise be able to afford.”
On Wednesday morning, the Rogers Cybersecure Catalyst announced the funding, which will help launch the Cyber Clinics Canada program. The national network of clinics will train post-secondary students and new cybersecurity professionals to deliver free cybersecurity consulting to public and community organizations. The program is the national expansion of the Catalyst Cyber Clinic, which launched last year to provide cybersecurity support for Canadian non-profits and community organizations.
In a statement, Catalyst’s founding executive director Charles Finlay likened cyber clinics to “a teaching hospital for the digital age.”
“Much like teaching hospitals give future healthcare professionals practical experience while serving patients, cyber clinics give learners the opportunity to tackle current cybersecurity challenges under expert supervision, while providing smaller organizations with support they may not otherwise be able to afford,” Finlay said.
Catalyst launched in 2018 as a national centre for cybersecurity out of Toronto Metropolitan University to promote training, research, and commercial innovation in the field of cybersecurity. Since then, cyberattacks have become more common, especially as AI tools have advanced. An IBM report earlier this year found a 44-percent year-over-year increase in attacks targeting public-facing software or system applications.
RELATED: An AI tried to hack Canada. Is that a warning?
In a statement, Google Canada vice-president and country manager Sabrina Geremia said that building a “strong, diverse, and skilled cybersecurity workforce is more important than ever.”
“Cyber clinics are a proven, scalable model, and expanding this program across Canada will meaningfully improve access to cyber education while delivering critical support to vulnerable organizations that serve Canadians,” Geremia said.
While cyber clinic students won’t handle active cyberattacks, they will help organizations with vulnerability and risk assessments, phishing and digital hygiene training, incident response planning, and regulatory and privacy compliance. The Catalyst said that its program will equip institutions like universities with the tools and knowledge to launch their own cyber clinics, helping build out Canada’s cybersecurity workforce.
Featured image courtesy Rogers Cybersecure Catalyst.

articles.title: Agentic AI Automates RTL Waveform Analysis And Debugging (Columbia, Google)
articles.text:
Researchers at Columbia University, Google DeepMind, and Google published a technical paper titled “Back to the Future: Rethinking EDA Infrastructure for Agentic Systems in Chip Design Verification.”
Abstract
“The unprecedented computational scale of modern artificial intelligence depends on complex, multi-billion-transistor Systems-on-Chip, yet the workflows that verify these chips remain stubbornly manual. Although Large Language Models (LLMs) have made rapid inroads into Electronic Design Automation (EDA), approximately 74.6% of existing studies target static Register-Transfer Level (RTL) code generation, leaving post-simulation verification and interactive waveform debugging largely untouched. We introduce Back-to-the-Future (BTTF), an end-to-end agentic framework that closes this infrastructural gap. BTTF distills massive, unstructured simulation dumps into a normalized relational SQLite database and couples it with a collaborative multi-agent orchestration engine that translates natural-language verification queries into schema-aware SQL while correlating signal anomalies with versioned RTL repositories. Across a 150-query benchmark, BTTF attains 95.33% execution accuracy, charting a practical path toward autonomous EDA verification.”
Find the technical paper here. October 2026.
Yang, Je, Ivan Lobov, and Thomas Karpati. “Back to the Future: Rethinking EDA Infrastructure for Agentic Systems in Chip Design Verification.” arXiv preprint arXiv:2610.06790 (2026).

articles.title: SA’s Kuunda completes $5m secondary share sale led by E4E Africa - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
South African digital lending infrastructure startup Kuunda has completed a US$5 million secondary share sale led by E4E Africa, returning capital to early investors while bringing the investment firm on board as a larger long-term shareholder.
Established in 2018, Kuunda is a B2B digital lending-as-a-service company that provides tailored liquidity solutions built through meaningful collaborative partnerships. By partnering with mobile money operators, POS network providers, e-commerce players and banks, Kuunda embeds credit products into existing digital platforms, using data-driven credit scoring to provide productive financing to mobile money agents, merchants, and consumers in emerging markets.
Disrupt Africa reported in October last year that the startup had raised a US$7.5 million pre-Series A round of funding, with E4E Africa among the participants alongside the likes of Portugal Gateway Fund, Seedstars Africa Ventures, 4Di Capital, Accion Ventures, and Nedbank.
Growth has continued since. Kuunda’s infrastructure has now disbursed more than 870 million loans, delivering over US$4.4 billion in credit to 14.6 million agents, merchants and consumers. The company is currently live in five markets, with launches planned in a further seven.
The new transaction sees E4E Africa expand its stake in the business, with existing investors Accion Ventures, Portugal Gateway Fund and Seedstars Africa Ventures also increasing their positions. Kuunda says the deal gives early backers a meaningful return, and shows African fintech companies can generate liquidity for shareholders well before an IPO or acquisition.
“This is an important milestone for Kuunda and our investors,” said Andrew Milne, Kuunda’s CEO. “Delivering a successful secondary at this stage reflects the strength of the business we’ve built – profitable, scalable lending infrastructure serving millions of people across Africa. We’re grateful to our early backers and excited to grow with a strong, aligned shareholder base.”
Bas Hochstenbach, managing partner at E4E Africa, said Kuunda was using technology, distribution and banking partnerships to deliver essential financial services where traditional institutions could not reach.
“Kuunda is an exceptional company, building a very healthy and fast-growing business while offering much needed products at fair prices to African small businesses and consumers,” he said.

articles.title: Amansa Investments, SBI Mutual Fund, others invest Rs 413 Cr in Tonbo Imaging ahead of IPO
articles.text:
Amansa Investments, SBI Mutual Fund, others invest Rs 413 Cr in Tonbo Imaging ahead of IPO
Amansa Investments, SBI Mutual Fund and HDFC Life Insurance Company, among others, have invested over Rs 413 crore in defence electronics maker Tonbo Imaging India Ltd through secondary share transactions, valuing the company at around Rs 4,000 crore.
This comes ahead of the company's Rs 852 crore Initial Public Offering (IPO).
The transactions, executed on September 29-30, involved existing investors CEAQ Singapore and CEAQ India transferring shares to a group of domestic and international institutional investors, according to the Red Herring Prospectus (RHP).
The buyers included Amansa Investments, Malabar India Fund, SBI Emergent India Fund, SBI Optimal Equity Fund, HDFC Life Insurance Company, Susquehanna Asia Technology, Valuequest Founders Conviction and 360 ONE Multi-Stage Defence and Space Fund, it showed.
Amansa Investments was the largest buyer, acquiring 24.32 lakh shares at Rs 700 apiece, the upper end of the IPO price band, for around Rs 170.24 crore.
Susquehanna Asia Technology Pty Ltd, Valuequest Founders Conviction LVF and 360 ONE Multi-Stage Defence and Space Fund each purchased 5.73 lakh shares for Rs 40.10 crore.
Akash Manek Bhanshali bought 5.66 lakh shares for Rs 39.59 crore, while SBI Emergent India Fund acquired 5 lakh shares worth Rs 35 crore. SBI Optimal Equity Fund and HDFC Life Insurance Company purchased shares valued Rs 20.09 crore and Rs 16.03 crore, respectively.
The company's IPO will open for public subscription on October 15 and close on October 19, with the price band of Rs 665-700 per share.
The issue comprises an Offer For Sale (OFS) of 1.22 crore equity shares by promoters and existing investors, with no fresh issue component.
Since the IPO is entirely an OFS, Tonbo Imaging will not receive any proceeds from the issue.
Founded in 2003 by technologists who had earlier worked with the US Department of Defense and Sarnoff Corporation, the company shifted its focus to defence product manufacturing in 2012 following a buyout by its current promoters.
Tonbo Imaging designs and manufactures sensing, processing, communication and guidance systems for surveillance, reconnaissance, targeting and control applications. Its product portfolio includes thermal imaging cores, weapon sights, handheld thermal imaging binoculars, targeting systems, missile seekers, fire control systems and missile guidance systems.
The company supplies its products to global defence forces, law enforcement agencies, homeland security organisations and defence original equipment manufacturers (OEMs).

articles.title: Un centro de datos es multado con 1,1 millones de dólares por operar 62 generadores de energía
articles.text:
Cuando los inspectores de Nueva Jersey visitaron el 29 de julio unas obras en medio de terrenos agrícolas, los generadores eran imposibles de no ver: 62 equipos del tamaño de un camión con remolque que alimentaban uno de los mayores centros de datos previstos en la costa este de EE. UU. Ninguno tenía los permisos para instalarse ni para funcionar.
El 22 de septiembre, el estado multó a DataOne, la operadora, con 1,07 millones de dólares (unos 933.000 euros al cambio de referencia del BCE de ese día) por violar su ley de control de la contaminación del aire. Según las autoridades estatales, es la mayor sanción que ha recibido un operador de centros de datos en Nueva Jersey.
Cada generador tiene 1.982 kilovatios, así que suman unos 123 megavatios. La ley exige permiso a partir de 37 kilovatios, más de 50 veces menos. El estado ordenó a DataOne pedir los permisos de inmediato y dejar de usar los generadores si no se aprueban en 45 días, que contados desde la orden del 22 de septiembre llegan al 6 de noviembre.
Hasta entonces, pueden seguir en marcha. La empresa dice que no está de acuerdo con la decisión, que solicitará los permisos para los generadores temporales y que está pasando a pilas de combustible de bajas emisiones y silenciosas.
Seis meses entre una pregunta y una inspección
La inspección anterior del estado, la de diciembre, no vio generadores. En febrero, el vecino Zac Landicini, fundador del grupo ecologista Sustain SJ, preguntó en una reunión pública por unos equipos que un agricultor había localizado en imágenes de satélite. No está claro por qué pasaron casi seis meses entre aquella reunión y la inspección del 29 de julio.
A mediados de agosto, una investigación con dron térmico comprobó que al menos 45 de los 62 estaban en marcha. Y un análisis de dos expertos, Xiaomeng Jin (Rutgers) y Bruce Buckheit (antiguo responsable de aplicación de la ley en la EPA), basado en datos técnicos de los equipos obtenidos por registros públicos, sitúa la llegada de los primeros en julio de 2025, con 16 funcionando en octubre de 2025, otros 16 en febrero de 2026 y los 62 en junio, con más de 46.000 horas de uso acumuladas. Esas fechas no encajan con la inspección de diciembre, y ninguna de las fuentes consultadas explica la diferencia.
¿Qué hemos estado respirando?
Tiffany Leone-Vespa lleva 18 años en el barrio y lo expresa de la siguiente manera: “¿Qué hemos estado respirando desde que funcionan estos generadores sin permisos?”. El complejo está cerca de campos de cultivo, viviendas y dos colegios, y los generadores de gas natural emiten dióxido de carbono, óxidos de nitrógeno, monóxido de carbono y otros contaminantes de combustión.
En la actualidad no existen mediciones públicas de lo emitido; lo que sí hay son estimaciones. Las de Jin y Buckheit dicen que son unas 140 toneladas de óxidos de nitrógeno en casi un año y más de 1.500 toneladas anuales si todos los equipos trabajaran a plena capacidad. El “problema” es que son cálculos de investigadores, no mediciones oficiales. Y el aire no es la única queja: bastantes vecinos presentaron una demanda por el ruido, y el departamento de salud del condado ha emitido órdenes de infracción a DataOne por exceso de ruido.
17.258 dólares por generador y un caso paralelo en Virginia
La multa es de 17.258 dólares por generador (unos 15.000 euros). Steve Brown, un vecino de la zona, la define como una gota en el océano para una empresa que, según sus propias estimaciones, tiene varios miles de millones de capital, y la propia Leone-Vespa pide que se hubiera multado por cada equipo.
Virginia ha puesto sobre la mesa otra cifra que es bastante buena para medir lo que ocurre. Su Departamento de Calidad Ambiental propone una sanción de 2,5 millones de dólares a Microsoft (tiene un acuerdo firmado el 3 de septiembre y abierto a comentarios hasta el 14 de octubre) por hacer funcionar 62 generadores durante siete días en agosto de 2025, tras el fallo de una subestación en Leesburg.
Esta es una multa unas 2,3 veces mayor que la de Nueva Jersey, y buena parte de ese dinero va a equipos de monitorización del aire. La comparación no es tampoco del todo exacta: allí hubo una emergencia en un centro con permiso para 104 generadores diésel, que superó sus límites anuales (102 toneladas de óxidos de nitrógeno frente a 94,67 permitidas). Aquí, la estimación de 140 toneladas corresponde a equipos sin permiso, y es una estimación frente a un dato declarado.
Gas como puente, pilas de combustible como destino
Actualmente, los centros de datos de IA buscan potencia más deprisa de lo que las eléctricas construyen red y algunos instalan fuentes propias. Los 123 megavatios de generadores equivalen al 35 % de los 350 megavatios que DataOne anuncia como capacidad máxima del campus (el 41 % de los 300 de los planes aprobados).
La solución definitoria pasa por pilas de combustible de Bloom Energy, pero la ciudad de Vineland ya paralizó dos trabajos: un depósito de gas natural licuado de 1,5 millones de galones, para el que la empresa pide aprobación, y unidades de esas pilas, ambos iniciados sin permiso de construcción.
La gobernadora, Mikie Sherrill, ha dicho que estos centros deben invertir en la red eléctrica e informar de su consumo de agua y energía, además de aportar beneficios a las comunidades. La pregunta es si los permisos llegarán antes que las primeras mediciones de lo que se ha respirado.
Imágenes | NJ.com

articles.title: CashAfrica brings mobile tap-to-pay to Chicken Republic outlets
articles.text: CashAfrica, a Nigerian contactless payment infrastructure provider, has partnered with Food Concepts, the quick-service restaurant company that owns Chicken Republic, PieXpress, and The Chop Box, to bring mobile tap-to-pay to Chicken Republic outlets across Nigeria. The partnership will let customers pay for their meals by tapping their smartphones on supported payment terminals. According to CashAfrica, the rollout will be phased, starting in Lagos before expanding to Abuja and other locations. Chicken Republic has more than 350 outlets across Nigeria and recorded ₦60.9 billion ($45.7 million) in sales in 2023. The scale of its operations gives CashAfrica a potential route to increase the adoption of tap-to-pay payments in Nigeria. “This is a strategic partnership to take Mobile Tap-to-Pay mainstream, while delivering the best-in-class payment experience,” Malik Asamu, CashAfrica’s chief executive officer, said in a statement. “Previously, Nigerian users and merchants could collect transfers, cards, QR code, and cash options. This strategic partnership delivers a whole new layer of payment possibilities, created the Pan-African way.” The deal follows CashAfrica’s partnership with ChamsSwitch , a licenced switching and electronic payment processing company, in May to address regulatory compliance and transaction-routing requirements that had slowed the adoption of its contactless payment infrastructure. It also builds on an earlier integration with PalmPay , which began rolling out contactless payment functionality on its point-of-sale (POS) terminals in February 2025, starting with a 1,000-device pilot. Founded in 2024 by Asamu and Bello Opeyemi, CashAfrica provides payment infrastructure that allows banks and fintechs to integrate contactless transactions into their existing services. Its CashTap technology uses near-field communication (NFC), a short-range wireless technology that allows compatible devices to exchange information when brought close together. CashAfrica’s mobile tap-to-pay product allows customers to initiate payments with their phones through participating banking and fintech apps. A customer opens a supported app, selects the tap-to-pay option, authenticates the transaction where required, and taps the phone against a compatible POS terminal. Depending on the device, payment authentication can involve features such as Face ID or fingerprint recognition, according to CashAfrica. Under the partnership with Food Concepts, users interact with PalmPay’s POS terminals for the payment, while CashAfrica supplies the technology that enables the contactless transaction. ChamsSwitch, meanwhile, supports the settlement side of the transaction. Asamu told TechCabal in an interview that the company acts as a regulatory and infrastructure partner, helping facilitate funds movement between the fintechs and operators involved in the payment. “ChamsSwitch is a regulatory partner that allows us to do a lot of cross settlements,” he said. “If Chicken Republic is collecting tap-to-pay, a lot of that money needs to be moving in the background, such as T+1 settlements and end-of-day settlements. ChamsSwitch is heavily involved in that.” CashAfrica said it will introduce the service gradually before making mobile tap-to-pay available across all 350-plus Chicken Republic outlets. The company also plans to work with more banks and fintechs to expand the number of customers who can use the feature through their existing apps. “Customer experience has always been at the heart of Chicken Republic, and we continuously look for ways to make every meal faster, easier and more convenient,” Solomon Ojelade, head of finance at Chicken Republic, said in the statement. “Our partnership with CashAfrica brings that commitment into the payment experience, giving our customers access to a fast and seamless Mobile Tap to Pay option across our outlets.” At Chicken Republic, customers will not pay a separate fee to use mobile tap-to-pay, Asamu told TechCabal. Instead, the merchant pays CashAfrica for transactions processed through its infrastructure. The company said it charges a percentage of each transaction, typically between 0.1% and 1.5%, depending on the arrangement. CashAfrica is looking to capitalise on Nigeria’s growing use of electronic payments. In 2024, electronic transactions processed through the Nigeria Inter-Bank Settlement System’s instant payment system surpassed ₦1 quadrillion ($803 billion). The company intends to turn that growth into the adoption of a newer payment method. Asamu said the company has signed other partnerships with businesses where customers regularly make in-person payments, including quick-service restaurants and supermarkets, and will announce them in the coming months. “The change in the average Nigerian customer consumption pattern in financial technology has allowed us to see wind in the sails of contactless payments,” he said. “We make the bet and continue to bet on contactless payments.” True scale demands moving beyond surface-level integrations to robust execution. articles.title: Ivanti Zero-Day Chain Gave Attackers Root Access to Fully Patched VPN
articles.text:
Ivanti on Tuesday warned customers that a zero-day vulnerability in its Connect Secure (ICS) VPN appliances has been exploited in the wild.
Tracked as CVE-2026-104935 and rated high severity, the issue is an authentication bypass that lets a remote, unauthenticated attacker execute arbitrary commands. Ivanti says it’s aware of exploitation affecting a limited number of customers.
Volexity discovered the in-the-wild exploitation while investigating an incident at one of its customers. A previously undocumented threat actor it tracks as UTA0576 had chained three zero-days to gain unauthenticated, root-level code execution on a fully patched ICS appliance.
According to Volexity, CVE-2026-104935 covers two of the flaws: an authentication bypass and a remote code execution bug. Ivanti has patched these vulnerabilities with the release of ICS versions 22.8R2.5, 25.1.1.2, 25.1.3.0, and 25.1.3.1.
The third vulnerability, a privilege escalation issue, remains unpatched, and the vendor plans to fix it over the coming weeks.
Volexity, which found evidence of exploitation starting on October 3, says UTA0576 focused primarily on credential theft, data exfiltration, network reconnaissance, and log tampering.
The attackers stole domain credentials stored on the appliance and exfiltrated limited Active Directory metadata. Using a custom tool, they searched Active Directory for LAPS passwords and BitLocker recovery keys.
They also ran password-spraying attacks, tested credentials with a custom Kerberos tool, and tried to extract credentials from captured network traffic. They also scanned the network, collected the appliance’s configuration data, and parsed authentication logs to identify valid usernames. Volexity found no backdoor or web shell on the device.
The operation was detected and disrupted before the attackers’ ultimate goals became clear. Volexity believes with high confidence that their actions pointed to preparation for lateral movement and a wider compromise of the network.
“Volexity assesses with low confidence that UTA0576 has criminal, rather than espionage, motivations based on the target of this activity,” the company says.
“As with many other threat actor operations Volexity has investigated in 2026, Volexity assesses with medium confidence that UTA0576 makes use of large language models (LLMs) for exploit development and post-exploitation activity,” it added.
