articles.title: Galaxy S27 Ultra : Samsung améliorerait l’écran qui protège votre vie privée, mais à quel prix ?
articles.text:
Le Privacy Display est l’une des principales curiosités du Galaxy S26 Ultra et notre 01lab s’était penché sur ce filtre de confidentialité qui modifie la diffusion lumineuse. En l’activant, le smartphone cherche à rendre illisible le contenu pour les regards indiscrets et ça marche, même si cela ne vient pas sans sacrifices. Loin d’abandonner son idée, Samsung plancherait sur la deuxième version de cet écran anti-regards.
Selon le leaker Sawyer Galox sur X, Samsung travaillerait sur un « Privacy Display v2 » pour le Galaxy S27 Ultra avec trois améliorations notables : de meilleurs angles de vision, une meilleure résolution quand la protection est activée, et une qualité et une clarté d’écran accrues. Samsung n’a, pour l’heure, rien confirmé alors que son nouveau modèle arriverait début 2027.
 Samsung is working on improving
Galaxy S27 Ultra Privacy Display v.2
Improved viewing angles
Better resolution when Privacy Display is enabled
Improved screen quality and clarity
Well, there are good hardware upgrades next year, so the price will be between $1,400-$1,500 https://t.co/vSa9LAcpl1
— Sawyer Galox (@Sawyergalox) October 10, 2026
Une estimation de prix, pas un tarif
Sur le S26 Ultra, Samsung a modifié certains pixels pour qu’ils n’émettent que vers l’avant, et la protection éteint les autres. Le prix à payer, selon nos mesures, est que la moitié des pixels sont retirés, ce qui donne une lecture moins confortable sur les textes et les motifs fins, ainsi qu’un écran moins lumineux. La deuxième et la troisième promesse du leaker répondent au premier de ces compromis, pas au second : il ne dit rien de la luminosité ni de la façon dont Samsung compte s’y prendre.
Le premier point est plus flou et Sawyer Galox parle d’« angles de vision » sans préciser s’il s’agit d’élargir la zone où le propriétaire voit bien l’écran, ou de mieux masquer l’image aux voisins.
Le Privacy Display pourrait aussi sortir de l’Ultra puisque d’autres fuites évoquent son arrivée sur un Galaxy S27 Pro, absent de la gamme actuelle. Ice Universe affirme de son côté que le S27 Ultra pourrait ne masquer qu’une seule application en écran partagé, comme le propose déjà le Xiaomi 18 Pro.
Une estimation de son prix qui inquiète
Sawyer Galox s’avance aussi sur le prix et écrit que, vu les « bonnes améliorations matérielles » de l’an prochain, le tarif sera compris entre 1 400 et 1 500 dollars aux États-Unis. Une déduction plus qu’une fuite qui s’inscrirait dans la hausse des prix des smartphones. Depuis le 1er octobre, le S26 Ultra de 256 Go est vendu 1 399,99 dollars outre-Atlantique, contre 1 299,99 dollars à son lancement, en raison du prix de la mémoire. Le bas de la fourchette correspond donc au tarif actuel, et le haut à 100 dollars de plus.
En France, ce même modèle est passé de 1 469 à 1 569 euros début octobre, comme nous l’avons détaillé plus tôt ce mois-ci. Rappelons au passage que les prix américains s’entendent hors taxes et qu’il ne faut pas les convertir tels quels.
Samsung présenterait ses Galaxy S27 vers février 2027, avec One UI 9.5 basée sur Android 17.

articles.title: La vérité sur les VPN : Ce qu'ils font vraiment, et ce qu'ils ne feront jamais
articles.text:
La vérité sur les VPN : Ce qu'ils font vraiment, et ce qu'ils ne feront jamais
Omniprésents dans nos publicités, les VPN (Virtual Private Networks) sont devenus la promesse d'une navigation sécurisée et sans entraves. On nous les vend comme la solution miracle pour l'anonymat, la sécurité absolue et un accès illimité à Internet. Mais que se cache-t-il vraiment derrière ces promesses marketing ? Entre les mythes tenaces et la réalité technique, il est facile de s'y perdre. Ce dossier lève le voile sur le fonctionnement réel des VPN : nous allons démêler le vrai du faux, expliquer ce qu'ils peuvent concrètement faire pour votre vie privée, et surtout, ce qu'ils ne feront jamais.
De YouTube aux podcasts, il est impossible d'échapper à la publicité pour les VPN (Virtual Private Networks). Leurs promesses sont immenses : anonymat total, sécurité infaillible, Internet sans limites... Mais dans ce marché saturé de discours marketing agressifs, il est devenu difficile de séparer la promesse technique de l'argument commercial. Un VPN est un outil puissant, mais ce n'est pas la cape d'invisibilité numérique que l'on nous vend. Il est temps de rétablir la vérité sur ce qu'un VPN fait réellement, comment il fonctionne, et ce qu'il ne pourra jamais faire pour vous.
Notre sélection des meilleurs VPN du moment :
Comment ça marche, un VPN ? (En clair)
Pour le grand public, un VPN est souvent une "boîte noire" : on appuie sur "Connecter" et la magie opère. En réalité, le processus est technique, mais très logique.
Imaginez que vous envoyez une lettre importante. Sans VPN, vous l'écrivez sur une carte postale. Tout le monde peut la lire en chemin : votre facteur, qui est votre Fournisseur d'Accès à Internet (FAI), le centre de tri, et toute personne qui intercepterait votre courrier.
Un VPN transforme cette carte postale en un colis blindé et sécurisé, en quatre étapes clés.
Premièrement, l'authentification et le "Tunnel". Quand vous lancez votre application VPN, votre appareil contacte un serveur VPN distant, par exemple à New York. Ils négocient alors une connexion sécurisée et créent ce qu'on appelle un "tunnel chiffré". C'est le cœur du VPN. Tout ce qui passera par ce tunnel devient illisible pour quiconque se trouve à l'extérieur. La qualité de ce tunnel dépend du "protocole" utilisé, les plus modernes comme WireGuard étant réputés pour leur vitesse et leur sécurité.
Deuxièmement, le chiffrement. Dès que le tunnel est actif, tout votre trafic Internet est chiffré avant même de quitter votre appareil. Si vous tapez "https://www.google.com/search?q=google.com", votre FAI ne voit plus cette demande. Il constate simplement un flux de données illisible, du charabia, à destination d'une seule adresse : celle du serveur VPN. Votre FAI sait donc que vous êtes connecté à un VPN, mais il ne sait absolument pas ce que vous faites.
Troisièmement, le masquage d'IP. Une fois vos données chiffrées arrivées au serveur VPN à New York, celui-ci déchiffre votre demande. Il voit que vous voulez aller sur "https://www.google.com/search?q=google.com" et envoie cette demande à Google, mais en utilisant sa propre adresse IP. Pour Google, la visite ne vient pas de votre box à Lyon, mais d'un serveur à New York. Votre adresse IP personnelle, votre "adresse postale" sur Internet, est masquée et remplacée.
Enfin, le voyage retour suit le même chemin. Google répond au serveur VPN (croyant que c'est vous), le serveur VPN chiffre cette réponse, et vous la renvoie via le tunnel sécurisé. Votre appareil déchiffre le tout, et la page s'affiche.
En résumé, un VPN agit comme un intermédiaire de confiance qui chiffre votre trafic pour le cacher de votre FAI et des pirates, et qui masque votre IP pour cacher votre localisation aux sites que vous visitez.
Fact-Checking : Les 5 grands mythes du VPN
Maintenant que le mécanisme est clair, attaquons-nous aux idées reçues les plus tenaces, souvent entretenues par le marketing des fournisseurs eux-mêmes.
Mythe 1 : "Un VPN me rend 100% anonyme."
C'est le mythe le plus répandu, et le plus faux. Un VPN ne fait que déplacer la confiance. Votre FAI ne voit plus ce que vous faites, mais votre fournisseur VPN, lui, peut le voir. Vous troquez la surveillance potentielle de votre FAI contre la promesse de non-surveillance de votre VPN.
C'est pourquoi le choix du VPN est crucial, notamment sa politique de "no-logs" (non-conservation des journaux de connexion). Plus important encore, il faut distinguer la confidentialité de l'anonymat. Un VPN protège votre confidentialité vis-à-vis de tiers, mais il ne vous rend pas anonyme. Si vous utilisez un VPN pour vous connecter à votre compte Google, Facebook ou Amazon, ces services savent parfaitement que c'est vous. Votre identité est trahie par vos cookies, votre "empreinte" de navigateur (fingerprinting), et le simple fait que vous vous soyez identifié.
Mythe 2 : "Je n'ai rien à cacher, je n'ai pas besoin de VPN."
C'est une confusion classique entre "vie privée" et "activités secrètes". Ce n'est pas parce que vous n'avez "rien à cacher" que vous laisseriez la porte de votre chambre ou de votre salle de bain ouverte. Il s'agit de protéger son espace privé.
Le cas d'usage le plus important et le plus légitime du VPN est la sécurité sur les réseaux Wi-Fi publics. Dans un aéroport, un hôtel ou un café, n'importe qui sur le même réseau peut intercepter vos communications en clair. Le VPN, en chiffrant tout ce qui sort de votre appareil, rend cette interception impossible. C'est l'équivalent numérique de ne pas crier son numéro de carte de crédit au milieu d'une foule.
De plus, un VPN empêche votre FAI de collecter et d'analyser l'intégralité de votre historique de navigation, une pratique qui, selon la législation, peut être utilisée à des fins de profilage publicitaire.
Mythe 3 : "Les VPN gratuits sont suffisants."
C'est une idée dangereuse. Sur Internet, il existe une règle d'or : "Si c'est gratuit, c'est vous le produit." Maintenir une infrastructure de serveurs VPN à travers le monde coûte extrêmement cher en bande passante et en matériel. Si le service est gratuit, l'entreprise doit se financer autrement.
Le scénario le plus probable est qu'elle enregistre votre historique de navigation et vend vos données à des courtiers en données ou des publicitaires, ce qui annule totalement l'intérêt premier du VPN. D'autres injectent de la publicité, utilisent des protocoles de sécurité obsolètes, ou limitent si drastiquement le débit qu'ils vous forcent à passer à une offre payante. Utiliser un VPN gratuit est souvent pire pour votre vie privée que de ne pas en utiliser du tout.
Mythe 4 : "Un VPN, c'est que pour le streaming et le piratage."
C'est une vision très réductrice, bien que ce soit un usage populaire. Oui, les VPN sont massivement utilisés pour le contournement du géo-blocage : accéder au catalogue Netflix américain depuis la France, ou regarder la télévision française lors d'un voyage à l'étranger.
Mais les usages légitimes et sérieux sont bien plus nombreux. Le premier usage historique du VPN est le télétravail, permettant aux employés de se connecter de manière sécurisée au réseau interne de leur entreprise. C'est aussi un outil vital pour contourner la censure dans les pays où l'accès à l'information est contrôlé, permettant aux journalistes et aux citoyens d'accéder à des sites bloqués. Enfin, il peut servir à éviter la discrimination par les prix sur certains sites d'e-commerce, comme les billets d'avion, qui adaptent parfois leurs tarifs en fonction de votre localisation IP.
Mythe 5 : "Mon VPN va forcément tuer ma vitesse de connexion."
Cette affirmation était vraie il y a dix ans, mais elle est beaucoup moins pertinente aujourd'hui. Il y aura toujours une perte de vitesse, c'est physiquement inévitable : le processus de chiffrement demande des ressources, et faire transiter votre trafic par un serveur à l'autre bout du monde (le "détour") ajoute de la latence.
Cependant, les protocoles modernes, en particulier WireGuard, sont désormais si rapides que l'impact sur la navigation ou le streaming est souvent imperceptible. Les fournisseurs payants investissent massivement dans des serveurs haute performance (souvent 10 Gbit/s) pour minimiser ce ralentissement. Paradoxalement, un VPN peut même améliorer votre débit dans un cas précis : si votre FAI bride (ralentit) volontairement votre connexion vers certains services (streaming, jeux, P2P). Le VPN, en masquant la nature de votre trafic, empêche le FAI d'appliquer ce bridage sélectif.
L'outil de la confidentialité, pas de l'invisibilité
En définitive, un VPN est un excellent outil, mais il doit être utilisé pour les bonnes raisons. Il n'est pas une cape d'invisibilité. C'est une ceinture de sécurité pour votre vie numérique. Elle vous protège en cas d'accident (une attaque sur un Wi-Fi public) et vous offre un confort indispensable (confidentialité vis-à-vis de votre FAI). Mais tout comme une ceinture de sécurité, elle ne vous empêche pas d'être suivi par une autre voiture (cookies et traceurs) ou de décliner votre identité au péage (vous connecter à vos comptes). C'est un outil de confidentialité et de sécurité, pas d'anonymat.

articles.title: AI can act exactly like a human, but we still don't think it's conscious
articles.text:
AI can act exactly like a human, but we still don't think it's conscious
- Date:
- October 13, 2026
- Source:
- Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München
- Summary:
- A new study reveals that people draw a surprisingly sharp line between human consciousness and artificial intelligence, even when both behave identically. Researchers found that participants considered even the most responsive AI less conscious than the least responsive human. Yet when asked about "awareness" instead, people judged humans and AI much more similarly.
- Share:
Even when artificial intelligence behaves exactly like a human, people are reluctant to consider it conscious, according to a new study from Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich (LMU).
As artificial intelligence becomes more advanced, reports of AI systems misleading users, working together, or appearing to pursue independent goals are becoming increasingly common. These behaviors often lead people to describe AI as though it can think, feel, or make decisions for itself. But does behaving like a human actually convince people that a machine has consciousness?
New research from LMU suggests that people make a clear distinction between displaying intelligent behavior and possessing a conscious mind, even when humans and AI act in precisely the same way.
How Scientists Tested Perceptions of AI Consciousness
Published in the journal Cognition, the study was led by Dr. Louis Longin of LMU's Chair of Philosophy of Mind, working alongside Dr. Bahador Bahrami, Professor Ophelia Deroy, and other researchers.
"Whereas previous studies have typically asked general questions about whether AI actually has mental states, our study is the first to directly compare how people attribute the same mental states to AI and humans behaving in exactly the same way, under identical circumstances," says Longin.
"We may be using mental terms to refer to AI, but this may only be because we lack better words," says Ophelia Deroy, philosopher and a senior author of the study. "After all, AI is trained to act and speak like a human, so these descriptions seem natural."
To investigate how people judge consciousness, the researchers conducted experiments involving nearly 1,100 participants. One group read brief descriptions of artificial agents that showed different levels of responsiveness to their environments. For example, some agents reacted to sounds or recognized the emotional states of others.
Another group encountered the same situations, except the characters were described as humans rather than AI systems. Participants then evaluated how conscious or aware each character seemed to be of its surroundings.
A Surprising Gap Between Human and AI Consciousness
The experiments revealed that responsiveness influenced how participants judged both humans and artificial intelligence. Characters that reacted more actively to their surroundings were generally considered more conscious and more aware.
However, a striking difference emerged when participants evaluated consciousness specifically. Even the most responsive AI was rated as less conscious than the least responsive human. In other words, identical behavior did not lead people to assign the same level of consciousness to humans and machines.
The results changed considerably when participants were asked about awareness instead. For this characteristic, judgments of humans and AI followed largely similar patterns, suggesting that people interpret awareness and consciousness in fundamentally different ways.
"There is a growing worry in public discussion that people will see AI behaving in a human-like way and start treating these systems as if they had human-like mental states," says Longin, lead author of the study. "We found something much more nuanced: People are quite willing to say that an AI notices things and is aware of its surroundings. But they clearly draw a line when it comes to the term 'consciousness'. People consistently attribute less consciousness to AI than humans -- even when their behavior is identical."
Although people sometimes describe AI as conscious when discussing its actions, the findings indicate that they still distinguish between artificial systems and human minds.
Why One Word Changes How We Perceive AI
The researchers believe the difference between consciousness and awareness offers an important insight into how people understand artificial intelligence.
Awareness is a relatively neutral term that can describe an agent's ability to detect and respond to information in its environment. Consciousness, however, carries deeper implications about subjective experience and what it means to have an inner mental life.
Because awareness focuses more directly on observable behavior, people appear comfortable applying it to both humans and AI. Consciousness carries a different meaning, leading people to judge the two much less similarly.
The findings also highlight why the language used to discuss artificial intelligence matters, particularly as AI systems become increasingly capable of producing convincing human behavior.
"Our study teaches us lessons for how we communicate about AI," says Bahador Bahrami, who is also a senior author of the study and an expert in social neuroscience. "Companies and journalists often reach for hyped descriptions of AI models, and credit them with intentions, plans, or even moral conscience and hesitation. What our study shows is that everyday judgments are much more discriminating: People do not simply put AI and humans on the same mental scale. But the boundary also depends on which terms we use. For more neutral descriptors such as 'awareness', the distinction can largely disappear. That makes our choice of language important."
Story Source:
Materials provided by Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Louis Longin, Jurgis Karpus, Nadine Meertens, Bahador Bahrami, Ophelia Deroy. AI is not as conscious as humans: Essentialism in mental state attributions to artificial systems. Cognition, 2027; 278: 106733 DOI: 10.1016/j.cognition.2026.106733

articles.title: Apple TV 4K con Siri AI: fecha de lanzamiento y sus características
articles.text:
Apple presentó una nueva generación del Apple TV 4K, su dispositivo para ver contenido en streaming y controlar accesorios del hogar inteligente. La principal novedad es Siri AI, una versión más conversacional del asistente que permite buscar películas y series, hacer preguntas sobre lo que se está viendo y manejar dispositivos compatibles mediante la voz.
Las reservas comenzaron el martes 13 de octubre en la tienda en línea y la aplicación Apple Store. El dispositivo llegará a las tiendas y empezará a entregarse el viernes 13 de noviembre, según el anuncio oficial de Apple. La compañía fijó su precio en 299 dólares en Estados Unidos.
Siri AI permite buscar contenido y hacer preguntas
Siri AI aparece en una interfaz a pantalla completa y permite buscar contenido con preguntas conversacionales. Por ejemplo, el usuario puede pedir recomendaciones de comedias premiadas y recibir sugerencias con imágenes tomadas directamente de la aplicación Apple TV.
El asistente también responderá preguntas mientras se reproduce una película o una serie. Se le podrá consultar dónde se filmó una escena o si un programa es adecuado para una persona de determinada edad. Las respuestas aparecerán en una ventana compacta para no cubrir toda la pantalla ni detener la reproducción.
Apple señala que Siri AI puede aprovechar el contexto personal de un iPhone compatible con Apple Intelligence. De ese modo, el usuario podrá pedirle que reproduzca una serie recomendada por uno de sus contactos. La disponibilidad inicial de Siri AI estará limitada a ciertos países e idiomas; Apple anunció que llegará en inglés a Estados Unidos, Australia, Canadá, India, Nueva Zelanda, Singapur, Sudáfrica y Reino Unido.
Chip A19 y control por voz sin el mando
El nuevo Apple TV 4K utiliza el chip A19. Según Apple, ofrece hasta un 50 % más de rendimiento de CPU y el doble de rendimiento gráfico frente a la generación anterior. El procesador también incluye un decodificador AV1, tecnología que permite reproducir contenido en streaming con mayor eficiencia y un menor consumo de ancho de banda.
El equipo incorpora tres micrófonos de campo lejano para controlar la reproducción y buscar contenido sin tener que sostener el Siri Remote. Apple indica que la cancelación de eco ayuda a que el dispositivo reconozca la voz incluso cuando el televisor está reproduciendo audio.
El Siri Remote conserva su diseño, pero ahora es compatible con la red Buscar de Apple. Desde un iPhone se podrá localizar el mando con indicaciones de precisión o activar un sonido para encontrarlo.
Sonido envolvente con cuatro HomePod
Por primera vez, el Apple TV 4K podrá utilizarse con cuatro altavoces HomePod para crear un sistema de sonido envolvente. La configuración es compatible con cuatro HomePod mini 2 o cuatro HomePod de segunda generación. También se pueden combinar ambos modelos, siempre que los altavoces delanteros sean iguales entre sí y los traseros también formen un par del mismo modelo.
El sistema detecta la ubicación de los altavoces y ajusta los niveles y tiempos del audio según la distribución de la sala. Apple lo presenta como su experiencia de sonido envolvente más inmersiva hasta la fecha.
Funciones para el hogar
El dispositivo mantiene su función de centro del hogar inteligente: permite controlar accesorios y automatizaciones, y recibir en el televisor notificaciones de timbres compatibles. Con Apple Intelligence, la aplicación Hogar sumará descripciones de la actividad detectada por cámaras y resúmenes de notificaciones.

articles.title: Forget rockets — Longshot wants to fire cargo into space from a gun. See it at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Rockets are, infamously, a real pain in the butt. Our old friend physics forces rockets to be built with almost no room for error, and even then only a small fraction of their weight makes it to orbit.
There are, at least in theory, other ways to do the job — space elevators, centrifuges, or a big chain hanging from a satellite in space and scooping up cargo from Earth. (Blue Origin spent some time thinking about that one before the idea wound up in a Neal Stephenson novel.)
And then there’s an idea dating all the way back to Jules Verne: Use a big gun to shoot a projectile into space.
Longshot Space Technology, a startup based in Alameda, California, is working on exactly that. The co-founders, CEO Mike Grace and CTO Nato Saichek, see an opportunity to take a technology that has already proven its worth and apply it to the pressing need for space launch. The startup has raised about $20 million from venture investors in service of its mission.
When it comes to frontier technology, Grace says, “you can build something that has a lot of novelty, or you can do something really hard. You don’t get to do both.” He points to SpaceX as an example of a company that has “taken classically de-risked technology and scaled it aggressively.” What SpaceX did with NASA rocket research, he says, Longshot will do with multi-injection guns — designs that give a projectile extra boosts as it moves down the barrel — built for World War II and during 1960s research programs.
The idea is to take all the work done by the first stage of a launch vehicle and collapse that into a reusable accelerator on the ground. Picture a steel pipe mounted horizontally over the ground, with tanks of high-pressure gas attached at ports spread across its length. When a projectile is fired and moves down the barrel, the tanks fire off at precise times to accelerate it — to speeds as high as Mach 4, thus far.
The company is currently firing a 70-foot gun with a six-inch diameter at its test site near Barstow, California, and says it can accelerate projectiles up to near-hypersonic speeds. Soon, it expects to start firing a 140-foot-long gun with a 30-inch diameter at its Alameda test site. After that, the company is preparing to build out a 30-inch diameter gun that is 328-feet long, with plans to extend it to about 3,000 feet — making it the largest gun on the planet. It will be capable of launching 220-pound payloads up to speeds of Mach 8, the team says.
These guns will let Longshot keep proving its technology works while also generating revenue from performing hypersonic testing for the U.S. military, which has awarded the company several contracts. Grace envisions building one of his guns on a U.S. military installation like Fort Bliss, where it could be part of the infrastructure for testing the next generation of U.S. interceptors. (And no, the guns don’t need to point up at an angle. Longshot’s projectile is a lifting body, meaning its shape generates lift, so it will aerodynamically gain altitude once it exits the barrel.)
“If you want to practice shooting down a Chinese or Russian hypersonic missile, wouldn’t it be nice not to pay $30 million for that?” Grace asks. “This is a way for half a million, a quarter of a million bucks, of doing hypersonic clay pigeons, throw them and shoot them down, and do it really fast and really cheap.”
The ultimate goal, however, is putting large payloads into space. The team is confident it can scale up its current design to accelerate payloads to as much as five kilometers per second (more than 11,000 mph). That’s fast enough to get into space if the payload, which effectively serves as the second stage of a rocket, has its own propulsion system. But doing that would require a gun 10 kilometers (about six miles) long and nearly 10 feet in diameter. As you might imagine, one problem the company faces is simply finding suitable worksites.
“The hard part is not building the thing, it’s finding a place where they will let you build the thing,” Saichek jokes.
But if Longshot can realize its vision, the math is very attractive: The system is cheap to construct and to fuel, and is highly reusable. Grace expects that if everything works out, they can send payloads to space for a hard-to-believe $50 per kilogram (about $22 per pound). Considering that the much-hyped orbital data center industry needs prices to fall to around $300 per kilogram to get off the ground, that leaves Longshot plenty of room to offer a competitive price.
It will require some modification to launch spacecraft in this form factor and conditions, but at that price point, satellite operators will be willing to try.
If you want to learn more about Longshot from the company itself — while also checking out dozens of startups, hearing their pitches, and listening to guest speakers on four different stages — join us this week at Disrupt, Tuesday to Thursday, in San Francisco. Learn more here.

articles.title: Dominion Dynamics strikes deal to build Ukrainian uncrewed ground vehicles in Canada | BetaKit
articles.text:
Dominion Dynamics has struck a partnership that will send uncrewed ground vehicles from Canada to Ukraine’s front lines.
The news: The Ottawa-based defence contractor signed a memorandum of understanding with Ukrainian defence tech firm Tencore at the Association of the United States Army defence conference in Washington, DC, on Tuesday afternoon. The agreement will see Dominion Dynamics manufacture Tencore’s TerMIT uncrewed ground vehicle in Canada and integrate its AuraNet command-and-control platform to Ukraine’s front lines.
The TerMIT is a modular light armour vehicle that can be modified for logistics, evacuation, or weaponry, and operate without a human on board. Tencore claims it has delivered more than 5,000 uncrewed ground vehicles to Ukrainian military units since 2024.
From the source: “Battlefield requirements change in weeks, so production, operational feedback, and engineering have to run as a loop: build, deploy, learn, change, scale,” Tencore co-founder Roman Tkachenko said in a statement. “Canada gives us the manufacturing base, suppliers and reliable power to run that loop alongside allies who need these vehicles.”
The context: Since launching in June 2025, Dominion Dynamics has raised $169 million CAD to become an explicitly Canadian competitor to big-name defence contractors like Lockheed Martin. Earlier this year, it raised a $139-million CAD Series A round and moved into a 25,000-square-foot manufacturing facility in Ottawa’s west end.
The Tencore agreement comes after Prime Minister Mark Carney and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy struck a 100-year partnership and drone collaboration agreement last month. As part of the partnership, Carney committed Canada to producing millions of drones within the next two years, with one third of those earmarked for Ukraine’s defence against Russia.
Hamilton-based drone company Sentinel R&D has inked similar deals with the Ukrainians and faced threats from Russian officials as a result. Dominion Dynamics CEO Eliot Pence told BetaKit in an email that his company isn’t concerned about potential threats, and that it “will never be afraid of defending democracy and western values.”
Final thought: While the companies are still ironing out a definitive agreement, Dominion Dynamics said initial TerMIT production is planned for 2027, following Tencore transferring its technology and training technicians in Canada. Dominion also said it is aiming to develop an “Arctic-hardened” version of the TerMIT for Canadian operations and to export to NATO allies.
Feature image courtesy Dominion Dynamics via X.

articles.title: Xbox is officially embracing the chaos of AI-powered game ports
articles.text:
Retro gaming is going through a wild time at the moment, thanks to decompilations and recompilations that are letting gamers port classic titles to new devices, or merge code from two different games into a single new experience. Microsoft has witnessed skateboarding being modded into Call of Duty and Halo being played in a web browser, and the company is now officially embracing the chaos of this new AI-powered era of game modding.
Xbox is officially embracing the chaos of AI-powered game ports
Microsoft has created a new Xbox Labs group to experiment with decompiling and recompiling games.
Microsoft is putting together a new Xbox Labs group to explore the rapid emergence of these mods, many of which use AI models to help modders remix games in ways we’ve rarely seen before. Xbox Labs will be a “small group of game makers, engineers and scientists whose job is to turn emerging ideas into things our players and developers can experience,” says Xbox CEO Asha Sharma. “We’ll build in the open, learn from what people do, and measure success by whether more people are playing and creating.”
Sharma thinks the experiments we’ve seen in recent weeks, where Windows PC builds have been translated to run on Apple Silicon or ported to run inside browsers, “challenge long-held assumptions about our industry: the tether between software and hardware, the boundary between creation and play, and how people discover and experience games.”
“While it is hard to predict the future of gaming, it is easy to see the possibilities in making great games easier to access, giving old games new life and allowing more players to become creators and co-creators,” says Sharma. “These are unmistakably good outcomes for players, even when (and sometimes because) they challenge our existing business models.“
Modders are now doing the type of work that Microsoft has been doing for decades with its Xbox backward compatibility program, letting old games run on modern hardware. But they’re doing it without the business model restrictions that Microsoft is tied to. It’s starting to feel like we’re just a model or two away from even more breakthroughs that decouple more modern games from their intended hardware.
Sharma clearly sees an opportunity here, particularly for AI agent use at Xbox. “I think Xbox has an important role to play here,” says Sharma. “Coding became the first major workload for agents because they can write, run, and test software. Games share many of those same properties, and people spend more than 72 billion hours a year playing XBOX games, roughly five times the estimated time spent writing code worldwide.”
Xbox Labs is clearly a way for Microsoft to experiment with how AI will shape where games are played, and Xbox will share any tools and learnings with developers. The bigger question is how Microsoft will respond to decompiles and recompiles of games where modders take its precious IP and make it freely available. Modding is fun, but I can’t see Microsoft and other publishers seeing the fun side if modern console games start to appear where they shouldn’t.
I asked Microsoft to comment about unauthorized IP use, but the company didn’t respond in time for publication.
Here’s Sharma’s full memo:
Team,
The first video games emerged some 75 years ago. In the time since, there have been booms and busts, but every year there are more great games to play, more devices to play them, and best of all, more people than ever playing. That growth helped make XBOX what it is today, and we’ve helped shape the industry in return, from bringing hard drives to consoles and online gaming through Xbox Live to Game Pass and cloud gaming, alongside franchises that have brought millions of people together.
In recent weeks, we’ve seen games rapidly decompiled and rebuilt to run on hardware they were never originally designed to support. Windows PC builds have been translated to run on Apple Silicon or ported to run inside a browser through WebAssembly and WebGPU, the latter now approaching 90% global browser support. Perhaps more surprisingly, we’ve seen many of the biggest games in the world have been remixed into the source code of another.
These experiments challenge long-held assumptions about our industry: the tether between software and hardware, the boundary between creation and play, and how people discover and experience games. While it is hard to predict the future of gaming, it is easy to see the possibilities in making great games easier to access, giving old games new life and allowing more players to become creators and co-creators. These are unmistakably good outcomes for players, even when (and sometimes because) they challenge our existing business models. To explore these possibilities, I’ve asked Scott to stand-up XBOX LABS, a small group of game makers, engineers and scientists whose job is to turn emerging ideas into things our players and developers can experience. We’ll build in the open, learn from what people do, and measure success by whether more people are playing and creating.
I think XBOX has an important role to play here. Coding became the first major workload for agents because they can write, run, and test software. Games share many of those same properties, and people spend more than 72 billion hours a year playing XBOX games, roughly five times the estimated time spent writing code worldwide. We’ve spent 25 years learning how to make great games, and I want our game makers to help shape what these new technologies make possible. As we learn, we’ll share the tools we build with developers across the industry, just as we always have.
Our priorities aren’t changing. We remain committed to the 4Cs, to making great games, to our hardware and to being responsible stewards of IP and the communities built around it. LABS gives us a way to explore new technology without abandoning the work already underway.
Asha

articles.title: Nintendo stands by physical games as Sony embraces a digital-only future — 'There's no plans to ditch physical. We know how much the fans like it as well, so our position has been to be agnostic,' says a Nintendo exec
articles.text:
Nintendo stands by physical games as Sony embraces a digital-only future — 'There's no plans to ditch physical. We know how much the fans like it as well, so our position has been to be agnostic,' says a Nintendo exec
While Sony remains committed to phasing out physical media, Nintendo is taking the opposite approach. In a recent interview with the Brazilian YouTube channel Coelho no Japão, Bill van Zyll, Nintendo's VP and General Manager for Latin America, confirmed that the company has no plans to abandon cartridges.
"Historically, we’ve been very agnostic, right?" stated van Zyll in the interview.
The Nintendo executive firmly continued, "We go off what the consumer prefers, and take that into account very heavily. We also have a platform that was just launched. We're barely just over a year into NS2. It's got both digital and physical – that capability. There's no plans to ditch physical. We know how much the fans like it as well, so our position has been to be agnostic."
In an era where the gaming industry is rapidly shifting toward digital distribution, it is comforting to see at least some companies still supporting physical media. The core issue with digital purchases is that you do not truly own what you buy; instead, you are purchasing a license to access the game, unlike owning a cartridge or game disc. Some storefronts, such as GOG or itch.io, offer DRM-free downloads of the titles you purchase, but only a handful of them exist.
However, even cartridges cannot completely escape the march toward digitalization. With the release of the Nintendo Switch 2, Nintendo introduced game-key cards, physical cards that contain a license to download the full game data. Modern AAA game releases have exceeded the storage capacity of traditional cartridges or discs. For instance, Black Myth: Wukong and the upcoming Grand Theft Auto VI use this code-in-a-box model.
On the Nintendo Switch and Switch 2, cartridges max out at 32GB and 64GB, respectively. That is not much capacity by modern standards, so publishers turn to game-key cards as a compromise for a physical release. Compared with fully digital releases, game-key cards bind the license to the card, so owners can still trade or sell them like normal cartridges.
Owning physical copies can sometimes cost more than going digital, especially for Nintendo’s first-party titles. Effective as of May 2026, physical versions of first-party Nintendo titles sell for $10 more than their digital counterparts. The price increase was due to manufacturing, packaging, and distribution costs for cartridges. However, Nintendo frames the pricing adjustment differently, claiming it lowered digital game prices by $10 to pass the savings on to consumers.

articles.title: Shareholder revolt leaves Africa Bitcoin Corporation with two directors
articles.text:
Africa Bitcoin Corporation (ABC), South Africa’s listed Bitcoin treasury firm and financial services group, faces a new battle over who joins its board after four directors, including its chairperson and interim chief executive, resigned following a shareholder push to remove them.
With just two directors remaining, the company must rebuild its board while a separate demand to appoint two new non-executive directors remains unresolved.
The dispute centres on two shareholder demands. Investors holding approximately 76% of ABC’s shares called for the appointment of two new non-executive directors, a move the board opposed on governance grounds. A subsequent demand, backed by shareholders holding approximately 71.8% of the company’s shares, sought the removal of four existing directors.
All four have since resigned, making the removal resolutions unnecessary, but the original demand for two new appointments remains in force.
ABC now faces a governance test at a critical point in its transformation from a small-business financier into a Bitcoin treasury company. Shareholders have forced out most of its board, but the fight over who should replace them remains unsettled, raising questions about how the company will balance investor control, regulatory scrutiny, and independent oversight as it pursues its new strategy.
The four directors who resigned are Norma Sephuma, board chairperson; Stafford Masie, the company’s interim chief executive officer (CEO); and independent non-executive directors Snowy Masakale and GG Alcock. The company disclosed the departures in a Stock Exchange News Service (SENS) announcement on Monday, following the supplementary shareholder demand.
The departing directors said they had not taken the decision lightly, but that differences with WGW Capital Proprietary Limited, an ABC shareholder, had become irreconcilable.
“Recently, however, material differences emerged between the Board and WGW,” ABC said in the announcement.
The remaining directors are Robin Coode, an independent non-executive director, and Jonathan Phillips, the company’s financial director. They are working with the company’s advisers to restore the board and committee structures in line with statutory, regulatory, and JSE listing requirements.
Shareholder push for new directors
The dispute began with the demand for two additional directors, which the board addressed in an October 8 announcement. ABC acknowledged that shareholders had validly demanded a meeting under section 61(3) of the Companies Act, but said it did not support the proposed appointments at that time.
“The Board’s concern relates primarily to governance and regulatory integrity given the exceptional circumstances currently facing the Group,” ABC said.
The company stressed that its objection was not a general assessment of the candidates’ professional experience or capabilities. It committed to taking the necessary steps to convene the meeting and put the proposed resolutions to shareholders in accordance with applicable legal and regulatory requirements.
However, the announcement did not identify the proposed candidates, specify a meeting date, or provide further details about the board’s objections.
The original appointment demand remains unresolved. The two remaining directors must oversee the company while addressing the shareholder request and restoring the board’s composition.
Before its Bitcoin treasury pivot, the company listed as Altvest Capital on the Cape Town Stock Exchange (CTSE) in May 2022, initially valued at R50 million ($3 million). It later introduced three additional share classes—Class A for Umgani Lodge, Class B for Bambanani, and Class C for Altvest Credit Opportunities Fund (ACOF)—to raise funding for investments, but trading in its securities remained thin.
Figures published in its 2024 prospectus show just 42,420 ordinary shares changing hands between July 2023 and July 2024, generating about R131,031.05 ($7,948) in reported turnover.
Altvest moved its equity listing to the Johannesburg Stock Exchange’s (JSE) AltX Market in October 2024, citing limitations in the Cape Town exchange’s ability to attract retail investors and support sizeable capital raises. In May 2026, it transferred its shares to the JSE Main Board.
In 2025, ABC expanded beyond small and medium-sized enterprise (SME) lending to adopt Bitcoin as a long-term treasury asset, making its first disclosed purchase in February. Shareholders approved its rebrand from Altvest to Africa Bitcoin Corporation on September 10, 2025, with the new name and ticker taking effect on the JSE two weeks later.
Since then, the company has retained its SME financing business, while aggressively pushing its Bitcoin investment strategy for institutional investors seeking access to the cryptocurrency.
Deepening leadership crisis
The boardroom dispute comes amid a series of leadership changes following enforcement action by the Financial Sector Conduct Authority (FSCA), South Africa’s financial services regulator, against three individuals associated with ABC, which previously operated as Altvest Capital.
The regulator found that former CEO Warren Wheatley, his wife Tatum Keshwar-Wheatley and former chief investment officer Akshay Karan manipulated Altvest shares in September 2022 to artificially inflate the share price and create a misleading impression of market demand and trading activity.
The three were fined a combined R9 million ($546,000) and debarred from the financial services industry for 20 years. The FSCA’s enforcement action was against the individuals, not ABC itself.
Wheatley has disputed the regulator’s findings, describing the transactions as three trades involving just 50 shares worth R301 ($18.26) that were intended to test the CTSE’s trading platform.
In a podcast interview with financial publication Moneyweb on October 9, Wheatley said those trades aimed to document pricing errors on the trading platform ahead of Altvest’s first public offering, disputing the regulator’s finding that they were part of a scheme to manipulate the share price for profit.
FSCA did not respond to a request for comment on its findings, the evidence supporting the market manipulation allegations, and the status of any appeals against its enforcement action.
In an email to TechCabal on September 8, Wheatley declined to comment, saying “none of the affected parties would be providing commentary” until their appeals are submitted.
In a September 1 SENS announcement, ABC said the affected individuals had informed the company that they disputed the findings and intended to seek reconsideration and suspension of the decisions before the Financial Services Tribunal, an independent body reviewing financial regulator decisions.
The Tribunal told TechCabal in September that it had not received applications for reconsideration or suspension involving the named parties at that time. Lwandiso Mgijima of the Financial Services Tribunal confirmed that no applications had been filed at the time.
“We confirm that the Tribunal has not received any applications for reconsideration or suspension involving the parties [Wheatley, Keshwar-Wheatley, and Karan] mentioned in your e-mail. The Tribunal is, accordingly, not in possession of any documents relating to the matter,” Mgijima said.
In a subsequent response to TechCabal, the Financial Services Tribunal confirmed that it received applications for reconsideration and suspension on September 25, 2026, after previously stating that no applications had been received. The matter, registered under case number A43/2026, lists Warren Gregory Wheatley, WGW Capital (Pty) Ltd, Tatum Lucy Wheatley, Tatum Keshwar Investments (Pty) Ltd, and Akshay Suresh Karan as applicants. The Tribunal said it had not yet ruled on the suspension application or set a hearing date.
“We confirm that applications for reconsideration and suspension involving the parties mentioned in your e-mail were received and processed by the Tribunal on 25 September 2026,” the Tribunal said. “We confirm that the Tribunal has not issued a ruling in respect of the suspension application. The process is ongoing.”
Wheatley, ABC’s co-founder and former CEO, resigned from the company with effect from September 21, 2026, after being placed on precautionary leave. Karan, who had also been placed on precautionary leave, resigned as chief investment officer with effect from October 1.
Masie took over as interim CEO after Wheatley was placed on precautionary leave. He has now also quit as interim CEO and director of Bitcoin Strategy, ABC’s Bitcoin investment subsidiary, with an intended final day of service of February 28, 2027.
ABC said Masie had agreed to continue fulfilling his executive responsibilities, supporting the management team, maintaining operational continuity and facilitating an orderly transition to permanent executive leadership.
Despite the board departures, ABC says its executive management team remains in place and will continue managing day-to-day operations within its existing lawful delegated authorities.
The company said its remaining directors, in consultation with its advisers, were addressing the steps needed to restore the appropriate board and committee composition.
Editor’s note: This article has been updated to include confirmation from the Financial Services Tribunal that it received applications for reconsideration and suspension. The case remains pending.

articles.title: Mitel WX bets next phase of unified communications will be won on the floor, not in the meeting room - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Mitel WX bets next phase of unified communications will be won on the floor, not in the meeting room
For the better part of my 30-year career as an analyst, unified communications has been designed around the person at a desk, bouncing between meetings, chat and email. That made sense when the pandemic pushed everyone onto video.
It makes far less sense when roughly 80% of the global workforce doesn’t sit at a desk at all. In fact, I’ve argued that front-line, non-deskbound workers have been forgotten by most of the UC industry, which is why so many nurses, warehouse workers and others rely on consumer devices and tools.
That’s the gap Mitel Networks Corp. is targeting with Mitel Workforce Experience, which the company recently launched. Mitel WX brings voice, messaging, meetings, contact center and vertical applications into a single client that adapts to the worker’s role rather than the device. Following a pre-briefing I attended with Eric Hanson, Mitel’s executive vice president and chief marketing officer, and Martin Bitzinger, executive vice president of product management, it’s apparent that “toggle tax” across disjointed applications has plagued users for years, so Mitel’s direction addresses a real problem.
Legacy UC is built for everyone, but optimized for no one
Hanson opened with a line that captures the problem with most UC platforms today.
“Many in the industry have attempted to build something that addresses the needs of everyone, but is optimized for no one,” he said. He’s right. The major platforms were built for knowledge workers and then pushed out to everyone else, which is how a nurse or plant technician ends up with a client designed around calendar invites. Those workers live in Epic or a dispatch console, and when something goes wrong, they pick up the phone.
Hanson also made a point I’ve been making for years: Communications was treated as a mature, almost commoditized part of the stack and “wasn’t really deemed to be strategic until it didn’t work.”
Mitel supported its thesis with a Vanson Bourne study it commissioned, which surveyed about 2,000 workers in Canada, France, Germany and the U.K. The study found that 57% of workers waste time switching among an average of seven tools, 79% reach for voice when rapid action is needed, and frontline workers are twice as likely to use unapproved tools.
It’s vendor-funded, so treat it as directional, but it aligns with what I hear from information technology leaders: When the sanctioned tool doesn’t fit the job, workers default to WhatsApp and IT loses control.
Starting over rather than bolting on
One of the more interesting decisions Mitel made was architectural. Mitel WX isn’t a MiCollab refresh or a rebrand of the clients Mitel inherited from Unify. “We basically started with a blank sheet of paper,” Bitzinger said. Only foundational functions, such as voice, are baked into the core client. Everything else is a plugin that administrators enable by role. While this is a longer path to a commercially available product, it will likely lead to greater success down the road because the code is cleaner and purpose-built.
In the demo, a hospital desk worker who also handles contact center queues sees chat and call queues, along with an electronic health record panel, on a single screen. An environmental services worker in the same hospital sees a streamlined view with work group log-in and task completion. A doctor driving in takes calls on a work number via Apple CarPlay or Android Auto. Calls migrate between mobile and desktop rather than being transferred, a small detail that matters when the caller is a patient.
Bitzinger stressed that IT, not the user, owns role design. “It can’t be left up to the user to do all of those things,” he said. That’s the right call. Frontline workers won’t customize their tools, and configurability without governance creates clutter. Administrators manage templated roles in Mitel Central, including across multiple domains common in health systems built through acquisition.
Control is the real product
For Mitel, WX’s competitive differentiation is deployment flexibility. Though every vendor supports public cloud today, Mitel also lets customers use hybrid, private cloud, on-premises, and edge deployments, with the same client built on a common application programming interface for both its CloudLink cloud back end and on-premises Mitel Central. Asked whether a customer could run Mitel WX fully air-gapped, Bitzinger answered: “They can run it completely air-gapped, completely on-prem in their basement if that’s what they prefer.”
The underrated feature is private push notifications. Most mobile UC apps rely on Apple and Google push services to ring a phone. WX can deliver push notifications over the customer’s own network, so calls and alerts still arrive in a hospital running private 5G or on a site that loses its internet connection. For regulated and mission-critical environments, that’s a meaningful differentiator.
Hanson noted that only about 25% of the industry’s 450 million to 500 million seats have moved to the multitenant public cloud and argued that hybrid is increasingly “a deliberate strategy” rather than a way station. With sovereignty pressure building in Europe and resilience concerns everywhere, I agree.
Mitel has a large European install base, and the deployment flexibility will serve it well in that region, where data sovereignty is a major issue, particularly in regulated verticals. I’ve discussed this with Tom Boyle at the NHS, who told me, “I need to ensure our clinicians can make calls regardless of what macro issues happen around the globe, so we will keep our communications system on-prem for the foreseeable future.”
Where the questions remain
The rollout of Mitel WX is phased. Initial availability begins in November, with full platform availability expected in 2027. MiVoice Business support is prioritized, with OpenScape Business and OpenScape Voice for the largest enterprises to follow in the next couple of quarters. OpenScape customers should receive firm dates before planning migrations.
Mitel will release artificial intelligence capabilities after launch. Mitel’s position on AI is that it makes people more capable rather than unnecessary, countering the view that “agents replace everyone,” particularly in contact centers, although I am seeing that opinion start to change. The Mitel AI Services Framework will include MCP support, and the incremental AI in the Elite tier is still to come.
Bitzinger’s view that “voice is the natural UI” for AI makes sense for front-line workers, and Mitel has decades of voice expertise to support this. Now it needs to ship.
The widget model for WX is only as good as its ecosystem. Mitel will build the core integrations itself and rely on services and technology partners for the rest. Bitzinger was candid about the channel, noting that most partners won’t become vertical workflow integrators: “Not for the overwhelming majority of channel partners. No illusions there.” That honesty is welcome, and integration depth will determine how quickly Mitel WX moves beyond early adopters.
Finally, there’s Microsoft Corp. Teams and Zoom Communications Inc. Mitel frames Mitel WX as complementary to both for knowledge workers. That’s sensible given the share those two vendors hold, but it means WX must win on the frontline against health care specialists and the frontline offerings from the big platforms.
Mitel has a real and growing opportunity. Hanson said two large, longtime customers, one in the U.S. and one in France, are already pushing to start migration plans after seeing MWX at Mitel’s User Group. Though the installed base is the “low-hanging fruit,” both Avaya and NEC have large install bases looking to move off those platforms as quickly as they can due to a lack of innovation. Moving a customer off an incumbent can be challenging, but Mitel can offer a “like-for-like” option for businesses that have stayed with a company such as Avaya because moving to the cloud doesn’t support the business.
Advice for IT leaders
- Map communications by role. Inventory your frontline, contact center, and knowledge worker roles and the tools each role uses. That’s the baseline for judging any role-based client.
- Audit your shadow IT. If frontline staff coordinate via consumer messaging apps, you already have a compliance problem.
- Test resilience, not features. Ask how calls and alerts are delivered when the internet path, a cloud region or a push service goes down.
- Get integration specifics in writing. “Integrates with EHR” can mean a deep workflow or a browser tab. Demand to see the integrations you need running on your systems.
- Use the in-place upgrade. Existing Mitel customers should take advantage of the migration path and the dual-run period to pilot Mitel WX with a single high-friction frontline group first.
Final thoughts
For Mitel, the WX strategy makes sense. Rather than chasing only the knowledge worker, where Microsoft and Zoom are entrenched, it targets the underserved frontline majority with a role-aware client, genuine deployment choice and voice at the center. Execution of the platform roadmap, the integration ecosystem and the AI layer will determine whether Mitel WX becomes Mitel’s growth engine or merely a better client for its installed base. Either way, it’s exciting to see UC come to the factory floor and hallways rather than to yet another meeting.
Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

articles.title: Apple presenta HomeView, su nueva apuesta para adueñarse del hogar inteligente
articles.text:
Apple acaba de presentar HomeView, su nuevo hub para controlar el hogar inteligente. Los de Cupertino no solo se meten en una nueva categoría de producto, sino que aspiran a darle batalla a propuestas ya establecidas como el Amazon Echo Show o el Google Nest Hub. Para ello sacan a relucir todas las capacidades de su ecosistema de software y hardware.
El HomeView de Apple equipa una pantalla táctil de 7 pulgadas y llega en dos variantes. Por un lado, una versión que se puede colgar en la pared; por el otro, con el panel acoplado a una base metálica que funciona como altavoz y que le permite residir sobre una mesa o cualquier otro mueble. Esta última cuenta con un brazo que permite ajustar la inclinación de la pantalla.
El nuevo dispositivo de la manzana puede llevar a cabo una gran cantidad de tareas y no se limita a ser el centro de control del hogar inteligente. Si bien el HomeView podrá controlar otros dispositivos conectados como termostatos, luces, persianas, timbres, etc., también servirá para ver fotos y vídeos, hacer videollamadas, escuchar música, pódcast y audiolibros, y más. Además, sacará provecho de la integración con Siri AI para aprovecharlo como asistente personal.
Quienes tengan una suscripción a iCloud+ podrán acceder a la función de reconocimiento de personas conocidas, paquetes, vehículos y mascotas al conectar HomeView con una cámara compatible. De acuerdo con Apple, esta característica funciona con cifrado de extremo a extremo para proteger la privacidad de los individuos y los datos procesados.
HomeView, el primer hub para el hogar inteligente de Apple
Un detalle interesante de HomeView es que puede reconocer hasta 6 usuarios diferentes y cambiar la apariencia de la pantalla de inicio, así como los widgets y las aplicaciones disponibles. Si bien el nuevo dispositivo de Apple no cuenta con acceso a la App Store, sí llega con algunas de las apps más importantes de la compañía (Mensajes, Apple Music, FaceTime, Calendar, etc.).
Apple menciona que al usar HomeView emparejado con un dispositivo compatible con Apple Intelligence, puede acceder al contexto personal del usuario. Vale aclarar que ese contexto personal no está disponible para todas las personas que utilizan el hub inteligente, sino que se mantendrá en privado solo para quien corresponda.
Apple ha dotado al HomeView de un chip A18 con Enclave Seguro. Esto significa que la información que ingresa por el micrófono y/o la cámara se procesan por separado del resto del sistema. Este sistema dividido en compartimientos ayuda a garantizar la privacidad de esos datos, impidiendo su acceso a terceros (incluyendo Apple).
Respecto del uso de Siri AI, algunas de las solicitudes de los usuarios se procesan de modo 100 % local, con modelos de inteligencia artificial que se ejecutan dentro del dispositivo. Sin embargo, para las tareas o consultas que requieren de mayor poder de procesamiento, HomeView se conecta con Private Cloud Compute, la red de servidores de Apple, pero sin poner en riesgo la privacidad de la información.
Una interfaz conocida
El software del HomeView de Apple llega con muchos elementos ya conocidos de las demás plataformas de la compañía. Si alguna vez usaste un iPhone o un Apple Watch, verás que la interfaz del nuevo dispositivo tiene varios puntos en común con la de dichos productos. El hub inteligente incluso permite seleccionar entre diferentes diseños, algunos similares a la pantalla de bloqueo del iPhone y otros más parecidos a una esfera del Apple Watch.
La idea de Apple es que HomeView sea fácil de usar, tanto con la voz como con los comandos táctiles. Y la posibilidad de utilizar el dispositivo apoyado sobre la mesa como montado en una pared, le brinda a los usuarios una versatilidad interesante pensando en la posibilidad de tener varios en la casa. Tengamos en cuenta que incluso es posible usar el aparato como intercomunicador entre las diferentes habitaciones del hogar.
Tal y como se rumoreaba, Apple también ha aprovechado para lanzar una línea de dispositivos para el hogar inteligente en colaboración con LG y Schneider Electric. Los productos en cuestión incluyen varios modelos de timbres con cámara, termostatos y cerraduras electrónicas. Todos estos, compatibles con el nuevo HomeView, por supuesto.
Disponibilidad y precio del Apple HomeView, con malas noticias para Europa
La disponibilidad inicial del HomeView será limitada, pues Apple lo lanzará primero en seis países: Estados Unidos, Reino Unido, Canadá, Australia, Nueva Zelanda e India. En dichos mercados se pueden reservar desde hoy, con las entregas comenzando el próximo 13 de noviembre. El dispositivo también llegará a Singapur y Sudáfrica. Sin embargo, hay malas noticias para quienes viven en la Unión Europea.
En la letra pequeña del anuncio, Apple ha informado que HomeView no se pondrá a la venta en la UE debido a la ausencia de Siri AI en el iPhone en la región. Así que si estás en España o cualquiera de los demás países que conforman el bloque, son muy malas noticias. Es lógico pensar que el nuevo hub inteligente llegará eventualmente a la Unión Europea, pero todavía es imposible saber cuándo. "Apple está trabajando constructivamente con la UE en un intento de encontrar una solución", indican los de Cupertino.
Respecto del preci0, tanto el HomeView con base como la versión para colgar tienen un precio de 299 dólares en Estados Unidos. La segunda opción necesita una montura para la pared que se vende por separado, con opciones que inician en los 59,95 dólares. Pero esto no es todo.
Ninguno de los modelos HomeView tienen batería integrada, así que funcionan enchufados. El modelo con base incluye el adaptador de corriente en la caja, pero la variante para colgar no. De modo que si eliges esta última tendrás que comprar el adaptador USB-C por separado o utilizar algún otro que ya tengas disponible en tu casa.
El HomeView con base se encuentra disponible en cuatro colores: plata, blanco estrella, rose pink y gris espacial. La opción para montar en la pared solo se consigue en gris espacial y plata.

articles.title: Einst milliardenschwer, jetzt Pleite: Gehyptes KI-Startup Character AI muss Insolvenz anmelden
articles.text:
Einst milliardenschwer, jetzt Pleite: Gehyptes KI-Startup Character AI muss Insolvenz anmelden
2021 von den Ex-Googlern Noam Shazeer und Daniel De Freitas gegründet, ermöglicht es Character AI Nutzerinnen, mit verschiedenen echten oder fiktiven Persönlichkeiten wie Elon Musk, Albert Einstein oder Super Mario zu chatten. Zudem können Nutzer:innen sich eine eigene KI-Persönlichkeit programmieren, um sich mit ihr zu unterhalten.
Milliardenbewertung ganz ohne Einnahmen
2023 erreichte die KI-Plattform monatlich 100 Millionen Besuche, hatte aber bis dahin noch keinen einzigen Cent eingenommen. Trotz fehlenden Umsatzes sammelte Character.ai in einer von Andreessen Horowitz angeführten Finanzierungsrunde 150 Millionen Dollar ein. Damit erreichte das Startup eine Bewertung von gut einer Milliarde Dollar.
Jetzt muss Character.ai Insolvenz nach dem Chapter-11-Verfahren anmelden. Es drücken Verbindlichkeiten in Höhe von 50 bis 100 Millionen Dollar. Das ist aber noch nicht alles. Als Grund für das Scheitern gab das Unternehmen „erhebliche rechtliche, regulatorische und operative Gegenwinde“ im vergangenen Jahr an.
Character AI: Finanzielle und rechtliche Probleme
Neben den finanziellen Schwierigkeiten musste sich Character.ai mit zahlreichen rechtlichen Problemen auseinandersetzen. So hatte Disney das KI-Startup im September 2025 per Unterlassungsaufforderung dazu gebracht, Chatbots mit Disney-Figuren aus dem Angebot zu entfernen.
Zudem gab es eine Reihe von Klagen von Familien in den USA. 2024 soll ein 14-Jähriger aus Florida nach langen Gesprächen mit einem Character-AI-Chatbot Suizid begangen haben. Eine entsprechende Klage der Mutter endete Anfang 2026 mit einem Vergleich. Außerdem hatten Familien aus Texas dem Unternehmen vor, mit seinen KI-Chatbots Jugendliche zu Gewalt und Selbstverletzung ermutigt zu haben, wie Trendingtopics schreibt.
Daraufhin hatte Character AI Altersprüfungen eingeführt. Seit Ende 2025 war es Nutzer:innen unter 18 Jahren außerdem verboten, offene Chats zu führen. Darüber hinaus hatte Character.ai 2024 seine Gründer Shazeer und De Freitas sowie weitere rund 30 Mitarbeiter:innen an Google Deepmind verloren. Erst im September 2026 war CEO Karandeep Anand als CTO zu Disney gewechselt.
Disney soll Startup-Teile kaufen wollen
Der Konzern soll auch das Vorkaufsrecht für zum Verkauf angebotene Teile des insolventen KI-Startups haben – das entsprechende Paket soll 20 Millionen Dollar in die klammen Kassen spülen. Weitere Interessenten könnten diesen Grundpreis aber noch überbieten. Der Verkauf soll bis Dezember 2026 abgeschlossen sein.
Mindestens bis dahin soll der Betrieb der Plattform weiterlaufen. Die Abos bleiben von der Insolvenz vorerst unberührt. Bei Änderung kostenpflichtiger Funktionen will das Unternehmen die Nutzer:innen informieren. Nutzer:innen können aber auch ihre Konten löschen und/oder die Daten exportieren.

articles.title: Laplace Intelligence red-teams robots and self-driving cars before they hit the real world | TechCrunch
articles.text:
If there’s one lesson the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident taught us, it’s that AI agents can be unpredictable.
“Imagine if something like that happened in the physical world,” Howie Sun, CEO and co-founder of Laplace Intelligence, told TechCrunch. “AI agents are moving from computers into the real world, and we don’t really want physical AI to fail in the real world.”
Ann Arbor-based Laplace is building automated red-teaming — essentially, stress-testing a system by deliberately trying to make it fail — for robotics and physical AI. The company is betting that the only way to make sure physical AI is safe is to have AI test it.
“Our goal is to help companies discover and fix problems before deployment — and, over time, build a shared foundation of evidence that customers, insurers, and regulators can trust,” Sun said.
Laplace is one of 20 startups competing in Startup Battlefield 200, the startup pitch competition taking place at TechCrunch Disrupt in San Francisco this week, October 13-15. It will present on the Disrupt Stage Tuesday afternoon, October 13.
Sun, alongside his co-founder and chief scientist Henry Liu, founded Laplace a year ago out of the University of Michigan. Sun has spent the last eight years in academia researching how to challenge autonomous driving AI in simulation. In 2023, he and Liu — his then-PhD adviser — published a paper on the subject that made it onto the cover of the top scientific journal Nature. That’s when the calls started coming in from autonomous vehicle companies interested in implementing their ideas.
“I realized that I wanted to build this and take it from purely academic research into a product that’s useful in the real world,” Sun said.
Using their academic research as a base, Sun and Liu built Laplace, so named for “Laplace’s demon,” an 1814 thought experiment by French scholar Pierre-Simon Laplace, who imagined that if you knew the exact state of everything in the universe, you could predict the future with total precision.
“We are essentially using simulation to predict the real world’s future,” Sun said.
At the startup’s core is a high-fidelity simulation reconstructed from the real world, paired with an AI agent that constantly probes for weaknesses and failure points. The goal is to ensure that any physical AI — be it a robot, autonomous vehicle, or smart city solution — is safe in simulation before it’s deployed in the real world.
The simulation environment is a post-trained version of Nvidia’s Cosmos, an AI world simulation platform, which is grounded in the real world, allowing Laplace to reconstruct anything from an Arizona highway to a Paris pedestrian crossing. Simulations are generated by blending a mesh of different real-world information. A Google Street View image could serve as a reference from which an entire street is generated. But rather than generating something random, the simulator combines real-world map data to re-create an environment that’s true to scale.
Developers can then use language prompts to change the setting in real time, like adding in afternoon traffic. Sun says Laplace pulls real-time traffic and congestion information from navigation providers like TomTom.
Within Laplace’s simulations, not only is the environment simulated, but also the behavior of other actors. For example, during a demo, Sun directed the test agent vehicle to swerve into oncoming traffic. The car it would have hit — or driven through, as is common among some generative world models — moved out of its way to avoid a collision.
“It’s truly an interactive simulation environment,” Sun said. “Everyone is reacting to everything … This is more like a world model with interactive participants.”
While the simulated environment is an important part of Laplace’s product, the real unique selling point is the AI agents the startup is developing to automatically design corner cases (tricky, rare scenarios that could trip up an AI system), moving the human further out of the loop.
“They can design from the news, from police reports on collisions — all kinds of information to actively challenge the autonomous vehicles and other physical AI agents,” Sun said.
Today, autonomous vehicle developers mostly train an AI to handle edge cases using recorded footage that they then turn into a simulation, or by relying on humans to come up with new ideas and design them. While many AV companies have done what Laplace is pitching and started embracing AI to create edge cases for training — self-driving truck company Waabi comes to mind — the need for this kind of technology will really become apparent when we start placing generalized robots in the real world.
“There’s less data on generalized robotics,” Sun said. “No one knows what the edge cases will be in the real world.”
Despite Sun and Liu coming from academia, with no shiny Silicon Valley tech company pedigrees, the two have managed to start generating revenue and even turn a modest profit. Most of the money is coming from autonomous driving use cases, with customers including Japanese trucking manufacturer Isuzu and Texas-based autonomous trucking firm Bot Auto.
Nvidia is also a customer, says Sun. The two companies, alongside T-Mobile, are working together on a free smart city pilot for San Jose, California, to provide high-level traffic operations. Laplace is also in the early stages of working with partners building humanoid robotics for warehouses.
Most of Laplace’s customer contracts are project-based today, and the company is working toward turning that into recurring revenue. The startup’s near-term goal — which it hopes will be aided by competing at Disrupt — is to raise funds and scale so it can compete with its rivals.
Chief among its rivals is Applied Intuition, a buzzy late-stage startup that’s raised $1.2 billion to date at a $15 billion post-money valuation. Isuzu is also one of Applied’s customers.
Sun isn’t too worried. He believes Laplace’s core methodology of using AI to test AI is a “new paradigm that changes the testing of physical AI entirely,” turning it into a “dynamic interactive testing process.”
“That will be the biggest moat,” he said.

articles.title: Geoffrey Hinton, Yoshua Bengio join 400 scientists calling for international AI regulator | BetaKit
articles.text:
More than 400 members of the scientific community are pushing for an international AI regulator to curb cybersecurity incidents.
The news: The open letter, released on Tuesday, calls for the creation of an international body to standardize AI containment practices and record and track containment failures. The letter recommends that every security incident involving containment failure be reported to the body and eventually made public, arguing that such transparency is required for learning and accountability.
The open letter counted signatories from all over the world, including nearly 70 Canadians, such as Nobel Prize winner Geoffrey Hinton and Turing Award winner Yoshua Bengio. Both AI pioneers have signed many previous open letters warning about AI’s potentially devastating effects.
From the source: “As scientists, we thought that the current situation with AI models breaking containment during testing was a concern,” University of Toronto professor and signatory David Lie told BetaKit over the phone. “We drafted this letter after talking with people across both the AI and security communities in hopes it would improve the situation.”
The context: The new open letter’s recommendations follow an OpenAI model escaping its test environment and breaching the systems of Hugging Face and other platforms this past summer. That incident was just the first in a growing number of similar disclosures.
The scientists’ proposed solution may already be in the works. Canada’s AI minister Evan Solomon recently floated the idea of an international “technology stability board,” which would regulate testing, model evaluation, and model release, as well as include incident reporting mechanisms.
Final thought: While Canada is talking about potential solutions, the threat of rogue AI cybersecurity incidents persists. The scientists behind the open letter say that more emphasis is needed on AI safety research and containment technologies, and warn that cybersecurity incidents will become “far more damaging” to critical infrastructure without immediate changes to AI development.
Feature image courtesy LawZero via LinkedIn.

articles.title: Street Fighter : que signifie la scène post-générique ?
articles.text:
La saga Street Fighter revient au cinéma ce mercredi 14 octobre, avec un nouveau film qui repart de zéro. Cette nouvelle adaptation est signée Kitao Sakurai et réunit notamment Jason Momoa, Noah Centineo, Andrew Koji, Callina Liang et 50 Cent.
Comme beaucoup de blockbusters récents, Street Fighter garde une scène bonus pour après son générique. Le film avec Jean-Claude Van Damme sorti en 1994 en avait déjà une, centrée sur la résurrection de M. Bison. Elle n’a débouché sur aucune suite.
Attention, la suite de cet article contient des spoilers sur Street Fighter.
La scène post-générique de Street Fighter prépare la suite
À l’instar des scènes flashback du film, la séquence post-générique est intégralement réalisée en animation. Elle montre les méchants, emmenés par M. Bison (David Dastmalchian), se rendre auprès de Sagat, personnage absent de toutes les scènes en prise de vues réelles.
On devine alors que Sagat cherchera à se venger de Ryu (Andrew Koji), qui l’a battu lors d’un premier grand tournoi organisé en 1987 (clin d’œil à l’année de sortie du tout premier jeu, où Sagat est le boss final), une défaite montrée en introduction du film. Une alliance avec M. Bison paraît tout indiquée pour se débarrasser de son rival.
Kitao Sakurai pense déjà à une suite. Avant même la sortie, le réalisateur a confié au site MovieWeb : « C’est quelque chose à quoi nous réfléchissons et que nous développons. Je ne veux rien dire qui puisse nous enfermer. Cela dépend aussi un peu de la réaction des gens à celui-ci, et de voir s’ils soutiennent cette vision de l’histoire. Nous avons vraiment beaucoup d’idées et nous sommes en train d’écrire en ce moment, mais vous savez, je ne voudrais faire aucune promesse dans un sens ou dans l’autre sur ce que nous allons faire exactement. »
Un éventuel Street Fighter 2 dépendra bien sûr du succès du premier opus. Si le feu vert est donné, tout porte à croire que l’histoire mettra en scène Sagat, colosse chauve pour lequel aucun acteur n’a encore été annoncé. Dans l’univers des jeux, ce maître de la boxe thaïlandaise fait partie des lieutenants de M. Bison au sein de l’organisation criminelle Shadaloo, aux côtés de Vega (Orville Peck) et Balrog (50 Cent).
