articles.title: Una app con IA que escucha todo lo que dicen sus usuarios ya consiguió USD 26 millones de recaudación
articles.text:
La empresa Ambi recaudó USD 26 millones en varias rondas de inversión para desarrollar una aplicación de inteligencia artificial que escucha de forma permanente a sus usuarios y les da sugerencias en tiempo real durante reuniones y tareas cotidianas.
La compañía, fundada por Peter Mo, exejecutivo de la empresa de grabadores con IA Plaud, confirmó que la ronda fue liderada por el fondo Luminous Ventures, que ya había invertido en Meituan y Unitree Robotics, junto al fabricante de diseño original Huaqin.
Cómo funciona la appp que escucha permanente
Ambi lanzó aplicaciones para iPhone, Mac y Apple Watch que actúan como anotadoras de reuniones, pero con una diferencia: los usuarios pueden dejarlas escuchando durante todo el día para que capturen contexto de forma continua.
“La forma en que interactuamos con la inteligencia es limitada. Muchas veces la inteligencia queda atrapada en la pantalla, y si usas un dispositivo como Plaud, tienes que esperar a que la grabación se transfiera al teléfono, se suba a la nube y se procese. Por eso estamos construyendo Ambi para usar IA en cualquier momento y lugar”, dijo Mo, cofundador y director ejecutivo de la compañía, a TechCrunch.
El agente de inteligencia artificial promete dar sugerencias de forma proactiva o mostrar información relevante mientras la persona está en una reunión, basándose en su calendario, sus encuentros previos, su base de conocimiento y datos de la web. Una tarea iniciada en un dispositivo puede continuarse en otro.
La empresa planea sumar una aplicación de escritorio que analice el trabajo que hacen los usuarios en la computadora y guarde en su memoria las partes más relevantes para generar sugerencias más personalizadas.
Asimismo, prepara su propio dispositivo de hardware, con pantalla, parlante, cámara y micrófonos para capturar contexto y mostrar información.
Las dudas sobre privacidad sobre Ambi
No está claro si las aplicaciones de Ambi, o su futuro dispositivo, alertarán a terceros cuando sus conversaciones estén siendo grabadas si el usuario no lo informa.
Mo aseguró que los usuarios pueden desactivar la captura de audio ambiental en cualquier momento y que esa función viene apagada por defecto. La empresa sostiene que no almacena grabaciones y que encripta los datos, aunque no precisó qué tipo de encriptación utiliza.
A pesar de esas medidas, la responsabilidad de avisarle a otras personas que están siendo escuchadas sigue recayendo en el usuario de la aplicación. Mo describió ese vacío como un problema de toda la industria, no exclusivo de su producto.
“Tenemos que informarles a nuestros usuarios que ellos deben avisarles a otras personas sobre la captura ambiental. Nosotros, como industria, todavía no resolvimos este problema de divulgación. Tratamos de poner la información sobre el aviso en todos los lugares posibles, pero si los usuarios intentan ocultar la captura, no podemos resolver el problema por ellos”, explicó Mo.
Ambi ya emplea a más de 50 personas distribuidas en oficinas de San Francisco, Beijing, Shanghai y Shenzhen y busca sumar personal comercial e ingenieros de inteligencia artificial especializados en reconocimiento de voz para seguir expandiendo el producto.
Meta opta por eliminar la cámara de sus gafas inteligentes
En medio del debate por privacidad y seguridad, hay empresas que optan por cambiar el enfoque de sus productos. Tal es el caso de Meta, que decidió eliminar la cámara de último modelo de gafas inteligentes.
En todos los juzgados y tribunales de Inglaterra y Gales, el Servicio de Tribunales (HMCTS) vetó el ingreso de estos dispositivos, que las autoridades pueden confiscar al momento de entrar.
Por otro lado, en Nueva York, desde el 20 de julio de 2026, las gafas inteligentes quedaron prohibidas en todas las sedes del Sistema Judicial Unificado

articles.title: Europe’s Advanced Packaging Gap: Fraunhofer, Swissbit Target the Missing Middle - EE Times
articles.text:
Europe has no shortage of semiconductor research. The harder problem often begins after the prototype works.
A company may need an advanced packaging process for a specialized product, but only at volumes of tens, hundreds, or thousands of units. That can be too much for a research organization to support indefinitely and far too little to interest a conventional high-volume outsourced semiconductor assembly and test provider.
Rolf Aschenbrenner, deputy director of the Fraunhofer Institute for Reliability and Microintegration (IZM), sees that gap regularly. “Companies come to us because their volume is too low to get access to advanced packaging,” he told EE Times. “We can help with prototypes, and in some cases we can also do small-volume manufacturing.”
That doesn’t mean Fraunhofer wants to become an outsourced semiconductor assembly and test (OSAT) provider. Its role, according to Aschenbrenner, is to adapt packaging processes to customer requirements, demonstrate their viability, and ultimately hand them off to industry. “The goal is that we also transfer our processes,” he said.
The problem is what happens when no industrial manufacturer is ready to take them.
Too small for the OSATs
Aschenbrenner cited fan-out wafer-level packaging as an example. A company developing RF products might require only around 100 wafers per year. For a large packaging provider, that volume barely registers.
“If you go to a large OSAT and ask for 100 wafers per year, that’s nothing for them,” he said. “They won’t do it.”
Fraunhofer has encountered even smaller production runs. Aschenbrenner described one customer making miniature cameras for medical applications that requires only about 20 wafers annually. A single wafer can contain tens of thousands of cameras, making that small wafer count sufficient for the customer’s entire market.
“Twenty wafers per year is the full volume,” he said. “They don’t need more. But nobody else can do those 20 wafers.”
He also pointed to work for a medical technology company on detector arrays for a novel CT scanner. The application requires sensors to be placed very close together; conventional wire bonding creates gaps that can affect imaging performance, so the design uses through-silicon vias to route connections to the backside.
The customer wanted that work performed in Europe, Aschenbrenner said. But again, the volume was too low to attract a conventional packaging house. “There was no company in Europe with the technology available at that volume,” he said. “So we do it.”
For Europe, that problem is especially relevant because many of its industrial strengths lie in specialized markets rather than mass consumer electronics. “We have many small and medium-sized companies that are champions in very narrow areas,” Aschenbrenner said. “They also need access to advanced packaging, and often no one is there to help them.”
The capital requirements make it harder for those companies to solve the problem themselves. Advanced packaging is no longer a matter of buying a few relatively inexpensive wire bonders. Wafer-level packaging lines require substantial investment.
That leaves a missing industrial layer between pilot production and mass manufacturing.
The industrial answer
Swissbit provides one example of how that middle ground might work. The company develops memory and security products in Europe and increasingly uses advanced packaging to move toward system-level products combining memory, controllers, security functions, compute, and potentially AI.
According to Lars Lust, executive director of Swissbit Germany, the company’s core competency is not semiconductor manufacturing. “We integrate semiconductors,” he told EE Times. “Advanced packaging is a must-have for our products.”
Lust argued that low-volume manufacturing doesn’t necessarily have to be uneconomic. The key is to avoid building a unique process flow for every product. “If you have a standard tool chain and a common platform, you can produce low volume in the same way as higher volume,” he said. “You don’t need a new setup every time.”
Swissbit’s own production illustrates the model. The company has roughly 3,500 products in its catalog and around 150 active products moving through production in a typical month. Some products may run in quantities of only hundreds, while others reach thousands or tens of thousands, but they can share equipment, process steps, and tooling.
“We scale over the platform,” Lust said. “If you have a good platform for low-volume products, you can produce them on the same line as volume products.” That changes the economics of the “missing middle.” The challenge is not necessarily low volume itself, but low volume combined with a bespoke process that cannot be reused.
For Europe, that could be important. Rather than trying to replicate the enormous Asian packaging ecosystem built around highly standardized, high-volume products, European manufacturers could aggregate many specialized products onto common advanced packaging platforms.
The handoff cannot come at the end
Lust also sees room for improvement in the way Europe transfers technology from research institutes to manufacturers. He argued that industry should become involved around technology-readiness levels five or six, once early demonstrators have shown that a process works, rather than waiting until researchers have pushed the technology close to production.
“The RTO should not develop everything to TRL seven or eight and then hand it over,” he said. “Industry needs to come in earlier, when the first demonstrators are there, to define applications, requirements, and scalability.” That makes the transition less like a relay race and more like an overlap between research and manufacturing.
Aschenbrenner described Fraunhofer’s current role in similar terms. Its packaging equipment is deliberately close to what’s used in industry, making it easier either to transfer processes or to manufacture initial volumes while an industrial route is established.
But he was clear that Fraunhofer should not remain the manufacturer indefinitely. “We can fill a gap,” he said. “But manufacturing should be industrialized. We are very interested in transferring our knowledge and processes so industry can do it.”
Build around Europe’s actual strengths
Both Aschenbrenner and Lust argued that Europe should be selective about what kind of packaging capacity it tries to build.
Aschenbrenner pointed to automotive and industrial markets, where Europe already has strong customers and specialized requirements. “We have to look at the real applications in Europe,” he said. “Do we really need to copy what is being done for extreme high-performance computing? I don’t think so. We should focus on the needs we actually have here.”
Lust made a similar argument. “Me-too is not the right approach,” he said. “Traditional packaging is already established elsewhere. Europe should strengthen the things it is already good at and scale those strengths into advanced packaging.”
That means complex integration, specialized industrial products, flexible manufacturing, and packaging platforms able to support many different applications rather than one enormous product family.
For Lust, Europe already has evidence that such a model can work. “In the industrial market, Europe is very strong,” he said. “We can handle complexity and variation. The key is to have your own platforms, your own ecosystem, and scale them across different applications.”
The missing piece is turning that capability into sustainable industrial infrastructure.
Fraunhofer can keep technologies alive through the dangerous interval between prototype and volume production. But if Europe wants a resilient advanced packaging supply chain, the final destination cannot be the pilot line.
It has to be industry.

articles.title: Could crypto give startups an edge? (Sponsored) | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Crypto can mean very different things to a startup. For one company, it could make international payments easier. For another, it might become part of a new financial product. And for plenty of businesses, it could simply be something they have no real need for.
Watching the Bitcoin price gives founders a sense of what is happening in the market, but it does not tell them whether crypto belongs in their own business.
Bitcoin crossed €74,222 ($85,000) on September 22 after ETF inflows hit €539.9 million ($617.6 million) in the previous session, according to Reuters reporting published by The Economic Times. That kind of movement is hard to ignore. It is also not necessarily the information a founder needs when deciding whether to adopt digital assets.
The better question is much more practical: where, if anywhere, could crypto make running a startup easier?
Why are startups exploring crypto?
Part of the interest comes down to how blockchain networks operate. They can run continuously, and digital assets can move between countries without following exactly the same route as a conventional bank payment.
For a young company working internationally, that can be interesting. A customer could be based in one country, contractors in another and suppliers somewhere else. Add different currencies and banking systems to the mix, and moving money can become even more complex.
Crypto is also becoming less separate from the financial system around it. Binance Research’s September 2026 Macro and Market Insights report found that equity holders’ share of crypto exposure rose from 64% to 72%. That suggests traditional market participants are playing a larger role in digital assets, too.
Where might it actually help?
There’s no standard crypto package that makes sense for every startup. A fintech business could have a clear use case, while a small software company selling locally might struggle to find one.
International payments are one possibility. A business dealing with customers or suppliers overseas could use digital assets as an additional way to move money. There are other options. A company could accept crypto payments from customers, build a product around tokenised assets or use existing blockchain networks as the infrastructure behind a financial service.
Smart contracts could also automate certain transactions where the conditions are straightforward.
Where does it get complicated?
The obvious concern is volatility. A company holding digital assets has to account for changes in their value. Even when crypto is only being accepted as payment, someone still has to decide how it will be stored, converted and recorded. And then there are the rules.
A startup operating across several countries can’t necessarily assume that the same approach will work everywhere. Digital assets, payments and taxation can all bring different requirements depending on the market.
Security is another practical issue. Blockchain transactions can be hard to undo, so losing control of a wallet or exposing private keys is not something a business can afford to treat casually. But there is an even more basic question worth asking: why use crypto in the first place?
If a startup already has a payment system that works and its customers are happy with it, adding crypto could simply create another thing to manage. There is little point taking on extra cost and complexity for the sake of having a new technology on the website.
Which startups might have a reason to try it?
Fintech startups are the clearest fit. Businesses working with payments, financial products or digital assets can use blockchain infrastructure as part of what they already do.
Other startups have more specific opportunities. An international marketplace could accept crypto payments. A gaming company could use blockchain for digital ownership. A creator platform could build services around digital assets.
Stablecoins are another option for businesses that want to accept crypto payments without holding large amounts of more volatile assets.
The key is having a clear use case. Startups don’t need to adopt crypto across the business. They can test one application and see whether it delivers a practical benefit.
What should a founder work out first?
Before adding a digital-asset feature, it is worth getting back to the basics. Ask what the technology is supposed to improve. Find out whether customers actually want the feature. Check the rules in every market involved. Decide who will handle security and custody.
Think about what happens if an asset’s value moves sharply. And, perhaps most importantly, work out whether the new system can slot into the tools the business already relies on.
Those answers will vary from startup to startup. There is no reason for a company with no obvious crypto use case to force one into its operations.
Crypto does not have to be the whole story
The growing overlap between crypto and traditional finance gives startups more choices, but choice doesn’t mean obligation.
For some founders, digital assets could solve a genuine problem or open up a service that would otherwise be difficult to build. For others, conventional financial infrastructure will remain the simpler route.
That’s probably the healthiest way to look at crypto in the startup world. It is a tool to consider, not a strategy in itself. If it makes something work better, there is a reason to explore it. If it does not, there is no need to force it.

articles.title: Pluto Security raises $42M as AI gives enterprise security teams a new headache | TechCrunch
articles.text:
The problem with giving everyone in a company access to AI tools is that people will use them in unexpected ways. And that fact is steadily seeding fears that companies now have new, gaping security holes in their systems or, at least, will soon.
Illustrating the pace of AI tool adoption within enterprises driving such fears, Shahar Bahat, CEO and co-founder of Pluto Security, says a newly announced AI tool can show up inside companies’ environment within a mere two hours of its release. And about 60% of the risks her company detects across its customer base are in tools vibe-coded by non-developers: Finance departments are the biggest source of such risks, she told TechCrunch, followed by marketing and legal teams. Developers rank fourth, she said.
Her startup’s tools apparently found a vibe-coded app made by a finance employee at a Fortune 500 company to manage customer information and churn, but the app was left exposed to the internet.
Pluto, fresh out of stealth with $42 million in funding, is the latest in a new crop of security startups that have quickly sprung up to help companies address those fears gaps, and all of them are raising big money from investors on the back of the conviction that only using existing security software to monitor and control AI tools, connectors, and usage is a square-peg-round-hole approach.
Bahat tells TechCrunch her startup started selling only in April and has already found some takers for its tech, which helps companies gain context, risk analysis, visibility, and control over how their employees use AI tools. She said Pluto began selling in April and has already crossed $2 million in annual recurring revenue, with more than 30 enterprise customers, including Oscar Health, Workato, Sixt, and AlphaSense.
Pluto’s funding spans an $8.5 million seed round led by TLV Partners, with cybersecurity firm Armis’ founders also investing. The company recently raised a Series A of $34 million led by Jump Capital, with Skinos (Check Point co-founder Shlomo Kramer’s venture firm), Ansa Capital, and other angel investors participating.
That’s decent traction for a young startup, though not unique in this AI era. But it may be because the breadth of the risk isn’t isolated to large tech companies that lead the AI adoption charts.
When I asked Bahat where she’s seeing the biggest risks, she said the issues are differentiated by the mindset of the CISO and how willing the organization is to adopt AI, but there were risks to be found anyway.
“In general, I’ll say there was not one POC in which we entered and didn’t find malicious stuff,” she said. “Whether those are extension packages or skills — some of them had active live attacks while we did the POC. Which again, for me, product-wise is amazing. For the companies, it’s not very good.”
Pluto’s entire bet is that securing such environments will require security tools to pay attention to what AI agents are doing in real time, in addition to keeping track of what and how employees are building and deploying.
“We’re moving from user behavior to agent behavior,” Bahat said.
In line with that vision, the startup’s software monitors the AI tools employees use, the skills, extensions, MCP servers, and other components those tools rely on, as well as the apps and agents being created. The company says it can identify risky components, spot potentially dangerous agent activity, and enforce security policies without stopping employees from using or making AI tools.
To do all that, Pluto connects to endpoint security and device management systems and can deploy its own sensors through them or directly onto devices. It gathers information, including prompts, commands, running processes, permissions, and users’ previous activity, and uses its own “lightweight” models on endpoints to help assess what an agent is trying to do.
What stood out is that Pluto’s system can intervene while an agent is working, Bahat said. If an agent tries to gain permissions beyond what a user intended, for example, the system can stop the action or add instructions into the session that prompt the agent to ask for confirmation.
“We can inject context back to the session, and this way I can change how the agent is working,” Bahat explained.
The startup also takes an unusual approach to finding customers. In April, it launched Plutonium, a free platform that lets anyone check risks associated with publicly available AI skills, connectors, and add-ons. There’s also an MCP scanner and a catalog of verified components. Bahat claims thousands of security professionals use Plutonium and that the community around it has become an important source of feedback and prospective customers.
She said 70% of Pluto’s sales pipeline now comes from inbound interest, although she didn’t break down how much of that comes directly through Plutonium.
Pluto said it plans to invest the new capital in developing its product, expanding its security research efforts, and growing its presence in the U.S. It has 40 employees in the U.S. and Israel.

articles.title: While WoW: Forever's Collector's Edition offers a game code, God of War Laufey's 'Collector's Box' is taking the GTA 6 approach and doesn't come with a copy of the game — 'Eventually the statue is going to be digital as well'
articles.text:
Like GTA 6, God of War Laufey's 'Collector's Box' doesn't come with a copy of the game, and fans are outraged — 'I see Rockstar is an inspiration for everyone'
The Collector's Box is priced at £130 / $149.99
- The God of War Laufey - Collector's Box has been revealed for £130 / $149.99
- The box doesn't include a copy of the game, just like Grand Theft Auto 6's collector's edition
- Fans are frustrated with the exclusion of the game from the collection, with some calling it "greedy"
Santa Monica Studio has revealed its God of War Laufey Collector's Box, and just like Rockstar's Grand Theft Auto 6 collector's edition, the pricey package doesn't include the game.
The studio shared the "Collector's Box" in a social media post, confirming that the £130 / $149.99 package includes a light-up Faye statue, 51-card Oracle Deck, and a mini art book, noting that the God of War Laufey game is "sold separately."
That's the part of the announcement that has fans talking, with many sharing their frustration over yet another collector's edition that doesn't offer a physical or digital copy of the game.
"I remember when collector's editions used to come with games. Not liking this new trend," one user responded, as another wrote, "'Game sold separately?' ...man, [the] gaming industry is getting greedier and greedier."
The lack of physical games has been a point of contention ever since Sony announced its plans to stop producing game discs by January 2028. The PlayStation company isn't alone; Rockstar Games is also skipping physical discs for GTA 6, the biggest game launch of all time, and players will instead receive a code in the box, a decision that initially caused an uproar.
On top of that, the studio recently announced The Goodtime State – Vice City Collection, a £349 / $399 premium collector's box featuring exclusive merchandise and no game.
"I see Rockstar is an inspiration for everyone," one redditor said about the Laufey - Collector's Box.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Another said, "We need to stop calling these collectors edition when they dont include the game and start calling them over priced cash grabs."
For now, it doesn't look like every company is cutting out games from their expensive collector's editions; Blizzard, for example, is selling its World of Warcraft: Forever's Collector's Edition with a digital download code included, and Tomb Raider: Legacy of Atlantis's version will also offer a physical copy and steelbook alongside other goodies.
Still, fans are particularly worried about the future of collector's editions, which used to typically offer more than just a pretty statue and artbook.
"They [Santa Monica Studio] soft launched this back in Ragnarok, when the collector's edition only had a download code, same for Horizon Forbidden West. Eventually the statue is going to be digital as well," remarked a fan.

articles.title: What’s old is new: Lightwell discovers novel zero-day vulnerability in core Java framework
articles.text:
Enterprise IT runs on decades-old foundational code. The prevailing assumption around these mature components is that if code has been sitting untouched in production for ten years without breaking, it must be safe. Libraries like the Eclipse Implementation of Jakarta XML Binding (JAXB) quietly power enterprise applications in the background. Embedded deep into middleware stacks and application servers, they carry heavy workloads without drawing attention.
Advanced AI security tooling doesn’t ignore these deep-stack layers, however. It finds zero-day flaws hidden in structural parsing logic that standard static analysis tools miss entirely. And discovery is only part of the story. Any new vulnerabilities impacting these load-bearing pillars need to be discovered, analyzed, and swiftly addressed by the community. This is exactly what Lightwell did with a novel vulnerability within JAXB, identified as CVE-2026-92877.
Addressing novel flaws across the software lifecycle
When a vulnerability is discovered in a new framework, communities and maintainers respond quickly. The code is fresh, developers are actively tweaking it, and patches roll out quickly. Legacy components face a different reality. Unaddressed flaws in fundamental XML binding logic can compromise every application server, middleware pipeline, and cloud service that relies on it.
Left unaddressed, a flaw like this could create severe operational consequences:
- Chained exploits: Isolated parsing bugs can be chained with other system vulnerabilities to escalate privileges, bypass access controls, or even execute arbitrary code.
- Unplanned downtime: Malformed payloads can trigger unhandled exceptions or resource exhaustion deep within key services, bringing critical business workflows to a sudden halt.
- Supply-chain amplification: Because JAXB is buried deep within thousands of enterprise software packages, downstream vendors and IT teams often don't realize they are exposed until an exploit hits production.
Discovering and addressing a novel vulnerability in a legacy codebase in real-time is key, not simply finding the problem and passing the hard work to the community. Lightwell’s work with JAXB shows the value that a collaborative, responsible, and technically innovative security practice brings to global IT infrastructure, as well as the health of upstream open source communities.
True security is upstream security
Scanning a container image and flagging a potential common vulnerability and exploit (CVE) is relatively easy with modern off-the-shelf tooling. Finding a zero-day flaw in a decade-old upstream project, engineering a fix, and contributing that patch back to the open source community is hard.
That is the core value proposition of Lightwell.
Lightwell centers on active engineering at the source and deep-level stewardship. When the Lightwell team uncovers a novel vulnerability or one is brought to our attention by a customer, our mission is to fix it upstream at the source.
By contributing this fix directly to the eclipse-ee4j community, Lightwell helps protect the broader open source ecosystem before downstream enterprise runtimes face exposure. These upstream contributions, however, are only part of the equation.
In many enterprise environments, critical infrastructure runs on older software versions that upstream communities no longer actively patch or maintain. Upstream maintainers eventually move on to new major releases. When a flaw impacts legacy versions, downstream systems are left exposed.
Lightwell steps in during those exact scenarios. Whether fixing current code upstream or backporting security patches to older releases that organizations still rely on, Lightwell helps protect critical workloads without forcing disruptive, unplanned upgrades. 
Durability is an active commitment
Durable enterprise software, the kind that allows critical infrastructure to run reliably for decades, isn’t easy to deliver. It requires continuous, active maintenance and rigorous upstream security engineering. Red Hat delivered this work for the better part of 30 years across Linux, Java, Kubernetes, and supporting projects.
The discovery and upstream acceptance of this patch to JAXB is a major milestone for Lightwell and further validates our core commitment to open source security. Protecting critical enterprise applications starts deep in the software stack, and Lightwell provides the engineering required to keep those foundations resilient.

articles.title: From Enterprise to Earthshot: UK’s Ecosystem Moves From Ambition to Application With NVIDIA
articles.text:
Across industries, the U.K. is putting the full stack to work — and the scale of deployment is growing fast, from enterprises transforming their businesses to startups solving some of the planet’s hardest problems.
NVIDIA is putting that principle into practice, including through a five-year, $250 million compute commitment to strengthen the U.K.’s agentic safety and security research.
In addition, NVIDIA is partnering with the Earthshot Prize, joining as a Global Alliance Founding Partner to bring compute and technical expertise to innovators working on solutions for the world’s greatest climate and sustainability challenges.
Technology Leaders Pioneer Intelligent Solutions Across the UK
In energy, Fuse Energy is moving its customer AI onto its own in-house infrastructure, built on NVIDIA B300 Blackwell Ultra, delivering faster, more responsive support to over 450,000 U.K. households.
Meanwhile, sovereign AI company Locai Labs released Nemotron-Personas-UK — an open source dataset of one million synthetic personas representing the UK’s demographic, regional and cultural diversity — helping developers build fairer, more representative AI systems.
Healthcare
In healthcare, OneAdvanced is deploying what it calls the U.K.’s first and most advanced fine-tuned LLM for Primary Care AI-triage — built with NVIDIA Agent Toolkit software and open models — supporting millions of National Health Service patients.
Heidi has now integrated NVIDIA Nemotron open models to give clinicians faster access to trusted medical evidence.
Speechmatics is deploying Oak, a multilingual medical speech recognition model, using NVIDIA Triton Inference — giving healthcare organizations control over where sensitive patient audio is processed.
Apian, Synnovis and NVIDIA are teaming up to use advanced computing and digital simulations using NVIDIA Cosmos to help hospital robots handle the heavy lifting of moving lab samples, freeing up medical staff to focus on patient care.
Danaher and NVIDIA are collaborating to advance autonomous science and help accelerate the pace of discovery by bringing accelerated computing, scientific and physical AI into laboratory workflows and instruments. Danaher’s recently announced AI-powered autonomous lab — designed to deliver up to 8x faster discovery of affinity reagents — is using NVIDIA BioNeMo open models within its AI-driven protein design workflows, data and automation technologies that connect design with experimental feedback.
Smart Cities
On the civic side, Liverpool City Region is building an NVIDIA-powered “City Brain” — a sovereign AI strategy designed as a blueprint for dozens of Unitary Authorities across the U.K.
Digital Jersey, Innovation City Belfast and Tees Valley Combined Authority are each exploring how trusted AI compute can serve communities and public services.
Financial Services
In financial services, LSEG and NVIDIA are bringing GPU-accelerated market analytics to global institutions.
Revolut introduced PRAGMA earlier in the year — a foundation model for banking event sequences, pre-trained on 26 million anonymised user histories. PRAGMA has moved from research to real-time scaling.
Lloyds Banking Group built ATUM, a transaction foundation model that converts billions of banking transactions into reusable AI. And Starling is developing a banking foundation model trained on Civo’s U.K. sovereign cloud infrastructure.
NatWest is collaborating with NVIDIA on Nemotron Voice to better understand how banking customers across the U.K. speak, while Modulr is deploying a network of agents using Nemotron for distinct parts of payment operations.
Quantum
Quantum is moving from research to systems deployable alongside classical AI, and the U.K. is at the heart of this shift.
Riverlane has shown how GPUs can accelerate decoder recalibration workflows used in quantum error correction, helping decoder performance keep pace with real-time changes in quantum hardware behaviour. The work forms part of a broader collaboration exploring how AI, accelerated computing and quantum error-correction technologies can work together to support future quantum systems.
Together, these announcements showcase how enterprises, organizations and startups in the U.K. are fostering innovation across the nation. This includes more than 3,100 U.K. companies that are a part of the NVIDIA Inception program for cutting-edge startups.
Tune in to NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang’s GTC Berlin keynote on Wednesday, Oct. 21, at 11 a.m. CEST.

articles.title: Russian bot farms are still trolling, even after Ukraine’s drone strikes on Yandex
articles.text:
Days after Ukrainian military drones took down several Russian data centers, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy claimed that the campaign had hurt Russia’s disinformation efforts. “It suddenly became a little easier to breathe on many social platforms,” Zelenskyy said Monday. “There was less hate, less division, and fewer provocations.”
Russian bot farms are still trolling, even after Ukraine’s drone strikes on Yandex
Zelenskyy celebrated ‘less division’ on social media after the strikes but the data isn’t backing that up yet.
Zelenskyy isn’t the first to assert that the drone operation, which targeted data centers belonging to the Russian technology company Yandex, has cut down on spam and disinformation campaigns fomented by Russian bot farms. Social media users have claimed they’ve noticed less traffic on posts by MAGA-affiliated accounts, as well as those associated with the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party. Some have even said they’ve noticed a steep drop in spam calls and messages.
But these people are wrong. The drone strikes appear to have affected Yandex’s web crawlers, not any disinformation or political operations.
In fact, the account antibot4navalny, which tracks state-sponsored troll farms, reports that bot traffic is steady as ever. On Monday, the same day Zelenskyy claimed that disinformation had died down, antibot4navalny reported that several Kremlin-aligned accounts posted videos falsely claiming that experts are demanding the European Union lift the ongoing sanctions on Russia. Danish analyst Valdemar Osted said interactions on MAGA and AfD accounts have actually increased since the strikes. And the charts purportedly showing a decline in bot activity appear to be AI-generated.
Ironically, claims that the drone strikes hindered Russian disinformation campaigns appears to be a form of disinformation itself, no matter what Zelenskyy says.

articles.title: Surround-System für Apple TV: Homepod Mini 2 vorgestellt
articles.text:
Verzögerungen bei dem neuen KI-System Siri AI sollen dafür gesorgt haben, dass Apple bisher mit der Veröffentlichung überarbeiteter Versionen von Homepod Mini und Apple TV noch warten musste. Dabei stammen die Geräte technisch gesehen aus den Jahren 2020 (Homepod Mini) beziehungsweise 2022 (Apple TV) und galten damit als veraltet.
Apple bringt Homepod Mini 2
Wie von Branchenbeobachter:innen erwartet, hat Apple dem Homepod Mini 2 und dem neuen Apple TV 4K eine Frischekur verpasst. Darüber hinaus stellte der iPhone-Konzern am 13. Oktober 2026 mit dem Homeview auch das ebenfalls prophezeite 7-Zoll-Smart-Display mit Siri AI vor. Letzteres kommt aber ebenso wie die gemeinsam mit LG Electronics und Schneider Electric entwickelte Smart-Home-Gerätereihe Apple Home Collection vorerst nicht in die EU.
Zum Preis von 169 Euro schon vorbestellen kann man dagegen in Deutschland den Homepod Mini 2 – allerdings ohne die KI-Funktionen von Siri. Die Auslieferung soll ab 30. Oktober 2026 erfolgen. Das Gerät gibt es in den Farben Rosa, Grün, Blau, Weiß und Mitternacht.
Die Funktion Sound Glow soll es möglich machen, dass die smarten Lautsprecher synchron zur Musik leuchten und pulsieren und in Echtzeit auf Bässe und Höhen reagieren. Die Farben entsprechen denen der Album-Gestaltung der gerade laufenden Titel. Auch Geräusche wie Regen lösen entsprechende visuelle Animationen aus.
Echtzeitanalyse von Musik
Im Inneren des Homepod Mini 2 arbeitet Apples S10-Chip, der gemeinsam mit Computational Audio eine Echtzeitanalyse von Musik ermöglichen soll. Dadurch sollen sich Dynamikbereich, Lautstärke und akustische Performance optimieren lassen.
Die Lautsprecher liefern 360-Grad-Sound und lassen sich Apple zufolge einzeln, als Stereopaar oder als Teil eines Multiroom-Setups betreiben. Als Smart-Home-Hub übernimmt der Homepod Mini 2 auch die Kommunikation mit anderen Smart-Home-Geräten wie Türschlösser oder Thermostate.
Inkludiert ist ebenfalls eine Geräuscherkennung, die Alarmsignale von Rauch- oder CO-Meldern erkennen und entsprechende Warnungen an iPhone, iPad und Apple Watch schicken soll. Die Home-App soll es zudem ermöglichen, dass externe Nutzer:innen live zuhören und mit Personen im Haushalt sprechen können sollen.
Surround-System für Heimkinofans
Heimkinofans können vier der Lautsprecher zusammen mit dem neuen Apple TV 4K zudem als Surround-System nutzen. Die Geräte sollen dabei Timing und Lautstärke des Audiosignals automatisch auf den Raum abstimmen können.
Das neue Apple TV 4K kostet 349 Euro und kann hier vorbestellt werden. In den Handel kommt das Gerät ab dem 13. November 2026. Mehr zu der Box und ihren Features liest du hier.

articles.title: Promise Robotics strikes deal to supply largest US homebuilder DR Horton
articles.text:
Toronto-based construction tech startup Promise Robotics is ready to grow south of the border after landing its first United States (US) customer: DR Horton, the nation’s largest homebuilder in terms of volume.
Through the multi-year commercial agreement, DR Horton will leverage Promise’s tech and “factory-as-a-service” capabilities to support the production of more than 1,250 largely single-story, single-family homes for buyers in the Phoenix, Arizona area.
Promise CEO Ramtin Attar said a deal like this “requires quite a bit of trust.”
Promise co-founder and CEO Ramtin Attar told BetaKit in an interview that a deal like this “requires quite a bit of trust.” He said the deal emphasizes the power of the startup’s platform, which aims to help developers build homes faster and more cheaply than traditional construction methods.
“That a company at that scale is able to look at what we have done and say, ‘We’re ready to work with you,’ that, to me, is very significant,” Attar added.
Promise announced the deal today, also revealing it intends to open a 16,000-square-foot factory in Phoenix. There, its AI-powered robots will assemble the components necessary to construct these houses in what marks the start of its broader US expansion. “This is our go-to-market facility in [the] US,” Attar said.
The hub, which will be Promise’s first outside of Canada and the company’s third of its kind after Calgary and Edmonton, is expected to begin manufacturing in early 2027.
“I was actually talking to an investor the other day who said, ‘I really love your odds. If you can build in the frost in Calgary, Phoenix is going to be pretty darn simple,’ and that’s exactly the case,” Attar said.
While the US housing market is very different from Canada’s, Attar said it faces similar challenges, from labour shortages to rising costs, and pressure to build more homes faster.
RELATED: Canada’s housing supply is in crisis. Can robots help?
Promise uses AI to interpret existing home designs, generate production plans and robotic instructions, orchestrate manufacturing, and connect that production with site installation as part of one integrated platform. The company equips off-the-shelf robots with its own tooling and software to produce everything from repeatable modular housing to custom builds.
“We are continuously focused on improving cycle times, increasing production capacity, and bringing greater consistency and predictability to our operations,” DR Horton senior vice president of strategic innovation Brad Conlon said in a statement. “Promise Robotics’ integrated platform gives us a new capability to support those goals.”
Attar claimed Promise, which is now contracted to build just over 2,500 homes for several different homebuilders, has completed over 200 builds to date for a group that includes Brookfield, Hopewell, and Mattamy.
“These are real market homes that people are living in,” the Autodesk alumnus said.
Promise’s factories are currently capable of producing many of the core components that make a house, from the interior and exterior walls to the flooring, stairs, and roof.
The 80-person startup is working to add heating, ventilation, and air conditioning, and plumbing, followed by drywall, insulation, and more over time as it looks to grow to 100 employees by the end of 2026.
Feature image courtesy Promise Robotics.

articles.title: Netflix compra los derechos exclusivos del Mundial 2030 y emitirá todo el torneo en España
articles.text:
Netflix acaba de anunciar que ha adquirido los derechos exclusivos de la Copa Mundial de la FIFA 2030. La plataforma de streaming redobla una vez más su apuesta por el contenido deportivo y emitirá el evento más importante del mundo del fútbol en España y Andorra. Así, el servicio ofrecerá en directo a sus suscriptores los 104 partidos de la mayor competición deportiva del planeta.
La Copa Mundial de la FIFA 2030 conmemorará el centenario de la competición. Curiosamente España, vigente campeona del mundo, será uno de sus tres países anfitriones. El país compartirá la organización con Portugal y Marruecos. Además, con motivo de ese centenario, Argentina, Paraguay y Uruguay acogerán algunos de los primeros partidos de la fase de grupos.
Todos esos encuentros del Mundial 2030 se podrán ver en Netflix tanto en España como en Andorra. Además, como parte del acuerdo, en España podrá verse gratis un partido de cada jornada. Y también se ofrecerá a una cadena nacional de televisión en abierto (todavía por determinar cuál) un paquete de partidos que incluirá todos los de España, las dos semifinales y la final.
Como parte de su estrategia de emisión del Mundial 2030, Netflix tiene previsto también ofrecer la cobertura íntegra y en directo del torneo, con emisión de programas —con un planteamiento genuinamente español— antes de cada partido, durante el descanso y después del encuentro, además de un programa resumen diario los días de partido y otros contenidos destinados a generar expectación en la antesala del torneo.
Netflix emitirá el Mundial 2030
El acuerdo se suma a la creciente oferta de deportes en directo de primer nivel de Netflix en todo el mundo, que abarca las ediciones del 2027 y 2031 de la Copa Mundial Femenina de la FIFA, partidos y eventos de la NFL, la MLB, WWE y algunos de los principales combates de boxeo y de artes marciales mixtas (MMA).
"Pocos acontecimientos unen tanto a la gente como un Mundial. Este año, yo estaba en el estadio cuando España levantó el trofeo y viví de primera mano la pasión, el orgullo y las historias que acaban formando parte de la cultura de un país y perduran en la memoria durante generaciones. Ahora que España va a ser uno de los países anfitriones en 2030, nos hace muchísima ilusión ofrecer en Netflix todos los partidos a los aficionados de España y Andorra", confiesa Bela Bajaria, directora jefe de Contenidos de Netflix, en un comunicado remitido a la prensa.
"Para los aficionados españoles al fútbol, recibir al mundo como vigentes campeones y poder seguir todos los partidos en Netflix hará que esta ocasión sea única. Además, nuestra creciente colaboración con la FIFA, que incluye las ediciones del 2027 y 2031 de la Copa Mundial Femenina de la FIFA en Estados Unidos y Canadá, refleja nuestro compromiso constante por acercar a los aficionados a los grandes momentos del deporte mundial", añade.

articles.title: Cómo crear contraseñas que protejan nuestra vida digital
articles.text:
Cómo crear contraseñas que protejan nuestra vida digital
El uso de claves débiles en dispositivos, programas y aplicaciones y el repetirlas en varias cuentas facilita el trabajo a los ciberdelincuentes. Pero hay maneras de no ponérselo fácil
Las contraseñas que protegen nuestros perfiles son uno de los principales objetivos de los ciberdelincuentes, que obtienen mediante el robo de bases de datos o a través del envío de correos y SMS en los que suplantan a instituciones y empresas. Si usamos la misma clave en diversas plataformas, como las de correo electrónico, las redes sociales o los comercios en línea, les resultarámás sencillo acceder a ellas en el caso de los ciberdelincuentes la consigan.
En 2025, se produjo una de las mayores filtraciones de credenciales en internet de la historia: quedaron expuestas 16.000 millones de claves de cuentas de Google, Apple y Facebook, entre otras plataformas, de acuerdo con una investigación de Cybernews, un medio de comunicación digital independiente especializado en tecnología y ciberseguridad. Existen páginas web como Haveibeenpwned.com, donde comprobar si una dirección de correo ha sido filtrada.
CÓMO OBTIENEN LOS CIBERDELINCUENTES LAS CONTRASEÑAS
'Phishing'
Campañas de correo electrónico, SMS o voz en las que los delincuentes suplantan la identidad de organismos públicos y empresas privadas para robar los datos de los usuarios. Al hacer clic en un enlace o al meter sus datos (usuario y contraseña) en una web falsa, los estafadores se hacen con ellos
'Infostealers'
Programas maliciosos que se cuelan en los dispositivos cuando el usuario hace clic en un enlace. Estos 'softwares' están especializados en extraer contraseñas almacenadas en navegadores, programas y sistemas
Ataque de fuerza bruta
Ofensiva automatizada que, mediante un programa informático, prueba millones de combinaciones hasta dar con la correcta
Filtración de credenciales
Los delincuentes piratean los sistemas informáticos de empresas para obtener las bases de datos de sus clientes, que posteriormente ponen a la venta en la web oscura
Ciberexperta
Nombre Virginia Fuster
Cargo Responsable de Cultura de Ciberseguridad y Fraude de CaixaBank
        “Las filtraciones de credenciales están a la orden del día. Para reducir su impacto es fundamental utilizar contraseñas robustas y diferentes para cada servicio”
0:00
CÓMO CREAR UNA CONTRASEÑA ROBUSTA
- 
                1
                Debe ser variada Una clave de acceso se puede componer a partir de distintos tipos de caracteres, como letras mayúsculas y minúsculas, números y caracteres especiales. Utilizar la mayor variedad posible aumenta la dificultad para ser descifrada
- 
                2
                Debe ser larga Como referencia, es preferible utilizar 16 caracteres o más, cuando el servicio lo permita. Utilizar una frase puede ser más fácil de recordar
- 
                3
                Evitar la información personal Eludir el propio nombre o el apellido, así como los de familiares, las fechas de nacimiento, los apodos, los nombres de mascotas, los de equipos de fútbol favoritos o cualquier otra información que se pueda encontrar en las propias redes sociales
- 
                4
                Evitar combinaciones predecibles Muchos usuarios recurren a composiciones como 123456, password y otras secuencias sencillas que conviene eludir
- 
                5
                Utilizar un gestor de contraseñas Existen programas seguros, de pago y gratuitos, que permiten generar y almacenar estos códigos sin tener que memorizarlos
- 
                6
                Activar la autenticación multifactor (MFA, por sus siglas en inglés) Un tipo de protección presente en algunas plataformas. Añade una segunda barrera de seguridad en caso de que alguien consiga la contraseña. Consisten en verificar el acceso desde otra aplicación o con un código que se envía en forma de e-mail o SMS
CASOS DE FILTRACIÓN DE CREDENCIALES TRAS UN CIBERATAQUE

articles.title: Docker Hub flaw let attackers impersonate users, tamper with images
articles.text:
Docker has disclosed a critical vulnerability (CVE-2026-105445) in Docker Hub that let attackers access another user’s container repositories using a personal access token (PAT).
Docker Hub is an online registry for storing, sharing, and downloading container images - templates that package everything needed for an application to run in an isolated environment.
In Docker Hub, a PAT serves as a secret used to authenticate tools and workflows. It allows you to pull, push, or delete container images.
According to a security bulletin from the Docker team, an attacker could create an account and PAT, then convert the account into an organization and name a target user as its owner.
The CVE-2026-105445 flaw stems from Docker Hub reassigning a personal access token (PAT) to a designated organization owner without changing its secret or obtaining the target's consent. This allowed the attacker to use the token to authenticate as the target.
Depending on the token’s scope and the target’s permissions, attackers could pull, push, or delete images in the target’s repositories and accessible organizations.
“Within the scope of the token, a re-assigned PAT acted as the target user at the registry level, meaning an attacker could potentially pull, push, and/or delete images in the target’s repositories and in organizations where the target had access,” Docker explained.
“Because that includes publishing images under a legitimate name, we treated this as a software supply chain risk and rated it critical.”
Although the flaw is critical, Docker noted that it did not provide Docker Hub web access or allow attackers to change passwords, email addresses, or two-factor settings, potentially locking legitimate account holders out.
The vulnerability was introduced on August 26, 2024, when the conversion started reassigning the personal account PAT to the new owner. This occurred without revoking or rotating the secret, and without asking the named owner to confirm the change.
On September 30, 2026, Docker received a vulnerability report describing the issue, confirmed it, and deployed a fix to production less than four hours later.
Docker says it found no evidence of exploitation after examining 304,000 pushes made with transferred tokens and analyzing high-risk public images.
Affected users and organization owners were notified on October 2, and transferred PATs were deactivated on October 8, except for those whose owners explicitly requested to retain them.
Docker says users who didn’t receive a notification should assume they were not impacted and did not need to take any action.
The platform no longer transfers PATs during conversion and requests user consent before naming them an organization owner.
Build your security blueprint for AI-powered attacks
Join Mikko Hyppönen and security leaders from the NFL, CHANEL, and Atlassian for a two-hour digital summit on what AI-speed attacks change, what defenders should stop doing, and how to validate, decide, fix, and re-validate at machine speed.
