articles.title: Ces chercheurs croient tellement en l'IA qu'ils se mettent à faire n'importe quoi
articles.text:
"Merci, j'essaie de commencer" dirait OSS 117 quand on lui tend une cigarette. C'est exactement ce que font des chercheurs, prétendant dur comme fer que l'intelligence artificielle leur permettra de guérir de tous leurs maux liés à des années de tabagisme.
On pourrait se demander quelle mouche les a piqués, mais aussi comprendre leur point de vue purement expérimental. L'idée n'en reste pas moins très douteuse, mais aussi coûteuse, tant sur le plan financier que sur le plan physique. Selon Shyam Sankar, directeur technique de Palantir, certains chercheurs en intelligence artificielle auraient commencé à fumer pour démontrer leur foi dans la capacité de cette technologie à guérir le cancer à l'avenir. Un pari risqué et … vraiment utile ?
Jouer sa santé comme une partie de poker
Shyam Sankar a présenté cette "expérience" lors d'une apparition sur le plateau de CBS Face the Nation dimanche.
Il a expliqué que cette pratique fonctionnerait comme un signal adressé à leurs pairs, illustrant l'ampleur de leur conviction envers l'IA. "Je crois tellement en l'IA pour guérir le cancer. Je montre ainsi que j'ai mis tous mes jetons sur la table," a-t-il déclaré, avant d'évoquer une "psychose de masse" autour de ce sujet.
Le responsable a également comparé cette foi à une forme de religiosité, en référence à la notion philosophique d'un vide spirituel que les travailleurs de la Silicon Valley comblent avec l'intelligence artificielle.
Des questions d'ordre sanitaire
Si cette affirmation s'avère fondée, elle soulève des questions d'ordre sanitaire. En effet, même si l'IA parvenait à contribuer au développement de traitements anticancéreux efficaces, le tabagisme reste responsable de plusieurs formes de cancer et de nombreux autres problèmes de santé à terme. S'ajoutent à cela les délais nécessaires pour tester ces traitements et les autres risques pour la santé liés à cette consommation.
Sankar pointe également une tendance plus large : plusieurs articles récents mentionnent une réapparition du tabagisme dans certains milieux des nouvelles technologies, ce qui pourrait partiellement valider ses observations.
Il en reste que même si l'intelligence artificielle était capable de guérir l'immense majorité des maladies, et tous les cancers, passer par cette étape reste tout de même une contrainte et un parcours parfois de plusieurs mois ou années pour s'en sortir.
Une croyance aveugle en l'IA qui en fait dérailler certains
Croire aveuglément que l'on peut se mettre à fumer pendant 40 ans, avoir un cancer et en guérir via les technologies de détection et de soin par IA reste un pari très risqué. Déjà, faut-il avoir le budget pour une telle expérience, fumer suffisamment d'années, puis avoir son cancer tant attendu, et évidemment ne pas faire de crise cardiaque ou ne pas avoir d'accident de voiture avant.
Dans 20, 30 ou 40 ans, les technologies d'intelligence artificielle auront largement évolué et sans aucun doute dans le bon sens en termes de santé. Mais s'il n'y avait pas suffisamment de maladies à traiter en ce moment, est-ce vraiment utile d'en rajouter volontairement ?

articles.title: GitHub’s model for secret detection: Finding more secrets with less noise
articles.text:
GitHub’s model for secret detection: Finding more secrets with less noise
GitHub’s context-aware secret classifier improves detection quality, raises weighted acceptance by 11.5%, and reduces median scan execution time by 86%.
Smarter secret scanning, at a fraction of the cost
11.5%
higher acceptance
Owner-weighted alert precision
86%
lower median scan execution time
Post-push scanning
98%
lower serving cost
Compact model vs. remote LLM calls
Secret scanning works best when developers are confident in the findings. Catch too little, and real credentials can remain in a repository. Alert too often, and developers may spend time investigating strings that aren’t secrets.
Generic secrets make that balance especially difficult. The same string could be a real credential or a documentation placeholder, so detecting it requires understanding the surrounding code and text.
To address this challenge, we trained a secret classifier specifically for GitHub’s product needs: distinguishing real credentials from lookalikes while meeting the speed and efficiency requirements of scanning at scale.
In our companion post, Secret protection must scale with software, we explained why secret protection must keep pace with AI-accelerated development. Here, we go behind the scenes of the context-aware classifier powering that effort: how we designed, trained, and evaluated it to find more real secrets with less noise.
What we enabled
GitHub secret scanning operates at two key moments:
Push protection helps prevent secrets from entering a repository by scanning changes before a push is accepted, giving developers an opportunity to address the finding.
Post-push scanning works after code has been committed, continuously scanning repository content and creating alerts when potential secrets are detected so developers and security teams can investigate and remediate them.
We developed a fast classifier that reduced median post-push scan execution time by 86% compared with the previous LLM-based pipeline. That efficiency made it practical to extend generic secret detection to push protection, returning results before developers push changes, not only after code is committed.
Why secrets are hard to detect
Structured credentials often include a distinctive prefix, length, alphabet, or checksum. Generic secrets may not. Their syntax overlaps with build identifiers, checksums, asset hashes, sample values, and other non-sensitive strings. Context is the deciding signal.
Likely real credential
Likely harmless lookalike
A password assigned beside a production database URL
The same password-shaped value in a test fixture
A connection string in deployment configuration
A localhost connection string in a setup guide
A high-entropy value bound to an API credential
A high-entropy checksum, build ID, or asset hash
These cases are hard negatives: strings that match a credential pattern but are not usable credentials. Adding more rules can suppress some of them, but each exception risks hiding a real secret. A learned classifier can instead use signals such as file path, secret type, variable names, and nearby code or text.
That is why we shipped a new scanner using a two-stage pipeline:
Candidate generation: Regex filters scan content for potential secrets with high recall. This stage is optimized to catch broad families of credential-like patterns quickly and deterministically.
Context-aware classification: A fine-tuned ModernBERT classifier evaluates each candidate and its surrounding context. It is trained to recognize the signals that separate real secrets from false positives, including placeholder values, examples, documentation snippets, generated content, and non-sensitive identifiers. Because the model is small and efficient to run on our inference infrastructure, it costs much less to serve and is simpler to scale than an LLM-based pipeline.
Impact:
11.5% user acceptance improvement, reducing false positives.
More than 98% cost savings compared with the LLM-based pipeline.
How our pipeline works
As content is scanned, regex patterns cast a wide net and flag anything that looks like a credential, so real secrets aren’t missed at the start. Each candidate then goes to a fine-tuned ModernBERT classifier, which reads the value together with its file path, variable names, and surrounding code. The classifier estimates how likely it is to be a real secret. High-confidence findings become alerts, and lookalikes such as placeholders, test fixtures, and checksums are filtered out before they reach developers.
HOW OUR PIPELINE WORKS
Broad first, careful second
STEP 1
Scan
Repository content, commits, pull requests, and other scanned surfaces.
STEP 2
Generate candidates
Regex patterns identify possible tokens, keys, and credential-like strings.
STEP 3
Classify
Fine-tuned ModernBERT evaluates candidate + context and assigns likelihood of a true secret.
STEP 4
Alert or suppress
High-confidence findings move forward; likely false positives are filtered.
The important design choice is that the model does not replace deterministic scanning. Instead, it complements it. Regexes remain the right tool for finding candidate strings quickly. The classifier is used where machine learning provides the most leverage: distinguishing “looks like a secret” from “is likely a real secret.”
A hard-negative problem: secrets that almost look real
Most false positives are not random. They are hard negatives: strings that match a credential pattern but are not usable credentials. Examples include documentation placeholders, toy examples in tests, redacted values, non-sensitive IDs, and generated fixtures. These cases are easy for a regex to match and hard for a purely rule-based system to suppress without accidentally losing real secrets.
ModernBERT helps because it can read the candidate together with nearby code and text providing contextual understanding comparable to an LLM without the latency and computational overhead of generating natural-language output. For example, a candidate surrounded by words like “example,” “dummy,” “fake,” or “replace-me” may be lower risk than a candidate assigned to an environment variable in a deployment file. The classifier learns these contextual differences from labeled examples rather than requiring engineers to encode every exception as another rule.
We chose ModernBERT because it provides a strong fit for this workload: it is compact, efficient, and well suited for classification over code-adjacent text. For secret scanning, the model needs to make a calibrated decision over short candidate windows with high throughput and low latency.
That makes a fine-tuned encoder classifier a better serving shape than a general-purpose LLM for this stage of the pipeline. The model can be trained directly on our decision boundary, and evaluated using the same recall and precision metrics that matter to secret scanning quality.
How we trained
The challenge was finding representative data for cases in which syntax alone is misleading. The training and evaluation strategy combines three sources:
Product-derived examples from GitHub repositories, using feedback from the secret detection experience and additional human validation.
High-recall regex candidates from GitHub repository data, including human-annotated examples and weak labels used to expand coverage.
Synthetic examples targeted at sparse and difficult cases, such as documentation secrets, test fixtures, public keys, checksums, structured lookalikes, and near-miss pairs.
Synthetic rows pass deterministic validation and model-based quality review before inclusion. Training emphasizes real secrets, realistic false positives, and hard negatives that frequently confuse regex-only approaches. Each model input includes the candidate value, file path, secret type, and a bounded amount of surrounding context. We select thresholds through offline evaluation and then validate behavior on production-like traffic before broader rollout.
Before splitting the data, we grouped rows that share a repository, candidate value, or example so near-duplicates could not appear in both training and evaluation.
Training focused on the cases that matter most for alert quality: real secrets, realistic false positives, and hard negatives that regexes frequently match. The input representation includes the candidate secret string, file path, type and a bounded amount of surrounding context. The output is a classification score used by the scanner to decide whether the candidate should proceed.
We optimized for the product tradeoff: preserve or improve recall while reducing false positives and serving cost. In practice, that means the classifier threshold is selected using offline evaluation, then validated against production-like traffic before rollout.
The most important training principle was to make the model see the confusing examples. We included candidates that are syntactically similar to real secrets but semantically different, so the model learns not only what a secret looks like, but also what a false positive looks like in context.
The trained model is exported to ONNX format with 8-bit quantization, enabling fast inference.
Evaluation results
Online result
Change vs. previous LLM pipeline
What it measures
Repository owner-weighted acceptance
11.5% higher
Customer acceptance of detected findings
Median post-push scan execution time
86% lower
Production scan execution time
Serving cost
More than 98% lower
Cost of the compact classifier compared with remote LLM calls
Customer A/B evaluation results for our fine-tuned model compared to the previous LLM pipeline.
We evaluated the new pipeline’s impact in production in two stages: first against the production baseline on the same public traffic and then through a customer A/B experiment.
Offline evaluation: On post-push scanning, the new pipeline achieved 13% higher precision and 19% higher recall than the previous LLM pipeline when evaluated on the same public traffic.
Online evaluation: We then validated whether these quality improvements translated to customer outcomes through an A/B experiment against the previous LLM pipeline. Repository owner-weighted acceptance increased by 11.5%. We weight acceptance by repository owner to reduce the influence of customers who bulk-resolve large volumes of alerts at once, which can otherwise distort a simple average.
Take this with you
The best security tool is the one developers trust enough to use. Higher precision means fewer distracting alerts. Higher recall means more real secrets are caught. Lower cost means we can keep improving coverage without making scanning prohibitively expensive.
For developers and security teams, this should translate into fewer false positives, and faster feedback in the places where secrets are most likely to be introduced: commits, pull requests, and everyday development workflows.
Hybrid systems are powerful. Regex gives us speed, transparency, and broad candidate coverage. ModernBERT gives us learned context understanding and false-positive reduction. The combination outperforms either approach used alone for this product constraint.
We also learned that model size is not the same as model usefulness. A smaller fine-tuned classifier can be the right answer when the task is narrow, the decision boundary is measurable, and serving efficiency is critical.
This is one step toward making secret scanning more accurate, scalable, and easy to use. Looking ahead, we are focused on two areas:
Building a continuous improvement flywheel. We will use production feedback loops to identify new false negatives and false positives, turning real-world signals into higher-quality training and evaluation data.
Exploring new model architectures. We are investigating approaches that can perform secret detection and extraction in a single step, reducing pipeline complexity while preserving accuracy and scale.
Acknowledgments
Huge thanks to the engineering, science and product teams across GitHub and Microsoft who helped build the training data, evaluation suite, serving stack, and rollout plan for this new secret scanner.
As a Senior Research Scientist in Microsoft CoreAI, I develop agentic model orchestration and routing techniques for GitHub Copilot. My research focuses on adaptive model selection, multi-model coordination, long-horizon agentic workflows, and developer security.
As a Partner Applied Science Manager in Microsoft CoreAI, I lead an applied research team that measurably boosts developer productivity with ML and AI. We evolve GitHub Copilot in Completion, Chat, Code Review, and agentic workflows by continuously refining models and applying in-context learning for deeper, context-aware assistance.
As we kick off Cybersecurity Awareness Month, the GitHub Bug Bounty team spotlights @vaib25vicky, exploring their methodology, techniques, and experiences hacking on GitHub.
Developers aren’t becoming more careless; they’re being outpaced. The tools that let developers create more software should also take on more of the work of protecting it.
We do newsletters, too
Discover tips, technical guides, and best practices in our biweekly newsletter just for devs.

articles.title: Build long-horizon agents with Grok 4.7 on Amazon Bedrock | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Build long-horizon agents with Grok 4.7 on Amazon Bedrock
SpaceXAI’s Grok 4.7 is now available on Amazon Bedrock, which offers a choice of foundation models (FMs) from multiple providers. According to SpaceXAI, Grok 4.7 is trained to work longer on more difficult tasks and knows when to check its own work. That matters most for agents, which carry a task through many steps and must verify what they find along the way.
An agent that works this way has to do more than look things up. It has to form a candidate answer, check it against what it has learned, and refine it until it fits. Grok 4.7 exposes a reasoning effort setting that controls how much deliberation happens before each response, and for agent workloads a practical question is which level to run.
In this post, we build a tool-calling agent on Grok 4.7 and evaluate it on three tasks that require search rather than lookup. The tasks are diagnosing a two-service outage from its alerts, scheduling maintenance under interacting constraints, and choosing an optimal set of migrations under a budget. Each task has exactly one correct answer, verified by brute force. We ran all three at every reasoning effort level, six times each, for 72 agent runs.
The agent answered 67 of the 72 runs correctly. At xhigh it answered all 18 correctly, and at low it answered 15 of 18 while using about an eighth of the output tokens. That gives a clear trade-off you can tune per request, and we show how to measure it on your own tasks and how to monitor it in production.
We report token counts rather than currency throughout. Token prices change, and the counts are what your own costs are derived from, so a measurement expressed in tokens stays valid.
What SpaceXAI reports about Grok 4.7
According to SpaceXAI, Grok 4.7 uses a larger base model than Grok 4.6 and was trained with a longer reinforcement learning run on a harder mix of tasks. This mix is weighted toward problems that take many hours to complete. SpaceXAI reports that the model is better at verifying its own work and at managing longer context.
SpaceXAI’s published benchmark results follow that emphasis. The largest reported gains over Grok 4.6 appear in the categories that measure sustained work rather than single-turn answers.
| Benchmark | Category | Grok 4.6 | Grok 4.7 | 
| Terminal-Bench 4.0 | Multi-hour terminal work | 20.3% | 37.6% | 
| EEBench | Electrical engineering | 53.0% | 64.0% | 
| Harvey Legal Agent Benchmark | Legal work | 15.8% | 19.6% | 
| CursorBench 4.0 | Longer-running coding | 40.4% | 46.3% | 
| HealthBench Professional | Clinical reasoning | 48.5% | 56.7% | 
| AA Briefcase v1.1 | Multi-hour office work | 1,546 | 1,657 | 
Source: SpaceXAI, Introducing Grok 4.7 (https://x.ai/news/grok-4-7). Scores are as published by SpaceXAI at the time of the model launch.
Benchmarks show how a model performs across standard tasks. For your own workload, the useful next step is to measure on tasks shaped like yours, which is what the rest of this post walks through.
SpaceXAI lists a 500K token context window for Grok 4.7, with text and image input and text output. On Amazon Bedrock, the model supports configurable reasoning effort, tool calling, and structured output.
How you access Grok 4.7 on Amazon Bedrock
Grok 4.7 runs on the bedrock-runtime endpoint and is accessed through a cross-Region inference profile. Two profiles are available:
| Inference profile | Routing | Use when | 
| us.xai.grok-4.7 | Within the US geography | You have US data residency requirements | 
| global.xai.grok-4.7 | Commercial AWS Regions | You have no residency constraints and want the widest capacity | 
Cross-Region inference routes requests across multiple AWS Regions, which gives you higher throughput without managing capacity Region by Region. Requests name one of the inference profiles rather than a bare model ID.
The model supports the OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions and Responses APIs, and the Amazon Bedrock Converse API. On Converse, reasoning is returned as a reasoningContent block alongside the text block. In inferenceConfig, set maxTokens only, and put model-specific parameters, such as reasoning effort, in additionalModelRequestFields.
For the current list of supported Regions, service tiers, and token prices, see the Grok 4.7 model card in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide and the Amazon Bedrock pricing page (https://aws.amazon.com/bedrock/pricing/).
Prerequisites
- An AWS account with access to Amazon Bedrock, and model access enabled for Grok 4.7.
- Python 3.9 or later, with openai, boto3, and aws-bedrock-token-generator installed.
- AWS credentials configured in your environment.
Your AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) identity needs bedrock:InvokeModel on both the inference profile and your account’s default project:
- arn:aws:bedrock:{region}::inference-profile/us.xai.grok-4.7 or the global. equivalent.
- arn:aws:bedrock:{region}:{account-id}:project/default.
Include both resources in the policy statement. The default project permission is required in addition to the inference profile.
Connect to the model
For production use, we recommend generating a short-term bearer token from your existing AWS credentials, so authentication stays tied to your IAM identity and no long-lived secret is stored:
Reasoning tokens count as output tokens and draw down max_completion_tokens before the answer text is produced, so size the limit to leave room for both. If the limit is reached during reasoning, the response returns without answer text, so check for empty content in agent code and raise the limit if you see it. Our runs used a limit of 32,768 tokens, which left headroom at every effort level.
Grok 4.7 supports four effort levels: low, medium, high, and xhigh. Effort levels can change between model versions, so it is worth confirming them against the service rather than hardcoding a list:
Design tasks that need reasoning
Many agent evaluations test diligence: read a record, filter it, add it up. Those tasks are worth having, but to see what reasoning effort contributes, a task has to require search: the answer can’t be read off the data, it has to be proposed and then checked.
We built a synthetic environment of 20 services, exposed through seven tools, and three tasks on top of it. Every task has exactly one correct answer, and each is built so that a quick heuristic is not enough to find it.
| Task | What the agent has to do | What makes it a reasoning task | 
| two_fault_diagnosis | Two services failed silently at 03:00 and 12 others raised alerts. Identify the two that failed | Failed services raise no alerts, so the answer is not among the alerting services. 190 possible pairs, and only one explains exactly the alerts observed | 
| maintenance_schedule | Patch eight services over four nights, two per night, under ten constraints and a rule that two services from the same team never share a night | 2,520 possible schedules, one valid. The team rule depends on data the agent has to look up | 
| migration_budget | Choose candidates to migrate that maximize risk reduction within a budget, including transitive prerequisites | 53 feasible sets, one optimal. Picking the best ratio first gives a set nine points short of the optimum | 
Four practices keep a measurement like this trustworthy, and they apply to most agent evaluations.
State every rule the grader relies on. If the prompt leaves an edge case open, a reasonable answer can be scored as wrong, and the evaluation ends up measuring the specification rather than the model. The diagnosis prompt, for example, says explicitly that a failed service raises no alert of its own.
Prove each task has one answer. Each environment is small enough to enumerate, so we checked every candidate answer before running anything. For the schedule, that is a few lines:
Grade a required final line, not the whole response. Each prompt asks the agent to end with a line such as FINAL: auth, checkout. The grader reads only that line, so a response that discusses other candidates while explaining its reasoning is graded on its conclusion:
Track format separately from correctness. A missing final line is a different signal from an incorrect one. In our runs, all 72 responses included a gradeable final line.
Constrain tool parameters with an enum where the valid values are known, so every tool call targets a real resource:
The system prompt is deliberately short, and asks the agent to check its answer before giving it:
The agent loop is a standard tool-calling loop: call the model with reasoning_effort set, execute each returned tool call, append the result keyed by tool_call_id, and repeat until the model stops requesting tools. Tracking prompt_tokens and completion_tokens across the loop gives the token counts reported in the following section.
Results
Six runs of each task at each effort level, 72 runs in total. The agent answered 67 correctly.
| Task | low | medium | high | xhigh | 
| two_fault_diagnosis | 5 of 6 | 6 of 6 | 6 of 6 | 6 of 6 | 
| maintenance_schedule | 5 of 6 | 5 of 6 | 5 of 6 | 6 of 6 | 
| migration_budget | 5 of 6 | 6 of 6 | 6 of 6 | 6 of 6 | 
| All three tasks | 15 of 18 | 17 of 18 | 17 of 18 | 18 of 18 | 
| Per run | low | medium | high | xhigh | 
| Mean output tokens | 1,184 | 6,430 | 6,778 | 9,147 | 
| Output tokens relative to low | 1.0x | 5.4x | 5.7x | 7.7x | 
| Mean tool calls | 17.2 | 18.7 | 17.8 | 18.1 | 
| Median elapsed time | 18s | 98s | 89s | 106s | 
Three observations.
xhigh answered every run correctly. All 18 runs across the three tasks were correct at xhigh, and medium and high answered 17 of 18 each. With six runs per task and level, the differences between levels are indicative rather than statistically conclusive, and the direction was consistent across all three tasks.
Effort changes how much the agent reasons, not how much it explores. Tool calls were essentially flat, between 17.2 and 18.7 per run at every level. The agent gathered the same facts regardless of effort, and what changed was how much reasoning it applied to them, with output tokens rising from 1,184 at low to 9,147 at xhigh.
low offers a strong cost-to-quality ratio. At low, the agent answered 15 of 18 runs correctly using about an eighth of the output tokens of xhigh, with a median run of 18 seconds. Where a slightly lower completion rate is acceptable, or where answers are reviewed downstream, low is an efficient choice. Where every answer needs to be right first time, higher levels are the safer default.
How effort level shapes the answer
The tasks were designed around a specific kind of difficulty, and looking at how each effort level handled them clarifies when the extra reasoning is worth it.
Optimization. The migration task rewards considering combinations rather than ranking options one at a time. Selecting the candidates with the best individual ratios produces a reasonable answer that is nine points short of the optimum. At medium and above, the agent found the optimal set in all 18 runs.
Hypothesis testing. The diagnosis task requires checking a candidate pair in both directions: every alert has to be explained, and every service that stayed silent has to be consistent with the answer. At medium and above, the agent identified the correct pair in all 18 runs.
Constraint satisfaction. The scheduling task combines ten listed constraints with a team rule that depends on looked-up ownership data. xhigh produced the valid schedule in every run, and this was the task where the highest level made the clearest difference.
The pattern across the three is that additional reasoning effort is most valuable where the agent has to weigh several candidate answers against each other, rather than follow a single path to the result.
Monitoring reasoning in production
In production you don’t have a known answer to grade against, but you do know how many output tokens and tool calls each run used. Those give you a useful operational signal.
Correct runs at each level stay above a clear floor of reasoning volume. Every correct run at medium and above used at least 1,739 output tokens, and the typical run used several thousand. A run that makes no tool calls, or that produces far less output than is normal for its level, is worth flagging for review:
Calibrate the baseline from runs you have graded, per task and per effort level, then apply it to runs you have not. Treat a flag as a prompt to inspect or re-run. At low, where every run is brief, output volume is a weaker signal, so pair it with spot checks.
Asking the agent to verify its answer in the system prompt is worth keeping, because it makes the agent’s reasoning straightforward to follow when you review a run. Pair it with automated grading wherever a known answer exists, so that quality is measured independently of the transcript.
Choosing a reasoning effort
These results suggest a few practical rules.
Match effort to the kind of task. Tasks that involve search, optimization, or testing a hypothesis benefit most from medium or higher. Tasks that follow a single path, or whose answers are reviewed downstream, can run efficiently at low.
Set effort per request, not per agent. Effort is a request parameter, so an agent can run its planning and verification steps at a higher level and its mechanical steps, such as formatting a tool result, at low. That combines much of the reliability of a higher level with a lower token cost.
Measure on your own tasks, with repeats. A single run per configuration gives a single observation. Repeating each configuration several times shows how consistent it is.
Monitor reasoning volume. Output tokens and tool calls per run, tracked by effort level, give you an early signal to review a run before its result is used.
Limitations of this measurement
Six runs per task and effort level. Enough to show a consistent direction across three tasks, not enough for a confidence interval. Treat the differences between levels as indicative.
A synthetic environment. The tools read from data generated in code, which is what makes it possible to prove each task has exactly one answer and to grade automatically. Real tools add latency, partial results and errors, none of which are tested here.
Minutes, not hours. Median run time ranged from 18 seconds at low to 106 seconds at xhigh. This is a scaled-down proxy for long-horizon work. The method transfers. The absolute figures do not.
One model version, one Region, one prompt per task. Different phrasings of the same task may change the results, which is part of why stating every rule explicitly matters.
Token counts, not costs. To convert to currency, apply the current rates for your inference profile and service tier from the Amazon Bedrock pricing page. The Global and US Geo profiles are priced differently, and the Flex and Priority service tiers apply multipliers.
Operational controls for agent workloads
Build in retries. Agents that issue a high volume of calls should treat retries as part of the design. Set a request timeout, retry only errors that are retryable, back off exponentially with jitter, and honor a Retry-After header when one is returned:
On-demand throughput scales up over time, so ramp a new high-volume workload gradually rather than starting at full rate.
Auditing a run. Model invocation logging writes request and response data to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) or Amazon CloudWatch Logs. This gives you the full transcript of runs you want to review after the fact.
Monitoring reasoning volume at scale. Amazon CloudWatch metrics give you the aggregate view of token usage, which is where the per-level baselines described earlier become something you can alarm on.
Attributing spend across agents. Cost itemization in AWS Cost Explorer and the AWS Cost and Usage Report breaks usage out per model, which combined with per-task token counts gives you both unit economics and the aggregate bill.
Matching cost to urgency. Service tiers are set per request, so one deployment can send an overnight analysis through the Flex tier and an interactive request through Priority. For a workload that runs at a higher effort level, tier selection is a further lever on cost.
Choosing a routing profile. Cross-Region inference widens the capacity pool a long run draws from. The Global profile serves from your choice of commercial AWS Region and is typically priced lower per token than geographic routing. The US profile keeps processing within the United States. Choose based on your data residency requirements as well as cost.
Clean up
The examples in this post do not create billable AWS resources beyond per-request token usage. If you generated a long-term Amazon Bedrock API key, delete it in the Amazon Bedrock console when you are finished, because it remains valid until revoked. Short-term tokens generated from IAM credentials expire on their own.
If you enabled model invocation logging to Amazon S3 while testing, review the bucket and remove objects you no longer need.
Conclusion
SpaceXAI trained Grok 4.7 to work longer on more difficult tasks and to know when to check its own work. On three tasks that required search rather than lookup, the agent answered 67 of 72 runs correctly, and every run at xhigh. Because reasoning effort is set per request, you can choose where each step of an agent sits on the trade-off between thoroughness and token cost.
Three things are worth carrying into your own evaluation. Design tasks with one provable answer and state every rule the grader depends on. Repeat runs, so you see how consistent each configuration is. And monitor output tokens and tool calls by effort level, so you have an operational signal alongside your quality measurements.

articles.title: Tesla confirme la présentation du Roadster le 15 octobre : cette fois, c’est la bonne - Numerama
articles.text:
Neuf ans après sa toute première apparition, la supercar électrique d’Elon Musk va enfin pouvoir faire ses preuves. Il aura fallu s’armer d’une patience presque infinie. Initialement calée au 1er octobre puis repoussée de deux semaines en raison de vents violents, la présentation du Tesla Roadster de seconde génération se tiendra bien ce jeudi 15 octobre à Waco, au Texas.
Pour le public français, il faudra veiller tard : le compte à rebours officiel renvoie à une diffusion en direct sur X (ex-Twitter) dans la nuit de jeudi à vendredi, à 3 h du matin (heure de Paris), enfin plus exactement 2h55 (7:55 PM CST).
Toutes les conditions sont enfin réunies pour le Tesla Roadster
Le choix d’un événement en plein air et la justification météorologique du premier report confirment qu’il s’agira d’une démonstration dynamique grandeur nature, promise comme « inoubliable » par Elon Musk.
Reste désormais à voir ce que la bête a réellement dans le ventre : au-delà des fantasmes sur le pack SpaceX et ses propulseurs à gaz froid, le constructeur américain devra surtout abattre ses cartes sur les caractéristiques définitives, le tarif final et une vraie fenêtre de livraison pour les clients qui ont bloqué jusqu’à 43 000 € d’acompte depuis 2017.
On a presque du mal à croire que cette présentation tant attendue va enfin avoir lieu. Espérons pour Tesla que tout se déroule sans couac.

articles.title: Tech30 2026: Meet the 30 startups building India’s next generation of technology
articles.text:
Tech30 2026: Meet the 30 startups building India’s next generation of technology
From spacetech and defence to clean energy and advanced materials, YourStory's Tech30 spotlights 30 promising startups developing technologies for India and beyond.
India’s startups are no longer just finding new ways to use existing technology. A growing number are building the technology itself, from satellites and autonomous robots to advanced materials, medical diagnostics and cleaner construction methods. Their work is taking them into sectors that demand years of research, specialised expertise, and significant investment, with the potential to change how industries operate.
This shift is at the heart of TechSparks 2026, YourStory's flagship startup-tech summit, themed ‘The New Tech Order’. One of its key highlights is Tech30, YourStory's annual selection of 30 promising startups working on technologies that could shape India’s future.
Sridhar Vembu, Chief Scientist and Co-founder of Zoho Corp, unveiled and presented this year's Tech30 at TechSparks 2026. Speaking on ‘Prosperity cannot be imported: The road to tech independence’, he emphasised the need for India to develop technologies that address its own challenges.
"The new tech order is to learn to solve our own problems — foundational problems from agritech to material science to lasers, and also AI. But AI is not to be the be all and end all of it,” Vembu said.
Yoonmin Cho, APJ Lead, Snowflake for Startups, and Amar Dixit, CEO, WOI India, also joined Vembu in celebrating this year's Tech30 cohort on stage.
Chosen from a pool of applicants, the startups are evaluated by a jury of experienced members of the startup ecosystem, along with YourStory's senior editorial and research teams. The Tech30 report was unveiled at TechSparks 2026, bringing attention to companies working across a range of sectors and technologies.
This year’s selection reflects the growing ambition of Indian startups to develop their own technologies and apply them to practical problems. From improving industrial processes and strengthening critical infrastructure to developing new products and markets, these companies are working on challenges in India and overseas.
Here are the 30 startups selected for Tech30 2026.
Apollyon Dynamics
Apollyon Dynamics develops autonomous drones and counter-unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) systems for defence applications. Its portfolio includes high-speed interceptor drones such as Ahuti Mk II, designed to neutralise hostile drones, and Nightshade ADX-1, an autonomous strike platform.
Arctus Aerospace
Arctus Aerospace is developing high-altitude, long-endurance unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) that operate at around 50,000 feet and can remain airborne for up to 24 hours. Equipped with onboard AI for autonomous navigation, obstacle avoidance, and flight planning, its platforms are designed to provide persistent aerial surveillance and high-resolution imaging for defence, agriculture, infrastructure monitoring, and disaster response.
Attox Research Laboratories
Attox Research Laboratories develops diagnostic technology to accelerate antibiotic sensitivity testing and help address antibiotic resistance. Its flagship device, Bactolizer, analyses electrical signals from patient samples using specialised algorithms to identify effective antibiotics and appropriate dosages in around two hours, compared with the 24–48 hours typically required by conventional methods. The system uses a reusable testing unit and disposable cartridges designed for hospital settings.
Balisto Agritech
Balisto Agritech has developed the Balisto 130 Pro, an electric farm machine that combines multiple agricultural operations, including weeding, sowing, spraying, rotavating, and harvesting, on a single platform. Powered by detachable batteries, the machine can be controlled through an onboard dashboard or remotely, while an internet-connected system enables cloud-based monitoring and remote diagnostics.
CaliperAI
CaliperAI builds AI infrastructure for robots and autonomous machines, using sensor fusion, localisation, and perception to help them navigate the physical world. Its platform captures, analyses, and annotates data from cameras, LiDAR, and navigation sensors, supporting the development of autonomous systems.
CraftifAI
CraftifAI builds AI software that automates development for embedded systems, edge AI, and IoT devices. Its Orbit platform generates, compiles, and validates code directly on target hardware, helping companies develop software for robotics, drones, industrial equipment, and automotive systems.
Curium Life
Curium Life is developing AI models that interpret surgical videos, anatomy, and operating-room workflows to support surgeons during procedures. Its technology aims to provide real-time guidance, identify anatomical structures, and flag potential risks, alongside tools that analyse CT scans to assess preoperative risks and abdominal-wall conditions.
Dognosis
Dognosis is developing BreathEasy, a non-invasive cancer screening test that analyses a person's breath to identify potential cancer risk across multiple cancer types. The system combines trained dogs' ability to detect cancer-related chemical patterns with brain-computer interfaces and machine learning to interpret their responses, flagging higher-risk individuals for confirmatory tests such as imaging and biopsies.
Ecopath
Ecopath turns industrial waste into construction materials, replacing conventional cement with alternatives designed to cut emissions and water use. Its EcoConcrete supports applications ranging from road construction to masonry products, while its soil-stabilisation and waterproofing solutions address other infrastructure needs.
Enerzolve Smart Technologies
From battery storage to grid infrastructure, Enerzolve works on the power electronics and instrumentation needed to manage electricity reliably. Its technology portfolio spans bidirectional power converters, software-driven solid-state transformers, and ultrasonic water, gas, and energy meters, serving utility developers, data centres, and defence organisations.
EON Space Labs
EON Space Labs’ MIRA imaging payload is now in orbit following a launch aboard SpaceX's Falcon 9, marking a milestone for its space-imaging technology. The startup develops electro-optical and infrared systems for space, aerial, and ground surveillance, including imaging payloads, gimbals, and fixed surveillance equipment, with more than 90% of its components built domestically.
Evoxia
Agricultural residues could offer an alternative route to producing polysilicon, a critical material for solar panels and semiconductors. Evoxia is developing a plasma-based process to turn this feedstock into high-purity silicon, reporting 6N purity in laboratory validation and targeting lower energy consumption and emissions than conventional production methods.
Folium Sensing
Folium Sensing turns standard optical fibre cables into sensors that detect vibrations, temperature changes, and mechanical strain over distances exceeding 100 km. Its AI-powered monitoring system helps identify pipeline leaks, railway-track cracks, and security threats across critical infrastructure.
Harvested Robotics
Harvested Robotics' RAKSHAK uses computer vision to identify weeds and high-powered lasers to remove them without damaging crops. Mounted on a tractor, the device can eliminate 80–100 weeds per minute, offering farmers an alternative to chemical herbicides and manual weeding.
Hyperonic Engineering
Hyperonic Engineering develops hydrogen technologies for mobility and industrial applications, including its H35 dispenser for safe, precision-controlled refuelling. It is also developing microgrids that combine electrolysers, hydrogen storage, and fuel cells for decentralised power generation.
Hypersonic Technologies
Hydrogen production need not come with direct CO₂ emissions or a single output. Hypersonic Technologies is developing plasma-based reactors that split methane and other gas feedstocks into hydrogen and solid carbon black, which can be used in tyres, plastics, paints, and coatings.
ImmunitoAI
Designing antibodies from scratch is the focus of immunitoAI, whose AbInitio platform uses AI to create proteins that bind to specific disease-linked targets. Trained on 3D protein structures, the system generates candidate antibodies for laboratory testing, with potential applications in cancer, autoimmune disorders, blood diseases, and neurological conditions.
Integra Robotics
Integra Robotics equips factories and defence teams with modular robots built for hazardous and hard-to-reach environments. The hardware ranges from robotic arms and underwater manipulators to mobile platforms capable of carrying 500 kg, while software uses field-operation data to train and improve machine capabilities.
Kubo Care
Kubo Care uses 60 GHz radar and AI to monitor older adults at home or in care facilities, detecting falls without cameras or wearable devices. Its system also tracks movement patterns, sleep interruptions, and vital signs to flag potential health changes, while alerting caregivers to events such as bed exits and wandering.
Metastable Materials
Discarded lithium-ion batteries contain valuable metals that Metastable Materials recovers for industrial reuse. Its proprietary recycling process separates lithium, nickel, cobalt, and copper without adding chemicals, supplying recovered materials to industries such as glass, ceramics, stainless steel, and automotive manufacturing.
MiCoB
From army bunkers to residential structures, MiCoB uses robotic 3D concrete printing to automate construction. Its integrated technology combines specialised concrete mixes, printers, and digital design software, enabling the company to produce structures with less labour and material waste; it has delivered more than 650 3D-printed structures across 13 states.
MumbaiSemi
MumbaiSemi's DhruvaPro chip enables satellite navigation receivers to work across India's NavIC system and global constellations including GPS, Galileo, and BeiDou. The fabless semiconductor startup is also developing integrated circuits for wireless communications, AI hardware, autonomous vehicles, and low-power IoT devices.
Neo San
Instead of transporting non-recyclable dry waste to disposal sites, Neo San's machines process it where it is generated, using induction heating to reach temperatures of 1,200 degrees Celsius. Its range handles between 25 kg and 500 kg or more of waste daily, serving buildings, hospitals, and industrial facilities, with the resulting ash tested for use in construction.
Pramatra Space
Pramatra Space is working on encryption systems designed to withstand future quantum-computing threats. Its integrated photonics chip generates entangled photons to create secure encryption keys, which the startup aims to distribute through fibre networks and satellites to protect enterprise communications and critical infrastructure.
Red Balloon Aerospace
Red Balloon Aerospace is building platforms to operate in near-space, the region between conventional airspace and outer space. Its portfolio includes high-altitude balloons, tethered aerostats, and autonomous stratospheric airships designed for long-duration communications, remote connectivity, disaster response, and surveillance missions.
Sanyark Space
Sanyark Space is developing low Earth orbit satellites to improve navigation accuracy from metres to centimetres. Its constellation will transmit correction data and stronger signals to support precise positioning, timing, and more resilient communications for defence and infrastructure applications.
Segritech
Segritech uses computer vision and deep learning to grade fruit by size, colour, and surface defects, processing up to two to three tonnes an hour with 95% reported accuracy. Its machines currently sort produce such as pomegranates and apples, while the startup is developing an autonomous robot to harvest fruit directly in the field.
SpaceFields
SpaceFields develops solid-propulsion systems for rockets, unmanned aerial vehicles, and defence applications, with capabilities spanning composite propellants, rocket motors, and energetic materials. Its portfolio also includes an aerospike rocket engine, while its in-house technologies are backed by 32 patent filings, 11 of which have been granted.
TeraLumen Solutions
Terahertz waves are at the core of TeraLumen Solutions’ imaging and testing systems. Its TeraXPLOR platform supports research and spectroscopy, while TeraNIM detects defects and measures coating thickness in industries such as aerospace, automotive, and oil and gas. The company is also developing a system for detecting cancer margins during surgery.
Yaanendriya
Yaanendriya develops motion sensors, navigation systems, and control software for autonomous machines, from drones to surgical robots. Its positioning technology is also being adapted for GPS-denied environments, including underwater and indoor settings.

articles.title: Meta Says Hackers Took Code, Personal Data of 1,500 in GitHub Breach
articles.text:
Meta is notifying roughly 1,500 people, most of them employees in the US, that their personal information was impacted after hackers got into some of the company’s GitHub repositories.
The intrusion was detected a few weeks ago. According to the tech giant, an outside group gained access to the repositories using an employee’s stolen credentials.
Meta’s security team shut down the attackers’ access and brought in GitHub and law enforcement. Notifications to the impacted individuals started going out on Tuesday.
Meta told SecurityWeek that 99% of the data the hackers took was business data, in the form of software code related to some of its products. The remaining 1% was personal data.
That personal data had been added to the repositories by mistake and should not have been there, as storing it on GitHub went against company policy. Meta has not said what types of personal information were involved.
The company also noted that a significant portion of what looked like personal data was actually synthetic or anonymized test data. As a result, the attackers may not readily be able to tell genuine records apart from test data.
Based on its investigation with GitHub so far, Meta does not believe the hackers were specifically after its data.
Meta is also notifying regulators, and the people whose information was involved are being offered credit and dark web monitoring services.
“This was not a vulnerability in any Meta product, and Meta’s internal systems were not breached. Meta business data held in a GitHub repository was improperly accessed using an employee’s stolen credentials – this included a small amount of personal data for a limited number of people, most of whom were Meta employees,” a Meta spokesperson told SecurityWeek.
In response to the incident, Meta rotated secrets it found in the affected repositories. It also hardened its product security to address risks stemming from access to its business data.
The company is working with its teams that use GitHub to keep user data off the platform. As a second line of defense, it is adding controls for proactive scanning to detect any user data uploaded by mistake.
“We’ve since rotated secrets found in the repositories, implemented new controls to prevent user data from being stored in GitHub, and worked with GitHub on additional measures to protect our repositories,” the spokesperson said.
Related: Cyberattack Prompts Ahold Delhaize to Disconnect Systems
Related: Refrigeration Controller Hack Spoils Food Across European Supermarkets

articles.title: Rivian partner Mind Robotics hires Doug Field as president
articles.text:
Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe’s startup Mind Robotics announced the appointment of Doug Field as president in a major coup for the CEO’s secretive robotics project.
Rivian partner Mind Robotics hires Doug Field as president
Ford’s former EV and software chief will run Rivian’s robotics startup at a time of maximum hype for physical AI.
Field was a VP of special projects at Apple, where he was the de facto head of the company’s ultimately unsuccessful Project Titan effort to make an autonomous electric car. He had a previous stint at Apple as VP of Mac hardware engineering, but he left the company in 2013 to become Tesla’s chief vehicle engineer, where he helped oversee the Model 3 sedan. He left Tesla in 2018 and rejoined Apple. In 2021, Field was hired by Ford to run the automaker’s electric vehicle and software division, a position he held until earlier this year.
Mind Robotics said Field will oversee its effort to build “universally capable robots” for the purpose of working in Rivian’s factories, as well as other applications. The startup was founded by Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe in 2025, and has since raised over $1 billion in financing. While the company has yet to show off any of its robots in public, the startup says its robots are being designed with “dexterity and physical reasoning” that’s required for industrial work.
“Doug is a remarkable leader with a track record of delivering new technologies in successful products, and I couldn’t be more excited to be building Mind with him,” Scaringe said in a statement. “He has an incredible ability to foster great teams that take on big, complex ideas and deliver products that reset expectations. That’s exactly what Mind needs as we deploy robots into real factories and beyond.”
Field joins Mind Robotics at a major turning point for the field of robotics, with rapid advances in physical AI colliding with major hurdles in hardware and software development. Several companies, like Tesla and Hyundai, are pursuing humanoid robots for factory and warehouse work — even as experts note that making a robot act like a human is easier than scaling the technology for practical work. Mind Robotics hasn’t confirmed whether it’s working on a humanoid design or something else entirely. The company has been on a hiring spree and currently has 32 open positions.
Scaringe, who serves as acting CEO and chair of Mind Robotics, has said he wants to keep the companies separate, rather than try to combine the work like Tesla. That said, the companies are certainly linked in several ways. Mind Robotics is using AI training data from Rivian, and the robots will be initially tested in Rivian’s factories. Rivian also owns equity in Mind Robotics and will be the first customer for its robots.
Field said he is excited for the challenge in running the new startup.
“Integrating AI and robotics is one of the most important—and difficult—engineering challenges of our time,” he said in a statement. “Mind has assembled an exceptional team and has a unique advantage: the ability to deploy and learn inside a real, high-volume factory from day one. I’m thrilled to join RJ in building a team, culture, and technology that will redefine what we can make in America.”
Correction October 13th: Mind Robotics is a partner of Rivian, but not a spinoff. A previous version of this story misstated the relationship between the companies.

articles.title: Physicists discover “astonishing” property of light that defies expectations
articles.text:
Physicists discover “astonishing” property of light that defies expectations
- Date:
- October 13, 2026
- Source:
- University of East Anglia
- Summary:
- Scientists have uncovered a surprising hidden ability of light that allows it to develop spinning, twisting behavior as it travels through empty space, without special lenses, mirrors, or materials. Researchers discovered that light’s internal geometry can naturally produce left- and right-handed patterns, challenging long-standing assumptions about how light behaves. By carefully arranging a beam’s structure, scientists can control where and how these spinning patterns emerge, unlocking a new way to manipulate light.
- Share:
Scientists have discovered a surprising ability of light that allows it to develop spinning patterns as it moves through empty space, without relying on special lenses, mirrors, or materials. The finding reveals that light possesses a hidden geometric structure that can influence its behavior in ways researchers previously thought were difficult to achieve.
The discovery comes from an international team led by researchers at the University of East Anglia (UEA) in the United Kingdom, working with scientists in South Africa. Their experiments demonstrate that carefully prepared light can be controlled through its own internal geometry, offering a new approach to manipulating how light spins and twists.
The findings challenge long-standing assumptions about how different properties of light interact. They could eventually lead to more sensitive medical tests, faster and more secure communications, and advanced quantum technologies that use light to transmit and protect information.
Why the Direction of Light's Spin Matters
One of the most intriguing aspects of the discovery involves chirality, a scientific term describing the difference between left-handed and right-handed structures.
Human hands provide a familiar example. Although they are mirror images of each other, a left hand cannot be perfectly superimposed on a right hand. Many molecules have a similar property, including compounds used in medicines. Two versions of the same molecule can have nearly identical chemical structures yet produce very different effects in the body.
Scientists can distinguish these molecular forms by studying how they interact with light that has a particular rotational behavior. Traditionally, producing and controlling such light has often involved specialized materials, carefully designed surfaces, or powerful lenses that focus beams extremely tightly.
The research demonstrates that appropriately prepared light can develop this behavior naturally as it travels, without requiring those additional optical components.
"Our work shows that light can naturally develop this handed behavior all on its own," said Dr. Kayn Forbes from UEA's School of Chemistry, Pharmacy and Pharmacology.
"You just have to prepare it in the right way.
"Most people think of light as traveling in straight lines. But scientists can also create structured light -- light whose brightness, shape, and direction are carefully arranged.
"One extreme example is light that twists as it travels, forming a corkscrew shape known as an optical vortex. Each twist can carry information, making this kind of light valuable for high-speed internet, secure communications, and advanced sensors.
"Light can also spin as it travels, depending on how it is polarized. This spin can be left-handed or right-handed -- another form of chirality."
Scientists Discover How Light Develops a Hidden Spin
Light can exhibit different kinds of rotational behavior. An optical vortex, for example, has a wave pattern that twists around its direction of travel, much like a corkscrew. Light also has a property known as polarization, which describes how its electric field oscillates. Certain polarization patterns produce a form of rotation called spin.
Physicists have long studied the relationship between these two properties. However, the interactions responsible for the newly observed effect were generally considered extremely weak and difficult to detect without specialized experimental conditions.
The researchers found that the situation changes when a beam of light is prepared in a particular balanced configuration.
Under those conditions, the beam can initially have no spin, yet distinct regions with spinning behavior emerge as it travels through free space. The effect does not require the light to pass through engineered materials or additional optical devices.
"It starts off with no spin at all," explained MSc student Light Mkhumbuza, who carried out key experiments. "But as the beam travels forward, spinning regions appear and separate out -- almost as if the spin was hiding and then revealed itself."
Rather than creating spin through an external optical component, the researchers demonstrated how the beam's existing internal structure can determine where spinning regions develop during propagation.
The Hidden Geometry That Controls Light
To explain this unexpected behavior, the researchers turned to topology, a mathematical field concerned with properties that remain unchanged when objects are continuously stretched, bent, or reshaped.
Dr. Isaac Nape, from the University of the Witwatersrand in Johannesburg, South Africa, offered a simple way to understand the concept.
"To explain it, imagine a mug and a doughnut," he said. "You can morph one into the other without tearing it, because they both have one hole. That hole is a topological feature."
The researchers found that structured light possesses its own topological characteristics, encoded in the arrangement of its polarization.
This underlying pattern acts like a mathematical fingerprint. Even as the light beam changes shape while traveling, its topological structure remains, influencing how different regions of the beam evolve.
As a result, the arrangement of the light itself can determine where its left-handed and right-handed spinning patterns become visible.
The discovery gives scientists a way to guide this behavior by designing the beam's initial structure, rather than depending on specialized materials to produce the desired effect.
"This gives us a completely new tuning knob for light. By adjusting its topology, we can decide how and where chirality appears," said Dr. Nape.
Potential Breakthroughs in Medicine and Communications
The ability to control light through its geometry could eventually make several important optical technologies simpler, more affordable, and more versatile.
One particularly promising application involves medical diagnostics and pharmaceutical research. Because many biologically important molecules have left-handed and right-handed forms, carefully structured light could help scientists identify these differences with greater sensitivity. Such tools could be valuable for evaluating drug safety and detecting biological markers associated with disease.
The same principles could support smaller optical sensors capable of identifying chemicals or biological substances without requiring large, sophisticated laboratory instruments.
Communications technology could also benefit. By encoding information into different twisting and spinning patterns, researchers may be able to increase the amount of data carried by individual light beams. This could contribute to faster optical communications, improved information security, and future quantum networks.
Other potential uses include manipulating microscopic particles, cells, and molecules with light, as well as developing more resilient quantum systems. Topological properties may help protect delicate quantum information against certain forms of noise and interference.
"The implications are wide-ranging," said Dr. Forbes. "This work could lead to simpler and more sensitive medical tests, especially in drug development.
"It could also be used to pack more information into laser beams -- boosting data capacity for communications, including future quantum networks.
"And because the effect doesn't rely on fragile materials or precision-engineered surfaces, it could be easier and cheaper to use in real-world technologies.
"This research could lay the foundations for a new generation of light-based technologies, by showing that light's behavior can be controlled using its own internal geometry," he added.
These applications remain possibilities for future development, but the underlying discovery provides researchers with another way to design and control the behavior of light.
A Hidden Property of Light Finally Revealed
For decades, scientists have relied on increasingly sophisticated optical equipment to produce and manipulate unusual forms of light. The findings suggest that some of these behaviors can instead arise from carefully designed structures already encoded within a light beam.
By showing how topology governs the emergence of spinning regions during propagation, the team has revealed a previously underappreciated connection between light's geometry and its physical behavior.
The discovery also illustrates how much remains to be learned about something as familiar and extensively studied as light.
"For something so familiar, light is proving to be far richer, stranger and more powerful than anyone imagined," said Dr. Forbes.
"And astonishingly, this new behavior has been there all along -- just waiting to be seen."
The research, 'Topological Control of Chirality and Spin with Structured Light', was published in the journal Light: Science & Applications.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of East Anglia. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Light Mkhumbuza, Pedro Ornelas, Angela Dudley, Isaac Nape, Kayn A. Forbes. Topological control of chirality and spin with structured light. Light: Science, 2026; 15 (1) DOI: 10.1038/s41377-026-02278-6
