I can’t wait for Kill Switch(´；ω；｀)
I tend to disagree with the statement that the large number of CVE’s are placing strains on IT teams in terms of patch prioritization. That’s not the issue. For most vendors, Microsoft included, a single cumulative security update is issued, or a small handful for core products (Windows, Office, .Net). Whether those updates patch 100 or 10,000 individual CVE’s, the number of updates to test hasn’t really changed all that much. What HAS changed is the potential for the update to break things since more code is being modified with each update. Testing and deployment processes haven’t changed; it’s the monitoring for unexpected behavior during the testing phase that has become the pain point.

articles.title: ¿A qué hora se estrena 'VisionQuest', la nueva serie del Universo Marvel?
articles.text:
Marvel estrena por fin su nueva serie, VisionQuest. El proyecto supone el segundo proyecto propio para el personaje de Paul Bettany para Disney+, que debutó hace ya una década en Avengers: La era de Ultrón. Precisamente, aquel villano regresa también al UCM en este título que apunta a convertirse en heredero directo de la aclamada serie Bruja Escarlata y Visión. Pero, ¿a qué hora se estrena VisionQuest?
Visión, reiniciado y tras escapar de quienes pretendían convertirlo en arma, ha permanecido oculto. En busca de un nuevo propósito, consulta a las distintas IA integradas en su programación, incluidas F.R.I.D.A.Y., E.D.I.T.H., J.A.R.V.I.S. y el infame Ultrón. Su discreta existencia llega a su fin cuando una recompensa por su captura lo obliga a huir junto a Thomas Shepherd, un misterioso joven que podría ser su hijo reencarnado. Mientras evita ser capturado, Visión deberá enfrentarse a su propia naturaleza, resistir la influencia de Ultrón y desentrañar el enigma de su joven acompañante si quiere sobrevivir.
En cuanto a dónde podrá verse, a diferencia de otros títulos, aquí no depende para nada del territorio. En Estados Unidos, España, Latinoamérica y en el resto del mundo, VisionQuest estará disponible únicamente en Disney+. La plataforma alberga los derechos de toda la serie, así como del resto del Universo Cinematográfico de Marvel. De esta forma, La Casa de las Ideas pondrá el punto y final a la conocida como Trilogía de Wanda, dando paso posteriormente a Avengers: Doomsday.
Hora de estreno de VisionQuest
Acerca de la hora de estreno de VisionQuest, en Estados Unidos se emitirá el martes 13 de octubre a las 6:00 pm P.T. En España y Latinoamérica, llegará a Disney+ en la conversión horaria de cada país:
- España: 3:00 h am del miércoles 14 de octubre.
- México, Guatemala, Honduras, El Salvador, Nicaragua, Costa Rica: 19:00 h.
- Perú, Colombia, Panamá, Ecuador: 20:00 h.
- Chile, Venezuela, Bolivia, República Dominicana, Puerto Rico: 21:00 h.
- Paraguay, Argentina, Brasil, Uruguay: 22:00 h.
Date de alta en Disney+ ahora y ahorra gracias a la suscripción anual, con la que podrás disfrutar de todo su catálogo de series y películas. Acceso a los últimos estrenos, al catálogo de Star y ESPN* y a los mejores documentales de National Geographic.
*ESPN solo está disponible en Latinoamérica. Ahorro respecto a 12 meses de suscripción mensual.
A esa hora, la serie de VisionQuest llegará a Disney+ con sus dos primeros episodios. La serie llevará a partir de entonces una estrategia de estreno semanal muy particular. Y es que cada martes (o madrugada de miércoles en España) se estrenarán dos episodios más. Sin embargo, esto cambiará de cara a los capítulos 7 y 8, que verán la luz de manera individual en sus respectivas semanas. De esta forma, la octava y última entrega verá la luz el 10 de noviembre.

articles.title: Mixture-of-Experts kernel engineering on Amazon SageMaker AI | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Mixture-of-Experts kernel engineering on Amazon SageMaker AI
Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) is a sparsely-activated architecture that scales large language model (LLM) capacity while keeping per-token compute low. Because its operations account for a large share of total compute time, inefficiencies there directly raise request latency and cost. Therefore, optimizing MoE operations through kernel engineering offers the largest opportunity for performance gains.
Fused MoE is a key optimization technique for the MoE architecture. A fused MoE system merges token routing, data shuffling, and specialized network calculations into a single batched operation on the GPU. This replaces executing those routing and expert computations as separate, sequential loop operations. While this provides latency advantages, it also brings complexity in kernel implementations and debugging capability. High GPU utilization for this architecture requires hardware-specific optimizations.
In this post, we describe the different kernel optimizations we implemented for fused MoE models and show you how you can benefit from this work. We used a representative MoE model as our primary example.
Swap-AB for WGMMA utilization
To maximize tensor processing throughput, the NVIDIA Hopper architecture relies on the Warp Group Matrix Multiply Accumulate (WGMMA) instruction protocol, which executes collectively across a cooperative warpgroup of 128 threads. This operand asymmetry is fundamentally an instruction set architecture (ISA)-level property. In the underlying wgmma.mma_async assembly definition, the hardware fixes the matrix row dimension (M) at a constant scale of 64 to define its parallel thread-mapping topology. The column dimension (N) remains highly variable. Operand A strictly maps across this fixed M dimension (using registers or shared memory), and Operand B maps across the variable N dimension (through a shared memory descriptor). These operand slots are therefore structurally non-interchangeable. Consequently, peak hardware tile utilization is governed by these rigid shape encodings, requiring that the M dimension equals or exceeds 64 to prevent compute execution lanes from sitting idle.
This structural preference stems from how Hopper Tensor Cores partition memory blocks. The hardware enforces a fixed minimum layout shape for the leading dimension of the first operand, locking the block height to exactly 64 (M=64). When a mathematical matrix possesses a large, continuous leading dimension in this primary slot, Hopper’s internal hardware schedulers can cleanly map and distribute data across the physical computing grid.
This structural asymmetry becomes a severe performance bottleneck during the decode phase of MoE networks. In a standard MoE layer, the linear algebra governing expert computation is formulated using traditional matrix notation:
A[M,K] x B[K,N] —> C[M,N]
Where (M) represents the token row count (or batch size), (K) represents the hidden feature dimension, and (N) represents the expansive expert output dimension.
During the decode phase, the system processes only one token per user sequence at a time. Consequently, the batch space or token row size is profoundly thin, regularly dropping to a profile where (M < 64), and frequently down to a single row (M = 1). Under this standard structural layout:
Matrix (A) transforms into a thin, fragmented horizontal vector (for example, 1 x 4096).
Matrix (B) (the core expert weights) remains in a large, dense vertical block (for example, 4096 x 8192).
Because the row count (M) is tiny, Matrix (A) is physically incapable of filling the hardware’s fixed (64)-row layout bucket for Operand A. When the WGMMA instruction executes over this layout, it leaves a vast portion of the physical Tensor Core capacity completely starved. The silicon spends clock cycles processing empty spatial slots, leading to poor hardware utilization.
In a standard dense LLM layer, weight matrices are static, unified, and perfectly contiguous. In an MoE layer, however, the workload is fractured across a fleet of independent subnetworks (experts). This creates unique memory and layout bottlenecks that make it hypersensitive to the WGMMA constraints of the Hopper GPU. In a standard dense layer, matrix multiplication multiplies a token vector by a single layer weight matrix. The output dimension (N) is the model’s hidden size (for example, 4096).
In a Fused MoE kernel, the GPU isn’t only multiplying against one expert. It’s grouping and running math for all active experts simultaneously to avoid launching individual kernels for each expert. For a standard dense layer, N is the hidden size (4,096). For a fused MoE layer, N is the number of experts chosen multiplied by the expert intermediate size. For a model running a topk=8 routine, the effective N dimension inside the fused kernel explodes into tens or hundreds of thousands of parameters. Because the N dimension is so disproportionately large compared to the tiny decode token size (M=1), the layout asymmetry becomes extreme. Transposing the matrices moves this large, combined MoE dimension into the primary slot, unlocking hardware prefetching at a scale that standard dense layers cannot match.
To resolve this hardware misalignment without altering the underlying mathematical integrity of the model, we exploit the algebraic property of matrix transposition:
BT[N,K] x AT[K,M] —> CT[N,M]
By programmatically flipping the matrix multiplication before it reaches the PTX assembly layer, we realigned the software to match the exact topography of the Hopper silicon. This transposition triggers two immediate architectural advantages on the GPU. First, it saturates the physical layout. The expansive expert dimension (N = 8192) is promoted to the first operand position (BT), and because (N) is large it easily floods the hardware’s mandatory (64)-row threshold. The Tensor Cores then operate at maximum local density with no wasted execution cycles. Second, it activates asynchronous prefetching. Hopper’s dedicated hardware copy engines can prefetch memory addresses asynchronously from shared memory straight into registers before the math execution block fires. Placing the continuous, large weight blocks (BT) in the leading slot lets these engines trace the data layout smoothly and keep the compute pipeline saturated without CPU intervention. This produced a 2–4 percent end-to-end output throughput improvement across large-scale MoE models on H200. We upstreamed this optimization to vLLM, and it is available in version 0.24.0 or later.
Backend routing for FP8 tensor quantization
Beyond kernel internals, the choice of which backend executes the MoE computation has a large effect on performance. The vLLM MoE oracle routes different quantization schemes to Triton, FlashInfer+CUTLASS, or other backends. Profiling revealed that for FP8 tensor-quantized models on Hopper, the Triton backend consistently outperforms the default FLASHINFER_CUTLASS path.
The Triton backend outperforms CUTLASS in low-concurrency MoE workloads primarily because it replaces rigid, framework-level matrix math configurations with custom, operator-level register fusion. CUTLASS relies on standard C++ template structures that treat FP8 tensor scaling, matrix multiplication, and expert aggregation as discrete mathematical operations. The Triton backend instead consolidates this entire pipeline into a single hardware pass. Data is pulled from global high-bandwidth memory (HBM) exactly once and processed entirely within the GPU’s ultra-fast local SRAM registers and compute execution files. It’s then streamed back to the final matrix destination. This removes the slow global VRAM read/write roundtrips that compromise CUTLASS when it is forced to constantly step through intermediate tensor scaling steps.
Furthermore, this register-level fusion is specifically paired with dynamic scheduling layouts designed around variable token bucketing, resolving a severe structural flaw in traditional compilation templates. CUTLASS is natively optimized for dense, large, and predictable matrix dimensions. When it encounters the fluid, ultra-thin batch profiles (M < 64 or M = 1) typical of the live decode generation phase, its default block-tiling and thread-mapping structures become profoundly inefficient. The result is heavy warp under-utilization or expensive memory padding overhead. Conversely, the Triton MoE backend excels at dynamically mapping these small, fragmented token arrays across the physical boundaries of the active expert weights. This keeps the hardware’s internal prefetch streams and Tensor Core pipelines fully saturated even when processing highly unstable workloads at very low batch sizes.
Updating the routing policy is a pure configuration change with no kernel code modified. Still, it yielded a 10 percent end-to-end throughput improvement for FP8 quantized fused MoE models on H200. This improvement is available in the AWS Large Model Inference (LMI) v28 container.
Triton JIT recompilation elimination
One of the most impactful performance pathologies in GPU inference is also one of the least obvious: unnecessary kernel recompilation. Triton, the compiler framework underlying many of vLLM’s custom kernels, specializes integer arguments by default. Every time a kernel is invoked with a previously unseen value for a specialized parameter, Triton triggers a fresh just-in-time (JIT) compilation. In serving workloads where sequence lengths and batch sizes vary continuously, this creates a steady stream of compilation overhead that inflates latency, particularly Time to First Token (TTFT).
In MoE model serving, the _fused_inv_rope_fp8_quant_per_head kernel (responsible for fused rotary position embedding and FP8 quantization) was recompiling on every new num_tokens value. Adding do_not_specialize annotations to the variable-length parameters removed these recompilations entirely, improving TTFT by 9 percent on H200 at 8-way tensor parallelism (PR #42849).
In a multi-GPU cluster, all 8 GPUs must execute their kernels in perfect, microsecond-level synchronization. If even one GPU must stop to recompile its local _fused_inv_rope_fp8_quant_per_head kernel because its local token batch count changed, the other seven GPUs sit idle and wait for it. By eliminating recompilations across the entire cluster, we smoothed out the multi-GPU coordination overhead, delivering a 9 percent speedup for the user’s initial response latency. The principle here is to treat the compiler as a first-class optimization surface. Understanding how Triton specializes semantics and recognizing when parameters are dead or variable unlocks latency improvements with minimal code change.
We upstreamed this optimization to vLLM, and it is available in version 0.22.0 or later.
Conclusion
Through our collaboration with the vLLM community, we implemented and open sourced multiple kernel optimizations for fused MoE models. We apply these optimizations in the LMI Deep Learning Container on Amazon SageMaker AI. Together, these optimizations have delivered up to 10 percent higher throughput and up to 9 percent faster TTFT. To get started with custom model hosting, see the Amazon SageMaker AI hosting documentation.

articles.title: How to Rewrite Apache Spark UDFs for GPU Acceleration with AI Agents | NVIDIA Technical Blog
articles.text:
Enterprise applications have become increasingly demanding. Agentic AI has compounded the need for vast amounts of enterprise data with frequent, complex queries across increasingly large datasets.
Meeting that demand requires greater data throughput without a proportional increase in cost. NVIDIA cuDF addresses this challenge by leveraging the massive parallelism and high-bandwidth memory of GPUs for data analytics. Particularly, the NVIDIA cuDF plugin for Apache Spark brings this acceleration to Apache Spark, the industry-leading platform for big data processing and analytics, to achieve better TCO performance in major workloads.
User-defined functions (UDFs) have long been problematic for accelerated query engines, introducing runtime overheads due to their opaque nature. While UDFs can often be replaced with more performant code, rewriting UDFs has long been a laborious process requiring careful validation.
This post describes how to use agents to rewrite UDFs into GPU-accelerated equivalents within minutes, achieving 22x+ speedups in Apache Spark jobs. We’ll introduce the cuDF skills for Apache Spark, a set of skills to quickly break through the UDF bottleneck for end-to-end development, from testing, to benchmarking, through integration.
The UDF challenge
cuDF achieves seamless GPU acceleration in part due to Apache Spark’s declarative programming interface. The SQL / Dataframe abstractions are powerful because they separate what a query should produce from how the system should execute it. This enables the cuDF plugin to transparently parallelize row-wise operations using the massive SIMD capabilities of GPUs, without any change in user code.
Apache Spark, however, also supports UDFs: custom routines to extend built-in functionality. While useful for implementing bespoke business logic, UDFs break the declarative abstraction—they contain arbitrary user code which the system cannot reason about or parallelize in any general sense. During execution, the GPU accelerator must convert the data from a columnar to row-wise format, and fall back to the CPU to execute the UDF row-by-row:
Thus in an otherwise accelerated query, UDFs have the following drawbacks:
- The UDF incurs a round-trip data transfer overhead due to fallback.
- The UDF forgoes potential compute speedup, had it been written using GPU-accelerated primitives.
Accelerating UDFs
With a small, targeted code change, many UDFs can be rewritten into a GPU-accelerable form by using the right primitives. Rewriting UDFs eliminates the overhead associated with accelerator fallback, and can yield speedups of over 20x.
We outline three approaches to rewrite UDFs:
| Approach | Complexity | Best For | 
|---|---|---|
| SQL | Low, highest level of abstraction | Simple relational logic, e.g. small or inlined functions | 
| cuDF | Medium, more flexibility and control over execution | Most cases, e.g. moderately complex logic like string parsing, nested types | 
| CUDA | High, maximum flexibility and kernel-level control | Most complex or performance critical logic | 
To make these approaches concrete, consider a simple Scala UDF that converts temperature from Celsius to Fahrenheit:
final class ToFahrenheit
    extends Function1[java.lang.Double, java.lang.Double]
    with Serializable {
  override def apply(celsius: java.lang.Double): java.lang.Double = {
    if (celsius == null) null
    else celsius * 9.0 / 5.0 + 32.0
  }
}
spark.udf.register("to_fahrenheit", new ToFahrenheit)
spark.sql("""
  SELECT
    *,
    to_fahrenheit(celsius) AS fahrenheit
  FROM temperatures
""")
Rewriting the UDF with SQL
The most direct solution for simple UDFs is to replace the UDF with an equivalent Spark SQL expression:
spark.sql("""
  SELECT
    *,
    celsius * 9.0 / 5.0 + 32.0 AS fahrenheit
  FROM temperatures
""")
This makes the function visible in Spark’s expression tree. During query planning, the cuDF plugin will replace these expressions with their corresponding GPU implementations, keeping the data and execution fully on the GPU.
Rewriting the UDF with cuDF
When SQL primitives are insufficient or undesirable, the UDF can instead operate directly on GPU columns using the RapidsUDF interface, a contract provided by the cuDF plugin. The contract requires a single method, evaluateColumnar:
import ai.rapids.cudf.{ColumnVector, Scalar}
import com.nvidia.spark.RapidsUDF
import scala.util.Using
final class ToFahrenheit
    extends Function1[java.lang.Double, java.lang.Double]
    with Serializable
    with RapidsUDF {
  override def apply(celsius: java.lang.Double): java.lang.Double = {
    if (celsius == null) null
    else celsius * 9.0 / 5.0 + 32.0
  }
  override def evaluateColumnar(
      numRows: Int,
      args: ColumnVector*): ColumnVector = {
    Using.Manager { use =>
      val scale = use(Scalar.fromDouble(9.0 / 5.0))
      val offset = use(Scalar.fromDouble(32.0))
      val scaled = use(args.head.mul(scale))
      scaled.add(offset)
    }.get
  }
}
The cuDF plugin recognizes instances of the RapidsUDF interface and passes a GPU-resident ColumnVector to the evaluateColumnar function. The function then composes operations from the Java API for cuDF operations to process the column in parallel. This approach provides a richer API for more complex processing.
Rewriting the UDF with CUDA
For highly complex logic that cannot be efficiently composed from existing cuDF operations, a RapidsUDF can invoke a custom CUDA kernel through the Java Native Interface (JNI). We’ve elided the code for brevity, but examples of CUDA conversions can be found in the cuDF examples for Spark UDFs.
Efficient rewrites with AI agents
Despite the performance benefits, UDF rewrites can require significant engineering effort. They demand careful API selection, semantic validation, and performance measurement, while columnar APIs can be unfamiliar to practitioners with less experience in vectorized programming.
Fortunately, much of this work is well suited to coding agents. With proper guardrails, an agent can search unfamiliar APIs, implement candidate rewrites, and iterate quickly while executable tests and performance measurements determine whether each change is acceptable.
Available skills
The cuDF skills for Apache Spark decompose the rewrite into four focused feedback loops. Each skill defines both the work to perform and the evidence required before proceeding to the next stage:
Figure 2. Four skills guide agents through testing, conversion, benchmarking, and optimization, with verification-driven feedback loops at each stage
Scaffolding and design
Reliable agent execution begins with a reliable development environment. The skills provide a complete project template containing the cuDF- and Spark-specific scaffolding required for end-to-end development. This includes test and benchmark harnesses, encoded routines for output verification, and build configuration. By encoding this knowledge into code, the agent can focus on the UDF rather than repeatedly reconstructing specialized infrastructure.
The skills also provide best practices for GPU programming with cuDF, including memory management and configuration. This serves as an advisory tips and tricks reference. To best leverage the power of frontier models, the agent remains free to explore different implementations based on surrounding context and select an approach based on measured correctness and performance.
Performance results
A major consumer technology company used this workflow to convert 30+ UDFs used in production data pipelines into GPU-accelerated implementations. The rewrites preserved the behavior of the original CPU UDFs while removing costly fallbacks from otherwise GPU-accelerated workloads. As an example, the following benchmark shows the resulting before-and-after performance for a UDF in one such workload:
This particular UDF was affecting more than 3,000+ jobs, and in this job, saw a 22x speedup when implemented as a cuDF-enabled RapidsUDF. With the help of agents, these performance gains are much more attainable, enabling practitioners to iterate on rewrites on the order of hours rather than days or weeks, without compromising correctness.
Get started
Converting UDFs to GPU implementations can unlock major speedups and contribute to overall cost savings in GPU-accelerated pipelines. With agent skills, the rewrite process can be made both easy and reliable.
To get started, install the cuDF skills for Apache Spark on GitHub, either directly or using the npx skill installer:
npx skills add NVIDIA/cudf-spark --skill ‘*’
For a deeper walkthrough of the workflow and practical lessons from building it, see the Data + AI Summit session, Coding with AI Agents to Supercharge Your Spark UDFs with GPU Acceleration.
To learn more about GPU acceleration for Apache Spark, follow the cuDF plugin for Apache Spark getting-started guide to unlock better performance and TCO across your Spark pipelines. Visit our webpage to learn more about NVIDIA cuDF: GPU-Accelerated Structured Data Processing, or you can read the docs for more information on NVIDIA cuDF plugin for Apache Spark.

articles.title: The MFA Gaps Attackers are Still Exploiting
articles.text:
On August 4, 2026, an Akira ransomware affiliate began spraying passwords against a SonicWall SSL VPN. Around seven minutes later, one attempt succeeded. The credentials were valid, and the VPN account had no multi-factor authentication (MFA) protecting it. Roughly two hours later, the attacker used RDP to access the domain controller and began enumerating Active Directory.
The ransomware deployment ultimately failed, but by then the attacker had already stolen credentials and file-share data.
It highlights an issue that is still common in 2026, where an organization might require MFA for Microsoft 365 and other SaaS applications while leaving certain access paths protected only by passwords. It’s this gap that attackers are regularly exploiting.
Stolen Credentials Remain a Valuable Tool for Attackers
Once an attacker has a valid account, they can begin interacting with the environment through the same authentication mechanisms used by legitimate employees and administrators. AI is adding another dimension to this problem by helping attackers operate at greater speed and scale.
The underlying identity tactics are largely unchanged: attackers still compromise identities, reuse credentials, escalate privileges and misuse legitimate access. The threat is that AI makes familiar techniques cheaper and easier to run at scale.
Mandiant’s ransomware investigations illustrate why that matters once credentials are obtained. Compromised legitimate credentials accounted for initial access in 21% of the 2025 incidents where the entry point could be established, typically through RDP or VPN.
RDP also appeared frequently later in the attack chain, with attackers using compromised or newly created accounts over RDP for lateral movement in around 85% of the ransomware incidents it investigated.
Identifying Stolen Credentials in Your Organization
Strong authentication helps limit what an attacker can do with a stolen password, but it is still worth finding exposed or risky credentials before they are used. Password reuse, weak choices and credentials that have appeared in previous breaches all increase the chance that an attacker will find a password that still works somewhere in the environment.
That makes regular password auditing a useful part of Active Directory security. Specops Password Auditor is a free, read-only password auditing tool that scans Active Directory for password-related vulnerabilities and presents the findings in an interactive report covering user and password policy information.
This gives IT teams another opportunity to reduce credential risk at source: identify password weaknesses, address them where possible, and make sure that a compromised password is not enough on its own to gain access.
Secure your Active Directory passwords with Specops Password Policy
Verizon’s Data Breach Investigation Report found stolen credentials are involved in 44.7% of breaches. 
Effortlessly secure Active Directory with compliant password policies, blocking 4+ billion compromised passwords, boosting security, and slashing support hassles!
Why Cloud MFA Doesn’t Necessarily Protect the Entire Windows Estate
Microsoft 365, identity providers and SaaS applications are obvious places to add additional authentication factors because they are internet-facing and frequently targeted. The problem is that cloud MFA does not automatically extend to every system that relies on the same user identity.
A user may need MFA to access a SaaS application through the corporate identity provider, but the same account could still be accepted elsewhere with just a password.
That creates a fragmented authentication environment where some routes are better protected than others, which leaves a gap for attackers to exploit.
VPNs are another potential gap. As the August Akira ransomware attack demonstrated, a threat actor that obtains or brute forces a valid username and password may be able to turn those credentials directly into remote network access if MFA isn’t enforced.
For IT and security teams, the useful question is therefore not simply whether MFA is deployed, but where a password is still enough on its own. Windows logon, RDP, VPN access and older AD-backed services are all worth including in that review.
Closing the Authentication Gaps
Closing these gaps means applying stronger authentication to the places where credentials are still being trusted, rather than treating MFA as something that only sits in front of cloud applications.
That is where solutions like Specops Secure Access fit by extending MFA to Windows logon, RDP and VPN authentication. This adds strong protection to some of the access paths attackers regularly target with stolen Active Directory credentials.
It also supports SSO for SaaS applications through OIDC and SAML, helping organizations apply a more consistent authentication approach across on-premises and cloud services.
Authentication is also a useful source of security telemetry. Specops Secure Access integrates with SIEM, SOC and analytics platforms, allowing authentication events and suspicious activity to feed into the wider monitoring process.
Protecting the user is only part of the picture, though. A second question is whether the device making the request should be trusted.
Mitigate the Risk of Stolen Passwords
In 2026, stolen passwords are still powerful tools for attackers if they are accepted by VPNs, RDP sessions or Windows systems without additional checks. That is why MFA coverage matters as much as adopting MFA in the first place. Protecting cloud applications is important, but it does not remove the risk created by authentication paths elsewhere in the environment that still rely on a password alone.
No single control will stop every intrusion, and MFA is no exception. But organizations can make credential theft much less useful by asking a simple question: where can a password still be used on its own?
Adding another protective layer to those areas with Specops Secure Access ensures that one stolen credential does not become the easiest route into the rest of the network.
If you’re looking to close gaps in your identity security strategy, book a demo with Specops today.

articles.text:
Nous vous en parlions récemment, SFR va augmenter les prix de certains de ses abonnements Internet et téléphoniques. L’opérateur a commencé à envoyer des mails d’avertissements aux clients concernés. Ces mails font état d’augmentations allant de 1,49 € à presque 5 €.
SFR annonce une hausse des tarifs de plusieurs de ses offres
Il est question de hausses de prix particulièrement importantes. Sur X, un client de SFR fait par exemple état d’une augmentation de 4,50 euros par mois sur sa facture initiale de 45 €, soit une hausse de 10 %. D’après nos confrères d’Univers Freebox, une offre fibre 1 Gb/s facturée 17,47 euros par mois passe à 22,46 euros par mois (+28 %). De notre côté, nous avons reçu un mail nous avertissant qu’un abonnement Internet facturé 27,98 € par mois allait augmenter de 3,29 € (+12 %). Les hausses varient donc en fonction du type d’abonnement.
Dans le mail adressé aux clients concernés, SFR indique : « Afin de continuer à vous proposer une expérience de qualité au quotidien, toujours plus fluide et toujours plus rapide, nous vous informons que le tarif de votre abonnement augmentera de X € par mois à compter de votre prochaine facture ».
Les clients concernés disposent de 4 mois pour résilier sans frais l’abonnement en cours
SFR explique : « Conformément à l’article L.224-33 du code de la consommation, vous avez la possibilité de résilier votre contrat sans frais et sans pénalité si vous n’acceptez pas ces nouvelles conditions contractuelles. Cette résiliation peut être effectuée dans un délai de 4 mois à compter du présent courriel ».
Si vous êtes concerné, vous disposez donc de 4 mois à partir de la réception du courrier d’avertissement pour résilier l’abonnement en cours sans frais et sans pénalité. Au-delà de ce laps de temps, des frais seront appliqués en cas de résiliation de votre abonnement.
SFR précise par ailleurs qu’il existe trois façons de résilier un abonnement concerné par une hausse de prix : par courrier (en indiquant que vous refusez cette modification contractuelle), depuis votre espace client en ligne (en indiquant le motif suivant : « Refus des modifications contractuelles/Motifs légitimes ») et, enfin, en cas de changement d’opérateur avec portabilité du numéro. Dans ce dernier cas, SFR vous adressera un e-mail ou un SMS à la suite de votre demande de portabilité, vous permettant de préciser le motif de votre résiliation : « Refus des modifications contractuelles (art. L.224-33 conso) ».
Notons enfin que certains clients dénoncent une hausse de leur abonnement alors que celui-ci leur avait été présenté comme étant à prix fixe « à vie ».

articles.title: "Je paie, je choisis” : Spliiit et Sharesub ripostent à Netflix, Disney+ et Apple avec une pétition
articles.text:
"Je paie, je choisis” : Spliiit et Sharesub ripostent à Netflix, Disney+ et Apple avec une pétition
Interview // Les Numériques a échangé avec les plateformes de coabonnement françaises Spliiit et Sharesub, qui rétorquent à Netflix, Apple et Disney+ via une pétition visant à défendre les droits des consommateurs.
Plus de quatre mois après la condamnation de Spliiit par le Tribunal judiciaire de Paris pour contrefaçon de marques et concurrence déloyale, les plateformes de coabonnement repartent au combat. Les entreprises Spliiit et Sharesub ont ainsi lancé une pétition nationale pour défendre les droits des consommateurs français, alors qu'une proposition de loi a été déposée à l'Assemblée nationale.
Les Numériques a pu s'entretenir avec Jonathan Lalinec, cofondateur du site de coabonnement Spliiit, et Jean-Brice de Cazenove, cofondateur du site Sharesub.
Partage d'abonnements numériques : la notion controversée de “foyer” au cœur des débats
Déposée le 23 juillet dernier à l'Assemblée nationale par les députés socialistes Mickaël Bouloux et Pierrick Courbon, la proposition de loi n° 3101 vise à légaliser et protéger le partage des abonnements numériques.
Le texte propose d'ajouter un article au Code de la consommation afin de garantir le droit pour un abonné de partager les accès à son compte avec les personnes de son choix sans restriction géographique, contournant ainsi la notion de “foyer” imposée il y a trois ans par les plateformes.
Avec leur texte, les députés Bouloux et Courbon souhaitent redonner de la liberté et du pouvoir d'achat aux Français, qui sont 80 % à disposer d'un abonnement numérique (vidéo à la demande, musique, jeux vidéo, logiciels) en 2026 et y consacrent en moyenne 54 € par mois.
Alors que Jonathan Lalinec rappelle que le tribunal de Paris a établi en mai dernier que l'activité de coabonnement n'était pas illicite, l'heure est plus que jamais à la pédagogie pour les leaders français du marché. C'est tout le sens de la pétition “Je paie, je choisis”, disponible via ce lien.
Pour rappel, les plateformes Spliiit et Sharesub permettent aux particuliers de partager les “places” disponibles de leur abonnement avec d'autres (amis ou inconnus), à la manière du covoiturage.
Spliiit et Sharesub face à Netflix et Disney+ : l'interview des cofondateurs
Jean-Brice de Cazenove Avec Jonathan, nous discutons depuis très longtemps et nous avons voulu faire un travail de sensibilisation sur le partage d'abonnements tel que nous le pratiquons aujourd'hui. Nous essayons de définir ce qu'est la co-souscription, un concept relativement nouveau pour le public. Aujourd'hui, cela a trouvé un écho auprès de nombreuses personnes, notamment des députés qui ont déposé cette proposition de loi.
Jean-Brice de Cazenove La plupart des CGU (conditions générales d'utilisation, NDLR) des plateformes sont des traductions de la version anglaise, et le droit européen n'est pas toujours pris en compte. Or la loi aujourd'hui peut suffire à protéger le consommateur.
Certaines mesures peuvent ainsi être considérées comme discriminatoires selon que vous apparteniez ou non à une même famille. Cela soulève aussi la question de ce qu’est cette dernière, car il existe des millions de familles atypiques. Ces personnes ne correspondent donc pas forcément à un modèle unique. Est-ce discriminatoire à leur égard ? Nous souhaitions donc que cela soit clarifié, car c'est tout simplement nécessaire.
	
Cette proposition de loi a le mérite de la lisibilité : à partir du moment où on achète un abonnement avec plusieurs places, l'acheteur en a la jouissance.
Jean-Brice de Cazenove Cette proposition a le mérite de la lisibilité. À partir du moment où on achète un abonnement avec plusieurs places, l'acheteur en a la jouissance. Il peut donc attribuer les places comme il le souhaite, car ce qui compte derrière, c'est que les droits d'auteur soient payés.
C'est ça qui est important, car dans le cadre de notre éthique avec Jonathan, ce qui nous intéresse, c'est de continuer à financer efficacement la création. Nous sommes donc attachés au fait que chaque abonnement paie ses droits, et notre modèle ne le remet pas en cause. L'important dans cette proposition de loi, c'est qu'elle garantirait la liberté et la transparence au consommateur.
Jonathan Lalinec D'un côté, il y a les députés qui font leur travail pour trouver des cosignataires. Mais avec Jean-Brice, nous avons un public concerné par cette proposition de loi et nous allons essayer de faire du bruit pour qu'il soit entendu. Là est le principe de la pétition : si nous parvenons à recueillir quelques milliers de signatures, nous pourrons inciter les députés à se pencher davantage sur le sujet.
Jonathan Lalinec En réalité, nous cherchons surtout à démontrer que le sujet intéresse les gens et que cette pétition mérite d'être débattue. Je pense qu'elle est d'autant plus pertinente aujourd'hui, compte tenu des problèmes de pouvoir d'achat.
	
Ce projet de loi défend le droit du consommateur à partager. C'est aussi simple que cela.
Jonathan Lalinec Il ne faut pas le cacher, ce projet de loi va dans notre sens. Mais en réalité, il ne mentionne ni Spliiit ni Sharesub, et il essaie simplement de faire comprendre aux autorités publiques que cela concerne les consommateurs français avant tout. Cette proposition de loi ne défend pas le principe d'entreprises comme la nôtre, mais bien le droit du consommateur à partager. C'est aussi simple que cela.
La pétition “Je paie, je choisis” est accessible via ce lien.

articles.title: Webs que se caen y bots desactivados: la consecuencia inesperada de bombardear centros de datos
articles.text: Un miembro de la Guardia Revolucionaria de Irán saluda junto a un dron durante un desfile el pasado 18 de septiembre. Ucrania ha asestado un importante golpe a la infraestructura digital rusa. Los drones ucranios han lanzado desde el pasado jueves una serie de ataques que han destrozado tres grandes centros de datos de Yandex, conocido como “el Google del Kremlin” , a las afueras de Moscú. La aplicación de transporte de viajeros Yandex Taxi y el servicio de pagos del grupo, Yandex Pay, han dejado de funcionar temporalmente. El presidente ucranio, Volodímir Zelenski, incluso aseguró que los bombardeos desactivaron bots rusos. Seguir leyendo

articles.title: Votre Livret A finance déjà le nucléaire des EPR2, et c'est l'État qui paie les intérêts — Frandroid
articles.text:
Le projet de loi de finances pour 2027, présenté le jeudi 1er octobre en Conseil des ministres, contient une ligne budgétaire inédite, alors même que l’État fait la chasse aux nouvelles dépenses pour tenter d’enrayer la dette. Intitulée « Soutien financier au nouveau nucléaire français » (programme 387), cette enveloppe de 137,8 millions d’euros a un rôle bien précis, et elle ne finance pas directement le chantier des six EPR2.
En réalité, cette enveloppe comble l’écart entre un taux d’intérêt soutenable pour EDF et le taux dont a besoin la Caisse des Dépôts, dont le Fonds d’épargne gère une partie de l’argent placé sur les Livrets A, LDDS et LEP.
Pour y voir plus clair, rappelons que le projet de loi prévoit les conditions suivantes pour la société de projet d’EDF, qui empruntera auprès du Fonds d’épargne de la Caisse des Dépôts : 0 % d’intérêt pendant la construction des EPR2, puis un taux fixe de 3 % dès lors que les EPR2 entrent en production.
Jusqu’à 330€ d’avantages avec nos offres Hello Prime ou Hello Prime Duo, dont 80€ cash à l’ouverture de compte !
Pour mesurer l’ampleur du montage, le Fonds d’épargne pourra prêter jusqu’à 60 milliards d’euros à la société de projet d’EDF, soit 60 % du devis de construction des six réacteurs, chiffré à 72,8 milliards d’euros (en euros de 2020). Les EPR2 doivent être construits par paires à Penly (Seine-Maritime), à Gravelines (Nord) et au Bugey (Ain), et l’État doit garantir ce prêt à 100 %, capital et intérêts compris, jusqu’au 31 décembre 2090. Les 137,8 millions d’euros inscrits pour 2027 ne couvrent donc que la première année d’intérêts.
Un mécanisme complexe pour protéger EDF
De son côté, la Caisse des Dépôts a un impératif : elle doit rémunérer les dépôts du Livret A, selon le taux qui lui est associé. L’accord qui a été trouvé avec la Caisse des Dépôts repose sur un taux d’intérêt correspondant au taux du Livret A + 1 point. Autrement dit, en phase de production, si le taux du Livret A est de 2 %, les 3 % payés par EDF correspondent exactement aux 3 % qu’attend la Caisse des Dépôts.
Aujourd’hui, ce seuil de 2 % joue en faveur de l’État. Avec un Livret A à 1,7 % depuis le 1er août 2026, le Fonds d’épargne prête à 2,7 % : si les réacteurs étaient déjà en service, EDF paierait plus que nécessaire et l’État encaisserait la différence. À l’inverse, un Livret A au-dessus de 2 % obligerait l’État à continuer de payer l’écart, même une fois les EPR2 en production.
Pendant la phase de construction, c’est l’État qui doit payer les intérêts auprès de la Caisse des Dépôts pour rémunérer les Livrets A. C’est exactement ce à quoi sert cette nouvelle ligne de 137 millions d’euros.
Rien n’est encore adopté pour autant. L’article 48, qui crée le compte de commerce, figure dans la première partie du budget, au programme des débats en séance à l’Assemblée nationale de ce mardi 13 au lundi 19 octobre, avant un vote solennel prévu le 20 octobre. L’article 69, qui autorise la garantie de l’État sur le prêt, sera examiné à partir du 27 octobre, avant le passage du texte au Sénat. Côté chantier, la première mise en service est visée à l’horizon 2038, à Penly.
Ça donne quoi, à l’échelle individuelle ?
Pour les épargnants, ce montage ne change rien : le livret reste rémunéré au taux réglementé, l’argent reste disponible, et l’État doit garantir le prêt à 100 %. Mais sachez que si vous avez 1 000 euros sur un Livret A, un LDDS ou un LEP, une partie de cette somme, centralisée par la Caisse des Dépôts, peut participer au programme de relance du nucléaire. Tant que les EPR2 sont en construction, c’est l’État qui verse au Fonds d’épargne les intérêts qu’EDF ne paie pas, ce qui permet de continuer à rémunérer cette épargne. Une fois les réacteurs en service, EDF prendra le relais à 3 %, et l’État réglera ou encaissera la différence selon le niveau du Livret A.
Un montage financier qui n’est pas sans risque pour l’État
Ce montage financier n’est pas sans risque, puisqu’il engendre un total d’intérêts qui peut très fortement varier. Dans l’exposé des motifs du projet de loi de finances, le gouvernement chiffre ce total à 44,2 milliards d’euros avec un Livret A à 1,5 %, à 53,6 milliards dans son scénario central (Livret A à 2 %), et jusqu’à 89 milliards avec un Livret A à 3 % et sept ans de retard sur les chantiers, une période pendant laquelle l’État compense l’absence d’intérêts payés par EDF. Ces montants ne sont pas la facture finale de l’État : une fois les réacteurs en service, EDF paie 3 % et l’État ne règle que l’écart.
Ce prêt bonifié s’ajoute à un autre engagement de l’État : lors du dernier Conseil de politique nucléaire, il s’est engagé à soutenir la production des EPR2 par un contrat pour différence d’une durée de quarante ans, qui fixe un prix maximal de 100 euros le mégawattheure.

articles.title: All Systems Go: Global PC App Ecosystem Ready for NVIDIA RTX Spark
articles.text:
NVIDIA RTX Spark is a new beginning for the PC — a reinvention combining the capabilities of a gaming PC, a creative studio and a personal AI supercomputer into a single superchip. With up to 128GB of unified memory and 1 petaflop of AI compute, RTX Spark delivers the full stack of NVIDIA RTX and CUDA technologies for creators, developers and gamers, while unlocking a new paradigm in personal computing via powerful local AI agents.
Last week, NVIDIA and Microsoft announced that RTX Spark laptops will be available on Friday, Oct. 16. Ahead of the launch, NVIDIA and its ecosystem partners are rolling out new software features and performance optimizations to expand what’s possible with local AI on RTX Spark.
New and upcoming RTX Spark updates — among the thousands of apps, games and models available at launch — include:
- New agent features, models and tools that enhance local agents on RTX Spark: 
  - Updates to top agent apps including GitHub Copilot, Hermes, OpenClaw, Perplexity, Pi and WorkBuddy streamline setup on RTX Spark, improve security with OpenShell and Microsoft Execution Containers (MXC), and enable hybrid local and cloud AI routing.
  - The NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B model, purpose-built for agentic AI on RTX Spark, releases on Thursday, Oct. 15.
  - NVIDIA PAIR moves out of beta and adds llama.cpp support.
- Top creative apps optimized for RTX Spark:
  - Up to 2x performance is coming soon to Adobe’s top apps. NVIDIA and Adobe have collaborated to rearchitect Photoshop for GPU-accelerated compositing and Premiere for playback, rendering, effects and more.
  - The NVIDIA Broadcast 2.3 release brings new Video Super Resolution, Video Frame Generation, offline file processing and agent Model Context Protocol (MCP) controls to the app.
  - NVIDIA RTX Video Frame Generation and high dynamic range (HDR) capabilities are available now in ComfyUI to accelerate AI generative video workflows.
  - NVIDIA DLSS Ray Reconstruction will be available in Blender 5.3 in November to improve interactivity in the viewport.
- Developer tools are now ready for RTX Spark:
  - Top developer frameworks are now available for RTX Spark, including PyTorch, Python and CUDA, as well as all CUDA libraries.
  - GitHub Copilot, Pi and other coding agents are now optimized for RTX Spark.
  - Llama.cpp adds support for decision models, and releases a Windows app.
- Hundreds of top games and anti-cheat are supported on RTX Spark, plus:
  - A 2x faster DLSS 5 AI model arrives Friday, Oct. 16, and a new Performance Mode for DLSS Frame Generation is available today via the NVIDIA App beta.
  - Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB, the third-generation small language model (SLM) for NVIDIA ACE AI game characters, releases Friday, Oct. 23.
  - The latest RTX Remix update, including DLSS 5 support, releases on Friday, Oct. 23.
Advancing Local AI Agents With New Apps, Models and Tools
AI is changing the way people interact with PCs. Agent popularity skyrocketed this year, with projects such as OpenClaw and Hermes topping popularity charts on GitHub. Local large language models (LLMs) surpassed the intelligence threshold to power agents, with models like Qwen 3.8-Flash-Next catching up to frontier cloud models released just a few months ago. As a result, local LLM downloads are already 5x higher than all of last year.
From models to agent harnesses to security to tools, NVIDIA is partnering closely with the local AI ecosystem to make RTX Spark the ideal hardware to run local agents.
Local AI Agents Made Easy On RTX Spark
From the first boot of RTX Spark, users will be greeted with a “Getting Started” screen to choose and install their agent app.
These agents will come with new, secure sandboxing technology thanks to NVIDIA OpenShell and MXC. MXC delivers operating system-level security, while OpenShell makes it simpler for agents to adopt MXC and adds advanced capabilities such as credential protection and security monitoring. Hermes Agent will integrate granular OpenShell controls and MXC by the end of the month. OpenClaw and GitHub Copilot now support MXC.
After installing an agent, setting up local AI is also now seamless in GitHub Copilot, Hermes Agent, OpenClaw, Perplexity, Pi and WorkBuddy. The apps will recommend an optimized local model and settings configuration for RTX Spark, and set it all up for users in a few clicks.
Many users want the best of both worlds — local models for free iteration, and cloud models for frontier intelligence. NVIDIA Switchyard, an open source model router library, enables agents to intelligently route queries between local and cloud LLMs, allowing the user to minimize cloud usage but still obtain similar results to just running on cloud. Hermes will be adding Switchyard later in October, and other agents like Perplexity Computer and GitHub Copilot have integrated their own routing solutions.
Software providers have made it simple for agents to connect to top Windows apps, with easy-to-use MCP libraries and command line interfaces (CLIs). NVIDIA has also now made available MCPs for its applications, including NVIDIA App, Broadcast, PAIR, Omniverse, RTX Remix and a large library of CUDA-X Skills.
NVIDIA is also releasing AI playbooks for RTX Spark, available on Friday, Oct 16. Users can set up their first agent, build an AI chief of staff, configure their system for development or design a creative assistant.
Meet Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B: Built for Local Agents on RTX Spark
NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB, available Thursday, Oct. 15, is a new LLM purpose-built for running local agents on RTX Spark.
This model is a 74B parameter, 9B-active-parameter mixture-of-experts (MoE) model, packed into 24GB using 2-bit quantization with advanced quantization-aware training techniques to retain quality. It aims to achieve the optimal balance between speed and intelligence, being faster than most popular dense models while smarter than most popular MoE models with a similar memory footprint.
Users will be able to run Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B at launch through llama.cpp, vLLM, Ollama, Unsloth and LM Studio. It will also be directly accessible via agents such as Hermes and OpenClaw.
Like other Nemotron models, Bolt 74B is fully open source — including training data, weights and recipes — so developers can fine-tune and customize their own agents.
The Perfect PAIR
Local AI doesn’t have to run on just one PC. NVIDIA PAIR, a personal AI router, is officially moving out of beta today, making it easier to tap into the total AI compute of compatible PCs on a local network. The free, open source software tool automatically discovers and connects devices, installs AI models and inference engines, and distributes AI workloads across available systems.
The official release adds llama.cpp support, direct model downloads from Hugging Face, customizable inference engine settings and RTX Spark support, along with a variety of inference and user experience improvements.
PAIR works on Windows, Linux and macOS. Developers can contribute to the open source project via Github — just one month after the initial PAIR release, the community has already contributed over 10 features and fixes to the release.
Sparking Creativity
RTX Spark brings over 130 accelerated apps, CUDA for fast video and image generation, and RTX technologies such as DLSS, NVENC and OptiX to advanced content creation workflows — all in a thin and light laptop with on-the-go performance.
Adobe Accelerates Creative Applications for RTX Spark
Adobe is optimizing its industry-leading creative applications, including Photoshop, Premiere and Substance 3D, for RTX Spark, delivering up to 2x faster AI, editing, color and effects across creative workflows.
In Photoshop, GPU-accelerated compositing makes complex image editing faster and more responsive, with improvements to the Remove Tool and effects such as Light Leaks. Premiere accelerates demanding video editing tasks, including playback, rendering, color grading and AI-powered features such as Enhance Speech and Object Mask. Meanwhile, Substance 3D Painter speeds up texture creation workflows, from baking high-resolution mesh maps to opening, saving and exporting large projects.
The updates will be rolling out in phases, with AI feature optimizations in Photoshop and Premiere now ready in beta, and with Adobe Substance 3D updates coming soon. Opt in to the beta to get access to the RTX Spark-optimized builds.
Latest NVIDIA Broadcast Brings New AI Effects to Live and Recorded Content
Available for download now, NVIDIA Broadcast 2.3 runs natively on RTX Spark, and adds new RTX Video Super Resolution and Frame Generation AI effects and Studio Voice profiles.
A new Offline File Processor lets creators apply Broadcast effects to prerecorded content, with many effects running at higher quality since there isn’t a need to maintain real-time performance. The update also introduces a new MCP server and skill that lets local AI agents adjust effects, change settings and process files directly through the Broadcast app.
RTX Video Brings Frame Generation and HDR to ComfyUI
ComfyUI is expanding its RTX Video tools with two new nodes: RTX Video Frame Generation and RTX Video HDR. It’s also providing the ability to export EXR files, giving creators more ways to enhance AI-generated video.
RTX Video Frame Generation increases video frame rates for smoother motion for GeForce RTX 40 Series GPUs and newer, while RTX Video HDR converts standard dynamic range (SDR) footage to HDR for greater flexibility in color grading. Combined with RTX Video Super Resolution, these tools enable creators to upscale, enhance and refine video within a single ComfyUI workflow.
For example, creators can combine LTX 2.5 with RTX Video Frame Generation and HDR to transform a 1080p, 30 frames-per-second (fps) SDR clip into a smoother 60 fps HDR video exported as EXR files ready for color grading.
Blender Adds DLSS 4.5 Ray Reconstruction
Blender has released a beta version of its popular 3D editor, adding compatibility for RTX Spark. Download Blender version 5.3 to get access.
Coming next month, Blender will also be adding support for DLSS Ray Reconstruction, allowing for real-time updates in the viewport so artists can navigate a scene while previewing it in real time.
Code, Text and Deploy From RTX Spark
Developers are moving from writing code to directing AI agents. This new development paradigm is requiring many to spread their work across their laptop, a cloud LLM and a cloud virtual machine, where they test and prototype.
RTX Spark enables developers to work on one machine, running all their workloads and libraries, testing and prototyping, and deploying. They can now do so directly in Windows with the new Windows Developer Config, which enhances the user experience for devs and installs all the top developer tools — or via Windows Subsystem for Linux, where they can get access to the same packages they’ll use to publish to the cloud.
Developer Tools Are RTX-Spark Ready
NVIDIA has partnered with Microsoft to ensure that developer tools are ready for RTX Spark. Alongside RTX Spark, the community is releasing:
- The first PyTorch-CUDA build for Windows on Arm.
- The first Python build that is native by default on Windows on Arm, with Python 3.15.
- The first native Conda installer for Windows on Arm, with over 2,000 Conda packages.
- 97% of the top 15,000 Python wheels are ready, thanks to work with the ecosystem. NVIDIA will be working closely with the community to ready the remaining wheels.
Development is now mostly done by agents. NVIDIA Skills — an open source GitHub repository that teaches agents how to use NVIDIA CUDA-X tools and libraries — lets users develop apps that are accelerated on NVIDIA technologies, even without knowing anything about CUDA.
Coding Agents Are Ready for Local AI
In addition to GitHub Copilot — one of the most popular coding agents, used by millions worldwide — adding support for MXC, it’s updating its model router HydraFusion with support for local models. This enables developers to use their local hardware to reduce token consumption while tapping into frontier intelligence.
Microsoft is making coding models, such as MAI 1.1 Coding Flash, available locally, and adding llama.cpp as a backend to Windows ML — extending the supported models and enabling the latest NVIDIA performance optimizations.
Get started with GitHub Copilot running locally when RTX Spark launches.
Llama.cpp Adds Support for Decision Models, Releases a Windows App
Decision models are the latest breakthrough in AI development. They give AI agents a near-instant way to make decisions, without lengthy reasoning loops. They can choose what to do next, from classifying requests to selecting the next action, up to 200x faster than traditional agents. Decision models are now supported in llama.cpp and Unsloth on RTX Spark and GeForce RTX GPUs.
Llama.cpp is also releasing today Llama Windows, a Windows-native companion app for llama.cpp, enabling an easy-to-use user interface to download and run models locally, without having to go into the command line. This app, like llama.cpp, is optimized for RTX Spark. Learn more on the Hugging Face blog.
Game On: RTX Spark Launches With Hundreds of Top Games and DLSS 5
RTX Spark is ready for gaming, with hundreds of top titles available when laptops launch on Friday, Oct. 16, including CONTROL Resonant, Cyberpunk 2077, Fortnite, Gears of War: E-Day, Genshin Impact, Hogwarts Legacy, Honkai: Star Rail, Marvel Rivals, NARAKA: BLADEPOINT, NBA 2K27, World of Warcraft and many more.
NVIDIA has worked to bring the full stack of RTX technologies, including DLSS, Reflex, Remix, G-SYNC and ray tracing, to the new platform, along with collaborating with game developers to enable anti-cheat support for popular multiplayer games. Learn more about gaming on RTX Spark.
DLSS 5 Brings Neural Rendering to RTX Spark
NVIDIA DLSS 5 with 3D-Guided Neural Rendering is also coming to RTX Spark on launch day. The technology uses AI to enhance lighting and materials with lifelike detail, making game worlds and characters more realistic while preserving developers’ artistic vision. A new, 2x faster DLSS 5 AI model debuts in NBA 2K27 on Friday, Oct. 16, boosting frame rates by up to 1.4x. The faster model will also power DLSS 5 in Hogwarts Legacy starting Thursday, Nov. 5, and Where Winds Meet in late November.
DLSS 5 is also coming to NVIDIA RTX Remix on Friday, Oct. 23, so modders can add better materials, lighting and shadows to classic characters and environments, as shown from modder Sparkles/Kim2091 in her in-development project, Fallout 4 RTX.
Read more about DLSS 5 on RTX Spark on GeForce.com.
Game Agents Running Locally on RTX Spark
Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB is the third-generation SLM for NVIDIA ACE, the suite of technologies for building in-game AI agents that deliver next-generation gaming experiences. The first-generation model was in a public beta earlier this year for PUBG, allowing players to team up with AI teammates, while the more efficient second-generation model previewed in Aniimo at Gamescom, turning standard creatures into voice-responsive companions.
Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B combines natural conversation with multi-turn tool use, instruction following and grounding in application state to power fast local voice and device assistants, interactive characters and embedded interfaces.
Designed for a low memory footprint and fast time to first token, this model enables responsive local experiences while leaving headroom for applications and other AI models. Its new conversational mode helps keep responses concise and speech-ready, and developers can turn reasoning on or off as needed.
Starting Friday, Oct. 23, test drive the third-generation Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB inside SkyrimNET, an AI nonplayable character (NPC) modding platform by MinLL for The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim. SkyrimNET transforms every NPC into an unscripted, interactive character equipped with personal memory, voice and autonomy for dynamic conversations and context-aware quests generated on the fly.
Now compatible with RTX Spark, SkyrimNET supports both cloud and local inference across multiple models, with the latest Nemotron models delivering best-in-class performance for efficient and fast in-game interactions. Download the build on GitHub.
Accelerating Modding Workflows in RTX Remix
As AI agents continue to help modders make their favorite classic games compatible with the RTX Remix renderer, NVIDIA is streamlining asset updates with a major overhaul to its AI-powered texture generation workflow. Launching Friday, Oct. 23, as part of Remix 1.6, ComfyUI Version 2 replaces complex REST application programming interface (API) node connections with a dedicated AI tools layout directly in the sidebar.
This update allows modders and artists to generate physically based rendering materials natively inside RTX Remix with zero API setup required. A new batch processing feature makes it easy to scale beyond single-texture experimentation to full modding projects, while an intuitive presets system lets non-technical creators adjust key settings without touching the node graph.

articles.title: BYD expands EV shipping fleet as wars upend freight costs and key trade routes
articles.text:
China’s BYDBYDBYD Auto is a Chinese carmaker that became the world’s leading EV manufacturer in 2023, competing with Tesla for market share and global attention.READ MORE is building cars faster than it can export, so it’s adding more ships.
The world’s largest electric vehicle maker will expand its fleet of car-carrying cargo ships to 18 from eight by 2029, according to shipping industry reports. Each new carrier will have the capacity to carry about 9,200 cars and will be built by China Merchants Industry.
Owning its fleet could cut BYD’s cost to ship each car abroad by as much as 40% compared with renting carriers, according to one industry estimate. BYD’s increasing export capacity could help it push further into global markets, intensifying competition for automakers including Tesla and traditional U.S. brands.
“Carmakers like BYD, which invested in the sector ahead of the surge, are reaping the rewards of that long-term strategy,” Andrea De Luca, a maritime analyst at Boston-based shipping data company Veson Nautical, told Rest of World. “By owning their ships, they can save money compared with chartering at today’s elevated rates, prioritize their most important markets, enter new ones more easily, and depend less on charter market swings.”
BYD did not respond to Rest of World’s request for comment.
Why BYD owns ships
In 2022, BYD announced a plan worth $687 million to build its own car carriers, to fix what founder Wang Chuanfu called a shortage of shipping capacity for exports. Between January 2024 and September 2025, the company put eight car carriers into service.
Earlier this year, BYD told investors that a shortage of shipping capacity had held back its exports. In September, the company sold 180,700 cars outside China, more than double a year ago and almost 40% of its monthly total sales.
Wars in the Red Sea and around the Strait of Hormuz have pushed up freight costs and forced ships onto longer routes around conflict zones. Renting a car carrier with capacity of about 6,500 cars now costs $95,000 a day, up from $50,000 in February, according to shipping data and analytics firm Clarksons Research. Chinese owners account for only about 10% of global car carrier capacity, including ships on order, so carmakers from the country hire ships from international shipping companies, the research arm of shipbroker Clarksons said.
With BYD aiming to sell more than 2.5 million cars overseas next year, up from a target of 1.9 to 2 million this year, owning a fleet cushions against higher shipping bills and gives more control over space and routes, analysts said.
2.5 million Number of cars BYD aims to sell overseas next year, up from a target of 1.9 to 2 million this year.
“The very strong growth in Chinese exports, fueling strong Asia-Europe fronthaul demand growth, is the biggest single factor behind the increase in charter rates,” Stephen Gordon, managing director of Clarksons Research, told Rest of World. “Additionally, conflict in the Middle East has caused regional disruption and inefficiencies, which have helped to further tighten markets after a two-year period of gradual normalization.”
Most car carriers on Asia-Europe routes are sailing around the Cape of Good Hope to avoid the Red Sea, adding about 25% to the distance and as many as 14 days to each voyage, De Luca said. With shipping through the Strait of Hormuz disrupted, the spot rate for moving cars from China to the Middle East has jumped to $220 per cubic meter of cargo space from $65 in February, he said.
Chinese EVs and exports
In China, industrywide sales of EVs and plug-in hybrids fell 12% in the first eight months of the year, after the government cut tax breaks for buyers. BYD sold 33% fewer cars at home over the same period.
Many Chinese carmakers have kept their factories busy by selling surplus cars abroad as changes to tax and subsidy incentives have cooled demand at home, George Whitcombe, a senior EV analyst at London-based battery data provider Benchmark Mineral Intelligence, told Rest of World.
Exports of China-made EVs are now rising faster than their registrations overseas, pointing to a growing stock of unsold cars, he said.
“Control over its distribution network is a strategy BYD has long pursued,” Whitcombe said. “With other Chinese automakers left without their own fleet of ships and exposed to rising shipping costs, it potentially leaves them in a less competitive position to grow their overseas presence.”
Tesla, BYD’s main U.S. rival, has relied on other companies’ carriers to export from China. Its Shanghai plant shipped more cars abroad than it sold at home in the first eight months of the year. Carmakers that charter ships are more exposed to swings in the charter market than those that own them, De Luca said.
BYD’s giant carriers are mainly a marketing exercise, Felipe Munoz, founder of research platform Car Industry Analysis, told Rest of World. Owning ships has its drawbacks and advantages, he said.
“By displaying these massive carriers, it aims to project an image of power and speed to the rest of the world,” Munoz said. “It is more a political statement against the established carmakers by telling the world that BYD is moving fast and has a lot of resources to make the most advanced EVs.”
BYD’s fleet is about control, and extending into logistics is a natural step now that it exports millions of cars amid geopolitical volatility and cost swings, Lei Xing, founder of AutoXing, a Chinese auto industry consultancy, told Rest of World. BYD ships only EVs and plug-in hybrids, which need specially configured carriers, and most of its fleet runs on liquefied natural gas as ports tighten green-fuel rules, he said.
Rival Geely began running its first car carrier in 2025, on a long-term charter from London-based shipowner Zodiac Maritime. Chery set up a venture with Wuhu Shipyard in 2023 to build car carriers for its own fleet in eastern China.
“Geely, on the other hand, will be running its own ships eventually,” Lei Xing said. “You can bet on that.”

articles.title: Les jaquettes iconiques de GTA sont nées à cause du 11 septembre
articles.text:
Aucune jaquette n’a un style plus iconique que celles des jeux GTA, composées d’un assemblage de petits carrés très graphiques. Ce style est né avec GTA 3, presque par accident. Dan Houser, cofondateur et ancien vice-président de Rockstar Games, en a raconté la genèse dans un long entretien paru ce mardi 13 octobre sur IGN.
À l’origine, GTA 3 ne devait pas avoir la jaquette que tout le monde connaît aujourd’hui, devenue depuis la signature visuelle de la saga. En réalité, Rockstar Games a dû la changer à la dernière minute en raison des attentats du 11 septembre 2001, qui ont eu lieu un peu plus d’un mois avant la sortie du jeu, le 22 octobre.
La jaquette de GTA est devenue iconique à cause du 11 septembre
Le style en mosaïque introduit par GTA 3 est donc une conséquence du 11 septembre. Dan Houser raconte : « Ce qui est marrant, c’est que la pochette qui est devenue la pochette emblématique de GTA, Stephen Bliss l’a faite en environ deux soirées parce que l’ancienne pochette était probablement jugée trop choquante pour être publiée après le 11 septembre, car on y voyait des bâtiments en feu. »
L’illustrateur Stephen Bliss a lui-même confirmé cette version. Selon lui, la jaquette d’origine avait demandé environ six mois de travail et partait déjà à l’impression pour les fêtes quand les attentats ont frappé New York.
Sans le 11 septembre, GTA 3 aurait donc conservé son design d’origine et, a priori, n’aurait pas amorcé le style en mosaïque conservé par tous les épisodes qui ont suivi — jusqu’à GTA 6, attendu pour le 19 novembre sur PS5, Xbox Series X et Xbox Series S. Le prochain opus va même jusqu’à garder l’hélicoptère, placé en haut à gauche.
Rockstar Games a par ailleurs été contraint de censurer certains éléments de GTA 3, dans l’urgence, car le jeu se déroule à Liberty City, une ville fictive inspirée de New York. Il explique : « Il y avait quelques éléments de contenu qui auraient été tout à fait acceptables en temps normal, mais qui, juste après le 11 septembre, étaient peut-être un peu de trop. Nous avons donc dû les retirer. L’équipe s’est mobilisée pour supprimer ces éléments, modifier quelques lignes de dialogue et faire un examen rapide du contenu, après quoi nous avons estimé que tout était bon. » Ces changements ont contraint le studio à décaler GTA 3 de près de trois semaines, du 3 au 22 octobre 2001.
Dès 2011, dans le magazine Edge, Dan Houser détaillait quelques retouches : la couleur des voitures de police, changée pour ne plus copier celles du NYPD, la trajectoire d’un avion qui semblait foncer vers un gratte-ciel, et une mission supprimée parce qu’elle faisait référence à des terroristes.

articles.title: YouTube teste ces 3 nouvelles icônes pour son application : mais que prépare Google ?
articles.text:
Une fois n’est pas coutume, c’est en allant chercher dans le code de l’application YouTube pour Android que l’on découvre des nouveautés qui n’ont pas encore été annoncées. C’est le cas aujourd’hui avec trois nouvelles icônes très énigmatiques sorties directement des laboratoires de Google. Voici ce que cette nouvelle identité graphique pourrait cacher.
Bientôt la possibilité de choisir son icône YouTube ?
En fouillant dans le code de cette mise à jour, on y trouve une référence explicite à une préférence d’icône, suggérant clairement que Google pourrait bientôt laisser le choix aux utilisateurs d’habiller l’application selon leurs préférences. Parmi les visuels, on retrouve trois icônes avec chacune un style très marqué.
Source : Android Authority
L’un des logos opte ainsi pour un style monochrome, tandis qu’un autre évoque la texture du glaçage d’un gâteau ou de la peinture fraîche, à moins que cela ne soit de la pâte à modeler. Le troisième design se distingue quant à lui par un effet néon qui peut aussi rappeler celui de l’affichage des anciens écrans à tube cathodique.
Une personnalisation réservée aux abonnés Premium ?
Impossible pour l’instant de savoir précisément à qui se destinent ces icônes ni de deviner la logique marketing qui se cache derrière. En effet, aucun libellé descriptif ou explicite dans les fichiers de l’application n’a été trouvé, ce qui laisse de la place aux spéculations en tous genres. Il pourrait s’agir d’un simple test de la part de YouTube, ou des prémisses d’une option réservée aux abonnements payants.
À lire : Gagner de l’argent sur YouTube devient beaucoup plus difficile
Pas de quoi sortir sa carte bleue immédiatement, mais cela pourrait être un « petit plus » pour les abonnements YouTube Premium ou Premium Lite. En attendant une éventuelle communication officielle de la part de Google, le mystère reste entier. N’hésitez pas à nous donner vos pronostics dans les commentaires.

articles.title: Microsoft is shutting its Nairobi engineering centre
articles.text:
Microsoft is winding down its Africa Development Centre (ADC) in Nairobi, putting nearly 400 jobs at risk and reversing a seven-year effort to make Kenya a hub for building technology for global markets.
Two employees, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, told TechCabal that staff at the centre, housed in Dunhill Towers in Nairobi’s Westlands district, were called to a meeting on Monday morning and asked to meet with their managers by Friday, October 16, to discuss exit options, including severance terms.
The closure comes seven years after the company pledged more than $100 million to develop African tech talent, to make Nairobi one of its engineering hubs outside the US. It would unwind a project built on the promise that African engineers could build products for global markets without leaving the continent, raising questions about Microsoft’s long-term plans for engineering in Africa.
“We are communicating directly with employees in Kenya about proposed changes to our engineering operations,” a Microsoft spokesperson told TechCabal on Monday. “We recognise the uncertainty this brings and are keeping those discussions private. Microsoft remains committed to Kenya and will continue to have employees in the country while supporting the country’s ongoing digital transformation and innovation ambitions.”
The statement did not confirm the centre’s closure or specify how many employees would remain or when the changes would take effect.
Two other employees, who asked not to be named as they aren’t authorised to discuss the matter, told TechCabal they expect their meetings with supervisors to focus on severance terms rather than on whether they will stay.
“Our case is sealed; we just didn’t know when,” one employee said.
Another person familiar with the matter said fewer than 10 employees are expected to remain, including staff in sales and recruiting, two in Microsoft Customer and Partner Solutions (MCAPS), which manages customer and partner relationships, and employees working on AI for Good, Microsoft’s initiative to apply AI to social and environmental challenges.
Microsoft’s seven-year bet on African engineering
When Microsoft launched the Africa Development Centre (ADC) in 2019, Michael Fortin, then a corporate vice president, said it would allow engineers to do “meaningful work from their home countries” while working within a global engineering organisation. Microsoft planned to hire 100 engineers by the end of 2019 and grow the workforce across Nairobi and Lagos to 500 by 2023.
By December 2022, Microsoft President Brad Smith said the Nairobi centre employed more than 450 engineers. The centre had met its original hiring ambition, making it harder to explain the closure as a failure to deliver on its initial promise.
The Nairobi closure follows Microsoft’s May 2024 decision to shut its sister centre in Lagos, a move the company said at the time would not affect its operations in Kenya. The Lagos closure caught staff by surprise, while Nairobi employees say they had seen signs of trouble for some time.
On Monday, Kenya’s ICT Minister William Kabogo said he met a Microsoft delegation led by Jeff Bullwinkel, the company’s vice president and deputy general counsel for Europe, the Middle East and Africa, with its East Africa team headed by Angela Ng’ang’a.
Microsoft briefed him on “its evolving operations in Kenya in the context of its global restructuring,” Kabogo said, while he pressed the company on “protecting jobs at Microsoft’s Nairobi engineering centre.”
The company reaffirmed its long-term commitment to Kenya, he said, and both sides agreed to draft a joint action plan. Neither has disclosed what the plan will contain or whether it could change a decision employees describe as final.
Microsoft has yet to disclose why it is closing the Nairobi centre, and people familiar with the matter point to several possible factors. The decision comes amid a wider round of cuts at the company, which announced about 4,800 job cuts in July 2026, or roughly 2.1% of its workforce, following about 15,000 cuts in 2025.
The reductions come as Microsoft pours record sums into AI infrastructure, raising questions about which parts of its business will continue to receive funding. A remote engineering centre could come under pressure, though no public evidence links the Nairobi closure directly to the global cuts.
Kenya has also struggled to advance another major Microsoft initiative. The $1 billion data centre that Microsoft planned with Abu Dhabi-based G42 in Olkaria has stalled amid concerns about electricity capacity and disagreements over the Kenyan government’s ability to guarantee payments for the facility’s capacity. President William Ruto has cited the country’s limited power supply as a problem. However, government officials have said the project has not been abandoned.
A third possible factor is the cost of maintaining a large local workforce, particularly its tax bill. One employee told TechCabal that Microsoft’s Kenyan employees generate at least KES 1.5 billion ($11.6 million) in annual Pay As You Earn (PAYE) taxes for the Kenya Revenue Authority. TechCabal could not independently verify the figures.
The closure would return hundreds of engineers to a job market Microsoft helped reshape when it opened the centre in 2019. The company recruited talent from Kenyan banks, telcos and technology firms to build its local engineering team.
Seven years later, those employers and other technology companies will be among the places its departing engineers may look to next, raising questions about where the specialised talent built at the centre will go and whether Kenya can retain the skills and experience it took Microsoft years to assemble.
True scale demands moving beyond surface-level integrations to robust execution.
